translations.an10.13:1: "Monks, there are these ten fetters. What ten? The five lower fetters and the five higher fetters. What are the five lower fetters? Identity view, doubt, grasping at rules and observances, sensual desire, ill will—these are the five lower fetters.
translations.an10.15:1: "Monks, as far as there are beings—whether without feet or with two feet or with four feet or with many feet, whether with form or formless, whether percipient or non-percipient or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata is declared the foremost of them: the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One; even so, monks, whatever wholesome states there are, all of them have heedfulness as their root, meet together in heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared the foremost of them.
translations.an10.15:2: Just as, monks, whatever tracks there are of creatures that roam in the forest, all of them meet together in the elephant’s footprint; the elephant’s footprint is declared the foremost of them, that is, because of its great size; even so, monks, whatever wholesome states there are, all of them have heedfulness as their root, meet together in heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared the foremost of them.
translations.an10.15:3: Just as, monks, whatever rafters there are of a peaked house, all of them go to the peak, slope to the peak, meet together in the peak; the peak is declared the foremost of them; even so, monks, whatever wholesome states there are, all of them have heedfulness as their root, meet together in heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared the foremost of them.
translations.an10.15:7: Just as, monks, whatever petty kings there are, all of them are followers of the wheel-turning king; the wheel-turning king is declared the foremost of them; even so, monks …
translations.an10.15:8: Just as, monks, whatever radiance there is of the forms of the stars, all of it does not amount to a sixteenth part of the moon’s radiance; the moon’s radiance is declared the foremost of them; even so, monks …
translations.an10.15:9: Just as, monks, in the autumn season, when the sky is clear and free of clouds, the sun, ascending into the sky, having struck down all the darkness that has gone into the sky, shines and burns and blazes; even so, monks …
translations.an10.17:1: "Live with a refuge, monks; do not live without a refuge. Without a refuge, monks, one lives in suffering. These ten things, monks, are refuge-making qualities. What ten? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous; he lives restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of conduct and resort, seeing fear in the slightest faults; having undertaken, he trains in the training rules. And whatever, monks, a monk is virtuous … having undertaken, he trains in the training rules—this, too, is a refuge-making quality.
translations.an10.17:2: Furthermore, monks, a monk is learned, a bearer of what has been heard, one who has stored up what has been heard; those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, proclaiming the completely full and purified spiritual life—such teachings are much heard by him, retained, repeated in speech, pondered in mind, and well penetrated by view. And whatever, monks, a monk is learned … well penetrated by view—this, too, is a refuge-making quality.
translations.an10.17:3: Furthermore, monks, a monk is a good friend, a good companion, a good associate. And whatever, monks, a monk is a good friend, a good companion, a good associate—this, too, is a refuge-making quality.
translations.an10.18:10: Furthermore, monks, a monk is mindful, endowed with the highest mindfulness and prudence, remembering and recollecting even what was done long ago and what was said long ago. "This monk is indeed mindful, endowed with the highest mindfulness and prudence, remembering and recollecting even what was done long ago and what was said long ago"—the elder monks, too, think that he should be spoken to and instructed; the middle monks … the new monks, too, think that he should be spoken to and instructed. For him, who is cared for by the elders, cared for by the middle monks, cared for by the new monks, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This, too, is a refuge-making quality.
translations.an10.18:11: Furthermore, monks, a monk is wise, endowed with wisdom that leads to rise and fall, noble and penetrative, rightly leading to the ending of suffering. "This monk is indeed wise, endowed with wisdom that leads to rise and fall, noble and penetrative, rightly leading to the ending of suffering"—the elder monks, too, think that he should be spoken to and instructed; the middle monks … the new monks, too, think that he should be spoken to and instructed. For him, who is cared for by the elders … not decline. This, too, is a refuge-making quality.
translations.an10.18:2: "Live with a refuge, monks; do not live without a refuge. Without a refuge, monks, one lives in suffering. These ten things, monks, are refuge-making qualities. What ten? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous … having undertaken, he trains in the training rules. "This monk is indeed virtuous, living restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of conduct and resort, seeing fear in the slightest faults, having undertaken, he trains in the training rules"—the elder monks, too, think that he should be spoken to and instructed; the middle monks … the new monks, too, think that he should be spoken to and instructed. For him, who is cared for by the elders, cared for by the middle monks, cared for by the new monks, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This, too, is a refuge-making quality.
translations.an10.18:4: Furthermore, monks, a monk is a good friend, a good companion, a good associate. "This monk is indeed a good friend, a good companion, a good associate"—the elder monks, too, think that he should be spoken to and instructed; the middle monks … the new monks, too, think that he should be spoken to and instructed. For him, who is cared for by the elders, cared for by the middle monks, cared for by the new monks, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This, too, is a refuge-making quality.
translations.an10.18:5: Furthermore, monks, a monk is easy to admonish, endowed with qualities that make one easy to admonish, patient, accepting instruction respectfully. "This monk is indeed easy to admonish, endowed with qualities that make one easy to admonish, patient, accepting instruction respectfully"—the elder monks, too, think that he should be spoken to and instructed; the middle monks … the new monks, too, think that he should be spoken to and instructed. For him, who is cared for by the elders, cared for by the middle monks, cared for by the new monks, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This, too, is a refuge-making quality.
translations.an10.18:6: Furthermore, monks, a monk is skilled and not lazy in the various duties, great and small, for his companions in the holy life; he is endowed with investigation into the means there, able to do it and able to arrange it. Thinking, ‘This monk is skilled and not lazy in the various duties, great and small, for his companions in the holy life; he is endowed with investigation into the means there, able to do it and able to arrange it,’ the elder monks consider him fit to be spoken to and instructed; the middle monks, too … and the new monks, too consider him fit to be spoken to and instructed. For him, supported by the elders, supported by the middle monks, supported by the new monks, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This, too, is a quality that is a source of protection.
translations.an10.18:7: Furthermore, monks, a monk is desirous of the Dhamma, one who speaks endearingly, one who has lofty joy in the higher Dhamma and the higher discipline. Thinking, ‘This monk is desirous of the Dhamma, one who speaks endearingly, one who has lofty joy in the higher Dhamma and the higher discipline,’ the elder monks consider him fit to be spoken to and instructed; the middle monks, too … and the new monks, too consider him fit to be spoken to and instructed. For him, supported by the elders, supported by the middle monks, supported by the new monks, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This, too, is a quality that is a source of protection.
translations.an10.18:8: Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells with aroused energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states, steadfast, firm in exertion, not laying down the burden in wholesome states. Thinking, ‘This monk dwells with aroused energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states, steadfast, firm in exertion, not laying down the burden in wholesome states,’ the elder monks consider him fit to be spoken to and instructed; the middle monks, too … and the new monks, too consider him fit to be spoken to and instructed. For him, supported by the elders, supported by the middle monks, supported by the new monks, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This, too, is a quality that is a source of protection.
translations.an10.18:9: Furthermore, monks, a monk is content with whatever robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and supplies for the sick he gets. Thinking, ‘This monk is content with whatever robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicines and supplies for the sick he gets,’ the elder monks consider him fit to be spoken to and instructed; the middle monks, too … and the new monks, too consider him fit to be spoken to and instructed. For him, supported by the elders, supported by the middle monks, supported by the new monks, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline. This, too, is a quality that is a source of protection.
translations.an10.20:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus, at a Kuru town called Kammāsadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the monks … etc. …
translations.an10.20:10: And how, monks, is a monk one whose bodily formation is calmed? Here, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and dejection, a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and includes purification of mindfulness by equanimity. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one whose bodily formation is calmed.
translations.an10.20:11: And how, monks, is a monk one whose mind is well liberated? Here, monks, a monk’s mind is liberated from lust, his mind is liberated from hatred, his mind is liberated from delusion. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one whose mind is well liberated.
translations.an10.20:2: These ten, monks, are noble dwellings—dwellings in which the noble ones dwelt in the past, dwell now, or will dwell in the future. What ten? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned five factors, is endowed with six factors, is guarded by one, has four supports, has expelled individual truths, has searches brought to rest, has untroubled intentions, has a calmed bodily formation, has a well-liberated mind, and has well-liberated wisdom.
translations.an10.20:3: And how, monks, is a monk one who has abandoned five factors? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned sensual desire, has abandoned ill will, has abandoned sloth and torpor, has abandoned restlessness and remorse, has abandoned doubt. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who has abandoned five factors.
translations.an10.20:4: And how, monks, is a monk endowed with six factors? Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk is neither glad nor upset; he dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending. Having heard a sound with the ear … having smelled an odor with the nose … having tasted a flavor with the tongue … having touched a tangible with the body … having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is neither glad nor upset; he dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is endowed with six factors.
translations.an10.20:5: And how, monks, is a monk guarded by one? Here, monks, a monk is endowed with a mind protected by mindfulness. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is guarded by one.
translations.an10.20:6: And how, monks, is a monk one who has four supports? Here, monks, after reflecting, a monk uses one thing; after reflecting, he endures one thing; after reflecting, he avoids one thing; after reflecting, he removes one thing. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who has four supports.
translations.an10.20:7: And how, monks, is a monk one who has expelled individual truths? Here, monks, whatever various individual truths there are among ordinary ascetics and brahmins, that is: ‘the world is eternal,’ or ‘the world is not eternal,’ or ‘the world is finite,’ or ‘the world is infinite,’ or ‘the soul is the same as the body,’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another,’ or ‘the Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—all of these are expelled, driven out, abandoned, cast away, vomited out, released, relinquished. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who has expelled individual truths.
translations.an10.20:8: And how, monks, is a monk one who has searches brought to rest? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the search for sensual pleasures, has abandoned the search for existence, and the search for the holy life has subsided. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who has searches brought to rest.
translations.an10.20:9: And how, monks, is a monk one with untroubled intentions? Here, monks, a monk has abandoned intentions of sensuality, has abandoned intentions of ill will, has abandoned intentions of harming. It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one with untroubled intentions.
translations.an10.24:1: At one time the Venerable Mahācunda was dwelling among the Cetīs at Sahajāti. There the Venerable Mahācunda addressed the monks: “Friends, monks.” “Friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Mahācunda. The Venerable Mahācunda said this:
translations.an10.24:10: Suppose, friends, that a man, being truly wealthy, would speak a wealthy talk; being truly rich, would speak a rich talk; being truly affluent, would speak an affluent talk. When some matter requiring money has arisen, he would be able to provide money or grain or silver or gold. People would know him thus: ‘This venerable one, being truly wealthy, speaks a wealthy talk; being truly rich, speaks a rich talk; being truly affluent, speaks an affluent talk. What is the reason for that? For this venerable one, when some matter requiring money has arisen, is able to provide money or grain or silver or gold.’
translations.an10.24:2: “When a monk, friends, is speaking a doctrine of knowledge: ‘I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma.’ If, friends, greed overwhelms that monk and remains, hate … delusion … anger … resentment … contempt … spite … jealousy … stinginess … evil envy … evil desire overwhelms him and remains, he should be understood thus: ‘This venerable one does not understand in such a way that, for one who understands, greed does not exist; for greed overwhelms this venerable one and remains. This venerable one does not understand in such a way that, for one who understands, hate does not exist … delusion … anger … resentment … contempt … spite … jealousy … stinginess … evil envy … evil desire does not exist; for evil desire overwhelms this venerable one and remains.’”
translations.an10.24:3: When a monk, friends, is speaking a doctrine of development: ‘My body is developed, my virtue is developed, my mind is developed, my wisdom is developed.’ If, friends, greed overwhelms that monk and remains, hate … delusion … anger … resentment … contempt … spite … jealousy … stinginess … evil envy … evil desire overwhelms him and remains, he should be understood thus: ‘This venerable one does not understand in such a way that, for one who understands, greed does not exist; for greed overwhelms this venerable one and remains. This venerable one does not understand in such a way that, for one who understands, hate does not exist … delusion … anger … resentment … contempt … spite … jealousy … stinginess … evil envy … evil desire does not exist; for evil desire overwhelms this venerable one and remains.’”
translations.an10.24:5: Suppose, friends, that a man, being truly poor, would speak a wealthy talk; being truly without wealth, would speak a rich talk; being truly without affluence, would speak an affluent talk. When some matter requiring money has arisen, he would not be able to provide money or grain or silver or gold. People would know him thus: ‘This venerable one, being truly poor, speaks a wealthy talk; being truly without wealth, speaks a rich talk; being truly without affluence, speaks an affluent talk. What is the reason for that? For this venerable one, when some matter requiring money has arisen, is not able to provide money or grain or silver or gold.’
translations.an10.24:9: When a monk, friends, is speaking both a doctrine of knowledge and a doctrine of development: ‘I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma; my body is developed, my virtue is developed, my mind is developed, my wisdom is developed.’ If, friends, greed does not overwhelm that monk and remain, hate … delusion … anger … resentment … contempt … spite … jealousy … stinginess … evil envy … evil desire does not overwhelm him and remain, he should be understood thus: ‘This venerable one understands in such a way that, for one who understands, greed does not exist; for greed does not overwhelm this venerable one and remain. This venerable one understands in such a way that, for one who understands, hate does not exist … delusion … anger … resentment … contempt … spite … jealousy … stinginess … evil envy … evil desire does not exist; for evil desire does not overwhelm this venerable one and remain.’”
translations.an10.29:1: “As far, bhikkhus, as the Kāsi-Kosalans extend, as far as the realm of King Pasenadi of Kosala extends, King Pasenadi of Kosala is declared the chief there. Yet even for King Pasenadi of Kosala, bhikkhus, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Being disenchanted with that, he becomes dispassionate toward what is chief—how much more toward what is inferior.”
translations.an10.29:10: Perceiving internally as without form, one sees externally forms that are blue, of blue color, of blue appearance, of blue radiance. Just as a flax-flower is blue, of blue color, of blue appearance, of blue radiance; or just as that Bārāṇasī cloth, smoothed on both sides, is blue, of blue color, of blue appearance, of blue radiance; even so, perceiving internally as without form, one sees externally forms that are blue, of blue color, of blue appearance, of blue radiance; ‘having mastered them, I know and see’—thus he is percipient. This is the fifth base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:11: Perceiving internally as without form, one sees externally forms that are yellow, of yellow color, of yellow appearance, of yellow radiance. Just as a kaṇikāra-flower is yellow, of yellow color, of yellow appearance, of yellow radiance; or just as that Bārāṇasī cloth, smoothed on both sides, is yellow, of yellow color, of yellow appearance, of yellow radiance; even so, perceiving internally as without form, one sees externally forms that are yellow, of yellow color, of yellow appearance, of yellow radiance; ‘having mastered them, I know and see’—thus he is percipient. This is the sixth base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:12: One perceives no form internally, yet sees forms externally that are red, of red color, of red appearance, of red radiance. Just as the bandhujīvaka flower is red, of red color, of red appearance, of red radiance, or as that Bārāṇasī cloth, polished on both sides, is red, of red color, of red appearance, of red radiance; even so one perceives no form internally, yet sees forms externally that are red, of red color, of red appearance, of red radiance; ‘Having dominated them, I know and see,’—thus they have such a perception. This is the seventh base of mastery.
translations.an10.29:13: One perceives no form internally, yet sees forms externally that are white, of white color, of white appearance, of white radiance. Just as the autumn star is white, of white color, of white appearance, of white radiance, or as that Bārāṇasī cloth, polished on both sides, is white, of white color, of white appearance, of white radiance; even so one perceives no form internally, yet sees forms externally that are white, of white color, of white appearance, of white radiance; ‘Having dominated them, I know and see,’—thus they have such a perception. This is the eighth base of mastery. These, bhikkhus, are the eight bases of mastery.
translations.an10.29:14: The foremost, bhikkhus, of these eight bases of mastery is this: one perceives no form internally, yet sees forms externally that are white, of white color, of white appearance, of white radiance; ‘Having dominated them, I know and see,’—thus they have such a perception. There are, bhikkhus, beings who have such a perception. But even for beings with such a perception there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Becoming disenchanted with that, they become dispassionate toward what is foremost, let alone toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:15: There are, bhikkhus, these four ways of practice. What four? A painful way of practice with slow direct knowledge, a painful way of practice with swift direct knowledge, a pleasant way of practice with slow direct knowledge, a pleasant way of practice with swift direct knowledge—these, bhikkhus, are the four ways of practice.
translations.an10.29:16: The foremost, bhikkhus, of these four ways of practice is this: a pleasant way of practice with swift direct knowledge. There are, bhikkhus, beings who practice in such a way. But even for beings practicing in such a way there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Becoming disenchanted with that, they become dispassionate toward what is foremost, let alone toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:17: There are, bhikkhus, these four perceptions. What four? One perceives the limited, one perceives the exalted, one perceives the immeasurable, one perceives the base of nothingness: ‘There is nothing’—these, bhikkhus, are the four perceptions.
translations.an10.29:18: The foremost, bhikkhus, of these four perceptions is this: one perceives the base of nothingness: ‘There is nothing.’ There are, bhikkhus, beings who have such a perception. But even for beings with such a perception there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Becoming disenchanted with that, they become dispassionate toward what is foremost, let alone toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:2: As far, bhikkhus, as the moon and sun revolve, shining and illuminating the quarters, so far extends a thousandfold world. In that thousandfold world are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, a thousand Sineru king-mountains, a thousand Jambudīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānas, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand Pubbavidehas, four thousand great oceans, four thousand hosts of Great Kings, a thousand of the Cātumahārājikas, a thousand of the Tāvatiṁsas, a thousand of the Yāmas, a thousand of the Tusitas, a thousand of the Nimmānaratīs, a thousand of the Paranimmita-vasavattīs, a thousand brahma worlds. As far, bhikkhus, as a thousandfold world-element extends, the Great Brahmā is said to be foremost there. But even for the Great Brahmā, bhikkhus, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Becoming disenchanted with that, they become dispassionate toward what is foremost, let alone toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:20: There are, bhikkhus, some ascetics and brahmins who proclaim ultimate purity. The foremost, bhikkhus, among those who proclaim ultimate purity is this: having entirely transcended the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. By direct knowledge of that, by realization of that, they teach the Dhamma. There are, bhikkhus, beings who speak thus. But even for beings who speak thus there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Becoming disenchanted with that, they become dispassionate toward what is foremost, let alone toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:3: There comes a time, bhikkhus, when this world contracts. When the world is contracting, bhikkhus, for the most part beings become bound for the Ābhassara realm. There they are mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the sky, abiding in beauty, and they remain for a long, long time. When the world is contracting, bhikkhus, the Ābhassara devas are said to be foremost. But even for the Ābhassara devas, bhikkhus, there is alteration, there is change. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Becoming disenchanted with that, they become dispassionate toward what is foremost, let alone toward what is inferior.
translations.an10.29:4: There are, bhikkhus, these ten bases of kasiṇa. What ten? One perceives the earth kasiṇa: above, below, across, non-dual, immeasurable; one perceives the water kasiṇa …; one perceives the fire kasiṇa …; one perceives the air kasiṇa …; one perceives the blue kasiṇa …; one perceives the yellow kasiṇa …; one perceives the red kasiṇa …; one perceives the white kasiṇa …; one perceives the space kasiṇa …; one perceives the consciousness kasiṇa: above, below, across, non-dual, immeasurable. These, bhikkhus, are the ten bases of kasiṇa.
translations.an10.29:5: "Of these ten kasiṇa bases, monks, the foremost is this: the consciousness-kasiṇa—where one person perceives (it) above, below, and across: non-dual, immeasurable. And there are, monks, beings who have such perception. Yet even for beings with such perception there is alteration; there is change. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with that. Becoming disenchanted with that, they become dispassionate toward what is highest, let alone toward what is inferior."
translations.an10.29:6: "There are, monks, eight bases of mastery. What eight? Having perception of form internally, one sees forms externally—limited, fair and foul; ‘having mastered them, I know and see,’—thus one is percipient. This is the first base of mastery."
translations.an10.29:7: "Having perception of form internally, one sees forms externally—immeasurable, fair and foul; ‘having mastered them, I know and see,’—thus one is percipient. This is the second base of mastery."
translations.an10.29:8: "Having perception of the formless internally, one sees forms externally—limited, fair and foul; ‘having mastered them, I know and see,’—thus one is percipient. This is the third base of mastery."
translations.an10.29:9: "Having perception of the formless internally, one sees forms externally—immeasurable, fair and foul; ‘having mastered them, I know and see,’—thus one is percipient. This is the fourth base of mastery."
translations.an10.51:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks!"—"Venerable sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an10.51:3: "And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the ways of their own mind? Just as, monks, a woman or a man, young, youthful, fond of adornment, examining their own facial reflection in a mirror that is clean and bright, or in a clear bowl of water—if they see there a speck of dust or a blemish, they strive for the removal of that very speck of dust or blemish; but if they do not see there a speck of dust or a blemish, they are glad because of that, with their intention fulfilled: ‘It is a gain for me! It is a purity for me!’ Even so, monks, a monk’s reviewing is very helpful in wholesome states: ‘Do I dwell often with covetousness, or do I dwell often without covetousness? Do I dwell often with a mind of ill will, or do I dwell often with a mind without ill will? Do I dwell often overcome by sloth and torpor, or do I dwell often free of sloth and torpor? Do I dwell often agitated, or do I dwell often unagitated? Do I dwell often with doubt, or do I dwell often having crossed beyond doubt? Do I dwell often angry, or do I dwell often not angry? Do I dwell often with a defiled mind, or do I dwell often with an undefiled mind? Do I dwell often with a rigid body, or do I dwell often with a non-rigid body? Do I dwell often lazy, or do I dwell often with aroused energy? Do I dwell often unconcentrated, or do I dwell often concentrated?’"
translations.an10.51:4: "If, monks, a monk, reviewing, knows thus: ‘I dwell often with covetousness; I dwell often with a mind of ill will; I dwell often overcome by sloth and torpor; I dwell often agitated; I dwell often with doubt; I dwell often angry; I dwell often with a defiled mind; I dwell often with a rigid body; I dwell often lazy; I dwell often unconcentrated,’ then, monks, by that monk for the abandoning of those very bad, unwholesome states, intense desire and effort and ardor and persistence and unrelentingness and mindfulness and clear comprehension should be undertaken. Just as, monks, someone whose robe is on fire or whose head is on fire would undertake intense desire and effort and ardor and persistence and unrelentingness and mindfulness and clear comprehension for the quenching of that very robe or head—so too, monks, by that monk for the abandoning of those very bad, unwholesome states, intense desire and effort and ardor and persistence and unrelentingness and mindfulness and clear comprehension should be undertaken."
translations.an10.54:2: "And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the ways of their own mind? Just as, monks, a woman or a man, young, youthful, fond of adornment, examining their own facial reflection in a mirror that is clean and bright, or in a clear bowl of water—if they see there a speck of dust or a blemish, they strive for the removal of that very speck of dust or blemish; but if they do not see there a speck of dust or a blemish, they are glad because of that, with their intention fulfilled: ‘It is a gain for me! It is a purity for me!’ Even so, monks, a monk’s reviewing is very helpful in wholesome states: ‘Am I a possessor of internal serenity of mind, or am I not a possessor of internal serenity of mind? Am I a possessor of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom, or am I not a possessor of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom?’"
translations.an10.54:5: "But if, monks, a monk, reviewing, knows thus: ‘I am not a possessor of internal serenity of mind; I am not a possessor of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom,’ then, monks, by that monk for the acquisition of those very wholesome states, intense desire and effort and ardor and persistence and unrelentingness and mindfulness and clear comprehension should be undertaken. Just as, monks, someone whose robe is on fire or whose head is on fire would undertake intense desire and effort and ardor and persistence and unrelentingness and mindfulness and clear comprehension for the quenching of that very robe or head—so too, monks, by that monk for the acquisition of those very wholesome states, intense desire and effort and ardor and persistence and unrelentingness and mindfulness and clear comprehension should be undertaken. After some time, that one becomes a possessor of internal serenity of mind and a possessor of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom."
translations.an10.54:6: "But if, monks, a monk, reviewing, knows thus: ‘I am a possessor of internal serenity of mind; (I am) a possessor of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom,’ then, monks, by that monk, standing in those very wholesome states, further exertion should be made for the destruction of the taints."
translations.an10.58:1: “Suppose, bhikkhus, the wanderers of other sects were to ask thus: ‘On what are all phenomena rooted, friends; from what are all phenomena born; from what do all phenomena arise; in what do all phenomena converge; what is foremost for all phenomena; what holds sway over all phenomena; what is highest for all phenomena; what is the essence of all phenomena; in what do all phenomena plunge; what is the end of all phenomena?’—when asked thus, bhikkhus, how would you answer those wanderers of other sects?” “Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, venerable sir, guided by the Blessed One, dependent on the Blessed One. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would make clear the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will retain it.”
translations.an10.58:2: “Then, bhikkhus, listen, attend carefully, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an10.59:1: “Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train thus: ‘Our mind will be familiar with renunciation, and arisen bad unwholesome states will not take possession of the mind and remain; our mind will be familiar with the perception of impermanence; our mind will be familiar with the perception of not-self; our mind will be familiar with the perception of the unattractive; our mind will be familiar with the perception of danger; having known what is even and what is uneven in the world, our mind will be familiar with that perception; having known the world’s existence and non-existence, our mind will be familiar with that perception; having known the world’s arising and passing away, our mind will be familiar with that perception; our mind will be familiar with the perception of abandoning; our mind will be familiar with the perception of dispassion; our mind will be familiar with the perception of cessation’—for thus, bhikkhus, you should train.
translations.an10.60:1: At one time the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. Now at that time the Venerable Girimānanda was sick, in pain, seriously ill. Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an10.60:10: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of cessation? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime—namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, cessation, Nibbāna.’ This is called, Ānanda, the perception of cessation.
translations.an10.60:11: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-delight in the whole world? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, abandoning those clinging, standpoints, adherences, and underlying tendencies of the mind in the world, dwells without clinging. This is called, Ānanda, the perception of non-delight in the whole world.
translations.an10.60:12: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of not desiring all formations? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is weary of, ashamed of, and disgusted with all formations. This is called, Ānanda, the perception of not desiring all formations.
translations.an10.60:13: And what, Ānanda, is mindfulness of breathing? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him. Mindful, he breathes in; mindful, he breathes out. Breathing in long, he understands: ‘I breathe in long.’ Breathing out long, he understands: ‘I breathe out long.’ Breathing in short, he understands: ‘I breathe in short.’ Breathing out short, he understands: ‘I breathe out short.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing rapture.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing rapture.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing pleasure.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing pleasure.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the mental formation.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the mental formation.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in calming the mental formation.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out calming the mental formation.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the mind.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the mind.’ Gladdening the mind …pe… concentrating the mind …pe… liberating the mind …pe… contemplating impermanence …pe… contemplating fading away …pe… contemplating cessation …pe… he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment.’ He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment.’ This is called, Ānanda, mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:14: If you, Ānanda, were to speak these ten perceptions to the bhikkhu Girimānanda, it is possible that, having heard these ten perceptions, the bhikkhu Girimānanda’s illness would subside on the spot.”
translations.an10.60:2: “The Venerable Girimānanda, venerable sir, is sick, in pain, seriously ill. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would go to the Venerable Girimānanda out of compassion.” “If you, Ānanda, were to speak the ten perceptions to the bhikkhu Girimānanda, it is possible that, having heard the ten perceptions, the bhikkhu Girimānanda’s illness would subside on the spot.
translations.an10.60:3: What ten? The perception of impermanence, the perception of not-self, the perception of the unattractive, the perception of danger, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of non-delight in the whole world, the perception of not desiring all formations, mindfulness of breathing.
translations.an10.60:4: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus: ‘Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.’ Thus he dwells contemplating impermanence in these five aggregates subject to clinging. This is called, Ānanda, the perception of impermanence.
translations.an10.60:5: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of not-self? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu—gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—reflects thus: ‘The eye is not-self, forms are not-self; the ear is not-self, sounds are not-self; the nose is not-self, odors are not-self; the tongue is not-self, tastes are not-self; the body is not-self, tangibles are not-self; the mind is not-self, mental phenomena are not-self.’ Thus he dwells contemplating not-self in these six internal and external sense bases. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of not-self.
translations.an10.60:6: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of the unattractive? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu reviews this very body—from the soles of the feet up, and from the crown of the head down, bounded by skin—as full of many kinds of impurity: ‘In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin; flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys; heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs; intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces; bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat; tears, grease, saliva, mucus, synovial fluid, urine.’ Thus he dwells contemplating the unattractive in this body. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of the unattractive.
translations.an10.60:7: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of danger? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu—gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut—reflects thus: ‘This body is very painful and has many dangers. In this body various diseases arise, such as: eye disease, ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, ear disease, mouth disease, tooth disease, lip disease; cough, asthma, catarrh, burning fever, fever, stomach disease, fainting, dysentery, colic, cholera; leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, epilepsy, ringworm, itch, scabies, nail-disease, skin-eruptions; blood-disorders, bile-disorders, diabetes; hemorrhoids, pimples, fistulas; diseases arising from bile, diseases arising from phlegm, diseases arising from wind, diseases arising from their combination; diseases due to change of season, diseases due to uneven care, diseases due to external causes, diseases due to the ripening of kamma; cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, urination.’ Thus he dwells contemplating danger in this body. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of danger.
translations.an10.60:8: And what, Ānanda, is the perception of abandoning? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu does not tolerate arisen sensual thoughts; he abandons them, dispels them, makes an end of them, brings them to nonexistence. He does not tolerate arisen ill-will thoughts; he abandons them, dispels them, makes an end of them, brings them to nonexistence. He does not tolerate arisen harmful thoughts; he abandons them, dispels them, makes an end of them, brings them to nonexistence. Whatever bad unwholesome states arise and arise, he does not tolerate them; he abandons them, dispels them, makes an end of them, brings them to nonexistence. This, Ānanda, is called the perception of abandoning.
translations.an10.61:1: “Monks, no first point is discerned of ignorance: ‘Before this, ignorance was not; then afterwards it came to be.’ Even so, monks, it is said; and yet it is discerned: ‘With this as condition, ignorance (comes to be).’
translations.an10.61:2: And I, monks, say that ignorance is with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for ignorance? ‘The five hindrances’—this is to be said. And I, monks, say that the five hindrances are with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the five hindrances? ‘The three kinds of bad conduct’—this is to be said. And I, monks, say that the three kinds of bad conduct are with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for the three kinds of bad conduct? ‘Non-restraint of the faculties’—this is to be said. And I, monks, say that non-restraint of the faculties is with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for non-restraint of the faculties? ‘Lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension’—this is to be said. And I, monks, say that lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension is with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension? ‘Unwise attention’—this is to be said. And I, monks, say that unwise attention is with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for unwise attention? ‘Lack of faith’—this is to be said. And I, monks, say that lack of faith is with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for lack of faith? ‘Listening to the false Dhamma’—this is to be said. And I, monks, say that listening to the false Dhamma is with nutriment, not without nutriment. And what is the nutriment for listening to the false Dhamma? ‘Association with bad persons’—this is to be said.
translations.an10.61:3: Thus, monks, association with bad persons, when fulfilled, fulfills listening to the false Dhamma; listening to the false Dhamma, when fulfilled, fulfills lack of faith; lack of faith, when fulfilled, fulfills unwise attention; unwise attention, when fulfilled, fulfills lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension; lack of mindfulness and clear comprehension, when fulfilled, fulfills non-restraint of the faculties; non-restraint of the faculties, when fulfilled, fulfills the three kinds of bad conduct; the three kinds of bad conduct, when fulfilled, fulfill the five hindrances; the five hindrances, when fulfilled, fulfill ignorance. Thus there is nutriment for this ignorance, and thus its fulfillment.
translations.an10.61:4: Just as, monks, when thick drops of rain fall on the upper mountain, (…) that water, flowing down according to the slope, fills the mountain clefts, gullies, and ravines; the mountain clefts, gullies, and ravines, when filled, fill the little ponds. The little ponds, when filled, fill the great ponds; the great ponds, when filled, fill the streams; the streams, when filled, fill the great rivers; the great rivers, when filled, fill the great ocean, the sea. Thus there is nutriment for this great ocean, the sea, and thus its fulfillment.
translations.an10.61:7: Thus, monks, association with good persons, when fulfilled, fulfills listening to the true Dhamma; listening to the true Dhamma, when fulfilled, fulfills faith; faith, when fulfilled, fulfills wise attention; wise attention, when fulfilled, fulfills mindfulness and clear comprehension; mindfulness and clear comprehension, when fulfilled, fulfills restraint of the faculties; restraint of the faculties, when fulfilled, fulfills the three kinds of good conduct; the three kinds of good conduct, when fulfilled, fulfill the four establishments of mindfulness; the four establishments of mindfulness, when fulfilled, fulfill the seven factors of awakening; the seven factors of awakening, when fulfilled, fulfill knowledge and liberation. Thus there is nutriment for this knowledge and liberation, and thus its fulfillment.
translations.an10.7:1: Then the Venerable Ānanda went to where the Venerable Sāriputta was; having gone, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta. When he had concluded the courteous and amicable talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.an10.7:2: “Could there be, friend Sāriputta, for a monk an attainment of such concentration that he would neither perceive earth in earth, nor perceive water in water, nor perceive fire in fire, nor perceive air in air; nor would he perceive the dimension of infinite space in the dimension of infinite space, nor perceive the dimension of infinite consciousness in the dimension of infinite consciousness, nor perceive the dimension of nothingness in the dimension of nothingness, nor perceive the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; nor would he perceive this world in this world, nor perceive the other world in the other world; and yet he would still be percipient”?
translations.an10.7:4: “But how, friend Sāriputta, could there be for a monk an attainment of such concentration that he would neither perceive earth in earth … and yet he would still be percipient”?”  “Once, friend Ānanda, at one time I was dwelling right here at Sāvatthī in Andhavana.  There I entered upon such a concentration that I was neither perceiving earth in earth, nor perceiving water in water, nor perceiving fire in fire, nor perceiving air in air; nor was I perceiving the dimension of infinite space in the dimension of infinite space, nor was I perceiving the dimension of infinite consciousness in the dimension of infinite consciousness, nor was I perceiving the dimension of nothingness in the dimension of nothingness, nor was I perceiving the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; nor was I perceiving this world in this world, nor was I perceiving the other world in the other world; and yet I was percipient.”
translations.an3.10:1: “Endowed with three things, monks, without abandoning three stains, one is thrown into hell as if carried off and laid down there.  What three?  One is immoral, and the stain of immorality has not been abandoned in him; one is envious, and the stain of envy has not been abandoned in him; one is stingy, and the stain of stinginess has not been abandoned in him.  Endowed with these three things, monks, without abandoning these three stains, one is thrown into hell as if carried off and laid down there.”
translations.an3.12:5: Furthermore, monks, in whatever region a monk understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering,’ understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’  This, monks, is the second thing that is to be remembered by a monk throughout life.
translations.an3.15:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana.  There the Blessed One addressed the monks:  “Monks.”  “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.  The Blessed One said this:
translations.an3.15:2: “Once upon a time, monks, there was a king named Saccetana.  Then, monks, King Saccetana addressed a chariot-maker:  ‘In six months’ time, my good chariot-maker, there will be a battle.  Will you be able, my good chariot-maker, to make me a new pair of wheels?’  ‘I will be able, Your Majesty,’ the chariot-maker replied to King Saccetana.  Then, monks, the chariot-maker in six months and four nights completed one wheel.  Then, monks, King Saccetana addressed the chariot-maker:  ‘In six days’ time, my good chariot-maker, there will be a battle; is the new pair of wheels finished?’  ‘With these six months and four nights, Your Majesty, one wheel has been completed.’  ‘But will you be able for me, my good chariot-maker, to complete the second wheel in these six days?’  ‘I will be able, Your Majesty,’ the chariot-maker replied; and having completed the second wheel in six days, taking the new pair of wheels, he approached King Saccetana.  Having approached, he said to King Saccetana:  ‘Here, Your Majesty, the new pair of wheels is finished.’  ‘And this wheel of yours, my good chariot-maker, finished in six months and four nights, and this wheel of yours finished in six days—what difference is there between them?  I do not see any difference at all.’  ‘There is, Your Majesty, a difference.  Let Your Majesty see the difference.’”
translations.an3.15:3: Then, monks, the chariot-maker rolled the wheel that was finished in six days.  As it rolled, it went as far as the momentum of the workmanship carried it, then it wobbled and fell to the ground.  But the wheel that was finished in six months and four nights, when he rolled it— as it rolled, it went as far as the momentum of the workmanship carried it, then it stood as though the axle had not been damaged.
translations.an3.15:5: Now, monks, you might think:  ‘Surely the chariot-maker at that time was someone else.’  But that, monks, should not be regarded so.  I was the chariot-maker at that time.  Then, monks, I was skilled in crookednesses of wood, in defects of wood, in impurities of wood.  But now, monks, I am an arahant, a perfectly awakened one, skilled in bodily crookednesses, bodily defects, bodily impurities; skilled in verbal crookednesses, verbal defects, verbal impurities; skilled in mental crookednesses, mental defects, mental impurities.  Whatever monk or nun, monks, has bodily crookedness not abandoned, bodily defect, bodily impurity; verbal crookedness not abandoned, verbal defect, verbal impurity; mental crookedness not abandoned, mental defect, mental impurity—thus they have fallen, monks, from this Dhamma and discipline, just like that wheel finished in six days.
translations.an3.15:6: Whatever monk or nun, monks, has bodily crookedness abandoned, bodily defect, bodily impurity; verbal crookedness abandoned, verbal defect, verbal impurity; mental crookedness abandoned, mental defect, mental impurity—thus they are established, monks, in this Dhamma and discipline, just like that wheel finished in six months and four nights.
translations.an3.1:3: Thus, monks, the fool is with fear; the wise one is without fear.  The fool is with trouble; the wise one is without trouble.  The fool is with affliction; the wise one is without affliction.  There is no fear from the wise one, monks; there is no trouble from the wise one; there is no affliction from the wise one.
translations.an3.20:1: "Monks, endowed with three qualities a shopkeeper in no long time attains greatness and expansion in wealth. What three? Here, monks, a shopkeeper is one with eyes, is competent, and is endowed with support. And how, monks, is a shopkeeper one with eyes? Here, monks, a shopkeeper knows merchandise: 'This merchandise, bought thus, when sold thus, will amount to such-and-such a principal, such-and-such a profit.' In this way, monks, a shopkeeper is one with eyes.
translations.an3.20:2: And how, monks, is a shopkeeper competent? Here, monks, a shopkeeper is skilled in buying and in selling merchandise. In this way, monks, a shopkeeper is competent.
translations.an3.20:3: And how, monks, is a shopkeeper endowed with support? Here, monks, those householders or householders' sons who are wealthy, very rich, with great property, know thus about the shopkeeper: 'This worthy shopkeeper is one with eyes, competent, capable of supporting wife and children, and of giving to us from time to time.' They provide him with wealth: 'With this, good shopkeeper, having made wealth, support wife and children, and give to us from time to time.' In this way, monks, a shopkeeper is endowed with support. Endowed with these three qualities, monks, a shopkeeper in no long time attains greatness and expansion in wealth.
translations.an3.20:4: Even so, monks, endowed with three qualities a monk in no long time attains greatness and expansion in wholesome qualities. What three? Here, monks, a monk is one with eyes, is competent, and is endowed with support. And how, monks, is a monk one with eyes? Here, monks, a monk understands as it really is: 'This is suffering'; understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering'; understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.' In this way, monks, a monk is one with eyes.
translations.an3.20:5: And how, monks, is a monk competent? Here, monks, a monk dwells with aroused energy for the abandoning of unwholesome qualities, for the acquisition of wholesome qualities—steadfast, firmly striving, not relinquishing the burden in wholesome qualities. In this way, monks, a monk is competent.
translations.an3.22:1: "Monks, these three sick people are found existing in the world. What three? Here, monks, some sick person—whether obtaining suitable foods or not obtaining suitable foods, whether obtaining suitable medicines or not obtaining suitable medicines, whether obtaining a suitable attendant or not obtaining a suitable attendant—does not recover from that illness.
translations.an3.22:3: Here, monks, some sick person obtains suitable foods and does not not obtain them, obtains suitable medicines and does not not obtain them, obtains a suitable attendant and does not not obtain one, and recovers from that illness.
translations.an3.22:4: Therein, monks, since this sick person—obtaining suitable foods and not not obtaining them, obtaining suitable medicines and not not obtaining them, obtaining a suitable attendant and not not obtaining one—recovers from that illness, with reference to this sick person sick-food is allowed, sick-medicine is allowed, and a sick-attendant is allowed. And, monks, with reference to this sick person other sick people also should be attended to. These, monks, are the three sick people found existing in the world.
translations.an3.22:5: Even so, monks, these three persons comparable to the sick are found existing in the world. What three? Here, monks, some person—whether obtaining the opportunity to see the Tathāgata or not obtaining the opportunity to see the Tathāgata, whether obtaining the opportunity to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata or not obtaining the opportunity to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata—does not enter the fixed course, rightness in wholesome qualities.
translations.an3.22:6: Here, monks, some person—whether obtaining the opportunity to see the Tathāgata or not obtaining the opportunity to see the Tathāgata, whether obtaining the opportunity to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata or not obtaining the opportunity to hear the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata—enters the fixed course, rightness in wholesome qualities.
translations.an3.24:1: "Monks, these three persons are of great help to a person. What three? That person, monks, relying on whom a person has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha: this person, monks, is of great help to this person.
translations.an3.24:2: Furthermore, monks, that person relying on whom a person understands as it really is: 'This is suffering'; understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering'; understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering'; understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering': this person, monks, is of great help to this person.
translations.an3.24:3: Furthermore, monks, that person relying on whom a person, by the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it: this person, monks, is of great help to this person. These, monks, are the three persons of great help to a person.
translations.an3.2:1: "Action is the mark of the fool, monks; action is the mark of the wise; wisdom is the beautifier of a good lineage. Endowed with three qualities, monks, a fool should be understood. What three? By bodily misconduct, by verbal misconduct, by mental misconduct. Endowed with these three qualities, monks, a fool should be understood.
translations.an3.2:2: Endowed with three qualities, monks, a wise person should be understood. What three? By bodily good conduct, by verbal good conduct, by mental good conduct. Endowed with these three qualities, monks, a wise person should be understood.
translations.an3.30:4: A man of inverted wisdom, dull-witted, undiscerning; even if he often goes to the presence of the monks,
translations.an3.30:5: such a one cannot grasp the beginning of the talk, the middle, and the end, for wisdom is not found in him.
translations.an3.30:6: A man of lap-wisdom is said to be better than that; even if he often goes to the presence of the monks,
translations.an3.30:8: And a man of broad wisdom is said to be better than these; even if he often goes to the presence of the monks,
translations.an3.32:4: “Here, Ānanda, a monk has this: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, that is, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the ending of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.’ In this way, Ānanda, a monk might obtain such a concentration that, in this conscious body, the underlying tendencies to ‘I-making’, ‘mine-making’, and conceit would not be; and externally, with regard to all signs, the underlying tendencies to ‘I-making’, ‘mine-making’, and conceit would not be; and having entered upon and dwelling in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in which, for one who has entered upon and dwells, the underlying tendencies to ‘I-making’, ‘mine-making’, and conceit are not, he would dwell having entered upon that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.”
translations.an3.33:1: Then Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As Venerable Sāriputta was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him: “Even in brief, Sāriputta, I would teach the Dhamma; even in detail, Sāriputta, I would teach the Dhamma; both briefly and in detail, Sāriputta, I would teach the Dhamma; but those who understand are hard to find.” “This is the time, Blessed One, this is the time, Fortunate One, for the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma even in brief, to teach the Dhamma even in detail, to teach the Dhamma both briefly and in detail. There will be those who understand the Dhamma.”
translations.an3.33:2: “Therefore, Sāriputta, you should train thus: ‘In this conscious body there will not be the underlying tendencies to “I-making”, “mine-making”, and conceit; and externally, with regard to all signs, there will not be the underlying tendencies to “I-making”, “mine-making”, and conceit; and having entered upon and dwelling in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in which, for one who has entered upon and dwells, the underlying tendencies to “I-making”, “mine-making”, and conceit are not, we will dwell having entered upon that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.’ Thus indeed, Sāriputta, should one train.”
translations.an3.33:3: And when, Sāriputta, for a monk, in this conscious body the underlying tendencies to ‘I-making’, ‘mine-making’, and conceit are not, and externally with regard to all signs the underlying tendencies to ‘I-making’, ‘mine-making’, and conceit are not, and having entered upon and dwelling in that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom in which, for one who has entered upon and dwells, the underlying tendencies to ‘I-making’, ‘mine-making’, and conceit are not, he dwells having entered upon that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; then this is said, Sāriputta: ‘The monk has cut off craving, turned back the fetter; by full understanding of conceit, he has made an end of suffering.’ And it was with reference to this that it was said in the Pārāyana, in the question of Udaya:
translations.an3.33:4: ‘The abandoning of perceptions of sensual pleasures, and both kinds of displeasure; the dispelling of sloth, the prevention of remorse.
translations.an3.34:1: “These three, monks, are causes for the arising of actions. What three? Greed is a cause for the arising of actions, hatred is a cause for the arising of actions, delusion is a cause for the arising of actions.
translations.an3.34:10: Whatever action, monks, is done without delusion, born of non-delusion, having non-delusion as its cause, having non-delusion as its origin—when delusion has disappeared, that action is thus abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made into nonexistence, not subject to arising in the future.
translations.an3.34:11: Just as, monks, seeds are unbroken, not rotten, not damaged by wind and sun, substantial, well stored. A man might burn them with fire. Having burned them with fire, he might make them into ashes. Having made them into ashes, he might winnow them in a strong wind or let them be carried away by the swift current of a river. Thus those seeds, monks, would be cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made into nonexistence, not subject to arising in the future. Even so, monks, whatever action is done without greed, born of non-greed, having non-greed as its cause, having non-greed as its origin—when greed has disappeared, that action is thus abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made into nonexistence, not subject to arising in the future.
translations.an3.34:13: Cast aside what is born of greed and born of hatred, and what is born of delusion; whatever action has been done by that, whether little or much, it is to be felt right here; no other ground is found.
translations.an3.34:2: Whatever action, monks, is done with greed, born of greed, having greed as its cause, having greed as its origin—wherever his individuality is produced, there that action ripens. Where that action ripens, there he experiences the result of that action, either in this very life, or having arisen (in another), or in some subsequent occasion.
translations.an3.34:5: Just as, monks, seeds are unbroken, not rotten, not damaged by wind and sun, substantial, well stored, placed in a good field on well-prepared ground; and rain would fall properly—thus those seeds, monks, would attain growth, increase, and fullness. Even so, monks, whatever action is done with greed, born of greed, having greed as its cause, having greed as its origin—wherever his individuality is produced, there that action ripens. Where that action ripens, there he experiences the result of that action, either in this very life, or having arisen (in another), or in some subsequent occasion.
translations.an3.34:6: Whatever action is done with hatred … whatever action is done with delusion, born of delusion, having delusion as its cause, having delusion as its origin—wherever his individuality is produced, there that action ripens. Where that action ripens, there he experiences the result of that action, either in this very life, or having arisen (in another), or in some subsequent occasion. These, monks, are the three causes for the arising of actions.
translations.an3.34:9: Whatever action, monks, is done without hatred, born of non-hatred, having non-hatred as its cause, having non-hatred as its origin—when hatred has disappeared, that action is thus abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made into nonexistence, not subject to arising in the future.
translations.an3.35:3: “Then, prince, I will question you about this in return. Answer it as it seems fit to you. What do you think, prince? Here there is the gabled house of a householder or a householder’s son, plastered inside and out, sheltered from the wind, with fitted bolts, with shut windows; there is a couch spread with a long-fleeced cover, a white cover, an embroidered cover, a cover of kadali-deer-skin, with a canopy above, with red pillows at both ends; and an oil lamp would be burning there; and four wives, pleasing and agreeable, would be standing by attending him. What do you think, prince—would he lie down pleasantly or not? Or how does it seem to you in this matter?” “He would lie down pleasantly, venerable sir. And among those in the world who lie down happily, he would be one of them.”
translations.an3.35:4: “What do you think, young man: would lust-born fevers—bodily or mental—arise in that householder or householder’s son, by which, being burned by those lust-born fevers, he would lie in suffering?” “Yes, sir.”
translations.an3.35:8: Always they lie happily, the brahmin who has become fully quenched; who is not smeared by sensual pleasures, cooled, without acquisitions.
translations.an3.39:10: As I dwelt thus, having understood the Dhamma that is without acquisitions; the intoxications that are in health, and in youth, and in life:
translations.an3.39:2: For me, bhikkhus, there were three mansions—one for winter, one for summer, one for the rainy season. And I, bhikkhus, in the rainy-season mansion, during the four months of the rainy season, being entertained by music without men, did not go down to the lower mansion. Whereas, bhikkhus, in the dwelling of others, the food of broken rice with sour gruel as the second is given to slaves, workers, and servants, so too for me, bhikkhus, in my father’s dwelling, boiled rice with meat was given to slaves, workers, and servants.
translations.an3.39:3: For me, bhikkhus, possessed of such prosperity and such delicacy, this occurred: ‘An uninstructed ordinary person, being oneself subject to aging, not having gone beyond aging, on seeing another who is aged, is horrified, ashamed, and disgusted, having overlooked oneself: “I too am subject to aging, I have not gone beyond aging. If I, being subject to aging, not having gone beyond aging, on seeing another who is aged, should be horrified, ashamed, and disgusted, that would not be fitting for me.”’ For me, bhikkhus, reflecting thus, the intoxication with youth that is in youth was entirely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:4: An uninstructed ordinary person, being oneself subject to illness, not having gone beyond illness, on seeing another who is ill, is horrified, ashamed, and disgusted, having overlooked oneself: ‘I too am subject to illness, I have not gone beyond illness. If I, being subject to illness, not having gone beyond illness, on seeing another who is ill, should be horrified, ashamed, and disgusted, that would not be fitting for me.’ For me, bhikkhus, reflecting thus, the intoxication with health that is in health was entirely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:5: An uninstructed ordinary person, being oneself subject to death, not having gone beyond death, on seeing another who is dead, is horrified, ashamed, and disgusted, having overlooked oneself: ‘I too am subject to death, I have not gone beyond death. If I, being subject to death, not having gone beyond death, on seeing another who is dead, should be horrified, ashamed, and disgusted, that would not be fitting for me.’ For me, bhikkhus, reflecting thus, the intoxication with life that is in life was entirely abandoned.
translations.an3.39:7: Intoxicated with the intoxication of youth, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having renounced the training, turns back to the inferior life. Or intoxicated with the intoxication of health, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu … or intoxicated with the intoxication of life, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having renounced the training, turns back to the inferior life.
translations.an3.39:8: Subject to illness, subject to aging, and also subject to death; being in accordance with their nature, being such, ordinary people are disgusted.
translations.an3.39:9: If I were to be disgusted at that in living beings with such natures, that would not be fitting for me, living thus.
translations.an3.40:1: “These three are authorities, bhikkhus. Which three? Authority of self, authority of the world, authority of Dhamma. And what, bhikkhus, is authority of self? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu gone to the wilderness, or gone to the root of a tree, or gone to an empty dwelling reflects thus: ‘It is not for the sake of a robe that I have gone forth from home to homelessness. Not for the sake of almsfood, not for the sake of lodging, not for the sake of becoming this or that that I have gone forth from home to homelessness. But I am afflicted by birth, aging, and death, by sorrows, lamentations, pains, displeasures, and despairs—afflicted by suffering, beset by suffering. Perhaps an end of this whole mass of suffering might be discerned. If I, having gone forth from home to homelessness abandoning such sensual pleasures, were to seek sensual pleasures of that kind or worse, that would not be fitting for me.’ He reflects thus: ‘My energy will be aroused and not slack, mindfulness established and unconfused, body tranquil and unagitated, mind concentrated and one-pointed.’ Making oneself alone the authority, he abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy, develops the blameless, and keeps himself pure. This is called, bhikkhus, authority of self.
translations.an3.40:3: And what, bhikkhus, is authority of Dhamma? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu gone to the wilderness, or gone to the root of a tree, or gone to an empty dwelling reflects thus: ‘It is not for the sake of a robe that I have gone forth from home to homelessness. Not for the sake of almsfood, not for the sake of lodging, not for the sake of becoming this or that that I have gone forth from home to homelessness. But I am afflicted by birth, aging, and death, by sorrows, lamentations, pains, displeasures, and despairs—afflicted by suffering, beset by suffering. Perhaps an end of this whole mass of suffering might be discerned. The Dhamma has been well proclaimed by the Blessed One: visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally known by the wise. And there are my companions in the holy life who dwell knowing and seeing. If I, having gone forth in this well-proclaimed Dhamma and discipline, were to dwell lazy and heedless, that would not be fitting for me.’ He reflects thus: ‘My energy will be aroused and not slack, mindfulness established and unconfused, body tranquil and unagitated, mind concentrated and one-pointed.’ Making the Dhamma alone the authority, he abandons the unwholesome, develops the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy, develops the blameless, and keeps himself pure. This is called, bhikkhus, authority of Dhamma. These, bhikkhus, are the three authorities.”
translations.an3.40:4: In the world there is no such thing as secrecy for one doing an evil deed; you yourself, man, know it—whether it is true or whether false.
translations.an3.40:5: You despise yourself as a witness, good sir; you who, having evil within yourself, hide yourself.
translations.an3.40:6: The gods see, and the Tathāgatas too, the fool in the world who behaves crookedly; therefore one who has self as authority, and the world as authority, prudent and meditative; and one who has the Dhamma as authority, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma—the sage does not decline, whose striving is for truth.
translations.an3.48:1: “Relying on the Himalayas, bhikkhus, the king of mountains, great sāla trees grow in three ways. In which three? They grow in branches, twigs, and leaves; they grow in bark and outer bark; they grow in sapwood and heartwood. Relying on the Himalayas, bhikkhus, the king of mountains, great sāla trees grow in these three ways.
translations.an3.48:2: Even so, bhikkhus, relying on a faithful householder, the people within grow in three ways. In which three? They grow in faith, they grow in virtue, they grow in wisdom. Relying on a faithful householder, bhikkhus, the people within grow in these three ways.”
translations.an3.48:3:
Just as a rocky mountain,
 in a wilderness, in a great forest;
 relying on it,
 those forest-lords, the trees, grow.
translations.an3.51:1: Then two brahmins, old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the end of life, two hundred years old by birth, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had concluded the greetings and friendly talk, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those brahmins said this to the Blessed One: “We, Master Gotama, are brahmins, old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the end of life, two hundred years old by birth; and we are without having done what is good, without having done what is wholesome, without having made a refuge from fear. Let Master Gotama advise us, let Master Gotama instruct us, so that it would be for our welfare and happiness for a long time.”
translations.an3.51:2: “Indeed, brahmins, you are old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the end of life, two hundred years old by birth; and you are without having done what is good, without having done what is wholesome, without having made a refuge from fear. This world, brahmins, is being led on by aging, illness, and death. When, brahmins, the world is being led on by aging, illness, and death, whoever here has restraint of body, restraint of speech, restraint of mind: that becomes for them, when they have passed away, a shelter and a refuge and an island and a safe haven and a final destination.”
translations.an3.51:3:
Life is being led on, of limited span;
 for one led on by aging there are no shelters.
 Seeing this danger in death,
 one should do meritorious deeds that bring happiness.
translations.an3.57:2: “Those, Vaccha, who have spoken thus: ‘The ascetic Gotama says this: “A gift should be given only to me …” … “what is given to others’ disciples is not of great fruit”’—they are not speaking what was said by me. They misrepresent me with what is false and untrue. Whoever, Vaccha, prevents another from giving a gift is a maker of obstacles to three things, a hinderer of three. Which three? He is a maker of obstacles to the giver’s merit, a maker of obstacles to the recipients’ gain, and moreover he has already hurt and harmed himself. Whoever, Vaccha, prevents another from giving a gift is a maker of obstacles to these three things, a hinderer of three.
translations.an3.5:1: “Endowed with three things, bhikkhus, a fool should be understood. With which three? He is one who asks a question improperly, he is one who answers a question improperly, and when another has properly answered a question with rounded words and phrases, smooth and connected, he does not approve. Endowed with these three things, bhikkhus, a fool should be understood.
translations.an3.60:1: Then Saṅgārava the brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When he had concluded the greetings and friendly talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Saṅgārava the brahmin said this to the Blessed One: “We, Master Gotama, are brahmins by name. We perform sacrifices and have them performed. There, Master Gotama, both the one who sacrifices and the one who has it performed—all of them undertake a course of merit involving many persons, namely, the occasion of sacrifice. But this one, Master Gotama, who from this or that family has gone forth from the household life to homelessness, tames only himself, calms only himself, quenches only himself—he undertakes a course of merit involving only one person, namely, the occasion of going forth.”
translations.an3.60:10: But here, brahmin, some one does not declare by a sign, but after hearing a sound of humans or non-humans or deities he declares: ‘So is your mind; so is your mind; such too is your thought.’ Though he declares much, it is just so and not otherwise.
translations.an3.60:11: But here, brahmin, some one does not declare by a sign, nor after hearing a sound of humans or non-humans or deities does he declare, but after hearing the sound produced by thought and examination as one is thinking and examining, he declares: ‘So is your mind; so is your mind; such too is your thought.’ Though he declares much, it is just so and not otherwise.
translations.an3.60:12: But here, brahmin, some one does not declare by a sign, nor after hearing a sound of humans or non-humans or deities does he declare, nor after hearing the sound produced by thought and examination as one is thinking and examining does he declare, but for one who has entered upon a concentration without thought and without examination, he understands mind with his mind: ‘As this good man’s mental formations are directed, immediately after this thought this mind will think such and such a thought.’ Though he declares much, it is just so and not otherwise. This is called, brahmin, the miracle of declaration.
translations.an3.60:13: And what, brahmin, is the miracle of instruction? Here, brahmin, some one instructs thus: ‘Think in this way; do not think in that way. Attend in this way; do not attend in that way. Abandon this; having attained this, dwell.’ This is called, brahmin, the miracle of instruction. These, brahmin, are the three miracles. Of these three miracles, brahmin, which miracle is acceptable, and more excellent and more sublime?”
