translations.an3.60:14: “There, Master Gotama, as to this miracle whereby here some one experiences various kinds of supernormal power … up to: he wields mastery with the body even as far as the brahmā world—this miracle, Master Gotama, whoever does it, he himself experiences it; whoever does it, it is his alone. This miracle, Master Gotama, appears to me to be like something involving illusion.”
translations.an3.60:16: And whatever is this, Master Gotama, the miracle: here someone instructs thus: ‘Think in this way; do not think in that way. Attend in this way; do not attend in that way. Abandon this; having attained this, dwell.’ This, Master Gotama, is the miracle that is acceptable, and it is more excellent and more sublime than these three miracles.
translations.an3.60:17: Wonderful, Master Gotama, marvelous, Master Gotama. How well this has been spoken by Master Gotama, and we hold Master Gotama to be endowed with these three miracles. For Master Gotama experiences various kinds of spiritual power … up to he wields mastery with the body even as far as the brahmā world; for Master Gotama, with mind, having encompassed the mind of one who has entered a concentration without thought and without examination, understands: ‘Just as this good man’s mental formations are directed, immediately after this state of mind he will think this thought by name.’ For Master Gotama instructs thus: ‘Think in this way; do not think in that way. Attend in this way; do not attend in that way. Abandon this; having attained this, dwell.’”
translations.an3.60:18: “Surely, brahmin, speech has been spoken by you that is offensive and insulting; nevertheless I will answer you. For I, brahmin, experience various kinds of spiritual power … up to I wield mastery with the body even as far as the brahmā world. For I, brahmin, with mind, having encompassed the mind of one who has entered a concentration without thought and without examination, understand: ‘Just as this good man’s mental formations are directed, immediately after this state of mind he will think this thought by name.’ For I, brahmin, instruct thus: ‘Think in this way; do not think in that way. Attend in this way; do not attend in that way. Abandon this; having attained this, dwell.’”
translations.an3.60:19: “But is there, Master Gotama, even another single monk who is endowed with these three miracles, apart from Master Gotama?” “No, brahmin, not just one hundred, not two hundred, not three hundred, not four hundred, not five hundred, but even more, the monks who are endowed with these three miracles.” “But where, Master Gotama, are those monks now dwelling?” “In this very Saṅgha of monks, brahmin.”
translations.an3.60:2: “Well then, brahmin, I will question you right here in return. Answer it as it seems fitting to you. What do you think, brahmin? Here a Tathāgata arises in the world, an arahant, a perfectly awakened one, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, awakened, blessed. He says this: ‘Come, this is the path, this is the practice, by following which I, having directly known and realized for myself the unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, proclaim it; come, you too practice likewise, by following which you too, having directly known and realized for yourselves the unsurpassed culmination of the holy life, will enter upon it and dwell.’ Thus this teacher teaches the Dhamma, and others practice for that very purpose; and those are many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands.
translations.an3.60:3: What do you think, brahmin? Since this is so, is this practice that is merit, namely going forth, involving one body or involving many bodies?” “Since this is so, Master Gotama, this practice that is merit, namely going forth, is involving many bodies.”
translations.an3.60:4: When this was said, Venerable Ānanda said this to the brahmin Saṅgārava: “Of these two practices of yours, brahmin, which practice is acceptable, and requires less aim and less undertaking, and is more fruitful and more beneficial?” When this was said, the brahmin Saṅgārava said this to Venerable Ānanda: “Such as Master Gotama, such as Master Ānanda. These are my objects of reverence, these are my objects of praise.”
translations.an3.60:5: A second time Venerable Ānanda said this to the brahmin Saṅgārava: “I do not ask you thus, brahmin: ‘Who are your objects of reverence, who are your objects of praise?’ Rather, brahmin, I ask you thus: ‘Of these two practices of yours, brahmin, which practice is acceptable, and requires less aim and less undertaking, and is more fruitful and more beneficial?’” A second time the brahmin Saṅgārava said this to Venerable Ānanda: “Such as Master Gotama, such as Master Ānanda. These are my objects of reverence, these are my objects of praise.”
translations.an3.60:7: Then it occurred to the Blessed One: “Even a third time the brahmin Saṅgārava, asked a question according to the Dhamma by Ānanda, evades it and does not answer. Why don’t I rescue him?” Then the Blessed One said this to the brahmin Saṅgārava: “What, brahmin, today was the topic of discussion that arose among the king’s men, seated and assembled in the royal palace?” “This, Master Gotama, today was the topic of discussion that arose among the king’s men, seated and assembled in the royal palace: ‘Formerly there were few monks, and many more displayed superhuman qualities, a miracle of spiritual power; but now there are many monks, and fewer display superhuman qualities, a miracle of spiritual power.’ This, Master Gotama, today was the topic of discussion that arose among the king’s men, seated and assembled in the royal palace.”
translations.an3.60:8: “There are, brahmin, these three miracles. What three? The miracle of spiritual power, the miracle of mind-reading, the miracle of instruction. And what, brahmin, is the miracle of spiritual power? Here, brahmin, someone experiences various kinds of spiritual power: ‘Having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; appearance and disappearance; he goes unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain, as though through space; he plunges into and emerges from the earth as though in water; he walks on water without breaking it, as though on earth; in the sky he travels cross-legged, as a winged bird; even these moon and sun, so mighty, so powerful, he touches and strokes with the hand; up to he wields mastery with the body even as far as the brahmā world.’ This is called, brahmin, the miracle of spiritual power.”
translations.an3.60:9: And what, brahmin, is the miracle of mind-reading? Here, brahmin, someone declares by means of a sign: ‘Thus is your mind, thus is your mind, thus is your thought.’ Even if they declare much, it turns out to be just so, not otherwise.
translations.an3.61:13: ‘These are the four noble truths’—monks, I have taught the Dhamma that is not open to censure, uncorrupted, blameless, not reproached, not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins. So it was said. And in reference to what was this said? Dependent on the six elements, monks, there is descent of an embryo; when there is descent, there is name-and-form; dependent on name-and-form, the six sense bases; dependent on the six sense bases, contact; dependent on contact, feeling. And for one who feels, monks, I designate: ‘this is suffering’; I designate: ‘this is the origin of suffering’; I designate: ‘this is the cessation of suffering’; I designate: ‘this is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.’
translations.an3.61:14: And what, monks, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, (…) death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair are suffering; association with the unloved is suffering; separation from the loved is suffering; not getting what one wants is suffering. In brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering. This is called, monks, the noble truth of suffering.
translations.an3.61:15: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. This is called, monks, the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
translations.an3.61:16: And what, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? With the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of formations; with cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness; with cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact; with cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with cessation of clinging, cessation of existence; with cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This is called, monks, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
translations.an3.61:3: But, monks, for those who return to what was done in the past as the essence, there is no desire or effort: ‘this should be done, this should not be done.’ And when what should be done and what should not be done cannot truly and really be found, for those who dwell forgetful and unguarded there is no personal, coherent ascetic doctrine. This, monks, is my first coherent refutation of those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such views.
translations.an3.61:8: These, monks, are the three grounds for sectarian views which, when examined by the wise, investigated, and discussed, even going beyond, end up in non-doing.
translations.an3.61:9: But, monks, I have taught the Dhamma that is not open to censure, uncorrupted, blameless, not reproached, not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins. And what, monks, is the Dhamma I have taught that is not open to censure, uncorrupted, blameless, not reproached, not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins? ‘These are the six elements’—monks, I have taught the Dhamma that is not open to censure, uncorrupted, blameless, not reproached, not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins. ‘These are the six spheres of contact’—monks, I have taught the Dhamma that is not open to censure, uncorrupted, blameless, not reproached, not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins. ‘These are the eighteen mental explorations’—monks, I have taught the Dhamma that is not open to censure, uncorrupted, blameless, not reproached, not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins. ‘These are the four noble truths’—monks, I have taught the Dhamma that is not open to censure, uncorrupted, blameless, not reproached, not despised by wise ascetics and brahmins.
translations.an3.62:1: “These three are motherless-and-sonless fears,” says the unlearned ordinary person. Which three? There is a time, monks, when a great conflagration breaks out. When a great conflagration has broken out, monks, thereby villages burn, towns burn, cities burn. When villages are burning, towns are burning, cities are burning, there a mother does not find her son, and a son does not find his mother. This, monks, is the first motherless-and-sonless fear,” says the unlearned ordinary person.
translations.an3.62:2: Furthermore, monks, there is a time when a great cloud breaks out. When a great cloud has broken out, monks, a great flood arises. When a great flood has arisen, monks, thereby villages are swept away, towns are swept away, cities are swept away. When villages are being swept away, towns are being swept away, cities are being swept away, there a mother does not find her son, and a son does not find his mother. This, monks, is the second motherless-and-sonless fear,” says the unlearned ordinary person.
translations.an3.62:3: Furthermore, monks, there is a time when there is danger: a forest uprising; provinces roaming about mounted on carts. When there is danger, monks, a forest uprising, provinces roaming about mounted on carts, there a mother does not find her son, and a son does not find his mother. This, monks, is the third motherless-and-sonless fear,” says the unlearned ordinary person. These, monks, are the three motherless-and-sonless fears,” says the unlearned ordinary person.
translations.an3.62:4: But these, bhikkhus, are just three fears that involve a mother and son, (yet) the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of them as fears that do not involve a mother and son. Which three? There is a time, bhikkhus, when a great fire breaks out. And when a great fire has broken out, then villages burn, towns burn, cities burn. When villages are burning, towns are burning, cities are burning, there is that time when sometimes, now and then, a mother finds her son, and a son finds his mother. This, bhikkhus, is the first fear that involves a mother and son (yet) the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of it as a fear that does not involve a mother and son.
translations.an3.62:5: Furthermore, bhikkhus, there is a time when a great cloud breaks out. And when a great cloud has broken out, a great flood arises. And when a great flood has arisen, then villages are swept away, towns are swept away, cities are swept away. When villages are being swept away, towns are being swept away, cities are being swept away, there is that time when sometimes, now and then, a mother finds her son, and a son finds his mother. This, bhikkhus, is the second fear that involves a mother and son (yet) the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of it as a fear that does not involve a mother and son.
translations.an3.62:6: Furthermore, bhikkhus, there is a time when there is fear, a forest uprising: countrymen mounted on wagons roam about. And when there is fear, bhikkhus, when there is a forest uprising, when countrymen mounted on wagons are roaming about, there is that time when sometimes, now and then, a mother finds her son, and a son finds his mother. This, bhikkhus, is the third fear that involves a mother and son (yet) the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of it as a fear that does not involve a mother and son. These, bhikkhus, are just three fears that involve a mother and son (yet) the uninstructed ordinary person speaks of them as fears that do not involve a mother and son.
translations.an3.62:7: There are, bhikkhus, three fears that do not involve a mother and son. Which three? The fear of aging, the fear of illness, the fear of death. A mother, bhikkhus, does not thus obtain a son who is aging: ‘I am aging; may my son not age’; or a son does not thus obtain a mother who is aging: ‘I am aging; may my mother not age.’
translations.an3.62:8: A mother, bhikkhus, does not thus obtain a son who is becoming ill: ‘I am becoming ill; may my son not become ill’; or a son does not thus obtain a mother who is becoming ill: ‘I am becoming ill; may my mother not become ill.’
translations.an3.62:9: A mother, bhikkhus, does not thus obtain a son who is dying: ‘I am dying; may my son not die’; or a son does not thus obtain a mother who is dying: ‘I am dying; may my mother not die.’ These, bhikkhus, are three fears that do not involve a mother and son.
translations.an3.63:1: Thus have I heard— At one time the Blessed One, wandering on tour among the Kosalans, arrived at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Venāgapura, together with a large saṅgha of bhikkhus. The brahmins and householders of Venāgapura heard: “Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama, the Sakyan son, who went forth from the Sakyan clan, has arrived at Venāgapura. And of that Master Gotama this good report has spread: ‘He is indeed the Blessed One, an arahant, perfectly awakened, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Fortunate One, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.’ He makes known this world—with its devas, with its Māras, with its Brahmās, this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—having realized it by his own direct knowledge. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with meaning and with phrasing; he reveals the perfectly complete and purified holy life. It is good to see such arahants.”
translations.an3.63:11: “Wonderful, Master Gotama, marvelous, Master Gotama. And who else would be one who gains at will, gains without trouble, gains without difficulty, such a noble one’s high bed and great bed, apart from Master Gotama?”
translations.an3.63:2: Then the brahmins and householders of Venāgapura went to the Blessed One; having gone, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after the exchange of friendly greetings and courteous talk, sat down to one side; some, with hands joined in reverence toward the Blessed One, sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan and sat down to one side; some sat down to one side in silence. While seated to one side, the Venāgapuran brahmin Vacchagotta said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an3.63:5: “There are, brahmin, these three high beds and great beds, which I now gain at will, gain without trouble, gain without difficulty. Which three? The divine high bed and great bed, the brahmā high bed and great bed, the noble high bed and great bed. These, brahmin, are the three high beds and great beds which I now gain at will, gain without trouble, gain without difficulty.”
translations.an4.10:10: Beings go on in saṁsāra, bound for birth and death; but those who, having fully understood sensual pleasures, and the yoke of becoming as well entirely.
translations.an4.10:9: Bound up with the yoke of sensual pleasures, and with the yoke of becoming as well—both; bound up with the yoke of views, with ignorance set in front.
translations.an4.18:1: “There are, bhikkhus, these four ways of going not astray. Which four? One does not go by favoritism, one does not go by aversion, one does not go by delusion, one does not go by fear— These, bhikkhus, are the four ways of going not astray.”
translations.an4.1:1: Thus have I heard— at one time the Blessed One was staying among the Vajjis at Bhaṇḍagāma. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an4.1:4: “Virtue, concentration, and wisdom too, and unsurpassed liberation; these things were awakened to by Gotama, the glorious one.”
translations.an4.24:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāketa in the Blackwood Monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this—
translations.an4.24:2: Whatever, bhikkhus, in the world with its devas, with its Māras, with its Brahmās, in this population with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought, and mentally explored— that I know.
translations.an4.24:5: Whatever, monks … that I might say: ‘I both know it and do not know it’—that would be just the same as that.
translations.an4.24:7: So, monks, with regard to what is to be seen, the Tathāgata, having seen, does not conceive of the seen, does not conceive of the unseen, does not conceive of what is to be seen, does not conceive of a seer; with regard to what is to be heard, having heard, he does not conceive of the heard, does not conceive of the unheard, does not conceive of what is to be heard, does not conceive of a hearer; with regard to what is to be sensed, having sensed, he does not conceive of the sensed, does not conceive of the unsensed, does not conceive of what is to be sensed, does not conceive of one who senses; with regard to what is to be cognized, having cognized, he does not conceive of the cognized, does not conceive of the uncognized, does not conceive of what is to be cognized, does not conceive of one who cognizes. So, monks, the Tathāgata is just such with respect to things that are to be seen, heard, sensed, and cognized—just such. And I say: ‘Apart from that such one, there is no other such one higher or more sublime.’
translations.an4.24:8: Whatever is seen or heard or sensed, adhered to as truth, taken up as truth of others—among those, the such one, self-restrained, would not posit as other either truth or falsehood.
translations.an4.28:1: “There are, monks, these four noble lineages—foremost, long-standing, of ancient lineage, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated; they are not being adulterated and will not be adulterated, and are not despised by ascetics, brahmins, or the wise. What four? Here, monks, a monk is content with whatever robe, and he speaks in praise of contentment with whatever robe; and for the sake of a robe he does not undertake improper seeking; and not obtaining a robe he is not anxious, and obtaining a robe he uses it without clinging, without infatuation, not obsessed, seeing danger, discerning escape; and with that contentment with whatever robe he neither exalts himself nor disparages others. For whoever is skilled there, not lazy, clearly comprehending, mindful—this one is called, monks, a monk standing in the ancient, foremost noble lineage.
translations.an4.28:4: Furthermore, monks, a monk is one who delights in development, who delights in development; he is one who delights in abandoning, who delights in abandoning; and by that delight in development, that delight in development, that delight in abandoning, that delight in abandoning, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others. For whoever is skilled there, not lazy, clearly comprehending, mindful—this one is called, monks, a monk standing in the ancient, foremost noble lineage. These, monks, are the four noble lineages—foremost, long-standing, of ancient lineage, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated; they are not being adulterated and will not be adulterated, and are not despised by ascetics, brahmins, or the wise.”
translations.an4.28:5: And, monks, a monk endowed with these four noble lineages—if he dwells in the eastern direction, he endures discontent itself; discontent does not endure him; if he dwells in the western direction, he endures discontent itself; discontent does not endure him; if he dwells in the northern direction, he endures discontent itself; discontent does not endure him; if he dwells in the southern direction, he endures discontent itself; discontent does not endure him. For what reason? For the wise one, monks, is one who endures discontent and delight.”
translations.an4.28:6: Discontent does not endure the wise one, nor does discontent withstand the wise one; the wise one indeed endures discontent, for the wise one is one who withstands discontent.
translations.an4.31:1: “There are, monks, these four wheels, endowed with which the four-wheeled (carriage) rolls for gods and humans, endowed with which gods and humans in no long time reach greatness and abundance in possessions. What four? Living in a suitable region, reliance on good persons, right self-directed resolve, and merit done previously—these, monks, are the four wheels, endowed with which the four-wheeled (carriage) rolls for gods and humans, endowed with which gods and humans in no long time reach greatness and abundance in possessions.”
translations.an4.32:1: “There are, monks, these four bases of social cohesion. What four? Giving, kindly speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality—these, monks, are the four bases of social cohesion.”
translations.an4.32:2: Giving and kindly speech, and whatever beneficial conduct there is here; and impartiality in things, here and there as is fitting—these indeed are cohesions in the world, like the linchpin of a moving chariot.
translations.an4.32:3: And if these cohesions were not, a mother would not obtain esteem or honor because of her children, nor would a father obtain esteem or honor because of his children.
translations.an4.33:1: “A lion, monks, the king of beasts, in the evening time comes out from his lair. Having come out from his lair, he stretches. Having stretched, he looks around in all four directions. Having looked around in all four directions, he roars a lion’s roar three times. Having roared a lion’s roar three times, he sets out in search of pasture. And those animals, monks, that hear the sound of the lion, king of beasts, roaring—most of them come to fear, agitation, and terror. They enter their burrows, they enter the water as their dwelling, they enter the forest as their dwelling; birds take to the sky. Even those royal elephants, monks, bound in villages, towns, and capital cities with strong leather straps and bonds—even they break and tear apart those bonds and, frightened, evacuating dung and urine, flee this way or that. So mighty in power, monks, is the lion, king of beasts, among animals; so influential, so great in might.”
translations.an4.33:2: “In just the same way, monks, when a Tathāgata arises in the world—an arahant, perfectly awakened one, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed—he teaches the Dhamma: ‘thus is personality, thus is the origin of personality, thus is the cessation of personality, thus is the way leading to the cessation of personality.’ And even those gods, monks, long-lived, beautiful, enjoying much happiness, long-standing in lofty mansions—having heard the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma, most of them come to fear, agitation, and terror: ‘Impermanent indeed, sirs, are we, though we thought, being as we are, that we are permanent; unstable indeed, sirs, are we, though we thought, being as we are, that we are stable; not eternal indeed, sirs, are we, though we thought, being as we are, that we are eternal. Indeed, sirs, we are impermanent, unstable, not eternal, included within personality.’ So mighty in power, monks, is the Tathāgata with the world of gods; so influential, so great in might.”
translations.an4.33:3: When the Buddha, by direct knowledge, set in motion the wheel of Dhamma, the teacher without equal for the world with its gods.
translations.an4.33:4: And personality and cessation, and the arising of personality; and the noble eightfold path leading to the calming of suffering.
translations.an4.34:1: “There are, bhikkhus, four kinds of highest confidence. What four? As far as, bhikkhus, there are beings—whether without feet or with two feet or with four feet or with many feet, whether with form or formless, whether percipient or non-percipient or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Those, bhikkhus, who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the highest. And for those who have confidence in the highest, the result is the highest.
translations.an4.34:2: As far as, bhikkhus, there are conditioned phenomena, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the foremost among them. Those, bhikkhus, who have confidence in the Noble Eightfold Path have confidence in the highest. And for those who have confidence in the highest, the result is the highest.
translations.an4.34:3: As far as, bhikkhus, there are phenomena, conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion is declared the foremost among them, that is: the removal of intoxication, the elimination of thirst, the uprooting of clinging, the cutting off of the round, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Those, bhikkhus, who have confidence in the dhamma of dispassion have confidence in the highest. And for those who have confidence in the highest, the result is the highest.
translations.an4.34:4: As far as, bhikkhus, there are communities or groups, the Saṅgha of the Tathāgata’s disciples is declared the foremost among them, that is: the four pairs of persons, the eight individuals—this is the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples, worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. Those, bhikkhus, who have confidence in the Saṅgha have confidence in the highest. And for those who have confidence in the highest, the result is the highest. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of highest confidence.”
translations.an4.34:5: For those confident in the highest, who understand the highest Dhamma: for those confident in the foremost Buddha, the unsurpassed one worthy of gifts;
translations.an4.34:6: for those confident in the highest Dhamma, in the happiness of the stilling of dispassion; for those confident in the highest Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit;
translations.an4.34:7: for those giving gifts to the highest, the highest merit grows: the highest lifespan and beauty, fame, renown, happiness, strength.
translations.an4.35:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding place. Then Vassakāra the brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, went to the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When he had exchanged courteous and friendly talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Vassakāra the brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.35:2: “With four qualities, Master Gotama, we describe a great wise man, a great person. With what four? Here, Master Gotama, one is learned; regarding this or that which has been heard, regarding this or that which has been spoken, one knows the meaning: ‘this is the meaning of this saying, this is the meaning of this saying.’ Moreover, one is mindful; one remembers and recollects even what was done long ago and what was said long ago. And as to those tasks that are to be done by householders, one is skillful there, not lazy, endowed with inquiry into the means, able to do and able to arrange. With these four qualities, Master Gotama, we describe a great wise man, a great person. If, Master Gotama, this should be approved by you, let Master Gotama approve it for me; but if it should be rejected by you, let Master Gotama reject it for me.”
translations.an4.35:6: He who knows the release of all beings from the snare of death; he proclaimed the beneficial Dhamma for devas and humans, the method; having seen and heard which, many people become serene.
translations.an4.36:1: At one time the Blessed One was traveling along the road between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setavyā. Doṇa the brahmin too was traveling along the road between Ukkaṭṭhā and Setavyā. Doṇa the brahmin saw on the Blessed One’s feet wheels with a thousand spokes, with rims and hubs, complete in every way; seeing this, he thought: “It is wonderful indeed, sir, it is amazing indeed, sir. These will not be the footprints of a human being.” Then the Blessed One, leaving the road, sat down at the root of a certain tree, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness in front of him. Then Doṇa the brahmin, following the Blessed One’s footprints, saw the Blessed One seated at the root of a certain tree, pleasing, inspiring confidence, with faculties calmed, mind calmed, having attained the highest taming and tranquility, tamed, guarded, with senses restrained, a nāga. Seeing him, he went to the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an4.36:2: “Will the honorable one be a deva?” “I will not be a deva, brahmin.” “Will the honorable one be a gandhabba?” “I will not be a gandhabba, brahmin.” “Will the honorable one be a yakkha?” “I will not be a yakkha, brahmin.” “Will the honorable one be a human being?” “I will not be a human being, brahmin.”
translations.an4.36:4: “Those taints, brahmin, by not abandoning which I might be a deva—those taints of mine are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made not to exist, of a nature not to arise in the future. Those taints, brahmin, by not abandoning which I might be a gandhabba … might be a yakkha … might be a human being—those taints of mine are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made not to exist, of a nature not to arise in the future. Just as, brahmin, a blue lotus or a pink lotus or a white lotus, born in the water, grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water; so too I, brahmin, born in the world, grown in the world, dwell having overcome the world, unsoiled by the world. Bear it in mind, brahmin: ‘Buddha.’”
translations.an4.37:1: “Possessed of four qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is incapable of decline, with Nibbāna close at hand. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is possessed of virtue, is one with guarded doors in the faculties, is moderate in eating, is devoted to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:2: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu possessed of virtue? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous, dwelling restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, endowed with proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults; having undertaken, he trains in the training rules. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is possessed of virtue.”
translations.an4.37:3: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu guarded at the sense doors? Here, bhikkhus, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu is not a grasped-at sign, nor a grasped-at detail. Since, when he dwells with the faculty of the eye unrestrained, evil unwholesome states of longing and dejection might invade him, he practices for its restraint; he guards the faculty of the eye; he comes to restraint in the faculty of the eye. Having heard a sound with the ear … having smelled an odor with the nose … having tasted a flavor with the tongue … having touched a tangible with the body … having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is not a grasped-at sign, nor a grasped-at detail. Since, when he dwells with the faculty of the mind unrestrained, evil unwholesome states of longing and dejection might invade him, he practices for its restraint; he guards the faculty of the mind; he comes to restraint in the faculty of the mind. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is guarded at the sense doors.
translations.an4.37:4: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who knows the measure in eating? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu takes food reflecting wisely: ‘Not for play, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification; but only for the maintenance and continuance of this body, for the ending of affliction, for assisting the holy life. Thus I shall allay old feeling and not arouse new feeling, and there will be sustenance for me, and blamelessness and comfortable abiding.’ In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who knows the measure in eating.
translations.an4.37:5: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu devoted to wakefulness? Here, bhikkhus, by day a bhikkhu purifies his mind of obstructive states while walking back and forth and while sitting; in the first watch of the night he purifies his mind of obstructive states while walking back and forth and while sitting; in the middle watch of the night he prepares the lion’s posture on the right side, placing foot on foot, mindful and clearly comprehending, having attended to the perception of rising; in the last watch of the night, having risen, he purifies his mind of obstructive states while walking back and forth and while sitting. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is devoted to wakefulness. Endowed with these four things, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is incapable of decline, and is close to nibbāna itself.
translations.an4.37:6: A bhikkhu established in virtue, and restrained in the faculties; knowing the measure in eating, he devotes himself to wakefulness.
translations.an4.37:7: Dwelling thus, ardent, tireless by day and night; developing the wholesome state, for the attainment of security from bondage.
translations.an4.38:1: “A bhikkhu, bhikkhus, who has expelled particularist truths is called ‘one whose search is balanced, whose bodily activity is calmed, who is withdrawn.’ And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one who has expelled particularist truths? Here, bhikkhus, whatever are the various particularist truths of various ascetics and brahmins, such as: ‘the world is eternal’ or ‘the world is not eternal’; ‘the world is finite’ or ‘the world is infinite’; ‘the soul is the same as the body’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another’; ‘the Tathāgata exists after death’ or ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death’; ‘the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ or ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’—all those have been pushed away, expelled, abandoned, vomited up, released, relinquished. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who has expelled particularist truths.
translations.an4.38:4: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu withdrawn? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s conceit ‘I am’ is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, done away with, not liable to arise in the future. In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is withdrawn. A bhikkhu, bhikkhus, who has expelled particularist truths is called ‘one whose search is balanced, whose bodily activity is calmed, who is withdrawn.’”
translations.an4.38:5: The search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search in connection with the holy life; thus, grasping at truth—accumulations of standpoints of views.
translations.an4.38:6: For one dispassionate toward all lust, freed by the destruction of craving; searches are relinquished, standpoints of views are uprooted.
translations.an4.52:1: “There are, bhikkhus, these four streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, nourishments of happiness, heavenly, yielding happiness as result, leading to heaven, conducing to what is desired, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and happy. Which four? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is endowed with confirmed confidence in the Buddha: ‘Itipi so bhagavā arahaṁ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṁ buddho bhagavā.’ This, bhikkhus, is the first stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, yielding happiness as result, leading to heaven, conducing to what is desired, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and happy.
translations.an4.52:2: Again, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is endowed with confirmed confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally known by the wise.’ This, bhikkhus, is the second stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, yielding happiness as result, leading to heaven, conducing to what is desired, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and happy.
translations.an4.52:3: Again, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is endowed with confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Blessed One’s community of disciples has practiced well; the Blessed One’s community of disciples has practiced straight; the Blessed One’s community of disciples has practiced rightly; the Blessed One’s community of disciples has practiced properly, namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight kinds of individuals; this is the Blessed One’s community of disciples: worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’ This, bhikkhus, is the third stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, yielding happiness as result, leading to heaven, conducing to what is desired, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and happy.
translations.an4.52:4: Again, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is endowed with virtues dear to the noble ones: unbroken, unpierced, unspotted, unblemished, liberating, praised by the wise, not misapprehended, leading to concentration. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nourishment of happiness, heavenly, yielding happiness as result, leading to heaven, conducing to what is desired, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and happy. These, bhikkhus, are the four streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, nourishments of happiness, heavenly, yielding happiness as result, leading to heaven, conducing to what is desired, lovely, agreeable, beneficial, and happy.”
translations.an4.52:5: One whose faith in the Tathāgata is unshakable and well established; and whose virtue is good, dear to the noble ones, praised.
translations.an4.52:6: One who has confidence in the Saṅgha, and whose view is straight; they call that one “not poor”; their life is not in vain.
translations.an4.53:1: At one time the Blessed One was travelling on the road between Madhurā and Verañjā. And several householder men and householder women were also travelling on the road between Madhurā and Verañjā. Then the Blessed One, leaving the road, sat down at the root of a certain tree (…). The householder men and householder women saw the Blessed One sitting at the root of a certain tree. Having seen him, they approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. When they were seated to one side, the Blessed One said this to those householder men and householder women:
translations.an4.53:10: Both are faithful and generous, self-restrained, living by Dhamma; they become husband and wife, speaking kindly to one another.
translations.an4.53:11: Many benefits come to them; comfort is born; enemies are displeased, since both are of the same virtue.
translations.an4.53:2: “Householders, there are these four kinds of cohabitation. What four? A corpse cohabits with a corpse, a corpse cohabits with a goddess, a god cohabits with a corpse, a god cohabits with a goddess.
translations.an4.53:3: And how, householders, does a corpse cohabit with a corpse? Here, householders, the husband is one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, is one who indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence; he is unvirtuous, of bad character, dwelling at home with a mind overcome by the stain of stinginess, an abuser and reviler of ascetics and brahmins. And his wife too is one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, is one who indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, the basis for negligence; she is unvirtuous, of bad character, dwelling at home with a mind overcome by the stain of stinginess, an abuser and reviler of ascetics and brahmins. Thus, householders, a corpse cohabits with a corpse.
translations.an4.53:8: The husband is unvirtuous, stingy, abusive; the wife is virtuous, generous, free of stinginess; she too, a goddess, cohabits with a husband who is a corpse.
translations.an4.53:9: The husband is virtuous, generous, free of stinginess; the wife is unvirtuous, stingy, abusive; she too, a corpse, cohabits with a husband who is a god.
translations.an4.5:1: “Bhikkhus, these four kinds of persons are found existing in the world. What four? The person who goes with the stream, the person who goes against the stream, the steadfast person, the one who has crossed over, gone beyond, stands on dry ground, a brahmin. And what, bhikkhus, is the person who goes with the stream? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person indulges in sensual pleasures and does bad deeds. This is called, bhikkhus, the person who goes with the stream.
translations.an4.5:2: And what, bhikkhus, is the person who goes against the stream? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person does not indulge in sensual pleasures and does not do bad deeds; even with suffering, even with displeasure, with a tearful face, weeping, they live the fulfilled, purified holy life. This is called, bhikkhus, the person who goes against the stream.
translations.an4.5:3: And what, bhikkhus, is the steadfast person? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person, through the destruction of the five lower fetters, is one who arises spontaneously, one who attains final Nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world. This is called, bhikkhus, the steadfast person.
translations.an4.5:4: And what, bhikkhus, is the person who has crossed over, gone beyond, stands on dry ground, a brahmin? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person, through the destruction of the taints, enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life. This is called, bhikkhus, the person who has crossed over, gone beyond, stands on dry ground, a brahmin. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
translations.an4.5:5: Whatever people are unrestrained in sensual pleasures, not free of lust here, enjoying sensual pleasures—again and again they go on to birth and aging, overcome by craving, going with the stream.
translations.an4.5:6: Therefore, the wise one here, established in mindfulness, not engaging in sensual pleasures and in evil, should abandon sensual pleasures even with suffering; they call that person “one who goes against the stream.”
translations.an4.5:7: Whoever, having abandoned the five defilements, is a perfected trainee, not of a nature to decline, having attained mastery of mind, with faculties collected in concentration—such a person is called “steadfast.”
translations.an4.62:2: “Householder, these four kinds of happiness are to be attained by a householder who enjoys sensual pleasures, from time to time, on an occasion, as the case arises. What four? The happiness of ownership, the happiness of wealth, the happiness of being debtless, the happiness of blamelessness.
translations.an4.62:3: And what, householder, is the happiness of ownership? Here, householder, a clansman has wealth gained by initiative and effort, acquired by strength of arm, earned by sweat, righteous, righteously obtained. Thinking, ‘I have wealth gained by initiative and effort, acquired by strength of arm, earned by sweat, righteous, righteously obtained,’ they attain happiness, they attain gladness. This is called, householder, the happiness of ownership.
translations.an4.62:5: And what, householder, is the happiness of being debtless? Here, householder, a clansman owes nothing to anyone, little or much. Thinking, ‘I owe nothing to anyone, little or much,’ they attain happiness, they attain gladness. This is called, householder, the happiness of being debtless.
translations.an4.62:6: And what, householder, is the happiness of blamelessness? Here, householder, a noble disciple is endowed with blameless bodily action, is endowed with blameless verbal action, is endowed with blameless mental action. Thinking, ‘I am endowed with blameless bodily action, endowed with blameless verbal action, endowed with blameless mental action,’ they attain happiness, they attain gladness. This is called, householder, the happiness of blamelessness. These, householder, are the four kinds of happiness to be attained by a householder who enjoys sensual pleasures, from time to time, on an occasion, as the case arises.”
translations.an4.62:7: Having known the happiness of being debtless, and then the supreme happiness of ownership; enjoying the happiness of wealth, a mortal then sees clearly with wisdom.
translations.an5.23:1: “There are these five impurities of gold, bhikkhus. When gold is corrupted by these impurities, it is neither soft nor workable, neither radiant nor malleable, and it does not properly lend itself to working. What five? Iron, copper, tin, lead, silver: these, bhikkhus, are the five impurities of gold. When gold is corrupted by these impurities, it is neither soft nor workable, neither radiant nor malleable, and it does not properly lend itself to working. But when, bhikkhus, gold is freed from these five impurities, then that gold is soft and workable, radiant and malleable, and it properly lends itself to working. And whatever kind of ornament one desires—whether a signet ring, or earrings, or a necklace, or a gold garland—it serves that purpose for him.
translations.an5.23:2: So too, bhikkhus, there are these five impurities of the mind. When the mind is corrupted by these impurities, it is neither soft nor workable, neither radiant nor malleable, and it is not properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. What five? Sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt: these, bhikkhus, are the five impurities of the mind. When the mind is corrupted by these impurities, it is neither soft nor workable, neither radiant nor malleable, and it is not properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. But when, bhikkhus, the mind is freed from these five impurities, then that mind is soft and workable, radiant and malleable, and it is properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. And whatever state that is to be realized by direct knowledge he inclines the mind toward for direct-knowledge realization, he reaches the capability of witnessing it there and then, whenever there is a basis.
translations.an5.23:3: If he wishes: ‘May I experience the various kinds of spiritual power: having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; I may appear and vanish; I may go unimpeded through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain, as if through space; I may plunge into and emerge from the earth, as if in water; I may walk on water without breaking it, as if on earth; I may travel through the sky cross-legged, like a winged bird; with my hand I may touch and stroke even this moon and sun, so powerful, so mighty; with the body I may wield mastery as far as the brahmā world’—he reaches the capability of witnessing it there and then, whenever there is a basis.
translations.an5.23:4: If he wishes: ‘With the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, may I hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, whether far or near’—he reaches the capability of witnessing it there and then, whenever there is a basis.
translations.an5.23:5: If he wishes: ‘May I understand the minds of other beings, other persons, having encompassed them with my own mind: I may understand a mind with lust as “a mind with lust”, and a mind without lust as “a mind without lust”; I may understand a mind with hate as “a mind with hate”, and a mind without hate as “a mind without hate”; I may understand a mind with delusion as “a mind with delusion”, and a mind without delusion as “a mind without delusion”; I may understand a contracted mind as “a contracted mind”, and a distracted mind as “a distracted mind”; I may understand an exalted mind as “an exalted mind”, and an unexalted mind as “an unexalted mind”; I may understand a mind with something beyond as “a mind with something beyond”, and a mind with nothing beyond as “a mind with nothing beyond”; I may understand a concentrated mind as “a concentrated mind”, and an unconcentrated mind as “an unconcentrated mind”; I may understand a liberated mind as “a liberated mind”, and an unliberated mind as “an unliberated mind”’—he reaches the capability of witnessing it there and then, whenever there is a basis.
translations.an5.25:1: “Supported by five factors, bhikkhus, right view is both the fruit of liberation of mind and has the benefit of the fruit of liberation of mind, and it is both the fruit of liberation by wisdom and has the benefit of the fruit of liberation by wisdom.
translations.an5.26:1: “There are these five bases of liberation, bhikkhus, where, as a bhikkhu dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, an unliberated mind is liberated, or unexhausted taints go to exhaustion, or he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained.
translations.an5.26:3: Furthermore, bhikkhus, it is not that the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, nor some venerable fellow practitioner; but rather, as he has heard it, as he has learned it, he teaches the Dhamma in detail to others. As the bhikkhu teaches the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard it, as he has learned it, so he becomes one who experiences the meaning in that Dhamma and one who experiences the Dhamma. For one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, gladness arises. For one who is gladdened, rapture arises. For one with rapture, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, he feels pleasure. For one who is pleased, the mind is concentrated. This, bhikkhus, is the second basis of liberation where, as a bhikkhu dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, an unliberated mind is liberated, or unexhausted taints go to exhaustion, or he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained.
translations.an5.26:4: Furthermore, bhikkhus, it is not that the Teacher teaches the Dhamma to a bhikkhu, nor some venerable fellow practitioner; and he does not teach the Dhamma in detail to others as he has heard it, as he has learned it, but rather, as he has heard it, as he has learned it, he recites the Dhamma in detail. As the bhikkhu recites the Dhamma in detail as he has heard it, as he has learned it, so he becomes one who experiences the meaning in that Dhamma and one who experiences the Dhamma. For one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, gladness arises. For one who is gladdened, rapture arises. For one with rapture, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, he feels pleasure. For one who is pleased, the mind is concentrated. This, bhikkhus, is the third basis of liberation where, as a bhikkhu dwells diligent, ardent … he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained.”
translations.an5.26:6: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu does not have the Teacher teach him the Dhamma, nor some respected fellow monk; nor does he teach others in detail the Dhamma as he has heard it and learned it; nor does he recite in detail the Dhamma as he has heard it and learned it; nor does he mentally think over, ponder over, and examine with his mind the Dhamma as he has heard it and learned it. But he has some sign of concentration that is well grasped, well attended to, well borne in mind, and well penetrated with wisdom. Insofar, bhikkhus, as a bhikkhu has some sign of concentration that is well grasped, well attended to, well borne in mind, and well penetrated with wisdom, to that extent he becomes one who experiences the meaning in that Dhamma and experiences the Dhamma. For one who experiences the meaning and experiences the Dhamma, joy arises. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with rapture, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, one feels pleasure. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth liberation-base, where, for a bhikkhu dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, the unliberated mind is liberated, or the unexhausted taints go to exhaustion, or the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained is attained.
translations.an5.27:1: “Develop concentration, bhikkhus, that is immeasurable, prudent, and mindful. For those developing concentration that is immeasurable, prudent, and mindful, five kinds of knowledge arise each for oneself. Which five? Knowledge arises each for oneself: ‘This concentration is pleasant here and now and has a pleasant result in the future.’ Knowledge arises each for oneself: ‘This concentration is noble, non-sensual.’ Knowledge arises each for oneself: ‘This concentration is not frequented by bad persons.’ Knowledge arises each for oneself: ‘This concentration is peaceful, sublime, attained by the calming down of acquisitions, attained to unity, not reached by being reined in and checked through fabrications.’ Knowledge arises each for oneself: ‘Mindful, indeed, I enter upon this, and mindful I emerge.’”
translations.an5.28:1: “I will teach, bhikkhus, the development of noble right concentration with five factors. Listen to that, attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an5.28:10: Just as, bhikkhus, on good ground at a four-way crossroads there might stand a thoroughbred chariot yoked, with the goad in hand. A skilled trainer, a master charioteer, having mounted it, holding the reins with his left hand and holding the goad with his right hand, could drive it forward and pull it back wherever he wished, as he wished. Even so, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has thus developed noble right concentration with five factors and has made it abundant, whatever thing is to be realized by direct knowledge he inclines his mind to for its realization by direct knowledge; and there and then he reaches the capability of witnessing it, whenever there is a basis.
translations.an5.28:15: If he wishes: ‘With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human … he might understand beings as they fare on according to their actions,’ there and then he reaches the capability of witnessing it, whenever there is a basis.
translations.an5.28:7: When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has thus developed noble right concentration with five factors and has made it abundant, whatever thing is to be realized by direct knowledge he inclines his mind to for its realization by direct knowledge; and there and then he reaches the capability of witnessing it, whenever there is a basis.
translations.an5.28:8: Just as, bhikkhus, there might be a water jar placed on a stand, full of water, filled to the brim, fit for a crow to drink. If a strong man were to tip it whichever way, would water come out?” “So it is, venerable sir.” “Even so, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has thus developed noble right concentration with five factors and has made it abundant, whatever thing is to be realized by direct knowledge he inclines his mind to for its realization by direct knowledge; and there and then he reaches the capability of witnessing it, whenever there is a basis.
translations.an5.28:9: Just as, bhikkhus, on level ground there might be a lotus pond, square, banked all around, full of water, filled to the brim, fit for a crow to drink. If a strong man were to open a bank whichever way, would water come out?” “So it is, venerable sir.” “Even so, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has thus developed noble right concentration with five factors and has made it abundant, whatever thing is to be realized by direct knowledge he inclines his mind to for its realization by direct knowledge … whenever there is a basis.”
translations.an5.2:1: “These, bhikkhus, are five strengths of a learner. What five? The strength of faith, the strength of conscience, the strength of fear of wrongdoing, the strength of energy, the strength of wisdom.
translations.an5.2:2: And what, bhikkhus, is the strength of faith? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is faithful; he has faith in the Tathāgata’s awakening: ‘Such indeed is that Blessed One: an Arahant, a perfectly awakened one, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’ This is called, bhikkhus, the strength of faith.
translations.an5.2:3: And what, bhikkhus, is the strength of conscience? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple has conscience; he is ashamed of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct; he is ashamed of engaging in evil, unwholesome states. This is called, bhikkhus, the strength of conscience.
translations.an5.2:4: And what, bhikkhus, is the strength of fear of wrongdoing? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple fears wrongdoing; he fears bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, mental misconduct; he fears engaging in evil, unwholesome states. This is called, bhikkhus, the strength of fear of wrongdoing.
translations.an5.2:5: And what, bhikkhus, is the strength of energy? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquiring of wholesome states—steadfast, strongly striving, not laying aside the burden in wholesome states. This is called, bhikkhus, the strength of energy.
translations.an5.2:6: And what, bhikkhus, is the strength of wisdom? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple is wise, endowed with wisdom that leads to arising and passing away—noble, penetrative, leading to the complete ending of suffering. This is called, bhikkhus, the strength of wisdom. These, bhikkhus, are the five strengths of a learner.”
translations.an5.30:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One, wandering on tour among the Kosalans, arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village named Icchānaṅgala, together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus. There the Blessed One was staying at Icchānaṅgala, in the woodland grove of Icchānaṅgala. The brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala heard: “The ascetic Gotama, the Sakyan son, gone forth from a Sakyan clan, has arrived at Icchānaṅgala; he is staying at Icchānaṅgala, in the woodland grove of Icchānaṅgala. Now a good report of that Master Gotama has been spread about: ‘He too is the Blessed One, an arahant, a perfectly awakened one, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Fortunate One, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, awakened, blessed.’ Having realized it by his own direct knowledge, he proclaims this world—with its devas, with Māra, with Brahmā, this population with ascetics and brahmins, with gods and humans. He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, meaningful and well phrased; he reveals a spiritual life that is entirely complete and purified. It is good indeed to see such arahants.” Then the brahmins and householders of Icchānaṅgala, when that night had passed, taking abundant food, both hard and soft, approached the woodland grove of Icchānaṅgala; having approached, they stood at the gatehouse outside, making a loud noise and a great noise.
translations.an5.30:3: “Let the Blessed One consent now, venerable sir; let the Fortunate One consent. Now is the time for the Blessed One’s consent. Wherever the Blessed One will go now, brahmins and householders, townsfolk and country folk, will go streaming after him. Just as, venerable sir, when thick drops of rain are falling, the waters flow along whatever is sloping down; even so, venerable sir, wherever the Blessed One will go now, brahmins and householders, townsfolk and country folk, will go streaming after him. For what reason? For such, venerable sir, is the Blessed One’s virtue and wisdom.”
translations.an5.31:1: At one time … in Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. Then Sumanā the princess, surrounded by five hundred chariots and five hundred princesses, approached the Blessed One; having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Sumanā the princess said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an5.31:10: In the same way, a person endowed with virtue, a faithful individual, outshines all the miserly in the world by generosity.
translations.an5.31:11: Just as a cloud, thundering, wreathed with lightning, fully rains upon the earth, filling high ground and low ground,
translations.an5.31:12: So, one accomplished in vision, a disciple of the perfectly awakened one, overcomes miserliness in five ways, the wise one.
translations.an5.31:2: “Here, venerable sir, there are two disciples of the Blessed One with equal faith, equal virtue, equal wisdom—one a giver, one not a giver. When their body breaks up, after death, they would be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. But for them as devas, venerable sir, would there be a distinction, would there be any difference?”
translations.an5.31:3: “There would be, Sumanā,” the Blessed One said. “That giver, Sumanā, being a deva, surpasses that non-giver in five ways—with divine life span, divine beauty, divine happiness, divine fame, and divine sovereignty. That giver, Sumanā, being a deva, surpasses that non-giver in these five ways.”
translations.an5.31:4: “But if, venerable sir, having passed away from there they come back to this state, then for them as humans, venerable sir, would there be a distinction, would there be any difference?” “There would be, Sumanā,” the Blessed One said. “That giver, Sumanā, being a human, surpasses that non-giver in five ways—with human life span, human beauty, human happiness, human fame, and human sovereignty. That giver, Sumanā, being a human, surpasses that non-giver in these five ways.”
translations.an5.31:5: “But if, venerable sir, both go forth from the household life into homelessness, then for them as gone-forth ones, venerable sir, would there be a distinction, would there be any difference?” “There would be, Sumanā,” the Blessed One said. “That giver, Sumanā, being gone forth, surpasses that non-giver in five ways—he enjoys much robe-cloth when asked, little when not asked; he enjoys much almsfood when asked, little when not asked; he enjoys much lodging when asked, little when not asked; he enjoys much in the way of medicines and requisites for the sick when asked, little when not asked. And those fellow practitioners with whom he lives together behave toward him mostly with pleasing bodily action, little with unpleasing; mostly with pleasing verbal action, little with unpleasing; mostly with pleasing mental action, little with unpleasing; they offer mostly pleasing gifts, little unpleasing. That giver, Sumanā, being gone forth, surpasses that non-giver in these five ways.”
translations.an5.31:6: “But if, venerable sir, both attain arahantship, then for them who have attained arahantship, venerable sir, would there be a distinction, would there be any difference?” “Here, Sumanā, I say there is no difference at all, that is, in liberation and in the liberated state.”
translations.an5.31:9: Just as the moon, spotless, moving through the element of space, outshines all the groups of stars in the world by its radiance,
translations.an5.34:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof. Then Sīha the general approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Sīha the general said this to the Blessed One: “Is it possible, venerable sir, for the Blessed One to point out the visible fruit of giving?”
translations.an5.34:2: “It is possible, Sīha,” the Blessed One said. “A giver, Sīha, a donor is dear and pleasing to many people. And whatever, Sīha, that a giver, a donor is dear and pleasing to many people—this too is a visible fruit of giving.”
translations.an5.34:8: Giving, one is dear; many associate with him; he gains renown and his fame increases; unconfused, he enters an assembly; a person without miserliness becomes confident.
translations.an5.34:9: Therefore wise people give gifts, removing the stain of miserliness, seekers of happiness; for a long time, established in the heaven of the Thirty-Three, having reached companionship with the devas, they rejoice.
translations.an5.36:1: “There are, bhikkhus, these five timely gifts.  What five?  One gives a gift to a guest;  one gives a gift to a traveler;  one gives a gift to the sick;  one gives a gift when there is famine;  whatever new crops and new fruits there are, one first establishes them among the virtuous.  These, bhikkhus, are the five timely gifts.”
translations.an5.36:2: The wise give at the right time,  generous, free from stinginess;  A gift given at the right time among the noble ones,  among such as are upright.
translations.an5.36:3: With a mind serene,  the offering is abundant;  Those who rejoice in it there,  or who render service—  by that the offering is not diminished;  they too are sharers in merit.
translations.an5.37:1: “When a donor gives food, bhikkhus, he gives recipients five things.  What five?  He gives life, he gives beauty, he gives happiness, he gives strength, he gives eloquence.  And having given life, one becomes a partaker of life, whether divine or human;  having given beauty, one becomes a partaker of beauty, whether divine or human;  having given happiness, one becomes a partaker of happiness, whether divine or human;  having given strength, one becomes a partaker of strength, whether divine or human;  having given eloquence, one becomes a partaker of eloquence, whether divine or human.  When a donor gives food, bhikkhus, he gives recipients these five things.”
translations.an5.37:2: A giver of life, a giver of strength, a wise one,  a giver of beauty, a giver of eloquence;  A giver of happiness, intelligent,  attains happiness.
translations.an5.38:2: “Just as, bhikkhus, on good ground at a crossroads a great banyan tree is a refuge for birds all around;  even so, bhikkhus, a faithful clansman is a refuge for many people—monks, nuns, male lay followers, and female lay followers.”
translations.an5.38:3: Endowed with branches, foliage, and fruits,  like a great tree with a solid trunk;  rooted, rich in fruits,  it is a support for birds.
translations.an5.38:4: In a delightful resort,  the birds frequent it;  those seeking shade go to its shade,  those seeking fruit eat its fruit.
translations.an5.38:5: Just so, one accomplished in virtue,  a faithful person;  one of humble ways, not stiff,  gentle, compliant, kindly, soft.
translations.an5.38:6: Free of lust, free of hate,  free of delusion, without taints;  fields of merit in the world,  they frequent such a man.
translations.an5.41:1: One time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park.  Then Anāthapiṇḍika the householder went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.  As he sat to one side, the Blessed One said this to Anāthapiṇḍika the householder:  “Householder, there are these five uses of wealth.  What five?  Here, householder, a noble disciple, with wealth acquired by energetic striving—amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous, righteously obtained—makes himself happy and pleased and properly maintains himself in comfort;  makes his mother and father happy and pleased and properly maintains them in comfort;  makes his children and wife, slaves, workers, and servants happy and pleased and properly maintains them in comfort.  This is the first use of wealth.
translations.an5.41:4: Furthermore, householder, a noble disciple, with wealth acquired by energetic striving—amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous, righteously obtained—makes the five offerings:  the offering to relatives, the offering to guests, the offering to departed ancestors, the offering to the king, the offering to the deities—this is the fourth use of wealth.
translations.an5.41:5: Furthermore, householder, a noble disciple, with wealth acquired by energetic striving—amassed by the strength of his arms, earned by the sweat of his brow, righteous, righteously obtained—establishes an uplifting gift among those ascetics and brahmins who have refrained from intoxication and heedlessness, who are established in patience and gentleness, who tame themselves, calm themselves, and extinguish themselves—such an offering that leads upward, leads to heaven, has happy result, and conduces to heaven.  This is the fifth use of wealth.  These, householder, are the five uses of wealth.
translations.an5.41:6: If, householder, while that noble disciple is using wealth in these five ways, his wealth comes to decline, it occurs to him:  ‘Indeed, the uses of wealth are things that I use, yet my wealth is coming to decline.’  Thus he has no remorse.  And if, householder, while that noble disciple is using wealth in these five ways, his wealth increases, it occurs to him:  ‘Indeed, the uses of wealth are things that I use, and my wealth is increasing.’  Thus he has no remorse in either way.”
translations.an5.41:7: Wealth has been enjoyed, dependents supported,  my hardships in times of trouble have been overcome;  uplifting gifts have been given, and the five offerings made;  the virtuous have been attended to,  the restrained, those living the holy life.
translations.an5.41:8: For whatever purpose a wise one, living the household life, might desire wealth,  that purpose of mine has been attained;  what should be done has been done, leaving nothing to regret.
translations.an5.43:1: Then Anāthapiṇḍika the householder went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.  As he sat to one side, the Blessed One said this:
translations.an5.43:4: A noble disciple, householder, who desires life is not fit to ask for life or to delight in it, or for the sake of life.  A noble disciple who desires life, householder, should practice the way that conduces to life.  For when he has practiced the way that conduces to life, it leads to the obtaining of life.  He becomes a receiver of life, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:5: A noble disciple, householder, who desires beauty is not fit to ask for beauty or to delight in it, or for the sake of beauty.  A noble disciple who desires beauty, householder, should practice the way that conduces to beauty.  For when he has practiced the way that conduces to beauty, it leads to the obtaining of beauty.  He becomes a receiver of beauty, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:6: A noble disciple, householder, who desires happiness is not fit to ask for happiness or to delight in it, or for the sake of happiness.  A noble disciple who desires happiness, householder, should practice the way that conduces to happiness.  For when he has practiced the way that conduces to happiness, it leads to the obtaining of happiness.  He becomes a receiver of happiness, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:7: A noble disciple, householder, ought not to request or delight in fame, or [act] for the sake of fame. A noble disciple, householder, who desires fame should practice the conduct that leads to fame. For when that conduct that leads to fame is practiced, it leads to the obtaining of fame. He obtains fame, whether divine or human.
translations.an5.43:9: Long life, beauty, fame, renown, heaven, high family; for one who longs for delights—exalted ones, again and again.
translations.an5.49:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
translations.an5.49:2: At that time Queen Mallikā had died. Then a certain man went to King Pasenadi of Kosala; having approached, he informed King Pasenadi of Kosala in his ear: “Queen Mallikā, lord, has died.” When this was said, King Pasenadi of Kosala, sorrowful and downcast, with shoulders drooping, face down, brooding, sat without reply.
translations.an5.51:3: It is impossible, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu, without abandoning these five obstructions, hindrances—overgrowths of the mind, weakeners of wisdom—to know his own welfare, or to know another’s welfare, or to know the welfare of both, or to realize any distinction in noble knowledge and vision beyond the human state, with weak wisdom and feeble wisdom. Suppose, bhikkhus, there is a river flowing down from the mountains, going far, with a swift current, carrying things along. A man would open up channels with plowshares on both banks. In that way, bhikkhus, the current in the middle of the river would be scattered, dispersed, diffused; it would not go far, nor have a swift current, nor carry things along. So too, bhikkhus, it is impossible for a bhikkhu, without abandoning these five obstructions, hindrances—overgrowths of the mind, weakeners of wisdom—to know his own welfare, or to know another’s welfare, or to know the welfare of both, or to realize any distinction in noble knowledge and vision beyond the human state, with weak wisdom and feeble wisdom.
translations.an5.56:1: Then a certain bhikkhu went to his own preceptor; having approached, he said this to his own preceptor: “Just now, venerable sir, my body is as though drugged, and the directions do not appear to me, and teachings do not occur to me, and sloth-and-torpor stands having taken over my mind; and I live the spiritual life without delight, and I have doubt about the teachings.”
translations.an5.56:3: “So it is, bhikkhu, for one with unguarded sense doors, one who is immoderate in eating, one who is not devoted to wakefulness, one who lacks insight into wholesome qualities, living not devoted, in the early and late night, to the practice of developing qualities that are on the side of awakening: that the body is as though drugged, the directions do not appear, teachings do not occur, sloth-and-torpor stands having taken over the mind, one lives the spiritual life without delight, and one has doubt about the teachings. Therefore, bhikkhu, you should train thus: ‘I will be guarded at the sense doors, moderate in eating, devoted to wakefulness, possessed of insight into wholesome qualities, and I will live devoted, in the early and late night, to the practice of developing qualities that are on the side of awakening.’ Thus, bhikkhu, you should train.”
translations.an5.56:4: Then that bhikkhu, instructed by the Blessed One with this exhortation, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and departed keeping him on his right. Then that bhikkhu, living alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, resolute, before long—having directly known and realized for himself in this very life the unsurpassed end of the spiritual life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness—entered upon it and dwelt. He understood: “Birth is ended, the spiritual life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.” And that bhikkhu became one of the arahants.
translations.an5.57:10: ‘It is not the case that only I will have separation and parting from all that is dear and pleasing; rather, for as many beings as there are—coming and going, passing away and reappearing—for all beings there is separation and parting from what is dear and pleasing.’ As he frequently reflects on that matter, the path arises. He cultivates that path, develops it, makes much of it. As he cultivates, develops, and makes much of that path, the fetters are completely abandoned, the underlying tendencies are ended.
translations.an5.57:11: ‘It is not the case that only I am the owner of my actions, heir to my actions, born of my actions, related through my actions, supported by my actions; whatever action I will do, good or bad, I will be its heir. Rather, for as many beings as there are—coming and going, passing away and reappearing—all beings are owners of their actions, heirs to their actions, born of their actions, related through their actions, supported by their actions; whatever action they will do, good or bad, they will be its heirs.’ As he frequently reflects on that matter, the path arises.
