He cultivates that path, develops it, makes much of it. As he cultivates, develops, and makes much of that path, the fetters are completely abandoned, the underlying tendencies are ended.
translations.an5.57:15: I have overcome all intoxications, having seen renunciation as safety; for me there was zeal, as I beheld Nibbāna.
translations.an5.57:7: That noble disciple, bhikkhus, reflects thus: ‘It is not the case that only I am subject to aging, not gone beyond aging; rather, for as many beings as there are—coming and going, passing away and reappearing—all beings are subject to aging, not gone beyond aging.’ As he frequently reflects on that matter, the path arises. He cultivates that path, develops it, makes much of it. As he cultivates, develops, and makes much of that path, the fetters are completely abandoned, the underlying tendencies are ended.
translations.an5.57:8: ‘It is not the case that only I am subject to illness, not gone beyond illness; rather, for as many beings as there are—coming and going, passing away and reappearing—all beings are subject to illness, not gone beyond illness.’ As he frequently reflects on that matter, the path arises. He cultivates that path, develops it, makes much of it. As he cultivates, develops, and makes much of that path, the fetters are completely abandoned, the underlying tendencies are ended.
translations.an8.13:1: “Bhikkhus, a king’s fine thoroughbred horse, endowed with eight factors, is worthy of a king, fit for royal use, and is counted among the king’s own qualities. With which eight? Here, bhikkhus, a king’s fine thoroughbred horse is well-born on both sides—on the mother’s side and on the father’s side. It is born in a region where other fine thoroughbred horses are born. Whatever food they give it—fresh or dry—it consumes it carefully, without scattering it. It is fastidious about sitting down on dung or urine, or lying down on it. It is gentle and pleasant to live with, and it does not disturb other horses. Whatever tricks, deceits, crookednesses, and evasions it has, it reveals them as they really are to the charioteer. The charioteer strives to suppress those in it. And it is a carrier. It generates the thought: ‘Let other horses pull or not, I myself will pull here.’ And when it goes, it goes by the straight path. It has strength, showing strength up to the end of life and death. Endowed with these eight factors, bhikkhus, a king’s fine thoroughbred horse is worthy of a king, fit for royal use, and is counted among the king’s own qualities.”
translations.an8.14:1: “Bhikkhus, I will teach eight horse-rogues and eight horse faults, and eight man-rogues and eight man faults. Listen to that, attend carefully, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.an8.14:2: “And what, bhikkhus, are the eight horse-rogues and the eight horse faults? Here, bhikkhus, some horse-rogue, when told ‘Go on!’—being struck and urged by the charioteer—backs up, pushing the chariot from behind. Such too, bhikkhus, is some horse-rogue here. This, bhikkhus, is the first horse fault.
translations.an8.14:3: Further, bhikkhus, some horse-rogue, when told ‘Go on!’—being struck and urged by the charioteer—jumps backward, strikes the pole, and breaks the crossbar. Such too, bhikkhus, is some horse-rogue here. This, bhikkhus, is the second horse fault.
translations.an8.14:4: Further, bhikkhus, some horse-rogue, when told ‘Go on!’—being struck and urged by the charioteer—having released a kick at the shaft, tramples on the shaft itself. Such too, bhikkhus, is some horse-rogue here. This, bhikkhus, is the third horse fault.
translations.an8.14:5: Further, bhikkhus, some horse-rogue, when told ‘Go on!’—being struck and urged by the charioteer—takes a wrong track and makes the chariot go off the road. Such too, bhikkhus, is some horse-rogue here. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth horse fault.
translations.an8.14:6: Further, bhikkhus, some horse-rogue, when told ‘Go on!’—being struck and urged by the charioteer—jumps up and lifts its forebody, lifting its front legs. Such too, bhikkhus, is some horse-rogue here. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth horse fault.
translations.an8.14:7: Further, bhikkhus, some horse-rogue, when told ‘Go on!’—being struck and urged by the charioteer—paying no attention to the charioteer, paying no attention to the goad-stick, tears apart the bit with its teeth and runs off wherever it wants. Such too, bhikkhus, is some horse-rogue here. This, bhikkhus, is the sixth horse fault.
translations.an8.14:8: Further, bhikkhus, some horse-rogue, when told ‘Go on!’—being struck and urged by the charioteer—neither goes forward nor goes back, but stands right there like a post. Such too, bhikkhus, is some horse-rogue here. This, bhikkhus, is the seventh horse fault.
translations.an8.14:9: Further, bhikkhus, some horse-rogue, when told ‘Go on!’—being struck and urged by the charioteer—folds in its front legs and folds in its hind legs and sits right there down on its four legs. Such too, bhikkhus, is some horse-rogue here. This, bhikkhus, is the eighth horse fault. These, bhikkhus, are the eight horse-rogues and the eight horse faults.”
translations.an8.19:1: At one time the Blessed One was living at Verañjā at the root of a naḷeru pucimanda tree. Then Pahārāda, lord of the asuras, went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. As Pahārāda, lord of the asuras, stood to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
translations.an8.22:1: At one time the Blessed One was living among the Vajjis at Hatthigāma. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, remember Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma as endowed with eight amazing and astonishing qualities.” The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.
translations.an8.22:10: But if I, venerable sir, were to die before the Blessed One, it would not be amazing that the Blessed One would declare about me thus: ‘There is no fetter by which Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma, bound, would come again to this world.’ This, venerable sir, is the eighth amazing and astonishing quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:11: These, venerable sir, are the eight amazing and astonishing qualities found in me. And I do not know: ‘By which eight amazing and astonishing qualities, possessed by me, have I been declared by the Blessed One?’”
translations.an8.22:12: Then that bhikkhu, having taken almsfood at the residence of Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma, rose from his seat and departed. Then that bhikkhu, after the meal, having returned from the alms round, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat to one side. Sitting to one side, that bhikkhu reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation he had had with Ugga the householder of Hatthigāma.
translations.an8.22:2: Then a certain bhikkhu, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, approached the residence of Uggā the householder of Hatthigāma; having approached, he sat down on a seat that had been prepared. Then Uggā the householder of Hatthigāma approached that bhikkhu; having approached, he paid homage to that bhikkhu and sat down to one side. When Uggā the householder of Hatthigāma was seated to one side, that bhikkhu said this to him: “Householder, you have been declared by the Blessed One as endowed with eight amazing and wonderful qualities. What, householder, are the eight amazing and wonderful qualities with which you are endowed, by which you have been declared by the Blessed One?”
translations.an8.22:3: “I do not know, venerable sir, ‘with which eight amazing and wonderful qualities I have been declared by the Blessed One as endowed.’ But, venerable sir, the eight amazing and wonderful qualities that are found in me—listen to that, attend to it carefully; I will speak.” “Yes, householder,” that bhikkhu replied to Uggā the householder of Hatthigāma. Uggā the householder of Hatthigāma said this: “When I was serving in the elephant-forest, venerable sir, I first saw the Blessed One from afar; with that very seeing, venerable sir, my mind became clear toward the Blessed One, and the intoxication with liquor was abandoned. This, venerable sir, is the first amazing and wonderful quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:4: “Then I, venerable sir, with a confident mind, attended upon the Blessed One. The Blessed One taught me a graduated talk, that is: talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on heaven; he explained the danger, the drawback, the defilement in sensual pleasures, and the benefit in renunciation. When the Blessed One knew me to have a mind that was ready, pliant, free from hindrances, uplifted, and confident, then he revealed the teaching that is distinctive to Buddhas—suffering, origin, cessation, path. Just as a clean cloth, with stains removed, would properly take up dye, so too, right there on that seat, the dust-free, stainless Dhamma-eye arose in me: ‘Whatever is of a nature to arise, all that is of a nature to cease.’ Then I, venerable sir, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, understood the Dhamma, fathomed the Dhamma, having crossed over doubt, having removed perplexity, having gained confidence, independent of others in the Teacher’s dispensation, went for refuge right there to the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, and undertook the training precepts that are five and pertain to the holy life. This, venerable sir, is the second amazing and wonderful quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:5: “For me, venerable sir, there were four young wives. Then, venerable sir, I approached those wives; having approached, I said this to those wives: ‘Sisters, I have undertaken the training precepts that are five and pertain to the holy life. Whoever wishes may enjoy wealth right here and do merits, or may go to her own relatives’ families. Or if there is an intention for a man, to whom shall I give you?’ When this was said, venerable sir, the eldest wife said this to me: ‘Give me, dear son, to the man named so-and-so.’ Then, venerable sir, having had that man summoned, taking the wife with my left hand and taking the water-pot with my right hand, I handed her over to that man. And, venerable sir, while giving up a young wife as a spouse, I do not recall any alteration of mind. This, venerable sir, is the third amazing and wonderful quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:6: “And there are, venerable sir, possessions found in my family. And they are not kept undistributed from virtuous ones with good qualities. This, venerable sir, is the fourth amazing and wonderful quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:7: “And whatever bhikkhu, venerable sir, I attend upon, I attend upon respectfully, not disrespectfully. If that venerable one teaches me the Dhamma, I listen respectfully, not disrespectfully. If that venerable one does not teach me the Dhamma, then I teach the Dhamma to him. This, venerable sir, is the fifth amazing and wonderful quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:8: “And it is not amazing, venerable sir, that when the Saṅgha has been invited, deities approach and inform: ‘So-and-so, householder, is one liberated in both ways; so-and-so is liberated by wisdom; so-and-so is a body-witness; so-and-so is one who has attained view; so-and-so is liberated by faith; so-and-so is a Dhamma-follower; so-and-so is a faith-follower; so-and-so is virtuous, of good qualities; so-and-so is immoral, of bad qualities.’ But, venerable sir, while serving the Saṅgha, I do not recall producing a mind like this: ‘To this one I give a little; to this one I give much.’ Rather, venerable sir, I give with an even mind. This, venerable sir, is the sixth amazing and wonderful quality found in me.
translations.an8.22:9: “And it is not amazing, venerable sir, that deities approach and inform me: ‘Well-proclaimed, householder, is the Dhamma by the Blessed One.’ When this is said, venerable sir, I say this to those deities: ‘Whether you deities were to say so or not to say so, still the Dhamma is well-proclaimed by the Blessed One.’ But I do not recall, venerable sir, because of that, an elation of mind: ‘Those deities approach me, or I converse together with the deities.’ This, venerable sir, is the seventh amazing and wonderful quality found in me.
translations.an8.23:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī, at the Aggāḷava shrine. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bear in mind Hatthaka of Āḷavī as endowed with seven amazing and wonderful qualities. With which seven? Hatthaka of Āḷavī, bhikkhus, is faithful; Hatthaka of Āḷavī, bhikkhus, is virtuous; Hatthaka of Āḷavī, bhikkhus, has a sense of shame; Hatthaka of Āḷavī, bhikkhus, has moral dread; Hatthaka of Āḷavī, bhikkhus, is learned; Hatthaka of Āḷavī, bhikkhus, is generous; Hatthaka of Āḷavī, bhikkhus, is wise—bear in mind Hatthaka of Āḷavī as endowed with these seven amazing and wonderful qualities.” The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.
translations.an8.23:2: Then a certain bhikkhu, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, approached the residence of Hatthaka of Āḷavī; having approached, he sat down on a seat that had been prepared. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī approached that bhikkhu; having approached, he paid homage to that bhikkhu and sat down to one side. When Hatthaka of Āḷavī was seated to one side, that bhikkhu said this:
translations.an8.23:3: “You, friend, have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed with seven amazing and astounding qualities. Which seven? ‘Hatthaka of Āḷavī is faithful, monks; virtuous … conscientious … morally afraid of wrongdoing … learned … generous … wise—Hatthaka of Āḷavī is wise, monks.’ You, friend, have been declared by the Blessed One to be endowed with these seven amazing and astounding qualities.” “But, venerable sir, was there not any householder there dressed in white?” “There was not, friend, any householder there dressed in white.” “Good, venerable sir, that there was not any householder there dressed in white.”
translations.an8.23:4: Then that monk, having taken almsfood at Hatthaka of Āḷavī’s residence, rose from his seat and departed. Then that monk, after the meal, having returned from his alms round, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk said this to the Blessed One:
translations.an8.24:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying in Āḷavī at the Aggāḷava shrine. Then Hatthaka of Āḷavī, surrounded by about five hundred lay followers, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said to Hatthaka of Āḷavī, who was sitting to one side: “This is a large assembly of yours, Hatthaka. But how do you gather in this large assembly?” “Venerable sir, by these four means of gathering in that have been taught by the Blessed One I gather in this large assembly. Venerable sir, what I know: ‘This one should be gathered in by giving,’ I gather in by giving; what I know: ‘This one should be gathered in by kind speech,’ I gather in by kind speech; what I know: ‘This one should be gathered in by beneficial conduct,’ I gather in by beneficial conduct; what I know: ‘This one should be gathered in by impartiality,’ I gather in by impartiality. Moreover, venerable sir, there are possessions in my family. One does not think it should be listened to in that way by one who is poor.” “Good, good, Hatthaka. This is indeed the proper way, Hatthaka, to gather in a large assembly. For whatever people, Hatthaka, in times past gathered in a large assembly, all of them gathered in a large assembly by just these same four means of gathering in. And whatever people, Hatthaka, in times future will gather in a large assembly, all of them will gather in a large assembly by just these same four means of gathering in. And whatever people, Hatthaka, at present gather in a large assembly, all of them gather in a large assembly by just these same four means of gathering in.”
translations.an8.26:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s mango grove. Then Jīvaka Komārabhacca approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Jīvaka Komārabhacca said this to the Blessed One: “To what extent, venerable sir, is one a lay follower?” “When, Jīvaka, one has gone for refuge to the Buddha, has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha: to that extent, Jīvaka, one is a lay follower.”
translations.an8.26:2: “But to what extent, venerable sir, is a lay follower virtuous?” “When, Jīvaka, a lay follower abstains from taking life … abstains from intoxicants, liquor and drugs that are a basis for negligence: to that extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower is virtuous.”
translations.an8.26:3: “But to what extent, venerable sir, is a lay follower practicing for their own benefit, not for the benefit of others?” “When, Jīvaka, a lay follower themselves is endowed with faith, and does not urge another to acquire faith … themselves, having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, practices in accordance with the Dhamma, and does not urge another to practice in accordance with the Dhamma. To that extent, Jīvaka, a lay follower is practicing for their own benefit, not for the benefit of others.”
translations.an8.28:5: Furthermore, venerable sir, in the monk with taints destroyed the four establishments of mindfulness are developed, well developed. And that the four establishments of mindfulness are developed, well developed, in the monk with taints destroyed: this too, venerable sir, is a strength of the monk with taints destroyed, relying on which the monk with taints destroyed acknowledges the destruction of the taints: ‘My taints are destroyed.’
translations.an8.28:6: Furthermore, venerable sir, in the monk with taints destroyed the four bases of spiritual power are developed, well developed … the five faculties are developed, well developed … the seven factors of awakening are developed, well developed … the Noble Eightfold Path is developed, well developed. And that the Noble Eightfold Path is developed, well developed, in the monk with taints destroyed: this too, venerable sir, is a strength of the monk with taints destroyed, relying on which the monk with taints destroyed acknowledges the destruction of the taints: ‘My taints are destroyed.’
translations.an8.2:1: “There are these eight, monks, causes, eight conditions that lead to the gaining of the wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been gained, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment when it has been gained. Which eight? Here, monks, a monk lives depending on the Teacher, or on some venerable fellow monk, where strong conscience and moral dread are present in him, and affection and reverence. This, monks, is the first cause, the first condition that leads to the gaining of the wisdom fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been gained, and to its increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment when it has been gained.
translations.an8.2:11: ‘And this venerable one, having heard the Dhamma, succeeds by means of two kinds of seclusion—by bodily seclusion and by mental seclusion. Surely this venerable one, knowing, knows; seeing, sees.’ This too is a quality that leads to dearliness, esteem, development, harmony, and unity.
translations.an8.2:15: ‘And this venerable one, having gone to the Saṅgha, is not one who speaks various talk, nor one who speaks excessive animal talk. Either they themselves speak Dhamma, or they ask another; or they do not look down on noble silence. Surely this venerable one, knowing, knows; seeing, sees.’ This too is a quality that leads to dearliness, esteem, development, harmony, and unity.
translations.an8.2:2: Living in dependence on that Teacher, he from time to time approaches a certain fellow spiritual companion who is to be respected, in whom strong conscience and concern are present for him, as well as affection and reverence, and he asks and inquires: ‘Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?’ Those venerable ones explain to him what has not been explained, make clear what has not been made clear, and dispel his doubt regarding various things that are grounds for doubt. This, bhikkhus, is the second cause, the second condition, that leads to the attainment of the wisdom that is fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been attained, and to the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of wisdom when it has been attained.
translations.an8.2:4: He is virtuous; he dwells restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults; he trains by undertaking the training rules. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth cause, the fourth condition, that leads to the attainment of the wisdom that is fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been attained, and to the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of wisdom when it has been attained.
translations.an8.2:5: He is learned, a bearer of what he has heard, one who stores up what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, meaningful and well-expressed, that proclaim the perfectly complete and purified spiritual life—such teachings are much heard by him, retained, rehearsed verbally, reviewed in mind, and thoroughly penetrated with view. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth cause, the fifth condition, that leads to the attainment of the wisdom that is fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been attained, and to the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of wisdom when it has been attained.
translations.an8.2:6: He dwells with aroused energy for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is strong, firm in exertion, not laying down the burden with regard to wholesome states. This, bhikkhus, is the sixth cause, the sixth condition, that leads to the attainment of the wisdom that is fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been attained, and to the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of wisdom when it has been attained.
translations.an8.2:7: Having gone to the Saṅgha, he is not a speaker of various kinds of talk, a speaker of excessive animal talk. Either he speaks Dhamma himself, or he invites another to speak, or he does not despise noble silence. This, bhikkhus, is the seventh cause, the seventh condition, that leads to the attainment of the wisdom that is fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been attained, and to the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of wisdom when it has been attained.
translations.an8.2:8: He dwells contemplating rise and fall in the five aggregates subject to clinging: ‘such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling, such is the origin of feeling, such is the passing away of feeling; such is perception … such are formations … such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’ This, bhikkhus, is the eighth cause, the eighth condition, that leads to the attainment of the wisdom that is fundamental to the spiritual life when it has not been attained, and to the increase, growth, development, and fulfillment of wisdom when it has been attained.
translations.an8.2:9: Then his fellow spiritual companions think of him thus: ‘This venerable one lives in dependence on the Teacher, or on a certain fellow spiritual companion who is to be respected, in whom strong conscience and concern are present for him, as well as affection and reverence. Surely this venerable one knows knowingly and sees seeing.’ This too is a quality that leads to being dear, being respected, to development, to fellowship, and to unity.
translations.an8.30:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Suṁsumāragiri, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park. Now at that time Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling among the Cetīs at the Eastern Bamboo Grove. Then, when Venerable Anuruddha was alone, secluded, and withdrawn, this train of thought arose in his mind: “This Dhamma is for one of few wishes, not for one of many wishes; this Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is discontent; this Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who delights in company; this Dhamma is for one with aroused energy, not for one who is lazy; this Dhamma is for one with mindfulness established, not for one with confused mindfulness; this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is unconcentrated; this Dhamma is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise.”
translations.an8.30:10: When you, Anuruddha, will think these eight thoughts of a great man, and you will be one who obtains at will, without trouble, without difficulty, these four jhānas that are higher in mind, pleasant abidings here and now, then for you, Anuruddha, just as for a householder or a householder’s son there might be a gabled house, plastered inside and out, sheltered from the wind, with fitted bolts, with windows shut; even so your dwelling at the root of a tree will appear to you, as you dwell content, for delight, without anxiety, for comfortable abiding, for entering upon Nibbāna.
translations.an8.30:11: When you, Anuruddha, will think these eight thoughts of a great man, and you will be one who obtains at will, without trouble, without difficulty, these four jhānas that are higher in mind, pleasant abidings here and now, then for you, Anuruddha, just as for a householder or a householder’s son there might be a couch with a long woolen cover, a white woolen cover, a flower-embroidered cover, a cover of fine deer hide, with a canopy above, with red bolsters at both ends; even so your grass-spread bed and seat will appear to you, as you dwell content, for delight, without anxiety, for comfortable abiding, for entering upon Nibbāna.
translations.an8.30:12: When you, Anuruddha, will think these eight thoughts of a great man, and you will be one who obtains at will, without trouble, without difficulty, these four jhānas that are higher in mind, pleasant abidings here and now, then for you, Anuruddha, just as for a householder or a householder’s son there might be various medicines, that is: ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses; even so your fermented-urine medicine will appear to you, as you dwell content, for delight, without anxiety, for comfortable abiding, for entering upon Nibbāna. Therefore, Anuruddha, in future too you should dwell right here among the Cetīs in the Eastern Bamboo Grove for the rains residence.” “Yes, venerable sir,” Venerable Anuruddha replied to the Blessed One.
translations.an8.30:13: Then the Blessed One, having exhorted the Venerable Anuruddha with this exhortation—just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm—so too, in the deer park at Bhesakaḷā Grove on the Crocodile Hill among the Bhaggas, he vanished from the Eastern Bamboo Park at Ceti and appeared. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. When he was seated, the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks, I will teach eight thoughts of a great man; listen to that … What, monks, are the eight thoughts of a great man? This Dhamma is for one of few wishes, monks, not for one of many wishes; this Dhamma is for one who is content, monks, not for one who is not content; this Dhamma is for one who is secluded, monks, not for one who delights in company; this Dhamma is for one with aroused energy, monks, not for one who is lazy; this Dhamma is for one with established mindfulness, monks, not for one with muddled mindfulness; this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, monks, not for one who is not concentrated; this Dhamma is for one who is wise, monks, not for one who is unwise; this Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation, for one who delights in non-proliferation, monks, not for one who delights in proliferation, who delights in proliferation.”
translations.an8.30:2: Then the Blessed One, having known with his mind the mental thought in the mind of the Venerable Anuruddha—just as a strong man might extend his bent arm or bend his extended arm—so too, in the deer park at Bhesakaḷā Grove on the Crocodile Hill among the Bhaggas, he vanished from the Eastern Bamboo Park at Ceti and appeared in the presence of the Venerable Anuruddha. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. And the Venerable Anuruddha, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. To the Venerable Anuruddha sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this:
translations.an8.30:22: Then the Venerable Anuruddha also lived there at Ceti in the Eastern Bamboo Park for the rains residence. Then the Venerable Anuruddha, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, resolute, in no long time—having directly known and realized for himself in this very life that unsurpassed consummation of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness—entered upon it and dwelt. He understood: “Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.” And the Venerable Anuruddha became one of the arahants. Then the Venerable Anuruddha, having attained arahantship, at that time spoke these verses:
translations.an8.30:23: “Knowing my intention, the Teacher, unsurpassed in the world, came by psychic power with a mind-made body.
translations.an8.30:24: As my intention was, he taught beyond that. The Buddha, delighting in non-proliferation, taught non-proliferation.”
translations.an8.30:3: “Good, good, Anuruddha. It is good, Anuruddha, that you thought the thought of a great man: ‘This Dhamma is for one of few wishes, not for one of many wishes; this Dhamma is for one who is content, not for one who is not content; this Dhamma is for one who is secluded, not for one who delights in company; this Dhamma is for one with aroused energy, not for one who is lazy; this Dhamma is for one with established mindfulness, not for one with muddled mindfulness; this Dhamma is for one who is concentrated, not for one who is not concentrated; this Dhamma is for one who is wise, not for one who is unwise.’ Therefore, Anuruddha, think also this eighth thought of a great man: ‘This Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation, for one who delights in non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation, who delights in proliferation.’”
translations.an8.30:4: When, Anuruddha, you will think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, as much as you wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, you will enter upon and dwell in the first jhāna, with thought and examination, born of seclusion, with rapture and pleasure.
translations.an8.30:5: When, Anuruddha, you will think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, as much as you wish, with the stilling of thought and examination, with inner tranquilizing, unification of mind, without thought, without examination, born of concentration, with rapture and pleasure, you will enter upon and dwell in the second jhāna.
translations.an8.30:6: When, Anuruddha, you will think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, as much as you wish, with the fading away of rapture, you will dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and you will feel pleasure with the body, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, one dwells in pleasure’; you will enter upon and dwell in the third jhāna.
translations.an8.30:7: When, Anuruddha, you will think these eight thoughts of a great man, then, Anuruddha, as much as you wish, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and displeasure, you will enter upon and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, with purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
translations.an8.39:1: “Monks, there are these eight streams of merit, streams of the wholesome, nutriments of happiness, heavenly, with happy result, leading to heaven, that lead to what is wished for, desired, pleasing, beneficial, and happy. What eight? Here, monks, a noble disciple has gone to the Buddha for refuge. This, monks, is the first stream of merit, stream of the wholesome, nutriment of happiness, heavenly, with happy result, leading to heaven, that leads to what is wished for, desired, pleasing, beneficial, and happy.
translations.an8.39:2: Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has gone to the Dhamma for refuge. This, monks, is the second stream of merit … leads to it.”
translations.an8.39:3: Furthermore, bhikkhus, a noble disciple has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha. This, bhikkhus, is the third overflow of merit, the overflow of the wholesome, a nutriment of happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, conducing to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and happy. There are these five gifts, bhikkhus—great gifts, foremost gifts, long-established, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated; they are not suspected and will not be suspected, and are uncriticized by ascetics, brahmins, and the wise. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life. Abstaining from taking life, bhikkhus, a noble disciple gives to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, gives non-hostility, gives non-ill will. Having given to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, having given non-hostility, having given non-ill will, one becomes a شریک of immeasurable freedom from fear, non-hostility, and non-ill will. This, bhikkhus, is the first gift, the great gift, the foremost gift, long-established, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated; it is not suspected and will not be suspected, and is uncriticized by ascetics, brahmins, and the wise. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth overflow of merit, the overflow of the wholesome, a nutriment of happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, conducing to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and happy.
translations.an8.39:7: Having abandoned intoxicants and fermented drinks that are a basis for heedlessness, one abstains from intoxicants and fermented drinks that are a basis for heedlessness. Abstaining from intoxicants and fermented drinks that are a basis for heedlessness, bhikkhus, a noble disciple gives to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, gives non-hostility, gives non-ill will. Having given to immeasurable beings freedom from fear, having given non-hostility, having given non-ill will, one becomes a sharer in immeasurable freedom from fear, non-hostility, and non-ill will. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth gift, the great gift, the foremost gift, long-established, traditional, ancient, unadulterated, never before adulterated; it is not suspected and will not be suspected, and is uncriticized by ascetics, brahmins, and the wise. This indeed, bhikkhus, is the eighth overflow of merit, the overflow of the wholesome, a nutriment of happiness, heavenly, resulting in happiness, leading to heaven, conducing to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and happy.
translations.an8.40:1: "Taking life, bhikkhus, when pursued, developed, and made much of, leads to hell, leads to the animal womb, leads to the realm of ghosts. Whatever is the lightest result of taking life, for one reborn as a human it leads to short life."
translations.an8.40:2: Taking what is not given, bhikkhus, when pursued, developed, and made much of, leads to hell, leads to the animal womb, leads to the realm of ghosts. Whatever is the lightest result of taking what is not given, for one reborn as a human it leads to loss of wealth.
translations.an8.40:3: Misconduct in sensual pleasures, bhikkhus, when pursued, developed, and made much of, leads to hell, leads to the animal womb, leads to the realm of ghosts. Whatever is the lightest result of misconduct in sensual pleasures, for one reborn as a human it leads to enmity with rivals.
translations.an8.40:4: False speech, bhikkhus, when pursued, developed, and made much of, leads to hell, leads to the animal womb, leads to the realm of ghosts. Whatever is the lightest result of false speech, for one reborn as a human it leads to being accused of what is not so.
translations.an8.40:5: Divisive speech, bhikkhus, when pursued, developed, and made much of, leads to hell, leads to the animal womb, leads to the realm of ghosts. Whatever is the lightest result of divisive speech, for one reborn as a human it leads to breaking with friends.
translations.an8.40:6: Harsh speech, bhikkhus, when pursued, developed, and made much of, leads to hell, leads to the animal womb, leads to the realm of ghosts. Whatever is the lightest result of harsh speech, for one reborn as a human it leads to unpleasant sounds.
translations.an8.40:7: Idle chatter, bhikkhus, when pursued, developed, and made much of, leads to hell, leads to the animal womb, leads to the realm of ghosts. Whatever is the lightest result of idle chatter, for one reborn as a human it leads to speech that is not heeded.
translations.an8.6:2: For an uninstructed ordinary person, bhikkhus, there arise gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. For an instructed noble disciple, bhikkhus, there also arise gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, pleasure and pain. In that case, bhikkhus, what is the difference, what is the distinction, what is the divergence between the instructed noble disciple and the uninstructed ordinary person?" "The teachings are rooted in the Blessed One for us, venerable sir, guided by the Blessed One, having the Blessed One as refuge. It would be good, venerable sir, if the meaning of this statement would occur to the Blessed One himself. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will retain it."
translations.an8.6:4: For that one, gain too occupies the mind and remains, loss too occupies the mind and remains, fame too occupies the mind and remains, disrepute too occupies the mind and remains, blame too occupies the mind and remains, praise too occupies the mind and remains, pleasure too occupies the mind and remains, pain too occupies the mind and remains. When gain has arisen, one welcomes it; with loss one resists. When fame has arisen, one welcomes it; with disrepute one resists. When praise has arisen, one welcomes it; with blame one resists. When pleasure has arisen, one welcomes it; with pain one resists. Being thus given to welcoming and resisting, one is not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrows, lamentations, pains, displeasures, and despairs. I say: 'One is not freed from suffering.'
translations.an8.6:7:
Gain and loss, and fame and disrepute,
Blame and praise, and pleasure and pain:
These phenomena among humans are impermanent,
Unlasting, of a nature to change.
translations.an8.6:8:
And having known these, the mindful and wise one
Reflects upon things of a nature to change;
Pleasant things do not stir the mind,
And in the face of the unpleasant, one does not come to opposition.
translations.an8.7:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Blessed One, referring to Devadatta, addressed the bhikkhus: “It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to review his own failure. It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to review another’s failure. It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to review his own success. It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu from time to time to review another’s success. Overcome by eight bad qualities, with a mind possessed and taken over, Devadatta is bound for a bad destination, bound for hell, to remain for an aeon, beyond remedy.”
translations.an8.7:2: Which eight? Overcome by gain, bhikkhus, with a mind possessed and taken over, Devadatta is bound for a bad destination, bound for hell, to remain for an aeon, beyond remedy. Overcome by lack of gain, bhikkhus … Overcome by fame, bhikkhus … Overcome by lack of fame, bhikkhus … Overcome by honor, bhikkhus … Overcome by lack of honor, bhikkhus … Overcome by evil desires, bhikkhus … Overcome by bad friendship, bhikkhus, with a mind possessed and taken over, Devadatta is bound for a bad destination, bound for hell, to remain for an aeon, beyond remedy. It is by these, bhikkhus, these eight bad qualities, that Devadatta—overcome, with a mind possessed and taken over—is bound for a bad destination, bound for hell, to remain for an aeon, beyond remedy.
translations.an8.7:3: It is good, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu to live having overcome again and again arisen gain; arisen lack of gain … arisen fame … arisen lack of fame … arisen honor … arisen lack of honor … arisen evil desire … arisen bad friendship, having overcome again and again.
translations.an8.8:4: Then Sakka, lord of the devas—just as a strong man might extend his bent arm, or bend his extended arm—disappeared from among the Tāvatiṁsa devas and appeared in the Cow-pen, on the Saṅkheyyaka mountain, at the hut of creepers, in the presence of Venerable Uttara. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached Venerable Uttara; having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Uttara and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to Venerable Uttara:
translations.an8.8:5: “Is it true, venerable sir, that Venerable Uttara taught the bhikkhus the Dhamma like this: ‘Good, friends, a bhikkhu from time to time reviews his own failure; good, friends, a bhikkhu from time to time … his own success … another’s success reviews’?” “It is so, lord of the devas.” “But, venerable sir, is this Venerable Uttara’s own inspiration, or is it the word of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One?” “Then, lord of the devas, I will make an analogy for you. By an analogy some wise men here understand the meaning of what is said.
translations.an8.8:6: Suppose, lord of the devas, not far from a village or town there is a great heap of grain. Then a large crowd of people might carry grain away—from carrying-poles, from baskets, from their laps, with cupped hands. If someone, lord of the devas, were to approach that large crowd and ask: ‘Where do you bring this grain from?’—how, lord of the devas, would that large crowd, answering correctly, answer?” “ ‘We bring it from that great heap of grain,’ venerable sir—thus, answering correctly, that large crowd would answer.” “So too, lord of the devas, whatever is well spoken, all that is the word of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Drawing on it and drawing on it, we and others speak.”
translations.an8.8:7: “Wonderful, venerable sir, marvelous, venerable sir. How well spoken is this by Venerable Uttara: ‘Whatever is well spoken, all that is the word of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Drawing on it and drawing on it, we and others speak.’ There was this one time, Venerable Uttara, when the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak, not long after Devadatta had left. There the Blessed One, referring to Devadatta, addressed the bhikkhus:
translations.mn108:1: Thus have I heard—at one time Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding place, not long after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna.
translations.mn108:13: “There are, brahmin, ten inspiring qualities that have been declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Insofar as these qualities are found in us, we now honor, respect, esteem, and venerate him; having honored and respected him, we live in dependence on him. What ten?
translations.mn108:14: Here, brahmin, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pāṭimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults; having undertaken them, he trains in the training rules.
translations.mn108:15: He is learned, a bearer of what has been heard, a store of what has been heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the meaning and with the phrasing, that proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings are much heard by him, retained, recited, mentally examined, and well penetrated by view.
translations.mn108:17: He is one who obtains at will—without trouble, without difficulty—the four jhānas, which are higher in mind and are pleasant dwellings here and now.
translations.mn108:18: He experiences various kinds of spiritual power: having been one he becomes many; having been many he becomes one; appearance and disappearance; he goes unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain, as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth as though in water; he walks on water without breaking through, as though on earth; seated cross-legged he travels through the sky like a winged bird; he touches and strokes with his hand these moon and sun, so powerful and so mighty; he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahmā world.
translations.mn108:19: With the divine element of hearing, purified and surpassing the human, he hears both kinds of sounds—divine and human, those far and near.
translations.mn108:2: At that time King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī princess, had Rājagaha fortified, fearing King Pajjoya.
translations.mn108:20: He understands the minds of other beings, other persons, having encompassed mind with mind. He understands a mind with lust as ‘a mind with lust’; he understands a mind without lust as ‘a mind without lust’; he understands a mind with hate as ‘a mind with hate’; he understands a mind without hate as ‘a mind without hate’; he understands a mind with delusion as ‘a mind with delusion’; he understands a mind without delusion as ‘a mind without delusion’; he understands a contracted mind as ‘a contracted mind’; he understands a distracted mind as ‘a distracted mind’; he understands an exalted mind as ‘an exalted mind’; he understands an unexalted mind as ‘an unexalted mind’; he understands a mind that has something higher as ‘a mind that has something higher’; he understands a mind that has nothing higher as ‘a mind that has nothing higher’; he understands a concentrated mind as ‘a concentrated mind’; he understands an unconcentrated mind as ‘an unconcentrated mind’; he understands a liberated mind as ‘a liberated mind’; he understands an unliberated mind as ‘an unliberated mind’.
translations.mn108:23: With the destruction of the taints, he dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it. These, brahmin, are the ten inspiring things that were declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. In whomsoever these things are found, we now honor, respect, esteem, and venerate him; having honored and respected him, we dwell relying on him.”
translations.mn108:25: Then Vassakāra the brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, said this to the Venerable Ānanda: “Where, then, does Master Ānanda now dwell?” “In the Bamboo Grove, brahmin, I now dwell.” “But surely, Master Ānanda, the Bamboo Grove is delightful, quiet and with little noise, secluded from the winds, hidden from people, suitable for seclusion?” “Indeed, brahmin, the Bamboo Grove is delightful, quiet and with little noise, secluded from the winds, hidden from people, suitable for seclusion, thanks to such protectors and guardians as you.” “Indeed, Master Ānanda, the Bamboo Grove is delightful, quiet and with little noise, secluded from the winds, hidden from people, suitable for seclusion, as befits you venerable meditators, devoted to meditation. You venerable ones are meditators and devoted to meditation. Once, Master Ānanda, at one time that Master Gotama was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof. Then I, Master Ānanda, went to the Great Wood, to the hall with the peaked roof, to where that Master Gotama was, and approached him. There that Master Gotama spoke in many ways about jhāna. And that Master Gotama was a meditator and devoted to jhāna. And that Master Gotama praised jhāna in every way.”
translations.mn108:28: “It is said, Master Ānanda, that that Master Gotama blamed jhāna, criticized it, and praised the snare. But now, Master Ānanda, let us go; we have much to do, much that must be done.” “When you think it is time, brahmin.” Then Vassakāra the brahmin, the chief minister of Magadha, approving and rejoicing in what the Venerable Ānanda had said, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn108:3: Then the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. Then this occurred to the Venerable Ānanda: “It is still too early to wander for alms in Rājagaha. Why don’t I go to the work place of the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, and approach the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna?”
translations.mn108:4: Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the work place of the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, and approached the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna. The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna saw the Venerable Ānanda coming from afar. Seeing the Venerable Ānanda, he said this: “Let Master Ānanda come. Welcome to Master Ānanda. It has been a long time, Master Ānanda, since you made this occasion, that is, coming here. Let Master Ānanda sit down; a seat is prepared.” The Venerable Ānanda sat down on the prepared seat. The brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna, taking another low seat, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmin Gopaka Moggallāna said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
translations.mn108:5: “Is there, Master Ānanda, even a single monk who is endowed in every way, in all respects, with those qualities with which that Master Gotama was endowed, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One?” “There is not, brahmin, even a single monk who is endowed in every way, in all respects, with those qualities with which that Blessed One was endowed, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. For that Blessed One, brahmin, was the originator of an unarisen path, the producer of an unproduced path, the declarer of an undeclared path; a knower of the path, a finder of the path, skilled in the path. And now his disciples dwell following the path, afterwards endowed with it.”
translations.mn108:7: “Is there, Master Ānanda, even a single monk appointed by that Master Gotama: ‘This will be your refuge after my passing,’ whom you would now put forward?” “There is not, brahmin, even a single monk appointed by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One: ‘This will be your refuge after my passing,’ whom we would now put forward.”
translations.mn108:9: “But since there is thus no refuge, Master Ānanda, what is the reason for harmony?” “We are not without a refuge, brahmin; we have a refuge, brahmin; we have the Dhamma as our refuge.”
translations.mn117:10: Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? He understands wrong intention as ‘wrong intention’; he understands right intention as ‘right intention’; this is his right view.
translations.mn117:11: And what, bhikkhus, is wrong intention? Intention of sensuality, intention of ill will, intention of harming—this, bhikkhus, is wrong intention.
translations.mn117:12: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention? Right intention, bhikkhus, I say is of two kinds: there is, bhikkhus, right intention that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions; and there is, bhikkhus, right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:13: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions? The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, the intention of non-cruelty: this, bhikkhus, is right intention that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions.
translations.mn117:14: And what, bhikkhus, is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? Whatever, bhikkhus, in one of noble mind, of taintless mind, possessed of the noble path, developing the noble path, is thought, thinking, intention, placing, directing, the mental fixing, the verbal formation—this, bhikkhus, is right intention that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:15: He strives for the abandoning of wrong intention and for the entering upon right intention; this is his right effort. Mindfully he abandons wrong intention; mindfully, having entered upon right intention, he dwells; this is his right mindfulness. Thus these three states run after and circle around right intention, that is: right view, right effort, right mindfulness.
translations.mn117:16: Therein, bhikkhus, right view is the forerunner. And how, bhikkhus, is right view the forerunner? He understands wrong speech as ‘wrong speech’, and right speech as ‘right speech’; this is his right view.
translations.mn117:18: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech? Right speech, bhikkhus, I say is of two kinds: there is, bhikkhus, right speech that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions; and there is, bhikkhus, right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:19: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter—this, bhikkhus, is right speech that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions.
translations.mn117:2: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you noble right concentration with its supporting conditions, with its requisites. Listen to that, attend carefully, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn117:20: And what, bhikkhus, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? Whatever, bhikkhus, in one of noble mind, of taintless mind, possessed of the noble path, developing the noble path, is abstaining, refraining, complete refraining, avoidance from the four kinds of verbal misconduct—this, bhikkhus, is right speech that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:22: Therein, bhikkhus, right view is the forerunner. And how, bhikkhus, is right view the forerunner? He understands wrong action as ‘wrong action’, and right action as ‘right action’; this is his right view.
translations.mn117:24: And what, bhikkhus, is right action? Right action, bhikkhus, I say is of two kinds: there is, bhikkhus, right action that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions; and there is, bhikkhus, right action that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:25: And what, bhikkhus, is right action that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions? Abstaining from killing living beings, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from misconduct in sensual pleasures—this, bhikkhus, is right action that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions.
translations.mn117:28: Therein, bhikkhus, right view is the forerunner. And how, bhikkhus, is right view the forerunner? He understands wrong livelihood as ‘wrong livelihood’, and right livelihood as ‘right livelihood’; this is his right view.
translations.mn117:29: And what, bhikkhus, is wrong livelihood? Deceit, flattery, hinting, disparaging, seeking gain by means of gain—this, bhikkhus, is wrong livelihood.
translations.mn117:30: And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood? Right livelihood, bhikkhus, I say is of two kinds: there is, bhikkhus, right livelihood that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions; and there is, bhikkhus, right livelihood that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:31: And what, bhikkhus, is right livelihood that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, makes his living by right livelihood—this, bhikkhus, is right livelihood that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions.
translations.mn117:34: Therein, bhikkhus, right view is the forerunner. And how, bhikkhus, is right view the forerunner? For one with right view, bhikkhus, right intention occurs; for right intention, right speech occurs; for right speech, right action occurs; for right action, right livelihood occurs; for right livelihood, right effort occurs; for right effort, right mindfulness occurs; for right mindfulness, right concentration occurs; for right concentration, right knowledge occurs; for right knowledge, right liberation occurs. Thus, bhikkhus, the trainee is possessed of eight factors, and the arahant is possessed of ten factors. There too, through right knowledge, many evil unwholesome states have disappeared, reaching the fulfillment of development.
translations.mn117:35: Therein, bhikkhus, right view is the forerunner. And how, bhikkhus, is right view the forerunner? For one with right view, bhikkhus, wrong view is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong view are worn away for him. Conditioned by right view, many wholesome states reach the fulfillment of development. For right intention, bhikkhus, wrong intention is worn away …pe… for right speech, bhikkhus, wrong speech is worn away … for right action, bhikkhus, wrong action is worn away … for right livelihood, bhikkhus, wrong livelihood is worn away … for right effort, bhikkhus, wrong effort is worn away … for right mindfulness, bhikkhus, wrong mindfulness is worn away … for right concentration, bhikkhus, wrong concentration is worn away … for right knowledge, bhikkhus, wrong knowledge is worn away … for right liberation, bhikkhus, wrong liberation is worn away. And the many evil unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong liberation are worn away for him. And conditioned by right liberation, many wholesome states reach the fulfillment of development.
translations.mn117:36: So, bhikkhus, twenty factors on the wholesome side and twenty factors on the unwholesome side—this exposition of the Dhamma called “the Great Forty” has been set in motion, not to be reversed by any ascetic or brahmin or deva or Māra or Brahmā or by anyone in the world.
translations.mn117:4: Therein, bhikkhus, right view comes first. And how, bhikkhus, does right view come first? One understands wrong view as ‘wrong view’, and understands right view as ‘right view’—this is one’s right view.
translations.mn117:5: And what, bhikkhus, is wrong view? ‘There is no giving, no offering, no sacrifice; there is no fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings who are reborn spontaneously; there are in the world no ascetics and brahmins who are rightly gone, rightly practicing, who having realized for themselves by direct knowledge this world and the other world, proclaim them’—this, bhikkhus, is wrong view.
translations.mn117:6: And what, bhikkhus, is right view? Right view, bhikkhus, I say is of two kinds: there is right view that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions; and there is right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:7: And what, bhikkhus, is right view that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions? ‘There is giving, there is offering, there is sacrifice; there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings who are reborn spontaneously; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who are rightly gone, rightly practicing, who having realized for themselves by direct knowledge this world and the other world, proclaim them’—this, bhikkhus, is right view that is with taints, partaking of merit, ripening in acquisitions.
translations.mn117:8: And what, bhikkhus, is right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path? Whatever, bhikkhus, is the wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor, the right view path-factor of one whose mind is noble, whose mind is taintless, who possesses the noble path, developing the noble path—this is called, bhikkhus, right view that is noble, taintless, supramundane, a factor of the path.
translations.mn117:9: He strives for the abandoning of wrong view and for the attainment of right view—this is his right effort. Mindfully he abandons wrong view; mindfully, having attained right view, he dwells—this is his right mindfulness. Thus these three states run along and revolve around right view, that is: right view, right effort, and right mindfulness.
translations.mn118:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, Migāra’s Mother’s mansion, together with many well-known, renowned elder disciples—Venerable Sāriputta, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, Venerable Mahākassapa, Venerable Mahākaccāyana, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika, Venerable Mahākappina, Venerable Mahācunda, Venerable Anuruddha, Venerable Revata, Venerable Ānanda, and other well-known, renowned elder disciples.
translations.mn118:15: Mindfulness of breathing, bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit and great benefit. Mindfulness of breathing, bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness. The four establishments of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven enlightenment factors. The seven enlightenment factors, when developed and cultivated, fulfill knowledge and liberation.
translations.mn118:17: Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, gone to the forest or gone to the root of a tree or gone to an empty hut, sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, having set his body upright, and having established mindfulness in front of him. Mindfully he breathes in, mindfully he breathes out.
translations.mn118:18: Breathing in long, he understands: ‘I breathe in long’; or breathing out long, he understands: ‘I breathe out long’. Breathing in short, he understands: ‘I breathe in short’; or breathing out short, he understands: ‘I breathe out short’. He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body’. He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation’.
translations.mn118:19: He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing rapture’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing rapture’. He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing pleasure’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing pleasure’. He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the mental formation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the mental formation’. He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in calming the mental formation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out calming the mental formation’.
translations.mn118:2: At that time the elder bhikkhus were instructing and exhorting the new bhikkhus. Some elder bhikkhus were instructing and exhorting ten bhikkhus; some elder bhikkhus were instructing and exhorting twenty bhikkhus; some elder bhikkhus were instructing and exhorting thirty bhikkhus; some elder bhikkhus were instructing and exhorting forty bhikkhus. And those new bhikkhus, being instructed and exhorted by the elder bhikkhus, came to know an excellent distinction, a progressive excellence.
translations.mn118:20: He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in experiencing the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out experiencing the mind’. He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in gladdening the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out gladdening the mind’. He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in concentrating the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out concentrating the mind’. He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in liberating the mind’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out liberating the mind’.
translations.mn118:21: He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating impermanence’. He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating dispassion’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating dispassion’. He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating cessation’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating cessation’. He trains thus: ‘I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment’; he trains thus: ‘I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment’.
translations.mn118:23: And how, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of breathing developed, and how is it cultivated, so as to fulfill the four establishments of mindfulness?
translations.mn118:24: At the time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu, breathing in long, understands “I breathe in long”, or breathing out long, understands “I breathe out long”; or breathing in short, understands “I breathe in short”, or breathing out short, understands “I breathe out short”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation”; at that time, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Of bodies, bhikkhus, I say that this is one kind of body, that is: inhalation and exhalation. Therefore, bhikkhus, at that time the bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:25: At the time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu trains thus: “I shall breathe in experiencing rapture”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out experiencing rapture”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in experiencing pleasure”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out experiencing pleasure”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in experiencing the mental formation”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out experiencing the mental formation”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in calming the mental formation”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out calming the mental formation”; at that time, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Of feelings, bhikkhus, I say that this is one kind of feeling, that is: close attention to inhalations and exhalations. Therefore, bhikkhus, at that time the bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:26: At the time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu trains thus: “I shall breathe in experiencing the mind”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out experiencing the mind”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in gladdening the mind”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out gladdening the mind”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in concentrating the mind”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out concentrating the mind”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in liberating the mind”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out liberating the mind”; at that time, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu dwells contemplating mind in mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. I do not say, bhikkhus, that mindfulness of breathing and in-breathing belongs to one who is unmindful and not clearly comprehending. Therefore, bhikkhus, at that time the bhikkhu dwells contemplating mind in mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:27: At the time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu trains thus: “I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out contemplating impermanence”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in contemplating fading away”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out contemplating fading away”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in contemplating cessation”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out contemplating cessation”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe in contemplating relinquishment”; he trains thus: “I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment”; at that time, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu dwells contemplating dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Having seen with wisdom the abandoning of those covetousness and displeasure, he is one who looks on with thorough equanimity. Therefore, bhikkhus, at that time the bhikkhu dwells contemplating dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.
translations.mn118:28: Thus developed, bhikkhus, mindfulness of breathing, thus cultivated much, fulfills the four establishments of mindfulness.
translations.mn118:29: And how, bhikkhus, developed and how cultivated much do the four establishments of mindfulness fulfill the seven factors of awakening?
translations.mn118:3: Now at that time the Blessed One, on that uposatha day, the fifteenth, at the invitation ceremony, on the full-moon night, was seated in the open air surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Then the Blessed One, after surveying the silent Saṅgha of bhikkhus, addressed the bhikkhus:
translations.mn118:30: At the time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world, at that time his mindfulness is established and unconfused. At the time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu’s mindfulness is established and unconfused, at that time the mindfulness factor of awakening is aroused in the bhikkhu. At that time the bhikkhu develops the mindfulness factor of awakening, and at that time the mindfulness factor of awakening comes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu.
translations.mn118:31: Dwelling thus mindful, he investigates that dhamma with wisdom, examines it, and enters upon inquiry. At the time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu dwelling thus mindful investigates that dhamma with wisdom, examines it, and enters upon inquiry, at that time the investigation-of-dhammas factor of awakening is aroused in the bhikkhu; at that time the bhikkhu develops the investigation-of-dhammas factor of awakening, and at that time the investigation-of-dhammas factor of awakening comes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu.
translations.mn118:33: For one whose energy is aroused, unworldly rapture arises. At the time, bhikkhus, when for a bhikkhu whose energy is aroused unworldly rapture arises, at that time the rapture factor of awakening is aroused in the bhikkhu; at that time the bhikkhu develops the rapture factor of awakening, and at that time the rapture factor of awakening comes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu.
translations.mn118:34: For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes calm, and the mind becomes calm. At the time, bhikkhus, when for a bhikkhu with a rapturous mind the body becomes calm and the mind becomes calm, at that time the tranquility factor of awakening is aroused in the bhikkhu; at that time the bhikkhu develops the tranquility factor of awakening, and at that time the tranquility factor of awakening comes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu.
translations.mn118:35: For one whose body is tranquil and who is happy, the mind is concentrated. At the time, bhikkhus, when for a bhikkhu whose body is tranquil and who is happy the mind is concentrated, at that time the concentration factor of awakening is aroused in the bhikkhu; at that time the bhikkhu develops the concentration factor of awakening, and at that time the concentration factor of awakening comes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu.
translations.mn118:36: He rightly looks on with equanimity at that mind so concentrated. At the time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu rightly looks on with equanimity at a mind so concentrated, the awakening factor of equanimity is aroused in the bhikkhu at that time; at that time the bhikkhu develops the awakening factor of equanimity; at that time the awakening factor of equanimity in the bhikkhu goes to fulfillment in development.
translations.mn118:4: "I am aroused in this practice, bhikkhus; I am of aroused mind in this practice, bhikkhus. Therefore, bhikkhus, arouse effort all the more for the attainment of what has not been attained, for the obtaining of what has not been obtained, for the realization of what has not been realized. Right here in Sāvatthī I will wait for the Komudī four-monthly festival"—so (he said).
translations.mn118:40: Thus developed, bhikkhus, and thus frequently practiced, the four establishments of mindfulness fulfill the seven awakening factors.
translations.mn118:41: And how, bhikkhus, when developed and frequently practiced, do the seven awakening factors fulfill knowledge and liberation?
translations.mn118:6: And those elder bhikkhus admonish and instruct the new bhikkhus all the more. Some elder bhikkhus admonish and instruct ten bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus admonish and instruct twenty bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus admonish and instruct thirty bhikkhus, some elder bhikkhus admonish and instruct forty bhikkhus. And those new bhikkhus, being admonished and instructed by the elder bhikkhus, come to know a lofty distinction, later and earlier.
translations.mn118:9: There are, bhikkhus, bhikkhus in this community of bhikkhus who are arahants, with taints destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own good, with the fetter of becoming exhausted, liberated by right knowledge—such, bhikkhus, there are bhikkhus in this community of bhikkhus.
translations.mn11:13: In such a teaching and discipline, bhikkhus, confidence in the Teacher is said to not be rightly directed; confidence in the Dhamma is said to not be rightly directed; fulfillment in virtue is said to not be rightly directed; being pleasing and agreeable among one’s fellows in the holy life is said to not be rightly directed. For what reason? For so it is, bhikkhus, as in a teaching and discipline that is badly proclaimed, badly made known, not leading out, not conducing to peace, proclaimed by one not perfectly awakened.
translations.mn11:14: But the Tathāgata, bhikkhus—an arahant, perfectly awakened one—professing to teach the full understanding of all acquisitions, lays down rightly the full understanding of all acquisitions: he lays down the full understanding of sensuality-acquisition, he lays down the full understanding of view-acquisition, he lays down the full understanding of rule-and-vow acquisition, he lays down the full understanding of self-doctrine acquisition.
translations.mn11:15: In such a teaching and discipline, bhikkhus, confidence in the Teacher is said to be rightly directed; confidence in the Dhamma is said to be rightly directed; fulfillment in virtue is said to be rightly directed; being pleasing and agreeable among one’s fellows in the holy life is said to be rightly directed. For what reason? For so it is, bhikkhus, as in a teaching and discipline that is well proclaimed, well made known, leading out, conducing to peace, proclaimed by one perfectly awakened.
translations.mn11:2: "Here, bhikkhus, there is a contemplative; here a second contemplative; here a third contemplative; here a fourth contemplative; empty are the doctrines of others of contemplatives other than these"—in this way, bhikkhus, roar the lion’s roar correctly.
translations.mn11:6: There are these two views, bhikkhus: the view of existence and the view of non-existence. Whatever contemplatives or brahmins, bhikkhus, cling to the view of existence, have gone over to the view of existence, have adhered to the view of existence, they are opposed to the view of non-existence. Whatever contemplatives or brahmins, bhikkhus, cling to the view of non-existence, have gone over to the view of non-existence, have adhered to the view of non-existence, they are opposed to the view of existence.
translations.mn11:7: Whatever contemplatives or brahmins, bhikkhus, do not understand as they really are the arising and the passing away, the gratification and the danger, and the escape in regard to these two views, they are with lust, they are with hatred, they are with delusion, they are with craving, they are with clinging, they are unlearned, they are compliant and opposing; they delight in proliferation, they rejoice in proliferation; they are not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrows, lamentations, pains, displeasures, and distresses; I say they are not freed from suffering.
translations.mn11:9: There are, bhikkhus, these four kinds of clinging. What four? Clinging to sensuality, clinging to views, clinging to rules and vows, clinging to a doctrine of self.
translations.mn12:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī, outside the city, in a wood, in the western district.
translations.mn12:10: Here, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands as it really is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible. And whatever, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata understands as it really is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible, this too, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata’s power of the Tathāgata, relying on which power the Tathāgata claims the bull-like position, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the wheel of brahma.
translations.mn12:19: Furthermore, Sāriputta, through the destruction of the taints the Tathāgata here and now enters upon and dwells in taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having directly known and realized it for himself. And whatever, Sāriputta, the Tathāgata through the destruction of the taints here and now enters upon and dwells in taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having directly known and realized it for himself, this too, Sāriputta, is a Tathāgata’s power of the Tathāgata, relying on which power the Tathāgata claims the bull-like position, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the wheel of brahma.
translations.mn12:2: Now at that time Sunakkhatta, the Licchavi’s son, had recently left this teaching and discipline. He speaks thus in the assembly at Vesālī: "There are no superhuman states in the ascetic Gotama, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. The ascetic Gotama teaches Dhamma hammered out by reasoning, following investigation, improvised. And for whoever that Dhamma is taught for, it leads him out for the right ending of suffering by that reasoning."
