translations.mn12:20: These, Sāriputta, are the ten powers of the Tathāgata, endowed with which powers the Tathāgata claims the bull-like position, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the wheel of brahma.
translations.mn12:22: There are, Sāriputta, these four confidences of the Tathāgata, endowed with which confidences the Tathāgata claims the bull-like position, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the wheel of brahma. What four?
translations.mn12:23: ‘Though you claim to be perfectly awakened, these things have not been fully understood by you.’ In this matter, Sāriputta, I do not see any sign that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could rightly challenge me in accordance with the Dhamma. Not seeing this sign, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained self-assurance.
translations.mn12:24: ‘Though you claim to be one whose taints are exhausted, these taints in you are not exhausted.’ In this matter, Sāriputta, I do not see any sign that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could rightly challenge me in accordance with the Dhamma. Not seeing this sign, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained self-assurance.
translations.mn12:25: ‘Those things that were said to be obstructive do not suffice for obstruction when one resorts to them.’ In this matter, Sāriputta, I do not see any sign that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could rightly challenge me in accordance with the Dhamma. Not seeing this sign, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained self-assurance.
translations.mn12:26: ‘The Dhamma that was taught for your purpose does not lead one who acts accordingly to the complete ending of suffering.’ In this matter, Sāriputta, I do not see any sign that any ascetic or brahmin or god or Māra or Brahmā or anyone in the world could rightly challenge me in accordance with the Dhamma. Not seeing this sign, Sāriputta, I dwell having attained security, having attained fearlessness, having attained self-assurance.
translations.mn12:32: There are these four kinds of wombs, Sāriputta. Which four? The egg-born womb, the womb of the womb-born, the moisture-born womb, the spontaneously arisen womb.
translations.mn12:33: And what, Sāriputta, is the egg-born womb? Those beings, Sāriputta, that are born after breaking out of an eggshell—this is called, Sāriputta, the egg-born womb. And what, Sāriputta, is the womb of the womb-born? Those beings, Sāriputta, that are born after breaking out of a membrane—this is called, Sāriputta, the womb of the womb-born. And what, Sāriputta, is the moisture-born womb? Those beings, Sāriputta, that are born in rotten fish or in a rotten corpse or in rotten porridge or in a cesspool or in a dung-pit—this is called, Sāriputta, the moisture-born womb. And what, Sāriputta, is the spontaneously arisen womb? Deities, hell-beings, some humans, and some beings in states of deprivation—this is called, Sāriputta, the spontaneously arisen womb. These, Sāriputta, are the four kinds of wombs.
translations.mn12:35: There are these five destinations, Sāriputta. Which five? Hell, the animal womb, the realm of the departed, humans, and deities.
translations.mn12:36: I understand hell too, Sāriputta, and the path leading to hell, and the course leading to hell; and I understand that one who has practiced in such a way, on the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn in the plane of misery, in a bad destination, in perdition, in hell. I understand the animal womb too, Sāriputta, and the path leading to the animal womb, and the course leading to the animal womb; and I understand that one who has practiced in such a way, on the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn in the animal womb. I understand the realm of the departed too, Sāriputta, and the path leading to the realm of the departed, and the course leading to the realm of the departed; and I understand that one who has practiced in such a way, on the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn in the realm of the departed. I understand humans too, Sāriputta, and the path leading to the human world, and the course leading to the human world; and I understand that one who has practiced in such a way, on the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn among humans. I understand deities too, Sāriputta, and the path leading to the world of the deities, and the course leading to the world of the deities; and I understand that one who has practiced in such a way, on the breaking up of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. I understand Nibbāna too, Sāriputta, and the path leading to Nibbāna, and the course leading to Nibbāna; and I understand that one who has practiced in such a way, through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it dwells in it.
translations.mn12:4: ‘He is angry, Sāriputta, that Sunakkhatta, the worthless man. And that speech of his was spoken out of anger. “I will speak dispraise,” Sāriputta, yet Sunakkhatta, the worthless man, speaks praise of the Tathāgata. It is praise, Sāriputta, of the Tathāgata if one were to say: “And that for the sake of which the Dhamma was taught leads one who acts accordingly to the complete ending of suffering.”
translations.mn12:43: Whoever, Sāriputta, knowing me thus, seeing me thus, would say thus: ‘There are no higher-than-human states in the ascetic Gotama, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones; the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma beaten out by reasoning, following inquiry, a self-originated inspiration’—not abandoning that speech, not abandoning that thought, not giving up that view, he is cast into hell just like that, as if carried off and laid down there. Just as, Sāriputta, a monk possessed of virtue, possessed of concentration, possessed of wisdom, might realize final knowledge in this very life; even so, Sāriputta, I say this is the case: not abandoning that speech, not abandoning that thought, not giving up that view, he is cast into hell just like that, as if carried off and laid down there.
translations.mn12:44: But I directly know, Sāriputta, that I lived the holy life endowed with four factors: I was an ascetic, supremely ascetic; I was coarse, supremely coarse; I was scrupulous, supremely scrupulous; I was secluded, supremely secluded.
translations.mn12:46: In that regard, Sāriputta, this was in me as one who was coarse: dirt and grime of many years accumulated on my body, forming a crust. Just as, Sāriputta, a tinduka stump with the passing of many years becomes accumulated, forming a crust, so too, Sāriputta, dirt and grime of many years accumulated on my body, forming a crust. Yet, Sāriputta, it did not occur to me: ‘Oh, if only I might rub off this dirt and grime with my hand, or if others might rub off this dirt and grime for me with their hand.’ Even so, Sāriputta, it did not occur to me. This, Sāriputta, was in me as one who was coarse.
translations.mn12:47: In that regard, Sāriputta, this was in me as one who was scrupulous: I would step forward mindfully, step back mindfully, and even regarding a drop of water, compassion was present in me: ‘Let me not bring harm upon tiny creatures that have come into misfortune.’ This, Sāriputta, was in me as one who was scrupulous.
translations.mn12:49: Then, Sāriputta, I went to those cattle-pens where the cows were penned up and the cowherds had gone away. There, having gone on all fours, I ate the dung of the calves, the young calves, and the milk-cows. And so long as my own urine and excrement were not exhausted, I ate my own urine and excrement. This, Sāriputta, was for me a coarse form of eating.
translations.mn12:5: For it may well be, Sāriputta, that for Sunakkhatta, that worthless man, there will be no devotion to me in the Dhamma: ‘Indeed the Blessed One is an arahant, a perfectly awakened one, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the awakened one, the Blessed One.’
translations.mn12:50:
Then, Sāriputta, having entered a certain fearful forest grove, I lived there. There, Sāriputta, in that fearful forest grove it was fearful—whoever with lust not faded entered that forest grove, for the most part their hairs stood on end. Then, Sāriputta, on those nights that were cold, wintry, in the interval between the seasons, in the time of snowfall—on such nights I lived at night in the open, by day in the forest grove; in the last month of the hot season I lived by day in the open, at night in the forest grove. And then, Sāriputta, this unastonishing verse occurred to me, unheard before:

‘Burned and scorched,
Alone in the fearful forest;
Naked, and not seated by a fire,
A sage intent on seeking.’
translations.mn12:51: Then, Sāriputta, I made my bed in a charnel ground, using bones of corpses for a pillow. And then, Sāriputta, groups from villages would approach and spit on me, and urinate on me, and even throw dust on me, and insert a stick into my ear-holes. But I do not recall, Sāriputta, ever having raised an evil mind toward them. This, Sāriputta, was for me a dwelling in equanimity.
translations.mn12:52: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who say this, who hold this view: ‘purity is by food.’ They say thus: ‘We live on jujubes.’ They eat jujubes, eat jujube powder, drink jujube water—they consume various kinds of jujube preparations. But I recall, Sāriputta, having taken just one jujube as food. Now, Sāriputta, you might think: ‘Surely at that time the jujube was large.’ But, Sāriputta, it should not be seen thus. Even then, the jujube was only so large, just as now. For me, Sāriputta, eating just one jujube as food, my body came to an extreme limit. Just as there are joints of reeds or joints of black beans, so too my limbs became because of that same meager intake. Just as a camel’s hoof, so too my buttocks became because of that same meager intake. Just as a string of balls, so too my spine became raised and bent because of that same meager intake. Just as, in an old shed, the rafters sink and sag, so too my ribs sank and sag because of that same meager intake. Just as in a deep well, water-stars are seen deep down, sunk and faint, so too in my eye-sockets my eye-stars were seen deep down, sunk and faint because of that same meager intake. Just as a bitter gourd, cut while unripe, shrivels and withers in wind and sun, so too the skin of my head shriveled and withered because of that same meager intake. Then, Sāriputta, thinking, ‘I will touch the skin of my belly,’ I grasped only my spine; thinking, ‘I will touch my spine,’ I grasped only the skin of my belly—so much so, Sāriputta, had the skin of my belly clung to my spine because of that same meager intake. Then, Sāriputta, thinking, ‘I will defecate or urinate,’ I fell down right there, face down, because of that same meager intake. Then, Sāriputta, comforting that very body, I stroked my limbs with my hand. For me, Sāriputta, as I stroked my limbs with my hand, hairs with rotten roots fell from my body because of that same meager intake.
translations.mn12:56: Yet even with that posture, Sāriputta, with that practice, with that arduous striving, I did not reach anything higher than the human state, any distinction of knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. For what reason? Because of not attaining that very noble wisdom—this noble wisdom that, when attained, is noble and leading onward; it leads one who acts accordingly to the complete ending of suffering.
translations.mn12:57: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who say this, who hold this view: ‘purity is by roaming on in saṁsāra.’ But, Sāriputta, there is no roaming on in saṁsāra easy to find that I have not roamed in during this long time, except among the gods of the Pure Abodes. And if, Sāriputta, I were to roam on among the gods of the Pure Abodes, I would not come back again to this world.
translations.mn12:6: For it may well be, Sāriputta, that for Sunakkhatta, that worthless man, there will be no devotion to me in the Dhamma: ‘Indeed the Blessed One experiences various kinds of spiritual power: having been one he becomes many; having been many he becomes one; he appears and disappears; he goes unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain, as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth, as though in water; he walks on water without breaking it, as though on earth; he travels through the sky cross-legged, like a winged bird; he touches and strokes with his hand even the moon and sun, so mighty and so powerful; he wields mastery with his body even as far as the brahmā world.’
translations.mn12:60: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who say this, who hold this view: ‘purity is by sacrifice.’ But, Sāriputta, there is no sacrifice easy to find that I have not performed in this long time—and that with a king or with a hundred consecrated khattiya nobles, or with a brahmin or a great wealthy man.
translations.mn12:61: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who say this, who hold this view: ‘purity is by worshiping fire.’ But, Sāriputta, there is no fire easy to find that I have not tended in this long time—and that with a king or with a hundred consecrated khattiya nobles, or with a brahmin or a great wealthy man.
translations.mn12:62: There are, Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus, who hold this view: ‘So long as this venerable person is young, youthful, with black hair, endowed with the blessings of youth, in the prime of life, only so long is he endowed with the highest acumen of wisdom. But when this venerable person becomes aged, old, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the end of life, eighty or ninety or a hundred years of age by birth, then from that acumen of wisdom he declines.’ But, Sāriputta, it should not be seen thus. For I, Sāriputta, am now aged, old, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the end of life; my age is now eighty. Here, Sāriputta, let there be for me four disciples, a hundred years long-lived, living a hundred years, endowed with the highest mindfulness and speed and steadiness, and with the highest acumen of wisdom. Just as, Sāriputta, a strong bowman, trained, practiced, skilled, could with a light arrow, with little effort, shoot across the shadow of a palm tree, so too they would be possessed of the utmost mindfulness, the utmost speed, the utmost steadiness, endowed with the highest acumen of wisdom. They might ask me question after question, taking up the four establishments of mindfulness; and questioned and questioned, I would answer them; and my answer they would retain as answered, and they would not question me a second time beyond that. Apart from eating, drinking, consuming, and tasting, apart from the work of defecation and urination, apart from dispelling sleep and weariness, unexhausted indeed, Sāriputta, would be the Tathāgata’s teaching of Dhamma; unexhausted indeed would be the Tathāgata’s words and phrases of Dhamma; unexhausted indeed would be the Tathāgata’s readiness in answering questions. Then those four disciples, a hundred years long-lived, living a hundred years, after the passing of a hundred years, might make an end of time. Even if you were to carry me about on a couch, Sāriputta, there is no change in the Tathāgata’s acumen of wisdom.
translations.mn12:7: Even so, Sāriputta, there will be no accordance with the Dhamma in me for Sunakkhatta, that worthless man: ‘Itipi so bhagavā, with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing the human, hears both kinds of sounds—divine and human, those far and near.’
translations.mn12:8: Even so, Sāriputta, there will be no accordance with the Dhamma in me for Sunakkhatta, that worthless man: ‘Itipi so bhagavā knows, having encompassed with his mind the minds of other beings, other persons: a mind with lust as a mind with lust he knows; a mind without lust as a mind without lust he knows; a mind with hate as a mind with hate he knows; a mind without hate as a mind without hate he knows; a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion he knows; a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion he knows; a contracted mind as a contracted mind he knows; a distracted mind as a distracted mind he knows; an exalted mind as an exalted mind he knows; an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind he knows; a mind with something superior as a mind with something superior he knows; a mind without anything superior as a mind without anything superior he knows; a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind he knows; an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind he knows; a liberated mind as a liberated mind he knows; an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind he knows.’
translations.mn12:9: There are, Sāriputta, these ten powers of the Tathāgata; possessed of which powers the Tathāgata claims the bull’s place, roars the lion’s roar in the assemblies, sets in motion the wheel of Brahmā. What are the ten?
translations.mn135:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park.
translations.mn135:13: Here, young man, a certain woman or man is not a giver to an ascetic or a brahmin of food, drink, clothing, a vehicle, garlands, scents and ointments, bedding, lodging, and lamps. By that action, thus accomplished, thus undertaken, with the breakup of the body, after death, they arise in the plane of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, hell. If, with the breakup of the body, after death, they do not arise in the plane of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, hell, then if they come to the human state, wherever they are reborn, they are of little wealth. This is the course, young man, that leads to little wealth, namely: not being a giver to an ascetic or a brahmin of food, drink, clothing, a vehicle, garlands, scents and ointments, bedding, lodging, and lamps.
translations.mn135:2: Then Subha the young man, Todeyya’s son, went to the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When he had concluded courteous and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Subha the young man, Todeyya’s son, said this to the Blessed One:
translations.mn135:20: Beings are owners of their actions, young man, heirs to their actions, born of their actions, related through their actions, supported by their actions. Action divides beings, that is—by inferiority and superiority.”
translations.mn135:3: “What then, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the condition, whereby among human beings—among those who have become human—there are seen inferiority and superiority? For, Master Gotama, humans are seen short-lived; they are seen long-lived. They are seen with many illnesses; they are seen with few illnesses. They are seen ugly; they are seen beautiful. They are seen of little influence; they are seen of great influence. They are seen of little wealth; they are seen of great wealth. They are seen of low family; they are seen of high family. They are seen of little wisdom; they are seen wise. What then, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the condition, whereby among human beings—among those who have become human—there are seen inferiority and superiority?”
translations.mn135:4: “Beings are owners of their actions, young man, heirs to their actions, born of their actions, related through their actions, supported by their actions. Action divides beings, that is—by inferiority and superiority.” “I do not understand the meaning of this spoken by Master Gotama in brief, without having analyzed the meaning in detail. It would be good if Master Gotama would teach me the Dhamma so that I might understand in detail the meaning of this spoken by Master Gotama in brief, without having analyzed the meaning in detail.” “Then, young man, listen and attend closely; I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” Subha the young man, Todeyya’s son, replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn135:5: “Here, young man, some woman or man is a killer of living beings, cruel, bloody-handed, given to killing and striking, without compassion for living creatures. By that action, thus undertaken and thus carried out, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, hell. But if, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are not reborn in deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, hell, then if they come to the human state, wherever they are reborn they are short-lived. This, young man, is the course of practice that leads to short life, that is: being a killer of living beings, cruel, bloody-handed, given to killing and striking, without compassion for living creatures.
translations.mn135:6: Here, young man, some woman or man, having abandoned killing living beings, abstains from killing living beings; with rod laid aside, with weapon laid aside, conscientious, compassionate, they dwell kind and sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings. By that action, thus undertaken and thus carried out, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. But if, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are not reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, then if they come to the human state, wherever they are reborn they are long-lived. This, young man, is the course of practice that leads to long life, that is: having abandoned killing living beings, abstaining from killing living beings; with rod laid aside, with weapon laid aside, conscientious, compassionate, dwelling kind and sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings.
translations.mn13:10: If, bhikkhus, for that clansman, as he makes such an effort, strives, and exerts himself, those possessions come to be. He experiences pain and displeasure on account of guarding those possessions: ‘How can it be that neither kings would take my possessions, nor thieves would take them, nor fire would burn them, nor water would carry them away, nor unloved heirs would take them?’ As he guards and protects them in this way, kings take those possessions, or thieves take them, or fire burns them, or water carries them away, or unloved heirs take them. He sorrows, grieves, and laments, beating his breast and weeping, and comes to bewilderment: ‘What I had, that too I no longer have.’ This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering, with sensual pleasure as its cause, sensual pleasure as its origin, sensual pleasure as its basis, sensual pleasure itself as the cause.
translations.mn13:11: Furthermore, bhikkhus, with sensual pleasure as the cause, sensual pleasure as the origin, sensual pleasure as the basis, sensual pleasure itself as the cause, kings dispute with kings, nobles dispute with nobles, brahmins dispute with brahmins, householders dispute with householders; a mother disputes with her son, a son disputes with his mother, a father disputes with his son, a son disputes with his father, a brother disputes with a brother, a brother disputes with a sister, a sister disputes with a brother, a friend disputes with a friend. Having fallen into quarrels, brawls, and disputes there, they attack one another with fists, they attack one another with clods, they attack one another with sticks, they attack one another with weapons. There they meet with death, and even mere death is suffering. This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering, with sensual pleasure as the cause, sensual pleasure as the origin, sensual pleasure as the basis, sensual pleasure itself as the cause.
translations.mn13:12: Furthermore, bhikkhus, with sensual pleasure as the cause, sensual pleasure as the origin, sensual pleasure as the basis, sensual pleasure itself as the cause, having taken shield and sword, having fastened on bow and quiver, they plunge into a battle drawn up on both sides, while arrows are being shot, spears are being hurled, and swords are flashing. There they are pierced by arrows, pierced by spears, and they cut off heads with swords. There they meet with death, and even mere death is suffering. This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering, with sensual pleasure as the cause, sensual pleasure as the origin, sensual pleasure as the basis, sensual pleasure itself as the cause.
translations.mn13:13: Furthermore, bhikkhus, with sensual pleasure as the cause, sensual pleasure as the origin, sensual pleasure as the basis, sensual pleasure itself as the cause, having taken shield and sword, having fastened on bow and quiver, the attackers, with plastered bodies, plunge in while arrows are being shot, spears are being hurled, and swords are flashing. There they are pierced by arrows, pierced by spears, they are drenched with cow dung, they are crushed under a mass, and they cut off heads with swords. There they meet with death, and even mere death is suffering. This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering, with sensual pleasure as the cause, sensual pleasure as the origin, sensual pleasure as the basis, sensual pleasure itself as the cause.
translations.mn13:15: Furthermore, bhikkhus, with sensual pleasure as the cause, sensual pleasure as the origin, sensual pleasure as the basis, sensual pleasure itself as the cause, they engage in misconduct by body, they engage in misconduct by speech, they engage in misconduct by mind. Having engaged in misconduct by body, having engaged in misconduct by speech, having engaged in misconduct by mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, they are reborn in deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, hell. This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures in the future, a mass of suffering, with sensual pleasure as the cause, sensual pleasure as the origin, sensual pleasure as the basis, sensual pleasure itself as the cause.
translations.mn13:16: And what, bhikkhus, is the escape from sensual pleasures? The removal and abandoning of desire and lust for sensual pleasures—this is the escape from sensual pleasures.
translations.mn13:17: Whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, do not truly understand as it is the gratification in sensual pleasures as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape, it is not possible that they will themselves fully understand sensual pleasures, or that they will lead another to such a state so that, practicing accordingly, they will fully understand sensual pleasures—there is no such possibility. But whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, truly understand as it is the gratification in sensual pleasures as gratification, the danger as danger, and the escape as escape, it is possible that they will themselves fully understand sensual pleasures, or that they will lead another to such a state so that, practicing accordingly, they will fully understand sensual pleasures—this is possible.
translations.mn13:18: And what, bhikkhus, is the gratification in forms? Suppose, bhikkhus, there is a noble girl, or a brahmin girl, or a householder girl, fifteen years old or sixteen years old, neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too fat, neither too dark nor too fair—at that time she is supremely beautiful, with a lovely complexion? ‘Yes, venerable sir.’ The pleasure and joy that arise dependent on that beautiful, lovely complexion—this is the gratification in forms.
translations.mn13:19: And what, bhikkhus, is the danger in forms? Here, bhikkhus, at another time one might see that same sister, eighty or ninety or a hundred years of age, old, bent like a roof-beam, crooked, leaning on a staff, trembling as she walks, afflicted, youth gone, with broken teeth, grey-haired, scanty-haired, bald, wrinkled, her body blotched with spots. What do you think, bhikkhus: has her former beauty and complexion vanished, and has the danger appeared? “Yes, venerable sir.” This too, bhikkhus, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:2: Then several bhikkhus, in the morning, having dressed and taken bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then it occurred to those bhikkhus: “It is too early to walk for alms in Sāvatthī. Suppose we go to the park of the wanderers of other sects.” Then those bhikkhus went to the park of the wanderers of other sects. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects; and after exchanging courteous and friendly talk, they sat down to one side. When those bhikkhus were seated to one side, those wanderers of other sects said this to them:
translations.mn13:20: Again further, bhikkhus, at another time one might see that same sister sick, suffering, gravely ill, lying fouled in her own urine and excrement, being lifted up by others, being set down by others. What do you think, bhikkhus: has her former beauty and complexion vanished, and has the danger appeared? “Yes, venerable sir.” This too, bhikkhus, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:23-28: Again further, bhikkhus, at another time one might see that same sister’s body thrown in a charnel ground— a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews; a skeleton smeared with flesh and blood, held together by sinews; a skeleton without flesh but smeared with blood, held together by sinews; bones disconnected, scattered in all directions—here a hand-bone, there a foot-bone, there an ankle-bone, there a shin-bone, there a thigh-bone, there a hip-bone, there a back-bone, there a rib-bone, there a spine-bone, there a shoulder-bone, there a neck-bone, there a jaw-bone, there a tooth-bone, there the skull. What do you think, bhikkhus: has her former beauty and complexion vanished, and has the danger appeared? “Yes, venerable sir.” This too, bhikkhus, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:29: Again further, bhikkhus, at another time one might see that same sister’s body thrown in a charnel ground— bones white, the color of a conch; bones heaped up, more than a year old; bones rotten, reduced to powder. What do you think, bhikkhus: has her former beauty and complexion vanished, and has the danger appeared? “Yes, venerable sir.” This too, bhikkhus, is the danger in forms.
translations.mn13:3: "Friends, the ascetic Gotama prescribes the full understanding of sensual pleasures; we too prescribe the full understanding of sensual pleasures. The ascetic Gotama prescribes the full understanding of forms; we too prescribe the full understanding of forms. The ascetic Gotama prescribes the full understanding of feelings; we too prescribe the full understanding of feelings. So here, friends, what is the distinction, what is the difference, what is the divergence between the teaching of the ascetic Gotama and ours—namely, as to a teaching of Dhamma or a teaching of Dhamma, an instruction or an instruction?"
translations.mn13:30: And what, bhikkhus, is the escape from forms? The removal of desire and lust for forms, the abandoning of desire and lust—this is the escape from forms.
translations.mn13:32: And what, bhikkhus, is the gratification in feelings? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. At the time, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, at that time he does not intend harm to himself, nor intend harm to others, nor intend harm to both; at that time he feels only a feeling that is harmless. Harmlessness is the highest: this, bhikkhus, I declare to be the gratification in feelings.
translations.mn13:36: And what, bhikkhus, is the danger in feelings? That feelings are impermanent, suffering, and of a nature to change—this is the danger in feelings.
translations.mn13:37: And what, bhikkhus, is the escape from feelings? The removal of desire and lust for feelings, the abandoning of desire and lust—this is the escape from feelings.
translations.mn13:4: Then those bhikkhus neither approved nor disapproved of what those wanderers of other sects had said. Without approving and without disapproving, they rose from their seats and departed: “In the Blessed One’s presence we shall understand the meaning of what has been said.”
translations.mn13:6: "Bhikkhus, wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be addressed as follows: ‘But, friends, what is the gratification in sensual pleasures, what is the danger, what is the escape? What is the gratification in forms, what is the danger, what is the escape? What is the gratification in feelings, what is the danger, what is the escape?’ When asked thus, bhikkhus, the wanderers of other sects would not be able to reply and, moreover, would meet with vexation. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, it is outside their domain. I do not see, bhikkhus, in this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, in this population with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, anyone who could satisfy the mind by answering these questions, apart from the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them."
translations.mn13:8: And what, bhikkhus, is the drawback of sensual pleasures? Here, bhikkhus, a clansman makes his living by some craft—whether by writing, whether by calculation, whether by accounting, whether by farming, whether by trade, whether by cattle-keeping, whether by archery, whether by the king’s service, or by some other craft—exposed to cold, exposed to heat, harassed by contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, dying of hunger and thirst; this too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering, caused by sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as its basis, with sensual pleasures themselves as the cause.
translations.mn13:9: If, bhikkhus, while that clansman is thus striving, struggling, and exerting himself, those possessions are not acquired, he sorrows, grieves, laments, beats his breast and wails, and falls into confusion: ‘My striving was in vain; my effort was fruitless!’ This too, bhikkhus, is a drawback of sensual pleasures, visible here and now, a mass of suffering, caused by sensual pleasures, originating from sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as its basis, with sensual pleasures themselves as the cause.
translations.mn140:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One, wandering on tour among the Magadhans, arrived at Rājagaha. Then he approached Bhaggava the potter; having approached, he said this to Bhaggava the potter:
translations.mn140:12: ‘One should not be negligent in wisdom, one should guard truth, one should cultivate relinquishment, one should train only in peace’—so it was said. And in reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:14: And what, bhikkhu, is the earth element? The earth element may be internal or external. And what, bhikkhu, is the internal earth element? Whatever internally, in oneself, is hard, solid, and appropriated, such as this—head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces; or whatever else internally, in oneself, is hard, solid, and appropriated—this is called the internal earth element, bhikkhu. And the internal earth element and the external earth element are simply the earth element. ‘That is not mine, I am not that, that is not my self’—thus it should be seen as it really is with proper wisdom. Seeing it thus as it really is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the earth element; one’s mind becomes dispassionate toward the earth element.
translations.mn140:15: And what, bhikkhu, is the water element? The water element may be internal or external. And what, bhikkhu, is the internal water element? Whatever internally, in oneself, is water, of the nature of water, and appropriated, such as this—bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, mucus, synovial fluid, urine; or whatever else internally, in oneself, is water, of the nature of water, and appropriated—this is called the internal water element, bhikkhu. And the internal water element and the external water element are simply the water element. ‘That is not mine, I am not that, that is not my self’—thus it should be seen as it really is with proper wisdom. Seeing it thus as it really is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the water element; one’s mind becomes dispassionate toward the water element.
translations.mn140:16: And what, bhikkhu, is the fire element? The fire element may be internal or external. And what, bhikkhu, is the internal fire element? Whatever internally, in oneself, is fire, of the nature of fire, and appropriated, such as this—by which one is warmed, by which one ages, by which one is consumed, by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested; or whatever else internally, in oneself, is fire, of the nature of fire, and appropriated—this is called the internal fire element, bhikkhu. And the internal fire element and the external fire element are simply the fire element. ‘That is not mine, I am not that, that is not my self’—thus it should be seen as it really is with proper wisdom. Seeing it thus as it really is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the fire element; one’s mind becomes dispassionate toward the fire element.
translations.mn140:17: And what, bhikkhu, is the air element? The air element may be internal or external. And what, bhikkhu, is the internal air element? Whatever internally, in oneself, is air, of the nature of air, and appropriated, such as this—upward-moving winds, downward-moving winds, winds in the belly, winds in the intestines, winds that course through the limbs, the in-breath and the out-breath; or whatever else internally, in oneself, is air, of the nature of air, and appropriated—this is called the internal air element, bhikkhu. And the internal air element and the external air element are simply the air element. ‘That is not mine, I am not that, that is not my self’—thus it should be seen as it really is with proper wisdom. Seeing it thus as it really is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the air element; one’s mind becomes dispassionate toward the air element.
translations.mn140:18: And what, bhikkhu, is the space element? The space element may be internal or external. And what, bhikkhu, is the internal space element? Whatever internally, in oneself, is space, of the nature of space, and appropriated, such as this—the ear-hole, the nostril, the mouth-opening by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is swallowed, where what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted rests, by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted exits below; or whatever else internally, in oneself, is space, of the nature of space, a hollow, of the nature of a hollow, a cavity, of the nature of a cavity, not filled with flesh and blood, and appropriated—this is called the internal space element, bhikkhu. And the internal space element and the external space element are simply the space element. ‘That is not mine, I am not that, that is not my self’—thus it should be seen as it really is with proper wisdom. Seeing it thus as it really is with proper wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with the space element; one’s mind becomes dispassionate toward the space element.
translations.mn140:2: “If it is not burdensome for you, Bhaggava, let us stay in the dwelling for one night.” “It is not burdensome for me, Bhante. But there is a renunciant here who first took up residence. If he permits it, stay, Bhante, as you please.”
translations.mn140:20: Then, further, only equanimity remains—pure, bright, soft and workable, and radiant. Just as, bhikkhu, a skillful goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice would prepare a crucible: having prepared the crucible, he would heat the mouth of the crucible; having heated the mouth of the crucible, he would take the gold with tongs and put it into the mouth of the crucible. From time to time he would blow on it, from time to time he would sprinkle it with water, from time to time he would just look on. And so that gold becomes well refined, well blown, taken out, with dross removed, soft and workable and radiant; and whatever kind of ornament he wants—whether a strip, or an earring, or a neck-ornament, or a gold garland—that purpose would be served. So too, bhikkhu, then further only equanimity remains—pure, bright, soft and workable, and radiant.
translations.mn140:23: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘That is impermanent’; he understands: ‘not clung to’; he understands: ‘not delighted in’. If he feels a painful feeling, he understands: ‘That is impermanent’; he understands: ‘not clung to’; he understands: ‘not delighted in’. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘That is impermanent’; he understands: ‘not clung to’; he understands: ‘not delighted in’.
translations.mn140:29: ‘One should not neglect wisdom, one should guard truth, one should cultivate giving up, one should train only in peace’—what was said, was said with reference to this.
translations.mn140:3: Now at that time a clansman named Pukkusāti had gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith in the Blessed One. He had come first to stay in that potter’s workshop. Then the Blessed One approached the venerable Pukkusāti; having approached, he said this to the venerable Pukkusāti: “If it is no burden to you, bhikkhu, let us dwell in the workshop for one night.” “The potter’s workshop is spacious, friend. Let the venerable one dwell as he likes.”
translations.mn140:30: ‘Where conceivings do not proceed for one who stands, and when conceivings do not proceed, the sage is said to be at peace’—so it was said. And with reference to what was this said?
translations.mn140:31: ‘I am’—bhikkhu, this is a conceiving; ‘I am this’—this is a conceiving; ‘I shall be’—this is a conceiving; ‘I shall not be’—this is a conceiving; ‘I shall be with form’—this is a conceiving; ‘I shall be formless’—this is a conceiving; ‘I shall be percipient’—this is a conceiving; ‘I shall be non-percipient’—this is a conceiving; ‘I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient’—this is a conceiving. Conceiving, bhikkhu, is a disease; conceiving is a tumor; conceiving is a dart. But with the complete overcoming of all conceivings, bhikkhu, the sage is said to be at peace. And the sage, bhikkhu, being at peace does not come to be born, does not age, does not die, does not get agitated, does not long. For him, bhikkhu, there is nothing by which he would be born. Not being born, how would he age? Not aging, how would he die? Not dying, how would he be agitated? Not being agitated, what would he long for?
translations.mn140:32: ‘Where conceivings do not proceed for one who stands, and when conceivings do not proceed, the sage is said to be at peace’—what was said, was said with reference to this. “So, bhikkhu, you should remember this brief exposition of the six elements.”
translations.mn140:33: Then the venerable Pukkusāti thought: “The Teacher has arrived for me; the Fortunate One has arrived for me; the perfectly awakened one has arrived for me.” Rising from his seat, arranging his robe over one shoulder, he fell with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and said to the Blessed One: “An offence has overcome me, venerable sir, in that, being foolish, being deluded, being unskillful, I thought I should address the Blessed One with ‘friend’. Let the Blessed One accept my offence as an offence, for my restraint in the future.” “Indeed, bhikkhu, an offence has overcome you in that, being foolish, being deluded, being unskillful, you thought you should address me with ‘friend’. But since you, bhikkhu, having seen the offence as an offence, make amends in accordance with the Dhamma, we accept it. For this is growth in the discipline of the noble one, bhikkhu: when one, having seen an offence as an offence, makes amends in accordance with the Dhamma, one comes to restraint in the future.”
translations.mn140:34: “Venerable sir, may I receive the full ordination in the Blessed One’s presence?” “But is your bowl and robes complete, bhikkhu?” “My bowl and robes are not complete, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhu, Tathāgatas do not give full ordination to one whose bowl and robes are incomplete.”
translations.mn140:35: Then the venerable Pukkusāti, having rejoiced in and approved of the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed in search of a bowl and robes. Then, while the venerable Pukkusāti was seeking a bowl and robes, a stray cow took his life.
translations.mn140:4: Then the Blessed One entered the potter’s workshop and, having spread a grass mat to one side, sat down folding his legs crosswise, setting his body upright, and establishing mindfulness in front of him. Then the Blessed One spent much of the night sitting. The venerable Pukkusāti also spent much of the night sitting. Then it occurred to the Blessed One: “This clansman’s conduct is pleasing. What if I were to question him?” Then the Blessed One said this to the venerable Pukkusāti:
translations.mn140:5: “For the sake of whom, bhikkhu, have you gone forth? Or who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you approve of?” “There is, friend, the ascetic Gotama, the Sakyan son, gone forth from a Sakyan clan. About that Blessed One Gotama a fine report has spread: ‘He is indeed the Blessed One, an arahant, a perfectly awakened one, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, Buddha, Blessed One.’ It is for the sake of that Blessed One that I have gone forth. And that Blessed One is my teacher. And I approve of the Dhamma of that Blessed One.” “But where, bhikkhu, is that Blessed One now dwelling, the arahant, the perfectly awakened one?” “There is, friend, in the northern countries a city named Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One now dwells, the arahant, the perfectly awakened one.” “But have you seen that Blessed One before, bhikkhu? And having seen him, would you recognize him?” “I have not seen that Blessed One before, friend; and having seen him, I would not recognize him.”
translations.mn140:6: Then it occurred to the Blessed One: “This clansman has gone forth with me in mind. Why don’t I teach him the Dhamma?” Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Pukkusāti: “I will teach you the Dhamma, bhikkhu. Listen to it and pay close attention; I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” Venerable Pukkusāti replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn140:7: “‘This person, bhikkhu, consists of six elements, has six bases of contact, eighteen kinds of mental exploration, and four determinations; standing where the outflows of conceiving do not proceed, and when the outflows of conceiving do not proceed the sage is said to be at peace. One should not be negligent with wisdom, one should preserve truth, one should cultivate relinquishment, one should train only in peace’—this is the summary of the Analysis of the Elements.
translations.mn146:12: “This simile has been made by me, sisters, for making the meaning understood. This is the meaning here: ‘the inner flesh-body’ is, sisters, a designation for these six internal sense bases; ‘the outer skin-body’ is, sisters, a designation for these six external sense bases; ‘in between the flesh, in between the sinew, in between the binding’ is, sisters, a designation for delight and lust; ‘with a threefold carving-knife for cattle’ is, sisters, a designation for noble wisdom, by which noble wisdom cuts through, cuts away, cuts off, and cuts all around the defilement, the fetter, the bondage.
translations.mn146:13: Now these, sisters, are seven awakening factors, by developing and cultivating which a bhikkhu, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, here and now, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it. What seven? Here, sisters, a bhikkhu develops the mindfulness awakening factor, supported by seclusion, supported by dispassion, supported by cessation, ripening in relinquishment. He develops the investigation-of-states awakening factor …pe… he develops the energy awakening factor … he develops the rapture awakening factor … he develops the tranquility awakening factor … he develops the concentration awakening factor … he develops the equanimity awakening factor, supported by seclusion, supported by dispassion, supported by cessation, ripening in relinquishment. These, sisters, are the seven awakening factors, by developing and cultivating which a bhikkhu, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, here and now, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.”
translations.mn146:14: Then Venerable Nandaka, having instructed those bhikkhunīs with this exhortation, dismissed them: “Go, sisters; it is time.” Then those bhikkhunīs, having delighted in and approved of what was spoken by Venerable Nandaka, rose from their seats, paid homage to Venerable Nandaka, and, keeping him on their right, went to the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. While standing to one side, those bhikkhunīs, the Blessed One said this: “Go, bhikkhunīs; it is time.” Then those bhikkhunīs, having paid homage to the Blessed One and, keeping him on their right, departed.
translations.mn146:3: Now at that time the elder bhikkhus were instructing the bhikkhunīs in turn. Venerable Nandaka did not wish to instruct the bhikkhunīs in turn. Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, whose turn is it today to instruct the bhikkhunīs in turn?” “It has been everyone’s turn, venerable sir, to instruct the bhikkhunīs in turn. This Venerable Nandaka, venerable sir, does not wish to instruct the bhikkhunīs in turn.”
translations.mn146:4: Then the Blessed One addressed Venerable Nandaka: “Instruct the bhikkhunīs, Nandaka; exhort the bhikkhunīs, Nandaka; you, brahmin, give the bhikkhunīs a talk on the Dhamma.” “Yes, venerable sir,” Venerable Nandaka replied to the Blessed One, and in the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, when he had returned from the almsround, he went alone to the Rājakārāma to approach it. Those bhikkhunīs saw Venerable Nandaka coming from afar. On seeing him, they prepared a seat and set out water for washing the feet. Venerable Nandaka sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, he washed his feet. Those bhikkhunīs too paid homage to Venerable Nandaka and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhunīs Venerable Nandaka said this:
translations.mn146:5: “There will be a talk by way of questions, sisters. Therein, those who understand should say: ‘We understand’; those who do not understand should say: ‘We do not understand.’ And whoever has doubt or uncertainty should ask me right there: ‘How is this, venerable sir? What is the meaning of this?’” “Even by this much, venerable sir, we are satisfied and pleased, that the master Nandaka invites us.”
translations.mn147:1: Thus have I heard—on one occasion the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind: “The dhammas that ripen Rahula’s liberation are mature. Why don’t I train Rahula further toward the destruction of the taints?” Then the Blessed One, in the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, when he had returned from the almsround, he addressed Venerable Rāhula: “Take a sitting-cloth, Rāhula; we will go to the Blind Men’s Grove for the day’s abiding.” “Yes, venerable sir,” Venerable Rāhula replied to the Blessed One, and taking the sitting-cloth, followed behind the Blessed One, close behind.
translations.mn147:2: Now at that time many thousands of deities were following the Blessed One, thinking: “Today the Blessed One will lead Venerable Rāhula further, to the destruction of the taints.” Then the Blessed One entered the Dark Wood and sat down on a seat spread out at the root of a certain tree. Venerable Rāhula too, after paying homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. When Venerable Rāhula was seated to one side, the Blessed One said this to him: “What do you think, Rāhula: is the eye permanent or impermanent?” “Impermanent, sir.” “But what is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?” “Suffering, sir.” “But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fitting to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?” “No, sir.”
translations.mn148:16: And this, bhikkhus, is the practice that leads to the arising of identity—one regards the eye as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’;
translations.mn148:2: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma, good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, meaningful and well-expressed; I will proclaim a holy life that is completely fulfilled and purified, that is— the six sixes. Listen to that, attend carefully, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn148:22: And this, bhikkhus, is the practice that leads to the cessation of identity—one regards the eye as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’
translations.mn148:3: “Six internal sense bases are to be understood, six external sense bases are to be understood, six classes of consciousness are to be understood, six classes of contact are to be understood, six classes of feeling are to be understood, six classes of craving are to be understood.
translations.mn148:34: Dependent on the eye, bhikkhus, and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; with contact as condition, feeling arises—pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. When touched by a pleasant feeling, they do not delight, do not welcome it, and do not remain holding to it. The underlying tendency to lust does not underlie them. When touched by a painful feeling, they do not sorrow, do not grieve, do not lament, do not beat their breast and weep, and do not fall into confusion. The underlying tendency to aversion does not underlie them. When touched by a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, they understand as it really is the arising and passing away of that feeling, its gratification, its danger, and the escape. The underlying tendency to ignorance does not underlie them. It is possible, bhikkhus, that one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to lust in regard to pleasant feeling, has dispelled the underlying tendency to aversion in regard to painful feeling, and has eradicated the underlying tendency to ignorance in regard to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, abandoning ignorance and giving rise to knowledge, will in this very life make an end of suffering—this is possible.
translations.mn148:40: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, becomes disenchanted with forms, becomes disenchanted with eye-consciousness, becomes disenchanted with eye-contact, becomes disenchanted with feeling, becomes disenchanted with craving.
translations.mn149:11: And which things, bhikkhus, are to be fully understood by direct knowledge? ‘The five aggregates affected by clinging’—this is the expression, that is: the form aggregate affected by clinging, the feeling aggregate affected by clinging, the perception aggregate affected by clinging, the formations aggregate affected by clinging, the consciousness aggregate affected by clinging. These things are to be fully understood by direct knowledge. And which things, bhikkhus, are to be abandoned by direct knowledge? Ignorance and craving for existence—these things are to be abandoned by direct knowledge. And which things, bhikkhus, are to be developed by direct knowledge? Serenity and insight—these things are to be developed by direct knowledge. And which things, bhikkhus, are to be realized by direct knowledge? Knowledge and liberation—these things are to be realized by direct knowledge.
translations.mn149:2: “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Discourse on the Great Six Sense Bases. Listen to that, attend carefully, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn149:3: “Not knowing, not seeing as it really is the eye; not knowing, not seeing as it really is forms; not knowing, not seeing as it really is eye-consciousness; not knowing, not seeing as it really is eye-contact; and not knowing, not seeing as it really is the feeling—pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises dependent on eye-contact; one lusts for the eye, lusts for forms, lusts for eye-consciousness, lusts for eye-contact, lusts for the feeling—pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises dependent on eye-contact. For one who is lustful, tied to it, confused, dwelling contemplating gratification, in the future the five aggregates affected by clinging grow. And their craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there, grows. Their bodily troubles grow, and their mental troubles grow; their bodily torments grow, and their mental torments grow; their bodily fevers grow, and their mental fevers grow. They experience bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:8: For one who is lustful, tied to it, confused, dwelling contemplating gratification, in the future the five aggregates affected by clinging grow. And their craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there, grows. Their bodily troubles grow, and their mental troubles grow; their bodily torments grow, and their mental torments grow; their bodily fevers grow, and their mental fevers grow. They experience bodily suffering and mental suffering.
translations.mn149:9: And, bhikkhus, knowing and seeing the eye as it actually is, knowing and seeing forms as they actually are, knowing and seeing eye-consciousness as it actually is, knowing and seeing eye-contact as it actually is, and knowing and seeing as it actually is whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact—whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he does not lust after the eye, he does not lust after forms, he does not lust after eye-consciousness, he does not lust after eye-contact, he does not lust after whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact—whether pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. For that one who is without lust, unfettered, unconfused, dwelling contemplating the danger, in the future the five clinging-aggregates go to decline. And his craving, which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting now here now there, is abandoned. His bodily distresses are abandoned, and his mental distresses are abandoned; his bodily torments are abandoned, and his mental torments are abandoned; his bodily fevers are abandoned, and his mental fevers are abandoned. He experiences bodily pleasure and mental pleasure.
translations.mn19:11: Whatever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon, in that way the mind inclines. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon the thought of renunciation, having abandoned the thought of sensuality, having made much of the thought of renunciation, then his mind inclines to that thought of renunciation. And if, bhikkhus, …pe… and if, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon the thought of non-harming, having abandoned the thought of harming, having made much of the thought of non-harming, then his mind inclines to that thought of non-harming.
translations.mn19:12: Just as, bhikkhus, in the last month of the hot season, when all the crops have been brought in and stored by the village, a cowherd might guard the cows, then, whether he has gone to the root of a tree or has gone out into the open, mindfulness is just what should be done: ‘Those are the cows.’ Even so, bhikkhus, mindfulness was just what should be done: ‘These are the states.’
translations.mn19:13: But, bhikkhus, my energy was aroused, not slack; mindfulness was established, not confused; the body was tranquil, not agitated; the mind was concentrated, unified.
translations.mn19:14: Then I, bhikkhus, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, entered upon and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is with thought and examination, born of seclusion, with rapture and pleasure.
translations.mn19:24: This, bhikkhus, was the third knowledge attained by me in the last watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose; as happens in one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn19:25: Just as, bhikkhus, in a forest wilderness there is a great low-lying marshy pond. A great herd of deer might depend on it and dwell. Then some man might arise who desires their harm, who desires their ill, who desires their insecurity. He might block the safe, secure, blissful path, open a bad path, set out a decoy, and place a decoy-man. For in that way, bhikkhus, that great herd of deer would at a later time meet with misfortune and disaster. But then, bhikkhus, for that very great herd of deer some man might arise who desires their good, who desires their welfare, who desires their security. He might open the safe, secure, blissful path, block the bad path, remove the decoy, and destroy the decoy-man. For in that way, bhikkhus, that great herd of deer would at a later time come to growth, increase, and abundance.
translations.mn19:26: This simile, bhikkhus, was made by me to make the meaning understood. And this is the meaning here: ‘a great low-lying marshy pond’ is a designation for sensual pleasures. ‘A great herd of deer’ is a designation for beings. ‘A man who desires their harm, who desires their ill, who desires their insecurity’ is a designation for Māra the Evil One. ‘The bad path’ is a designation for the wrong eightfold path, that is: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration. ‘The decoy’ is a designation for delight and lust. ‘The decoy-man’ is a designation for ignorance. ‘A man who desires their good, who desires their welfare, who desires their security’ is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the perfectly awakened one. ‘The safe, secure, blissful path’ is a designation for the noble eightfold path, that is: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. Thus, bhikkhus, the safe, secure, blissful path has been opened by me, the bad path blocked, the decoy removed, the decoy-man destroyed.
translations.mn19:3: While I, bhikkhus, was dwelling thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, a thought of sensuality arose in me. I understood thus: ‘This thought of sensuality has arisen in me. And it leads to my own affliction, it leads to others’ affliction, it leads to the affliction of both; it blocks wisdom, is on the side of distress, and does not lead to Nibbāna.’ When I reflected, bhikkhus, ‘it leads to my own affliction,’ it vanished in me; when I reflected, bhikkhus, ‘it leads to others’ affliction,’ it vanished in me; when I reflected, bhikkhus, ‘it leads to the affliction of both,’ it vanished in me; when I reflected, bhikkhus, ‘it blocks wisdom, is on the side of distress, and does not lead to Nibbāna,’ it vanished in me. Then I, bhikkhus, abandoned, dispelled, ended, and obliterated each and every arisen thought of sensuality.
translations.mn19:6: Whatever, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon, in that way the mind inclines. If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon the thought of sensuality, having abandoned the thought of renunciation, having made much of the thought of sensuality, then his mind inclines to that thought of sensuality. And if, bhikkhus, a thought of ill will …pe… and if, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu frequently thinks and ponders upon the thought of harming, having abandoned the thought of non-harming, having made much of the thought of harming, then his mind inclines to that thought of harming.
translations.mn19:7: Suppose, bhikkhus, in the last month of the rainy season, at the time of autumn, when the crops are close together, a cowherd were to guard the cows. He would strike and beat those cows from place to place with a stick; he would block them and keep them back. For what reason? For that cowherd, bhikkhus, sees from that a beating or binding or loss or blame. Even so, bhikkhus, I saw the danger, the degradation, the defilement in unwholesome states, and the benefit of renunciation, the side of cleansing, in wholesome states.
translations.mn19:8: For me, bhikkhus, abiding thus diligent, ardent, resolute, a thought of renunciation arises. I understand thus: ‘This thought of renunciation has arisen in me. It does not lead to afflicting myself, it does not lead to afflicting others, it does not lead to afflicting both; it is productive of wisdom, on the side of non-distress, leading to Nibbāna.’ Even if, bhikkhus, I were to think and ponder upon it during the night, I see no danger arising from that. Even if, bhikkhus, I were to think and ponder upon it during the day, I see no danger arising from that. Even if, bhikkhus, I were to think and ponder upon it night and day, I see no danger arising from that. But as I think and ponder upon it for too long, my body would become tired. When the body is tired, the mind becomes strained. With the mind strained, the mind is far from concentration. Then, bhikkhus, I steady the mind within myself, settle it, make it unified, and concentrate it. For what reason? ‘Let not my mind be strained.’
translations.mn1:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Ukkaṭṭhā in the Subhaga Grove at the root of a royal sāla tree. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn1:10: They perceive Brahmā as Brahmā; having perceived Brahmā as Brahmā, they conceive about Brahmā, they conceive in Brahmā, they conceive from Brahmā, they conceive ‘Brahmā is mine’, they delight in Brahmā. For what reason? I say, ‘It has not been fully understood by them.’
translations.mn1:11: They perceive the Ābhassara gods as Ābhassara gods; having perceived the Ābhassara gods as Ābhassara gods, they conceive about the Ābhassara gods, they conceive in the Ābhassara gods, they conceive from the Ābhassara gods, they conceive ‘The Ābhassara gods are mine’, they delight in the Ābhassara gods. For what reason? I say, ‘It has not been fully understood by them.’
translations.mn1:123: And that bhikkhu too, bhikkhus, who is an arahant, with taints destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, with the fetters to existence exhausted, liberated by right final knowledge—he too directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive about earth, he does not conceive in earth, he does not conceive from earth, he does not conceive ‘Earth is mine’, he does not delight in earth. For what reason? Through the ending of delusion, because he is free from delusion.
translations.mn1:13: They perceive the Vehapphala gods as Vehapphala gods; having perceived the Vehapphala gods as Vehapphala gods, they conceive about the Vehapphala gods, they conceive in the Vehapphala gods, they conceive from the Vehapphala gods, they conceive ‘The Vehapphala gods are mine’, they delight in the Vehapphala gods. For what reason? I say, ‘It has not been fully understood by them.’
translations.mn1:14: They perceive the Overlord as Overlord; having perceived the Overlord as Overlord, they conceive about the Overlord, they conceive in the Overlord, they conceive from the Overlord, they conceive ‘The Overlord is mine’, they delight in the Overlord. For what reason? I say, ‘It has not been fully understood by them.’
translations.mn1:147: The Tathāgata too, bhikkhus, an arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive about earth, he does not conceive in earth, he does not conceive from earth, he does not conceive ‘Earth is mine’, he does not delight in earth. For what reason? I say, ‘It has been fully understood by the Tathāgata.’
translations.mn1:171: The Tathāgata too, bhikkhus, an arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive about earth, he does not conceive in earth, he does not conceive from earth, he does not conceive ‘Earth is mine’, he does not delight in earth. For what reason? ‘Delight is the root of suffering’—having thus known, ‘From existence comes birth, and for what has come to be, aging-and-death.’ Therefore, bhikkhus, I say: ‘The Tathāgata, by the destruction of all craving, through fading away, cessation, relinquishment, and letting go, has awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.’
translations.mn1:19: They perceive the seen as the seen; having perceived the seen as the seen, they conceive about the seen, they conceive in the seen, they conceive from the seen, they conceive ‘The seen is mine’, they delight in the seen. For what reason? I say, ‘It has not been fully understood by them.’
translations.mn1:2: “I will teach you, bhikkhus, the exposition of the root of all things. Listen to that, attend to it closely; I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn1:20: They perceive the heard as the heard; having perceived the heard as the heard, they conceive about the heard, they conceive in the heard, they conceive from the heard, they conceive ‘The heard is mine’, they delight in the heard. For what reason? I say, ‘It has not been fully understood by them.’
translations.mn1:22: They perceive the known as the known; having perceived the known as the known, they conceive about the known, they conceive in the known, they conceive from the known, they conceive ‘The known is mine’, they delight in the known. For what reason? I say, ‘It has not been fully understood by them.’
translations.mn1:23: They perceive unity as unity; having perceived unity as unity, they conceive about unity, they conceive in unity, they conceive from unity, they conceive ‘Unity is mine’, they delight in unity. For what reason? I say, ‘It has not been fully understood by them.’
translations.mn1:24: They perceive diversity as diversity; having perceived diversity as diversity, they conceive about diversity, they conceive in diversity, they conceive from diversity, they conceive ‘Diversity is mine’, they delight in diversity. For what reason? I say, ‘It has not been fully understood by them.’
translations.mn1:25: They perceive all as all; having perceived all as all, they conceive about all, they conceive in all, they conceive from all, they conceive ‘All is mine’, they delight in all. For what reason? I say, ‘It has not been fully understood by them.’
translations.mn1:27: And that bhikkhu too, bhikkhus, who is a trainee, not yet attained in mind, dwelling aspiring to the unsurpassed security from bondage—he too directly knows earth as earth; having directly known earth as earth: ‘May he not conceive about earth; may he not conceive in earth; may he not conceive from earth; may he not conceive “Earth is mine”; may he not delight in earth.’ For what reason? I say, ‘It is to be fully understood by him.’
translations.mn1:3: "Here, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person—one who has not seen the noble ones, unskilled in the noble Dhamma, untrained in the noble Dhamma; one who has not seen true persons, unskilled in the Dhamma of true persons, untrained in the Dhamma of true persons—perceives earth as earth. Having perceived earth as earth, they conceive about earth, they conceive in earth, they conceive from earth, they conceive 'earth is mine', they delight in earth. For what reason? I say: 'It has not been fully understood by them.'
translations.mn1:4: They perceive water as water. Having perceived water as water, they conceive about water, they conceive in water, they conceive from water, they conceive 'water is mine', they delight in water. For what reason? I say: 'It has not been fully understood by them.'
translations.mn1:5: They perceive fire as fire. Having perceived fire as fire, they conceive about fire, they conceive in fire, they conceive from fire, they conceive 'fire is mine', they delight in fire. For what reason? I say: 'It has not been fully understood by them.'
translations.mn1:51: "And that bhikkhu too, bhikkhus, who is an arahant, with taints destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, with the fetter of existence exhausted, liberated by right knowing—he too directly knows earth as earth. Having directly known earth as earth, he does not conceive about earth, he does not conceive in earth, he does not conceive from earth, he does not conceive 'earth is mine', he does not delight in earth. For what reason? I say: 'It has been fully understood by him.'
translations.mn1:7: They perceive beings as beings. Having perceived beings as beings, they conceive about beings, they conceive in beings, they conceive from beings, they conceive 'beings are mine', they delight in beings. For what reason? I say: 'It has not been fully understood by them.'
translations.mn1:8: They perceive devas as devas. Having perceived devas as devas, they conceive about devas, they conceive in devas, they conceive from devas, they conceive 'devas are mine', they delight in devas. For what reason? I say: 'It has not been fully understood by them.'
translations.mn1:9: They perceive Pajāpati as Pajāpati. Having perceived Pajāpati as Pajāpati, they conceive about Pajāpati, they conceive in Pajāpati, they conceive from Pajāpati, they conceive 'Pajāpati is mine', they delight in Pajāpati. For what reason? I say: 'It has not been fully understood by them.'
translations.mn20:2: "Bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind, five signs should from time to time be attended to. What five?
translations.mn22:12: Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever meaning you understand of what I have said, you should bear it in mind accordingly. But whatever meaning you do not understand of what I have said, you should question me about it, or else the competent bhikkhus.
translations.mn22:14: Bhikkhus, I have taught you the Dhamma comparable to a raft: for those who understand, even dhammas should be abandoned—how much more what is not Dhamma.
translations.mn22:18: When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: "Could there be, venerable sir, anxiety when what is external does not exist?" "There could be, bhikkhus," the Blessed One said. "Here a bhikkhu has this in some case: 'Oh, I had that, but now I do not have it; oh, I might have that, but I do not get it.' He grieves, languishes, laments, beats his breast and weeps, and falls into confusion. Thus, bhikkhu, there is anxiety when what is external does not exist."
translations.mn22:19: "But could there be, venerable sir, no anxiety when what is external does not exist?" "There could be, bhikkhus," the Blessed One said. "Here a bhikkhu does not in some case have this: 'Oh, I had that, but now I do not have it; oh, I might have that, but I do not get it.' He does not grieve, does not languish, does not lament, does not beat his breast and weep, and does not fall into confusion. Thus, bhikkhu, there is no anxiety when what is external does not exist."
translations.mn22:20: "Could there be, venerable sir, anxiety when what is internal does not exist?" "There could be, bhikkhus," the Blessed One said. "Here, bhikkhu, someone has this view: 'That world is the self; after death I will be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change; I will stand just the same for eternity.' He hears the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata teaching the Dhamma for the uprooting of all standpoints for views, fixations, obsessions, and underlying tendencies; for the stilling of all formations; for the relinquishing of all acquisitions; for the destruction of craving; for dispassion; for cessation; for Nibbāna. It occurs to him: 'I will be annihilated! I will perish! I will be no more!' He grieves, languishes, laments, beats his breast and weeps, and falls into confusion. Thus, bhikkhu, there is anxiety when what is internal does not exist."
translations.mn22:23: Bhikkhus, would you take up that clinging to a doctrine of self such that, when taking up that clinging to a doctrine of self, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would not arise? Do you see, bhikkhus, that clinging to a doctrine of self such that, when taking up that clinging to a doctrine of self, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would not arise?" "No, venerable sir." "Good, bhikkhus. I too, bhikkhus, do not see that clinging to a doctrine of self such that, when taking up that clinging to a doctrine of self, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would not arise."
translations.mn22:24: Bhikkhus, would you rely on that support of views such that, when relying on that support of views, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would not arise? Do you see, bhikkhus, that support of views such that, when relying on that support of views, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would not arise?" "No, venerable sir." "Good, bhikkhus. I too, bhikkhus, do not see that support of views such that, when relying on that support of views, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would not arise."
translations.mn22:25: "Bhikkhus, when there is a self, would there be (the notion) 'what belongs to my self'?" "Yes, venerable sir." "Bhikkhus, when there is what belongs to a self, would there be (the notion) 'my self'?" "Yes, venerable sir." "But when a self and what belongs to a self are not found as real and true, then that very standpoint for views—'that world is the self; after death I will be permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change; I will stand just the same for eternity'—is it not, bhikkhus, sheer and complete foolishness?" "How could it not be, venerable sir? For it is, venerable sir, sheer and complete foolishness."
