translations.mn22:27: “Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever form there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ Whatever feeling … whatever perception … whatever formations … whatever consciousness there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’
translations.mn22:28: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, becomes disenchanted with feeling, becomes disenchanted with perception, becomes disenchanted with formations, becomes disenchanted with consciousness,
translations.mn22:29: through disenchantment they become dispassionate; through dispassion they are liberated; when liberated there is the knowledge: ‘Liberated.’ They understand: ‘Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’
translations.mn22:30: This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu with the bar removed, and also one with the moat filled in, and also one with the pillar uprooted, and also one without a bar, and also a noble one with the banner lowered, the burden laid down, detached.
translations.mn22:31: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one with the bar removed? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s ignorance is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more, of a nature not to arise again in the future. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one with the bar removed.
translations.mn22:32: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one with the moat filled in? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s round of rebirth, the cycle of birth and wandering on, is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more, of a nature not to arise again in the future. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one with the moat filled in.
translations.mn22:33: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu one with the pillar uprooted? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s craving is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more, of a nature not to arise again in the future. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one with the pillar uprooted.
translations.mn22:34: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu without a bar? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s five lower fetters are abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that they are no more, of a nature not to arise again in the future. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is without a bar.
translations.mn22:35: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu a noble one with the banner lowered, the burden laid down, detached? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s conceit ‘I am’ is abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, obliterated so that it is no more, of a nature not to arise again in the future. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is a noble one with the banner lowered, the burden laid down, detached.
translations.mn22:38: In this case, bhikkhus, if others honor the Tathāgata, respect him, esteem him, and venerate him, there is no delight for the Tathāgata in that, no gladness, no elation of mind. And if others honor the Tathāgata, respect him, esteem him, and venerate him, then, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata thinks: ‘This has been fully understood before; such courtesies are being done to me in regard to that.’
translations.mn22:39: Therefore, bhikkhus, even if others should abuse you, revile you, anger you, and harass you, in that you should not produce resentment, displeasure, or dissatisfaction of mind. Therefore, bhikkhus, even if others should honor you, respect you, esteem you, and venerate you, in that you should not produce delight, gladness, or elation of mind. Therefore, bhikkhus, even if others should honor you, respect you, esteem you, and venerate you, then you should think thus: ‘This has been fully understood before; such courtesies are being done to me in regard to that.’
translations.mn22:40: Therefore, bhikkhus, abandon what is not yours; when you have abandoned it, that will be for your welfare and happiness for a long time.
translations.mn22:42: Thus, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me—plain, open, made manifest, with the patchwork cut off. In the Dhamma thus well proclaimed by me—plain, open, made manifest, with the patchwork cut off—those bhikkhus who are arahants, with taints ended, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, with the fetters to existence exhausted, liberated by right understanding: there is no round for them for designation.
translations.mn22:43: Thus, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me—plain, open, made manifest, with the patchwork cut off. In the Dhamma thus well proclaimed by me—plain, open, made manifest, with the patchwork cut off—those bhikkhus for whom the five lower fetters are abandoned, all of them are spontaneously arisen; there they attain final Nibbāna, not subject to return from that world.
translations.mn22:44: Thus, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me—plain, open, made manifest, with the patchwork cut off. In the Dhamma thus well proclaimed by me—plain, open, made manifest, with the patchwork cut off—those bhikkhus for whom three fetters are abandoned, and lust, hate, and delusion are weakened, all of them are once-returners: returning to this world only once, they will make an end of suffering.
translations.mn22:45: Thus, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me—plain, open, made manifest, with the patchwork cut off. In the Dhamma thus well proclaimed by me—plain, open, made manifest, with the patchwork cut off—those bhikkhus for whom three fetters are abandoned, all of them are stream-enterers, not subject to perdition, fixed in destiny, bound for enlightenment.
translations.mn22:46: Thus, bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been well proclaimed by me—plain, open, made manifest, with the patchwork cut off. In the Dhamma thus well proclaimed by me—plain, open, made manifest, with the patchwork cut off—those bhikkhus who are followers of the Dhamma and followers by faith, all of them are bound for enlightenment.
translations.mn22:6: “How could you, foolish man, understand that I have taught the Dhamma in this way? Have I not, foolish man, in many ways said that obstructive things are obstructive? And it is enough to lead you, if you indulge in them, to obstruction. I have said that sensual pleasures have little gratification, much suffering, much misery, and that the danger in them is even greater. Sensual pleasures have been said by me to be like a skeleton … sensual pleasures have been said by me to be like a piece of meat … sensual pleasures have been said by me to be like a grass torch … sensual pleasures have been said by me to be like a pit of coals … sensual pleasures have been said by me to be like a dream … sensual pleasures have been said by me to be like something borrowed … sensual pleasures have been said by me to be like fruits on a tree … sensual pleasures have been said by me to be like a sword and butcher’s block … sensual pleasures have been said by me to be like a spear and stake … sensual pleasures have been said by me to be like a snake’s head, with much suffering, much misery, and the danger in them even greater. Yet you, foolish man, by your own wrongly grasped view, misrepresent us, and you harm yourself, and you generate much demerit. For that, foolish man, will be for your harm and suffering for a long time.”
translations.mn22:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “What do you think, bhikkhus? Has not this bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-killer, even been warmed by this Dhamma and discipline?” “How could it be, venerable sir? Certainly not, venerable sir.” When this was said, the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-killer, became silent, embarrassed, with drooping shoulders, head down, brooding, sitting without a reply. Then the Blessed One, knowing the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-killer, to be silent, embarrassed, with drooping shoulders, head down, brooding, without a reply, said this to the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-killer: “You will be recognized, foolish man, by this your own evil adherence to a view. Here I will question the bhikkhus.”
translations.mn22:9: That, bhikkhus, apart from sensual pleasures, apart from perceptions of sensual pleasures, apart from thoughts of sensual pleasures, he would indulge in sensual pleasures—no such case is found.
translations.mn26:10: And what, bhikkhus, do you call things liable to sorrow? Children and wives, bhikkhus, are things liable to sorrow; male and female slaves are things liable to sorrow; goats and sheep are things liable to sorrow; chickens and pigs are things liable to sorrow; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are things liable to sorrow. These supports, bhikkhus, are things liable to sorrow. Here one is tied to them, infatuated with them, engrossed in them; oneself being of a nature liable to sorrow, one seeks only what is liable to sorrow.
translations.mn26:11: And what, bhikkhus, do you call things liable to defilement? Children and wives, bhikkhus, are things liable to defilement; male and female slaves are things liable to defilement; goats and sheep are things liable to defilement; chickens and pigs are things liable to defilement; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are things liable to defilement; gold and silver are things liable to defilement. These supports, bhikkhus, are things liable to defilement. Here one is tied to them, infatuated with them, engrossed in them; oneself being of a nature liable to defilement, one seeks only what is liable to defilement. This, bhikkhus, is the ignoble search.
translations.mn26:13: I too, bhikkhus, before my awakening, when I was not yet fully awakened but was only a bodhisatta, being myself subject to birth sought what is subject to birth; being myself subject to aging sought what is subject to aging; being myself subject to sickness sought what is subject to sickness; being myself subject to death sought what is subject to death; being myself subject to sorrow sought what is subject to sorrow; being myself subject to defilement sought what is subject to defilement. Then, bhikkhus, it occurred to me: ‘Why am I, being myself subject to birth, seeking what is subject to birth; being myself subject to aging … being myself subject to sickness … being myself subject to death … being myself subject to sorrow … being myself subject to defilement, seeking what is subject to defilement? What if I, being myself subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, were to seek the unborn, the unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to aging, having understood the danger in what is subject to aging, were to seek the unaging, the unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to sickness, having understood the danger in what is subject to sickness, were to seek the unsick, the unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to death, having understood the danger in what is subject to death, were to seek the deathless, the unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to sorrow, having understood the danger in what is subject to sorrow, were to seek the sorrowless, the unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna; being myself subject to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, were to seek the undefiled, the unsurpassed security from bondage, Nibbāna.’
translations.mn26:14: Then I, bhikkhus, at a later time, being young, with black hair, endowed with the blessings of youth, in the prime of life, having shaved off my hair and beard though my mother and father did not wish it, with tearful faces weeping, and having put on ochre robes, went forth from the household life into homelessness.
translations.mn26:17: Then I, bhikkhus, seeking what is wholesome, searching for the unsurpassed state of sublime peace, while wandering by stages on tour among the Magadhans, came to Uruvelā, the market town of Senānī. There I saw a delightful stretch of ground and a pleasing grove, and a river flowing with clear water, with a pleasant ford, delightful, and nearby a village for alms. Then, bhikkhus, it occurred to me: ‘This is indeed a delightful stretch of ground, and the grove is pleasing, and the river flows with clear water, with a pleasant ford, delightful, and nearby is a village for alms. This is enough for the striving of a clansman who wishes to strive.’ So I, bhikkhus, sat down right there: ‘This is enough for striving.’
translations.mn26:21: Then, bhikkhus, having understood Brahmā’s request and out of compassion for beings, I surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye. As I surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye, bhikkhus, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to instruct and hard to instruct, some dwelling seeing fear in blame and in the other world, and some dwelling not seeing fear in blame and in the other world. Just as in a pond of blue lotuses, or in a pond of red lotuses, or in a pond of white lotuses, some blue lotuses, or red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, do not rise above the water, and thrive submerged; some blue lotuses, or red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, do not rise above the water, and stand level with the water; some blue lotuses, or red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, rise above the water, and stand unstained by the water; even so, bhikkhus, as I surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye, I saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with keen faculties and with dull faculties, with good qualities and with bad qualities, easy to instruct and hard to instruct, some dwelling seeing fear in blame and in the other world, and some dwelling not seeing fear in blame and in the other world. Then, bhikkhus, I replied to Brahmā Sahampati in verse: ‘Opened are the doors of the deathless for them; let those who have ears release faith. Thinking “it is harmful”, I did not speak the refined Dhamma; among humans, Brahmā, (I will speak) the sublime Dhamma.’ Then, bhikkhus, Brahmā Sahampati, (thinking) ‘the Blessed One has given me the opportunity for teaching the Dhamma,’ paid homage to me, circumambulated me on the right, and disappeared right there.
translations.mn26:25: Upaka the Ājīvaka saw me, bhikkhus, on the road between Gayā and the Bodhi tree. Seeing me, he said this: ‘Your faculties are bright, friend, your complexion is pure and clear. In reference to whom, friend, have you gone forth? Or who is your teacher? Or whose Dhamma do you approve of?’ When this was said, bhikkhus, I addressed Upaka the Ājīvaka in verses: ‘I am one who has overcome all, one who knows all; in regard to all dhammas I am unsoiled. Having abandoned all, freed through the destruction of craving, having directly known by myself—whom should I point to? I have no teacher, and one like me is not found. In the world with its devas, there is no counterpart of mine. For I am an arahant in the world, I am the unsurpassed teacher; I alone am a perfectly awakened one; I am cooled, I am quenched. To set in motion the wheel of Dhamma, I go to the city of Kāsi; in a world become blind, I beat the drum of the deathless.’ ‘According as you claim, friend, you are an arahant, an infinite victor.’ ‘Such as I are victors, those who have reached the destruction of the taints; evil states are conquered by me; therefore, Upaka, I am a victor.’ When this was said, bhikkhus, Upaka the Ājīvaka, saying ‘May it be so, friend,’ shook his head, took a bypath, and departed.
translations.mn26:26: Then, bhikkhus, wandering on tour by stages, I approached Bārāṇasī, the deer park at Isipatana, where the group of five bhikkhus were. The group of five bhikkhus saw me coming from afar. Seeing me, they agreed among themselves: ‘This recluse Gotama is coming—indulgent, turned away from striving, reverted to indulgence. He should not be greeted, nor should one rise up for him; nor should his bowl and robe be received. But a seat should be set out; if he wants, he will sit down.’ Yet as I approached, bhikkhus, the group of five bhikkhus were unable to keep to their own agreement. Some came out to meet me and received my bowl and robe, some prepared a seat, some brought water for washing my feet. But they addressed me by name and with the word “friend”.
translations.mn26:28: When this was said, bhikkhus, I said this to the group of five bhikkhus: ‘Do you acknowledge, bhikkhus, that you have ever known me before as speaking in this way?’ ‘No, venerable sir.’ ‘The Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is an arahant, a perfectly awakened one. Lend ear, bhikkhus; the deathless has been attained; I will instruct you, I will teach Dhamma. Practising according to the instruction, before long—having directly known and realized for yourselves in this very life, you will enter upon and dwell in the consummation of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life to homelessness, that unsurpassed goal.’
translations.mn26:29: I was able, bhikkhus, to convince the group of five bhikkhus. I instructed two bhikkhus, while three bhikkhus went for alms. Whatever the three bhikkhus brought back from their almsround, with that we sustained the group of six. I instructed three bhikkhus, while two bhikkhus went for alms. Whatever the two bhikkhus brought back from their almsround, with that we sustained the group of six.
translations.mn26:30: Then, bhikkhus, the group of five bhikkhus, being thus instructed by me, thus guided, though themselves subject to birth, having understood the danger in what is subject to birth, seeking the unborn, unsurpassed security from bondage—nibbāna—they attained the unborn, unsurpassed security from bondage—nibbāna; though themselves subject to aging, having understood the danger in what is subject to aging, seeking the unaging, unsurpassed security from bondage—nibbāna—they attained the unaging, unsurpassed security from bondage—nibbāna; though themselves subject to illness …pe… though themselves subject to death … though themselves subject to sorrow … though themselves subject to defilement, having understood the danger in what is subject to defilement, seeking the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage—nibbāna—they attained the undefiled, unsurpassed security from bondage—nibbāna. And knowledge and vision arose in them: ‘Unshakable is our liberation; this is the last birth; now there is no more renewed existence.’
translations.mn26:31: There are, bhikkhus, these five cords of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye—agreeable, pleasing, charming, endearing, connected with sensuality, alluring; sounds cognizable by the ear … smells cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … tangibles cognizable by the body—agreeable, pleasing, charming, endearing, connected with sensuality, alluring. These, bhikkhus, are the five cords of sensual pleasure.
translations.mn26:34: Just as, bhikkhus, a forest deer wandering in a woodland thicket goes about confident, stands confident, sits confident, and lies down confident. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, it has not come within range of the hunter. So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu—quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states—enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This is called, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has made Māra blind, made him trackless; having struck down Māra’s eye, he has gone to where the Evil One cannot see him.
translations.mn26:35: Again, bhikkhus, with the stilling of thought and examination, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and without examination, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This is called, bhikkhus … the Evil One.
translations.mn26:36: Again, bhikkhus, with the fading away of rapture too, a bhikkhu dwells equanimous, mindful and fully aware, and feels pleasure with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, one dwells in pleasure.’ This is called, bhikkhus … the Evil One.
translations.mn26:37: Again, bhikkhus, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the earlier passing away of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purification of mindfulness by equanimity. This is called, bhikkhus … the Evil One.
translations.mn26:38: Again, bhikkhus, with the complete transcending of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of resistance, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space, thinking: ‘Infinite is space.’ This is called, bhikkhus … the Evil One.
translations.mn26:39: Again, bhikkhus, with the complete transcending of the base of infinite space, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness, thinking: ‘Infinite is consciousness.’ This is called, bhikkhus … the Evil One.
translations.mn26:4: Then the Blessed One approached the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka. Now at that time several bhikkhus were sitting together in the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka engaged in talk on the Dhamma. Then the Blessed One stood outside at the door, waiting for the talk to end. Then, knowing that the talk had ended, the Blessed One coughed and knocked on the door-bolt. The bhikkhus opened the door for the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One entered the hermitage of the brahmin Rammaka and sat down on the seat that had been prepared. When he was seated, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “What are you sitting together discussing now, bhikkhus? And what talk of yours was left unfinished?” “Venerable sir, it was talk on the Dhamma about the Blessed One himself that was left unfinished; then the Blessed One arrived.” “Good, bhikkhus. For you, bhikkhus, this is fitting—sons of good families who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith—that you should sit together for talk on the Dhamma. When you have gathered together, bhikkhus, there are two things to be done: either talk on the Dhamma or noble silence.”
translations.mn26:40: Again, bhikkhus, with the complete transcending of the base of infinite consciousness, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of nothingness, thinking: ‘There is nothing.’ This is called, bhikkhus … the Evil One.
translations.mn26:41: Again, bhikkhus, with the complete transcending of the base of nothingness, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This is called, bhikkhus … the Evil One.
translations.mn26:5: There are, bhikkhus, these two quests: the noble quest and the ignoble quest. And what, bhikkhus, is the ignoble quest? Here, bhikkhus, someone, being himself subject to birth, seeks what is subject to birth; being himself subject to aging, seeks what is subject to aging; being himself subject to illness, seeks what is subject to illness; being himself subject to death, seeks what is subject to death; being himself subject to sorrow, seeks what is subject to sorrow; being himself subject to defilement, seeks what is subject to defilement.
translations.mn26:6: And what, bhikkhus, do you call ‘subject to birth’? Wives and children, bhikkhus, are subject to birth; female and male slaves are subject to birth; goats and sheep are subject to birth; chickens and pigs are subject to birth; elephants, cattle, horses, and mares are subject to birth; gold and silver are subject to birth. These possessions, bhikkhus, are subject to birth. Bound up, infatuated, and immersed herein, being himself subject to birth, he seeks what is subject to birth alone.
translations.mn27:12: He hears that Dhamma—either a householder or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family. Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata. Endowed with that gaining of faith, he reflects thus: ‘The household life is cramped, a dusty path; going forth is open. It is not easy, living in a home, to live the holy life entirely complete, entirely pure, polished like a conch-shell. Suppose I were to shave off hair and beard, put on saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.’ Then at a later time, abandoning a small or a great mass of wealth, abandoning a small or a great circle of relatives, shaving off hair and beard, putting on saffron robes, he goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
translations.mn27:13: Having gone forth in this way, he lives in accordance with the training and way of life of the bhikkhus. Having abandoned the taking of life, he abstains from taking life; with rod laid down, with weapon laid down, modest, compassionate, he dwells kind and sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings. Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given, taking only what is given, expecting only what is given. With himself thus purified, he dwells. Having abandoned unchastity, he is chaste, living apart, abstaining from the village practice of sexual intercourse. Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech; he speaks truth, is devoted to truth, reliable, trustworthy, not a deceiver of the world. Having abandoned divisive speech, he abstains from divisive speech: having heard here he does not tell it there to cause division among these; or having heard there he does not tell it here to cause division among those. Thus he is one who reunites the divided, promotes the united, delights in concord, rejoices in concord, is glad of concord, and speaks speech that makes for concord. Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech. He speaks such speech as is gentle, pleasing to the ear, agreeable, going to the heart, courteous, liked by many, pleasing to many. Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, what is beneficial, speaks Dhamma, speaks Vinaya; he speaks words worth treasuring, timely, with reasons, well bounded, connected with benefit. He abstains from damaging seed and plant life; he eats once a day, abstains from food at night, refrains from eating at the wrong time; he abstains from dancing, singing, music, and shows; he abstains from wearing garlands, using perfumes and cosmetics, and from adornment and beautification; he abstains from high and luxurious beds; he abstains from accepting gold and silver; he abstains from accepting raw grain; he abstains from accepting raw meat; he abstains from accepting women and girls; he abstains from accepting male and female slaves; he abstains from accepting goats and sheep; he abstains from accepting fowl and pigs; he abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares; he abstains from accepting fields and land; he abstains from running errands and carrying messages; he abstains from buying and selling; he abstains from false weights, false metal, and false measures; he abstains from bribery, deception, fraud, and trickery; he abstains from cutting, killing, binding, robbery, plunder, and violence.
translations.mn27:14: He is content with a robe for protecting the body and with almsfood for sustaining the belly. Wherever he goes, he goes taking only these with him. Just as a bird, wherever it flies, flies carrying its wings as its only burden; so too the bhikkhu is content with a robe for protecting the body and with almsfood for sustaining the belly. Wherever he goes, he goes taking only these with him. Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself the blameless happiness.
translations.mn27:15: On seeing a form with the eye, he is not a grasper of signs and not a grasper of details. Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of the eye unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint; he guards the faculty of the eye; he undertakes restraint of the faculty of the eye. On hearing a sound with the ear … on smelling an odor with the nose … on tasting a flavor with the tongue … on touching a tangible with the body … on cognizing a mind-object with the mind, he is not a grasper of signs and not a grasper of details. Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of the mind unguarded, evil unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint; he guards the faculty of the mind; he undertakes restraint of the faculty of the mind. Endowed with this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself happiness that is unblemished.
translations.mn27:16: He is one who acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside; he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching; he acts with clear comprehension in wearing the outer robe and carrying bowl and robe; he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension in defecating and urinating; he acts with clear comprehension when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking, speaking, and keeping silent.
translations.mn27:17: Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, endowed with this noble contentment, endowed with this noble restraint of the faculties, and endowed with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, he resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a forest thicket, the open air, a heap of straw.
translations.mn27:18: After his meal, on returning from his almsround, he sits down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him. Having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness. Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind without ill will, kind and sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred. Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, perceiving light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor. Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with mind inwardly stilled; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse. Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having crossed beyond doubt, without perplexity regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.
translations.mn27:19: Having abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of the mind that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This too is called, brahmin, the Tathāgata’s track, also the Tathāgata’s resort, also what is gladdened by the Tathāgata. But still the noble disciple does not arrive at the conclusion: ‘The Blessed One is perfectly awakened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced well.’
translations.mn27:2: Now at that time the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi was leaving Sāvatthī in the daytime by an all-white chariot drawn by mares. He saw the wanderer Pilotika coming from afar. On seeing the wanderer Pilotika, he said this: “Come, where is the venerable Vacchāyana coming from in the daytime?” “For I, sir, am coming from the presence of the ascetic Gotama.” “What does the venerable Vacchāyana think—does the ascetic Gotama have excellence in wisdom? He is clever, I think.” “Who am I, sir, and who is to know the ascetic Gotama’s excellence in wisdom? Surely one would have to be such a one as to know the ascetic Gotama’s excellence in wisdom.” “Indeed the venerable Vacchāyana praises the ascetic Gotama with lofty praise.” “And who am I, sir, and who am I to praise the ascetic Gotama? That venerable Gotama is the best of those praised by the praised among devas and humans.” “But seeing what reason does the venerable Vacchāyana have such confidence in the ascetic Gotama?”
translations.mn27:20: Furthermore, brahmin, with the stilling of thought and examination, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without thought and without examination, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This too is said, brahmin …pe… ‘The Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples has practiced well.’
translations.mn27:21: Furthermore, brahmin, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and feels pleasure with the body, that of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, one dwells in pleasure’—and he enters and dwells in the third jhāna. This too is said, brahmin …pe… ‘The Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples has practiced well.’
translations.mn27:22: Furthermore, brahmin, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the earlier disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This too is said, brahmin, ‘the Tathāgata’s track’ as well, ‘frequented by the Tathāgata’ as well, ‘visited by the Tathāgata’ as well. But still the noble disciple does not yet reach a conclusion: ‘The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples has practiced well.’
translations.mn27:3: “Just as, sir, a skilled elephant hunter might enter an elephant wood. He would see in the elephant wood a large elephant footprint, long in length and broad across. He would come to a conclusion: ‘Surely it is a great elephant.’ Even so, sir, when I saw in the ascetic Gotama these four tracks, then I came to the conclusion: ‘The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples has practiced well.’”
translations.mn27:4: “What four? Here, sir, I see certain learned noblemen—astute, trained in the doctrines of others, hair-splitting debaters, who go about as though they were breaking up the views established by wisdom. They hear: ‘Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama will enter such-and-such a village or town.’ They prepare a question: ‘We will go to the ascetic Gotama and ask him this question. If, when asked by us, he answers thus, we will refute him in this debate. And if, when asked by us, he answers thus, we will refute him in this debate.’ They hear: ‘Indeed, sirs, the ascetic Gotama has entered such-and-such a village or town.’ Then they go to where the ascetic Gotama is and approach him. The ascetic Gotama instructs them, urges them, rouses them, and gladdens them with a talk on Dhamma. Having been instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the ascetic Gotama with a talk on Dhamma, they neither ask the ascetic Gotama a question, nor how could they refute him in debate? Rather, they become disciples of that very ascetic Gotama. When, sir, I saw in the ascetic Gotama this first track, then I came to the conclusion: ‘The Blessed One is perfectly enlightened, the Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples has practiced well.’”
translations.mn27:9: Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi went to the Blessed One; having gone, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When he had concluded the courteous and cordial talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi reported to the Blessed One all the conversation and discussion he had had with the wanderer Pilotika. When this was said, the Blessed One said this to the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi: “Not just to this extent, brahmin, is the simile of the elephant’s footprint fulfilled in detail. But, brahmin, listen to how the simile of the elephant’s footprint is fulfilled in detail; attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn28:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. There the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus.” “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn28:10: If, friends, that monk, while recollecting the Buddha in this way, recollecting the Dhamma in this way, recollecting the Saṅgha in this way, does not establish equanimity grounded in the wholesome, then he is stirred and comes to a sense of urgency: ‘It is a loss for me, indeed it is not a gain for me; it is ill-gotten by me, indeed it is not well-gotten by me, that while I recollect the Buddha in this way, recollect the Dhamma in this way, recollect the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity grounded in the wholesome does not become established.’ Just as, friends, a daughter-in-law, seeing her father-in-law, is stirred and comes to a sense of urgency; even so, friends, if that monk, while recollecting the Buddha in this way, recollecting the Dhamma in this way, recollecting the Saṅgha in this way, does not establish equanimity grounded in the wholesome, he is stirred and comes to a sense of urgency: ‘It is a loss for me, indeed it is not a gain for me; it is ill-gotten by me, indeed it is not well-gotten by me, that while I recollect the Buddha in this way, recollect the Dhamma in this way, recollect the Saṅgha in this way, equanimity grounded in the wholesome does not become established.’ But if, friends, that monk, while recollecting the Buddha in this way, recollecting the Dhamma in this way, recollecting the Saṅgha in this way, establishes equanimity grounded in the wholesome, he becomes glad because of that. Even by this much, friends, much has been done by that monk.
translations.mn28:12: There is a time, friends, when the external water element becomes disturbed. It carries off even villages, carries off towns, carries off cities, carries off districts, carries off even parts of districts. There is a time, friends, when in the great ocean waters subside even for a hundred leagues, subside for two hundred leagues, subside for three hundred leagues, subside for four hundred leagues, subside for five hundred leagues, subside for six hundred leagues, subside for seven hundred leagues. There is a time, friends, when in the great ocean water stands even to seven palm-trees, stands to six palm-trees, stands to five palm-trees, stands to four palm-trees, stands to three palm-trees, stands to two palm-trees, stands to just one palm-tree. There is a time, friends, when in the great ocean water stands even to seven men, stands to six men, stands to five men, stands to four men, stands to three men, stands to two men, stands to just one man. There is a time, friends, when in the great ocean water stands even to half a man, stands to the waist, stands to the knee, stands to the ankle. There is a time, friends, when in the great ocean there is not even water enough to wet the joint of a finger. For in that case, friends, the impermanence of even that great external water element would be evident; its nature to be destroyed would be evident; its nature to vanish would be evident; its nature to change would be evident.
translations.mn28:13: But what of this body of a mere measure, taken up through craving: ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’? Then it would not be so for him here …
translations.mn28:14: But if, friends, that monk, while recollecting the Buddha in this way, recollecting the Dhamma in this way, recollecting the Saṅgha in this way, establishes equanimity grounded in the wholesome, he becomes glad because of that.
translations.mn28:17: There is a time, friends, when the external fire element becomes disturbed. It burns even villages, burns towns, burns cities, burns districts, burns even parts of districts. Having reached a green stretch or a bare stretch or a rocky stretch or a watery stretch or a lovely region of ground, it goes out for lack of fuel. There is a time, friends, when they look for fire even with a chicken’s feather, even with a tendon-scrap. For in that case, friends, the impermanence of even that great external fire element would be evident; its nature to be destroyed would be evident; its nature to vanish would be evident; its nature to change would be evident. But what of this body of a mere measure, taken up through craving: ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’?
translations.mn28:18-20: Then it would not be so for him here … if, friends, that monk, while recollecting the Buddha in this way, recollecting the Dhamma in this way, recollecting the Saṅgha in this way, establishes equanimity grounded in the wholesome, he becomes glad because of that. Even by this much, friends, much has been done by that monk.
translations.mn28:2: “Just as, friends, whatever footprints there are of creatures that roam the wild, all of them meet together in the elephant’s footprint; the elephant’s footprint is declared chief among them in terms of its great size; even so, friends, whatever wholesome states there are, all of them are included in the four noble truths. Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.mn28:22: There is a time, friends, when the external wind element becomes disturbed. It carries off even villages, carries off towns, carries off cities, carries off districts, carries off even parts of districts. There is a time, friends, when, in the last month of the hot season, they look for wind even with a palm-leaf fan and with a winnowing basket, and at the mouth of a bellows they do not want even blades of grass. For in that case, friends, the impermanence of even that great external wind element would be evident; its nature to be destroyed would be evident; its nature to vanish would be evident; its nature to change would be evident. But what of this body of a mere measure, taken up through craving: ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’? Then it would not be so for him here.
translations.mn28:23: And if, friends, others abuse that monk, revile him, provoke him, harass him, he understands thus: ‘This painful feeling born of ear-contact has arisen in me.’ And it is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. And he sees that contact too as impermanent; he sees feeling as impermanent; he sees perception as impermanent; he sees formations as impermanent; he sees consciousness as impermanent. His mind leaps toward, grows confident in, becomes steady on, and is resolved upon just the element as its object.
translations.mn28:24: If, friends, others mistreat a monk with what is unwanted, displeasing, and disagreeable—by contact with the hand, by contact with clods, by contact with sticks, by contact with weapons—he understands thus: ‘Such indeed is this body, that in a body that is such, contacts with the hand occur, contacts with clods occur, contacts with sticks occur, contacts with weapons occur. And this was said by the Blessed One in the instruction on the simile of the saw: “Even if, monks, bandits were to carve you limb by limb with a two-handled saw, even then whoever would corrupt their mind there would not be one who carries out my teaching.” Therefore my energy will be aroused and unflagging, mindfulness established and unconfused, the body tranquil and untroubled, the mind concentrated and one-pointed. Let now, in this body, contacts with the hand occur, contacts with clods occur, contacts with sticks occur, contacts with weapons occur. For this is how the Buddha’s teaching is done.’
translations.mn28:26: Just as, friends, dependent on wood and dependent on creepers and dependent on grass and dependent on clay, space enclosed by them comes to be reckoned simply as ‘a house’; even so, friends, dependent on bone and dependent on sinews and dependent on flesh and dependent on skin, space enclosed by them comes to be reckoned simply as ‘form.’
translations.mn28:27: And if, friends, the internal eye is intact, and external forms do not come into its range, and there is no corresponding bringing-to-mind, then there is, as yet, no manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness. And if, friends, the internal eye is intact, and external forms come into its range, but there is no corresponding bringing-to-mind, then there is, as yet, no manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness. But when, friends, the internal eye is intact, and external forms come into its range, and there is corresponding bringing-to-mind, then there is the manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness.
translations.mn28:28: Whatever form there is for one who is such, that is included in the form clinging-aggregate; whatever feeling there is for one who is such, that is included in the feeling clinging-aggregate; whatever perception there is for one who is such, that is included in the perception clinging-aggregate; whatever volitional formations there are for one who is such, those are included in the formations clinging-aggregate; whatever consciousness there is for one who is such, that is included in the consciousness clinging-aggregate. He understands thus: ‘So indeed there is this inclusion, gathering, and coming together of these five clinging-aggregates. And this was said by the Blessed One: “One who sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma; one who sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination.” And these five clinging-aggregates are dependently arisen. Whatever desire, attachment, inclination, and clinging there is in regard to these five clinging-aggregates, that is the origin of suffering. Whatever removal of desire and lust, abandonment of desire and lust, there is in regard to these five clinging-aggregates, that is the cessation of suffering.’ Even to this extent, friends, much has been done by a monk.
translations.mn28:3: And what, friends, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair are suffering; not getting what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five clinging-aggregates are suffering. And what, friends, are the five clinging-aggregates? That is: the form clinging-aggregate, the feeling clinging-aggregate, the perception clinging-aggregate, the formations clinging-aggregate, the consciousness clinging-aggregate.
translations.mn28:37: The mind is intact, and external mental phenomena do not come into its range, and there is no corresponding bringing-to-mind; then there is, as yet, no manifestation of the corresponding portion of consciousness.
translations.mn28:7: There is, friends, a time when the external water element becomes agitated. At that time the external earth element disappears. For even in the case of that external earth element, great though it is, impermanence will be evident, its nature to decay will be evident, its nature to vanish will be evident, its nature to change will be evident. How much more, then, in this body a mere measure, taken up by craving, is there ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’? Rather, indeed, it is not so in this case.
translations.mn29:1: Thus have I heard— At one time the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak, not long after Devadatta had departed. There the Blessed One, in reference to Devadatta, addressed the monks:
translations.mn29:3: Here, monks, some clansman, out of faith, has gone forth from the household life into homelessness: ‘I am submerged by birth, aging, and death; by sorrows, lamentations, pains, displeasures, and despairs; submerged in suffering, overwhelmed by suffering—perhaps an end of this whole mass of suffering might be made known.’ Having gone forth thus, he produces gain, honor, and fame. He is not satisfied with that gain, honor, and fame, nor is his resolve fulfilled. Because of that gain, honor, and fame he does not exalt himself or disparage others. Because of that gain, honor, and fame he does not become intoxicated, does not become negligent, does not fall into negligence. Being heedful, he accomplishes the attainment of virtue. He is satisfied with that attainment of virtue; his resolve is fulfilled. Because of that attainment of virtue he exalts himself and disparages others: ‘I am virtuous, of good qualities; but these other monks are unvirtuous, of bad qualities.’ Because of that attainment of virtue he becomes intoxicated, becomes negligent, falls into negligence; being negligent, he dwells in suffering. Just as, monks, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, would come upon a great tree standing, possessing heartwood, and—having passed over the heartwood, passed over the sapwood, passed over the inner bark—would cut off and take away the outer bark, thinking it “heartwood.” A man with good eyes, seeing him, would say thus: ‘This good man did not know heartwood, did not know sapwood, did not know inner bark, did not know outer bark, did not know branches and foliage. For this good man, needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, searching for heartwood, came upon a great tree standing, possessing heartwood, and—having passed over the heartwood, passed over the sapwood, passed over the inner bark—cut off and took away the outer bark, thinking it “heartwood”; and he will not obtain the benefit for which heartwood is needed.’
translations.mn2:10: And what, bhikkhus, are things that should not be attended to, such that one does not attend to those things? When, bhikkhus, one attends to things, an unarisen influx of sensual desire arises, or an arisen influx of sensual desire increases; an unarisen influx of being arises, or an arisen influx of being increases; an unarisen influx of ignorance arises, or an arisen influx of ignorance increases—these are things that should not be attended to, such that one does not attend to those things. And what, bhikkhus, are things that should be attended to, such that one attends to those things? When, bhikkhus, one attends to things, an unarisen influx of sensual desire does not arise, or an arisen influx of sensual desire is abandoned; an unarisen influx of being does not arise, or an arisen influx of being is abandoned; an unarisen influx of ignorance does not arise, or an arisen influx of ignorance is abandoned—these are things that should be attended to, such that one attends to those things. By not attending to things that should not be attended to, and by attending to things that should be attended to, unarisen influxes do not arise and arisen influxes are abandoned.
translations.mn2:11: They attend wisely: ‘This is suffering,’ they attend wisely: ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ they attend wisely: ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ they attend wisely: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’ For one who attends wisely in this way, three fetters are abandoned—identity view, doubt, and adherence to rules and observances. These are called, bhikkhus, the influxes to be abandoned by seeing.
translations.mn2:12: 2. Influxes to be abandoned by restraint  And what, bhikkhus, are the influxes to be abandoned by restraint? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having reflected wisely, dwells restrained with the restraint of the faculty of the eye. For one, bhikkhus, who dwells unrestrained in the restraint of the faculty of the eye, influxes of distress and fever might arise; for one who dwells restrained in the restraint of the faculty of the eye, those influxes of distress and fever are not. Having reflected wisely, they dwell restrained with the restraint of the faculty of the ear … the restraint of the faculty of the nose … the restraint of the faculty of the tongue … the restraint of the faculty of the body … they dwell restrained with the restraint of the faculty of the mind. For one, bhikkhus, who dwells unrestrained in the restraint of the faculty of the mind, influxes of distress and fever might arise; for one who dwells restrained in the restraint of the faculty of the mind, those influxes of distress and fever are not. For one, bhikkhus, who dwells unrestrained in restraint, influxes of distress and fever might arise; for one who dwells restrained in restraint, those influxes of distress and fever are not. These are called, bhikkhus, the influxes to be abandoned by restraint.
translations.mn2:14: Having reflected wisely, they use almsfood: ‘not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for adornment, not for beautification, but only for the maintenance and continuance of this body, for ending affliction, for supporting the holy life; thus I shall destroy old feeling and not give rise to new feeling, and there will be for me sustenance and blamelessness and comfortable abiding.’
translations.mn2:16: Having reflected wisely, they use medicines and provisions for the sick: ‘only for the warding off of arisen painful feelings of illness, for the highest freedom from affliction.’
translations.mn2:17: For one, bhikkhus, who would not use them, influxes of distress and fever might arise; for one who uses them, those influxes of distress and fever are not. These are called, bhikkhus, the influxes to be abandoned by use.
translations.mn2:3: ‘Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the influxes is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. And what, bhikkhus, do I say is the destruction of the influxes for one who knows and sees? Wise attention and unwise attention. For one who attends unwisely, bhikkhus, unarisen influxes arise and arisen influxes increase; but for one who attends wisely, bhikkhus, unarisen influxes do not arise and arisen influxes are abandoned.
translations.mn2:6: And what, bhikkhus, are things that should not be attended to, such that one attends to those things? When, bhikkhus, one attends to things, an unarisen influx of sensual desire arises, or an arisen influx of sensual desire increases; an unarisen influx of being arises, or an arisen influx of being increases; an unarisen influx of ignorance arises, or an arisen influx of ignorance increases—these are things that should not be attended to, such that one attends to those things. And what, bhikkhus, are things that should be attended to, such that one does not attend to those things? When, bhikkhus, one attends to things, an unarisen influx of sensual desire does not arise, or an arisen influx of sensual desire is abandoned; an unarisen influx of being does not arise, or an arisen influx of being is abandoned; an unarisen influx of ignorance does not arise, or an arisen influx of ignorance is abandoned—these are things that should be attended to, such that one does not attend to those things.
translations.mn2:7: By attending to things that should not be attended to and by not attending to things that should be attended to, unarisen influxes arise and arisen influxes increase. They attend unwisely in this way: ‘Was I in the past? Was I not in the past? What was I in the past? How was I in the past? Having been what, what was I in the past? Will I be in the future? Will I not be in the future? What will I be in the future? How will I be in the future? Having been what, what will I be in the future?’ Or else, regarding the present period, they are inwardly perplexed: ‘Am I? Am I not? What am I? How am I? Where has this being come from? Where will it go?’
translations.mn2:8: As he attends in an unwise way, one of six views arises in him: either the view ‘I have a self’ arises in him as true and established; or the view ‘I have no self’ arises in him as true and established; or the view ‘By self I perceive self’ arises in him as true and established; or the view ‘By self I perceive not-self’ arises in him as true and established; or the view ‘By not-self I perceive self’ arises in him as true and established; or else he has this view: ‘This self of mine that speaks and feels, that experiences the results of good and bad deeds here and there—this self of mine is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain the same for eternity.’ This is called, bhikkhus, a thicket of views, a wilderness of views, a contortion of views, a writhing of views, a fetter of views. Bound by the fetter of views, bhikkhus, the uninstructed ordinary person is not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair; I say, ‘he is not freed from suffering.’
translations.mn2:9: But the instructed noble disciple, bhikkhus—one who has seen the noble ones, who is skilled in the noble Dhamma, well trained in the noble Dhamma; who has seen good persons, who is skilled in the Dhamma of good persons, well trained in the Dhamma of good persons—understands what things are to be attended to and understands what things are not to be attended to. Understanding what things are to be attended to and what things are not to be attended to, he does not attend to those things that are not to be attended to; he attends to those things that are to be attended to.
translations.mn31:10: “Good, good, Anuruddhas. But, Anuruddhas, while you dwell thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, have you attained any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, any peaceful abiding, beyond the human state?” “How could there not be, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, we enter upon and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, born of seclusion, with rapture and pleasure. This, venerable sir, is for us—dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute—a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, attained as a peaceful abiding, beyond the human state.”
translations.mn31:11-13: “Good, good, Anuruddhas. But, Anuruddhas, with the going beyond of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, have you attained any other distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, any peaceful abiding, beyond the human state?” “How could there not be, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we wish, with the stilling of thought and examination, with inner confidence and unification of mind, we enter upon and dwell in the second jhāna, which is without thought and without examination, born of concentration, with rapture and pleasure. With the going beyond of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, this other distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, attained as a peaceful abiding, beyond the human state.”
translations.mn31:14: “Good, good, Anuruddhas. But, Anuruddhas, with the going beyond of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, have you attained any other distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, any peaceful abiding, beyond the human state?” “How could there not be, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we wish, with the fading away of rapture we dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and we feel pleasure with the body, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, one dwells in pleasure’; we enter upon and dwell in the third jhāna. With the going beyond of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, this other distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, attained as a peaceful abiding, beyond the human state.”
translations.mn31:15: “Good, good, Anuruddhas. But, Anuruddhas, with the going beyond of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, have you attained any other distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, any peaceful abiding, beyond the human state?” “How could there not be, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we wish, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and displeasure, we enter upon and dwell in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, with purification of mindfulness by equanimity. With the going beyond of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, this other distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, attained as a peaceful abiding, beyond the human state.”
translations.mn31:16: “Good, good, Anuruddhas. But, Anuruddhas, with the going beyond of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, have you attained any other distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, any peaceful abiding, beyond the human state?” “How could there not be, venerable sir? Here, venerable sir, whenever we wish, by completely going beyond perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, (perceiving) ‘Infinite is space,’ we enter upon and dwell in the base of infinite space. With the going beyond of this abiding, with the calming of this abiding, this other distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, attained as a peaceful abiding, beyond the human state.”
translations.mn31:19: Then the Blessed One, having instructed, encouraged, inspired, and gladdened the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila with a Dhamma talk, rose from his seat and departed.
translations.mn31:2: Now at that time the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila were dwelling in the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree wood.
translations.mn31:3: Then the Blessed One, in the evening, having emerged from seclusion, approached the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree wood. The park keeper saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Seeing the Blessed One, he said this: “Do not enter this park, ascetic. There are three young men of good family dwelling here, seeking their own good. Do not cause them discomfort.”
translations.mn31:4: The Venerable Anuruddha heard the park keeper conversing with the Blessed One. Having heard, he said this to the park keeper: “Do not, friend park keeper, prevent the Blessed One. Our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.” Then the Venerable Anuruddha approached the Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimila; having approached, he said this to the Venerable Nandiya and the Venerable Kimila: “Come, venerable sirs, come, venerable sirs, our Teacher, the Blessed One, has arrived.”
translations.mn31:5: Then the Venerable Anuruddha, the Venerable Nandiya, and the Venerable Kimila went out to meet the Blessed One: one took the Blessed One’s bowl and robe, one prepared a seat, one set out water for washing the feet. The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One washed his feet. Those venerable ones too, having paid homage to the Blessed One, sat down to one side. Then the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Anuruddha as he was sitting to one side: “I hope you are well, Anuruddhas; I hope you are getting by; I hope you are not weary because of almsfood?” “We are well, Blessed One, we are getting by, Blessed One; and we are not weary because of almsfood, venerable sir.”
translations.mn31:6: “But, Anuruddhas, are you living in concord, with mutual appreciation, without disputing, like milk and water, looking on one another with loving eyes?” “Indeed, venerable sir, we are living in concord, with mutual appreciation, without disputing, like milk and water, looking on one another with loving eyes.” “But how, Anuruddhas, are you living in concord, with mutual appreciation, without disputing, like milk and water, looking on one another with loving eyes?”
translations.mn31:9: “Indeed, venerable sir, we live diligent, ardent, resolute.” “But how, Anuruddhas, do you live diligent, ardent, resolute?” “Here, venerable sir, whoever of us returns first from the village after going for alms sets out the seats, sets out drinking water and water for washing, and sets out the refuse bowl. Whoever returns later from the village after going for alms, if there are leftovers and if he wants, he eats; if he does not want, he throws them away where there is little greenery, or tips them into water without living beings. He puts away the seats, puts away the drinking water and water for washing, puts away the refuse bowl, and sweeps the dining hall. Whoever sees a water pot for drinking or a water pot for washing or a pot for the toilet empty and void sets it out. If it is too much for him, by a gesture of the hand having summoned a second, we set it out with a hand-carrying; but we do not, venerable sir, on that account break into speech. Every five days, venerable sir, we sit together all night in talk on the Dhamma. Thus, venerable sir, we live diligent, ardent, resolute.”
translations.mn36:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was living at Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof.
translations.mn36:10: “Thus I am confident in Master Gotama. For Master Gotama is one who has developed body and has developed mind.” “Surely you have spoken this, Aggivessana, in words that are attacking and offensive; but I will answer you. From the time when I, Aggivessana, having shaved off hair and beard, having put on the ochre robes, went forth from the household life into homelessness, it is not possible that arisen pleasant feeling would invade and remain holding sway over my mind, or that arisen painful feeling would invade and remain holding sway over my mind.”
translations.mn36:12: “For what should it be, Aggivessana? Here, Aggivessana, before my awakening, when I was still unawakened, being just a bodhisatta, this occurred to me: ‘Crowded is the household life, a dusty road; open is going forth. It is not easy, while living in a house, to practice the holy life utterly complete and utterly pure, like a polished shell. What if I were to shave off hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?’
translations.mn36:2: At that time the Blessed One, in the morning, was well dressed and, taking bowl and robe, was wanting to enter Vesālī for alms.
translations.mn36:20: Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me: ‘What if I were to press tongue to palate and, clenching my teeth, were to restrain, subdue, and torment the mind with the mind?’ So I, Aggivessana, clenching my teeth and pressing my tongue to the palate, restrained, subdued, and tormented the mind with the mind. As I, Aggivessana, clenched my teeth and pressed my tongue to the palate and restrained, subdued, and tormented the mind with the mind, sweat poured from my armpits. Just as, Aggivessana, a strong man might seize a weaker man by the head or by the shoulders and restrain him, subdue him, and torment him; even so, Aggivessana, as I clenched my teeth and pressed my tongue to the palate and restrained, subdued, and tormented the mind with the mind, sweat poured from my armpits. But my energy, Aggivessana, was aroused, unflagging; mindfulness was established, not confused; and my body was tense, uncalmed, because I was afflicted by that painful striving, being one who strives. Yet such arisen painful feeling does not invade and remain holding sway over my mind.
translations.mn36:26: And some deities, Aggivessana, seeing me, said thus: ‘The ascetic Gotama is dead.’ Some deities said thus: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not dead, but he is dying.’ Some deities said thus: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not dead, nor is he dying; the ascetic Gotama is an arahant; such is indeed the dwelling of an arahant.’
translations.mn36:27: Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me: ‘What if I were to undertake the complete cutting off of food?’ Then, Aggivessana, deities came up to me and said this: ‘Do not, good sir, undertake the complete cutting off of food. If you, good sir, undertake the complete cutting off of food, then we will infuse divine nourishment into you through the pores of your skin; by that you will get by.’ Then, Aggivessana, this occurred to me: ‘If I were to declare that I am completely fasting, and these deities were to infuse divine nourishment into me through the pores of my skin, and I were to get by by that, that would be a lie for me.’ So I, Aggivessana, refused those deities; I said, ‘Enough.’
translations.mn36:28: Then it occurred to me, Aggivessana: ‘Why don’t I take food little by little, a handful at a time—either bean soup, or vetch soup, or pea soup, or lentil soup?’ So I took food little by little, a handful at a time—either bean soup, or vetch soup, or pea soup, or lentil soup. As I took food little by little, a handful at a time—either bean soup, or vetch soup, or pea soup, or lentil soup—my body came to an extreme state of emaciation. Just as there are joints like the eighty-knot or the black-knot; so too my limbs became like that, because of eating so little. Just as a camel’s hoof; so too my buttocks became like that, because of eating so little. Just as a string of beads; so too my backbone became protruding and bent, because of eating so little. Just as in an old shed the rafters become sagging and drooping; so too my ribs became sagging and drooping, because of eating so little. Just as in a deep well the water-stars, sunk deep down, appear as if looking up; so too in my eye-sockets my eye-stars, sunk deep down, appeared as if looking up, because of eating so little. Just as a bitter gourd, cut raw, becomes shriveled and withered by wind and sun; so too the skin of my head became shriveled and withered, because of eating so little. When I thought, ‘I will touch the skin of my belly,’ I grasped only the backbone; when I thought, ‘I will touch the backbone,’ I grasped only the skin of my belly, so much so, Aggivessana, did the skin of my belly cling to the backbone, because of eating so little. When I thought, ‘I will urinate or defecate,’ I fell face down right there, because of eating so little. When I soothed this very body, I stroked my limbs with my hand. As I stroked my limbs with my hand, the hairs, rotten at the roots, fell from my body, because of eating so little.
translations.mn36:29: And people, Aggivessana, seeing me, said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is black.’ Some people said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is not black; the ascetic Gotama is brown.’ Some people said: ‘The ascetic Gotama is neither black nor brown; the ascetic Gotama has a sallow complexion.’ So much so, Aggivessana, was my formerly clear, bright complexion ruined, because of eating so little.
translations.mn36:3: Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son, while walking and wandering for exercise, went to the great wood, to the hall with the peaked roof. Venerable Ānanda saw Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son coming from afar. Seeing him, he said this to the Blessed One: “This, venerable sir, is Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son coming—a debater, a clever speaker, well regarded by many people. He is one who wants to disparage the Buddha, wants to disparage the Dhamma, wants to disparage the Saṅgha. It would be good, venerable sir, for the Blessed One to sit down for a moment out of compassion.” The Blessed One sat down on the seat that had been prepared. Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after the exchange of courteous and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son said this to the Blessed One:
translations.mn36:30: Then it occurred to me, Aggivessana: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past have felt painful, intense, sharp, severe feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost; there is none beyond this. And whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will feel painful, intense, sharp, severe feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost; there is none beyond this. And whatever ascetics or brahmins now feel painful, intense, sharp, severe feelings due to exertion, this is the utmost; there is none beyond this. But I do not attain, by this painful austerity, anything higher than the human state, a distinction of noble knowledge and vision. Might there be another path to awakening?’
translations.mn36:32: Then it occurred to me, Aggivessana: ‘Why am I afraid of that happiness—that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states?’ Then it occurred to me, Aggivessana: ‘I am not afraid of that happiness—that happiness which is apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states.’
translations.mn36:34: So I, Aggivessana, having eaten solid food and regained strength, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, entered upon and dwelt in the first jhāna, with thought and examination, born of seclusion, with rapture and happiness. Yet even such arisen pleasant feelings, Aggivessana, do not take hold of and overwhelm my mind.
translations.mn36:38: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, pliant, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of recollection of past lives. I recollected manifold past lives, that is—one birth …pe… thus with aspects and details I recollected manifold past lives.
translations.mn36:39: This, Aggivessana, was my first knowledge attained in the first watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose—as happens for one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute. Yet even such arisen pleasant feelings, Aggivessana, do not take hold of and overwhelm my mind.
translations.mn36:4: “There are, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who live devoted to the practice of developing the body, but not of developing the mind. For they, Master Gotama, experience bodily painful feeling. Formerly, Master Gotama, when one is experiencing bodily painful feeling, there will be even stiffness of the thighs, the heart will even split, hot blood will even gush from the mouth, and one will even reach madness, mental derangement. In that case, Master Gotama, the mind is dependent on the body, it proceeds in accordance with the body. What is the reason for that? Because the mind has not been developed. But there are, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who live devoted to the practice of developing the mind, but not of developing the body. For they, Master Gotama, experience mental painful feeling. Formerly, Master Gotama, when one is experiencing mental painful feeling, there will be even stiffness of the thighs, the heart will even split, hot blood will even gush from the mouth, and one will even reach madness, mental derangement. In that case, Master Gotama, the body is dependent on the mind, it proceeds in accordance with the mind. What is the reason for that? Because the body has not been developed. It occurs to me, Master Gotama, thus: ‘Surely Master Gotama’s disciples live devoted to the practice of developing the mind, but not of developing the body.’”
translations.mn36:40: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, pliant, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearing of beings. With the divine eye, purified, surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good destinations and bad destinations; I understood beings according to their actions …
translations.mn36:42: When my mind was thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement, pliant, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of the destruction of the taints. I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is suffering.’ I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering.’ I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering.’ I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’ I directly knew as it really is: ‘These are taints.’ I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the origin of taints.’ I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of taints.’ I directly knew as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of taints.’
translations.mn36:43: When I knew thus and saw thus, my mind was liberated from the taint of sensuality, my mind was liberated from the taint of existence, my mind was liberated from the taint of ignorance. When it was liberated, there came the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’ I directly knew: ‘Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’
translations.mn36:45: Moreover, Aggivessana, I recollect teaching the Dhamma to an assembly of many hundreds. Yet perhaps each one thinks thus: ‘It is about me that the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma.’ But, Aggivessana, it should not be seen like that; the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to others only for the sake of making them understand. Then I, Aggivessana, at the end of that very talk, in that same earlier sign of concentration, steady my mind internally alone, settle it, unify it, concentrate it, by which I dwelled habitually.” “That is believable of Master Gotama, as is fitting for an arahant, a perfectly awakened one. But does Master Gotama recollect sleeping during the day?”
translations.mn36:46: “I recollect, Aggivessana, in the last month of the hot season, after the meal, returning from the alms-round, having spread out the outer robe folded in four, I lay down on my right side, mindful and fully aware, and fell asleep.” “Some ascetics and brahmins, Master Gotama, say this is dwelling in delusion.” “Aggivessana, not just by this is one deluded or not deluded. But, Aggivessana, how one is deluded and how one is not deluded—listen to that, attend carefully, I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn36:47: “Whoever, Aggivessana, has taints that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, ripening in suffering, resulting in future birth, aging, and death, not abandoned—I say that person is ‘deluded.’ For, Aggivessana, by not abandoning the taints one is deluded. Whoever, Aggivessana, has taints that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, ripening in suffering, resulting in future birth, aging, and death, abandoned—I say that person is ‘not deluded.’ For, Aggivessana, by abandoning the taints one is not deluded. But for the Tathāgata, Aggivessana, the taints that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, ripening in suffering, resulting in future birth, aging, and death have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made into nonexistence, not liable to arise again in the future.
