Just as, Aggivessana, a palm tree with its top cut off is incapable of growing again, so too, Aggivessana, for the Tathāgata the taints that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, accompanied by distress, ripening in suffering, resulting in future birth, aging, and death have been abandoned, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made into nonexistence, not liable to arise again in the future.”
translations.mn36:5: “But what, Aggivessana, have you heard is the development of the body?” “That is, Master Gotama—Nanda Vaccha, Kisa Saṅkicca, Makkhali Gosāla—these, Master Gotama, are naked ascetics, of free conduct, lickers of the hand, they do not accept ‘Come, good sir,’ they do not accept ‘Stand, good sir,’ they do not accept what is brought, what is prepared for them, or an invitation; they do not accept from the mouth of a pot, they do not accept from the mouth of a bowl, not from between doorposts, not from between sticks, not from between pestles, not from two people eating, not from a pregnant woman, not from a woman giving suck, not from a woman living with a man, not from where food is distributed, not where a dog is standing, not where flies swarm, they do not drink fish, meat, liquor, spirits, or rice-water. They are one-house eaters and one-mouthful eaters; or they are two-house eaters and two-mouthful eaters … up to they are seven-house eaters and seven-mouthful eaters. They live on even one gift, they live on two gifts … up to they live on seven gifts. They take food once a day, they take food every two days … up to they take food every seven days. Thus they live devoted to the practice of eating by turns even for half a month.”
translations.mn36:6: “But, Aggivessana, do they get by on just that much?” “No, Master Gotama. Sometimes, Master Gotama, they eat the finest solid foods, they eat the finest meals, they taste the finest delicacies, they drink the finest drinks. They take strength into this body, they build it up, they fatten it.” “Whatever, Aggivessana, they gave up earlier and later accumulate, thus there is increase and decrease of this body. But what, Aggivessana, have you heard about the development of mind?” When Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha’s son was questioned by the Blessed One about development of mind, he could not answer.
translations.mn36:8: “And how, Aggivessana, is there an undeveloped body and an undeveloped mind? Here, Aggivessana, in an uninstructed ordinary person a pleasant feeling arises. Being touched by a pleasant feeling, they become infatuated with pleasure and fall into infatuation with pleasure. That pleasant feeling of theirs ceases. With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises. Being touched by a painful feeling, they sorrow, grieve, lament, beat their breast and weep, and fall into confusion. In this way, Aggivessana, even a pleasant feeling that has arisen occupies the mind because the body is undeveloped; even a painful feeling that has arisen occupies the mind because the mind is undeveloped. Whoever, Aggivessana, is in such a two-sided way— even a pleasant feeling that has arisen occupies the mind because the body is undeveloped, and even a painful feeling that has arisen occupies the mind because the mind is undeveloped— thus, Aggivessana, there is an undeveloped body and an undeveloped mind.
translations.mn36:9: And how, Aggivessana, is there a developed body and a developed mind? Here, Aggivessana, in an instructed noble disciple a pleasant feeling arises. Being touched by a pleasant feeling, they do not become infatuated with pleasure and do not fall into infatuation with pleasure. That pleasant feeling of theirs ceases. With the cessation of the pleasant feeling, a painful feeling arises. Being touched by a painful feeling, they do not sorrow, do not grieve, do not lament, do not beat their breast and weep, and do not fall into confusion. In this way, Aggivessana, even a pleasant feeling that has arisen does not occupy the mind because the body is developed; even a painful feeling that has arisen does not occupy the mind because the mind is developed. Whoever, Aggivessana, is in such a two-sided way— even a pleasant feeling that has arisen does not occupy the mind because the body is developed, and even a painful feeling that has arisen does not occupy the mind because the mind is developed— thus, Aggivessana, there is a developed body and a developed mind.”
translations.mn38:10: “‘This is something that has come to be, isn’t it?’—monks, when one is in doubt, does doubt arise?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘It has arisen from that nutriment, isn’t it?’—monks, when one is in doubt, does doubt arise?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘From the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is of a nature to cease, isn’t it?’—monks, when one is in doubt, does doubt arise?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:11: “‘This is something that has come to be’—monks, whatever doubt there is, when one sees with correct wisdom as it actually is, that doubt is abandoned.” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘It has arisen from that nutriment’—monks, whatever doubt there is, when one sees with correct wisdom as it actually is, that doubt is abandoned.” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘From the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is of a nature to cease’—monks, whatever doubt there is, when one sees with correct wisdom as it actually is, that doubt is abandoned.” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:12: “‘This is something that has come to be’—monks, in this you too are free from doubt.” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘It has arisen from that nutriment’—monks, in this you too are free from doubt.” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘From the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is of a nature to cease’—monks, in this you too are free from doubt.” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:13: “‘This is something that has come to be’—monks, as it actually is it is well seen with correct wisdom.” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘It has arisen from that nutriment’—monks, as it actually is it is well seen with correct wisdom.” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘From the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is of a nature to cease’—monks, as it actually is it is well seen with correct wisdom.” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:14: “And if you, monks, would cling to this view—so pure, so clear—would be attached to it, cherish it, treasure it, and take possession of it, would you then understand the teaching I have taught as like a raft: for crossing over, not for holding on to?” “No, venerable sir.” “And if you, monks, would not cling to this view—so pure, so clear—would not be attached to it, would not cherish it, would not treasure it, and would not take possession of it, would you then understand the teaching I have taught as like a raft: for crossing over, not for holding on to?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:15: “There are, monks, these four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of beings that have come to be, or for the support of those seeking existence. What four? Edible food, coarse or fine; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; consciousness as the fourth.
translations.mn38:17: So, monks, with ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:19: “Good, monks. So, monks, you too say thus, and I say thus—when this exists, that is; with the arising of this, that arises; that is: with ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact; with contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:2: Now at that time, in the bhikkhu named Sāti, the fisherman’s son, there had arisen this kind of bad view: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is just this consciousness that runs and wanders on, that transmigrates, and not another.”
translations.mn38:20: But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance there is cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.mn38:22: “Good, bhikkhus. So, bhikkhus, you too speak thus, and I also speak thus: when this is not, that is not; with the cessation of this, that ceases; that is: with the cessation of ignorance, cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”
translations.mn38:23: “But, bhikkhus, knowing thus and seeing thus, would you run back to the past: ‘Were we indeed in the past, were we not indeed in the past? What indeed were we in the past? How indeed were we in the past? Having been what, what indeed were we in the past’?” “No, venerable sir.” “But, bhikkhus, knowing thus and seeing thus, would you run on to the future: ‘Will we indeed be in the future, will we not indeed be in the future? What indeed will we be in the future? How indeed will we be in the future? Having been what, what indeed will we be in the future’?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.mn38:25: “Good, bhikkhus. You have been led by me, bhikkhus, by this Dhamma that is visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. ‘This Dhamma, bhikkhus, is visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise’—what was said as far as that, it was said in dependence on this.”
translations.mn38:26: “But, bhikkhus, from the coming together of three there is descent into the womb. Here, mother and father come together, but the mother is not in season and the gandhabba is not present—then there is no descent into the womb. Here, mother and father come together, and the mother is in season, but the gandhabba is not present—then there is no descent into the womb. But when, bhikkhus, mother and father come together, and the mother is in season, and the gandhabba is present—thus from the coming together of three there is descent into the womb.”
translations.mn38:27: “Then, bhikkhus, the mother carries him in the womb for nine or ten months, with great concern, a heavy burden. Then, bhikkhus, after nine or ten months have passed, the mother gives birth to him with great concern, a heavy burden. Then, when he is born, she nourishes him with her own blood. For that, bhikkhus, is blood in the discipline of the noble ones, that is, mother’s milk.”
translations.mn38:28: “And that boy, bhikkhus, as he grows up, as his faculties mature, plays with the kinds of toys that belong to boys, such as a crooked stick, a toy cart, a toy windmill, a toy top, a toy plate, a toy chariot, a toy bow.”
translations.mn38:39: “Having abandoned these five hindrances, the defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is with thought and examination, born of seclusion, with rapture and pleasure. And further, bhikkhus, with the calming of thought and examination, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, with internal confidence and unification of mind, without thought, without examination, born of concentration, with rapture and pleasure … the third jhāna … the fourth jhāna, and dwells.”
translations.mn38:6: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “What do you think, bhikkhus? Is this bhikkhu Sāti, the fisherman’s son, even warm in this Dhamma and discipline?” “How could that be, venerable sir? No indeed, venerable sir.” When this was said, the bhikkhu Sāti, the fisherman’s son, became silent, abashed, with drooping shoulders, head down, brooding, unable to reply, and sat there. Then the Blessed One, knowing the bhikkhu Sāti, the fisherman’s son, to be silent, abashed, with drooping shoulders, head down, brooding, unable to reply, said this to the bhikkhu Sāti, the fisherman’s son: “You will be known, foolish man, by that bad view of your own. Now I will question the bhikkhus.”
translations.mn38:7: Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Do you too, bhikkhus, understand the Dhamma taught by me in the way this bhikkhu Sāti, the fisherman’s son, having wrongly grasped it himself, misrepresents us, and digs himself up, and produces much demerit?” “No indeed, venerable sir. For in many ways, venerable sir, dependent-arisen consciousness has been spoken of by the Blessed One; apart from a condition there is no coming-to-be of consciousness.” “Good, good, bhikkhus. It is good that you, bhikkhus, understand the Dhamma taught by me thus. For in many ways, bhikkhus, dependent-arisen consciousness has been spoken of by me; apart from a condition there is no coming-to-be of consciousness.” But this bhikkhu Sāti, the fisherman’s son, having wrongly grasped it himself, misrepresents us, and digs himself up, and produces much demerit. For that will be for that foolish man’s harm and suffering for a long time.
translations.mn38:9: “Do you see, bhikkhus, that ‘this has come to be’?” — “Yes, venerable sir.” “Do you see, bhikkhus, that it arises from nutriment?” — “Yes, venerable sir.” “Do you see, bhikkhus, that whatever has come to be, with the cessation of that nutriment, is of a nature to cease?” — “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn41:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One, wandering on tour among the Kosalans, arrived with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus at a brahmin village of the Kosalans named Sālā.
translations.mn41:10: And how, householders, is there threefold misconduct and wrong conduct by mind? Here, householders, someone is covetous; they covet what belongs to another, another’s property and possessions: ‘Oh, if only what belongs to another were mine!’ And they have a mind of ill will, with thoughts of a corrupted mind: ‘May these beings be killed or slaughtered or annihilated or destroyed, or may they not exist!’ And they are of wrong view, of distorted vision: ‘There is no gift, no offering, no sacrifice; there is no fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings who are reborn spontaneously; there are in the world no ascetics and brahmins who have gone rightly, who practice rightly, who having directly known and realized this world and the other world proclaim them.’ Thus, householders, there is threefold misconduct and wrong conduct by mind. Because of misconduct and wrong conduct, householders, thus some beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell.
translations.mn41:12: And how, householders, is there threefold good conduct and right conduct by body? Here, householders, someone, abandoning killing living beings, abstains from killing living beings; with rod laid down, with weapon laid down, conscientious, compassionate, they dwell kind and sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings. Abandoning taking what is not given, they abstain from taking what is not given. What belongs to another, another’s property and possessions, whether in a village or in the wilderness, they do not take as theft what has not been given. Abandoning misconduct in sensual pleasures, they abstain from misconduct in sensual pleasures. Those who are protected by mother, protected by father, protected by both mother and father, protected by brother, protected by sister, protected by relatives, protected by clan, protected by Dhamma, who have a husband, who are punishable, even those enclosed with a garland of flowers—among such they do not commit misconduct. Thus, householders, there is threefold good conduct and right conduct by body.
translations.mn41:13: And how, householders, is there fourfold good conduct and right conduct by speech? Here, householders, someone, abandoning false speech, abstains from false speech. Having gone to an assembly or to a meeting, or into the midst of relatives, or into the midst of a guild, or into the midst of the royal family, if they are brought forth and asked as a witness: ‘Come now, good man, say what you know’—not knowing, they say ‘I do not know’; knowing, they say ‘I know’; not seeing, they say ‘I do not see’; seeing, they say ‘I see.’ Thus they do not knowingly speak falsehood for their own sake, or for another’s sake, or for the sake of some trivial material gain. Abandoning divisive speech, they abstain from divisive speech: having heard here, they do not tell it there to cause division among these; or having heard there, they do not tell it here to cause division among those. Thus they are one who reconciles those who are divided, who promotes friendship among those who are united, delighting in concord, rejoicing in concord, enjoying concord, speaking words that make for concord. Abandoning harsh speech, they abstain from harsh speech. They speak words that are gentle, pleasing to the ear, affectionate, going to the heart, courteous, dear and pleasing to many people. Abandoning idle chatter, they abstain from idle chatter. They speak at the right time, speak what is true, speak what is beneficial, speak Dhamma, speak Vinaya; they speak words worth treasuring, timely, with reasons, measured, and connected with the goal. Thus, householders, there is fourfold good conduct and right conduct by speech.
translations.mn41:14: And how, householders, is there threefold good conduct and right conduct by mind? Here, householders, someone is not covetous; they do not covet what belongs to another, another’s property and possessions: ‘Oh, if only what belongs to another were mine!’ And they have a mind without ill will, with thoughts of an uncorrupted mind: ‘May these beings be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from trouble, and may they look after themselves happily!’ And they are of right view, of undistorted vision: ‘There is what is given, there is what is offered, there is what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings who are reborn spontaneously; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have gone rightly, who practice rightly, who having directly known and realized this world and the other world proclaim them.’ Thus, householders, there is threefold good conduct and right conduct by mind. Because of good conduct and right conduct, householders, thus some beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, the heavenly world.
translations.mn41:15: If a dhamma-conducting, right-conducting person should wish, householders: ‘Oh, if only with the breakup of the body, after death, I might be reborn in companionship with the great Khattiya families’—there is a possibility for that, that with the breakup of the body, after death, they might be reborn in companionship with the great Khattiya families. For what reason? For they are a dhamma-conducting, right-conducting person.
translations.mn41:3: Then the brahmins and householders of Sālā went to the Blessed One; having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One, and after friendly and courteous talk sat down to one side; some raised their joined palms toward the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some announced their name and clan in the Blessed One’s presence and sat down to one side; and some, remaining silent, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the brahmins and householders of Sālā said this to the Blessed One:
translations.mn41:4: “What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the condition, by which some beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell? And what, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the condition, by which some beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, the heavenly world?”
translations.mn41:43: Householders, if a person of good conduct and right conduct should wish: ‘Oh, may I—with the destruction of the taints—realize for myself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it dwell’; it is possible that—with the destruction of the taints—they would realize for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it dwell. For what reason? For they are of good conduct and right conduct.”
translations.mn41:5: “It is due to wrong conduct and unrighteous conduct, householders, that in this way some beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of loss, an unhappy destination, downfall, hell. It is due to good conduct and right conduct, householders, that in this way some beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.”
translations.mn41:6: “We do not understand the meaning of this that has been spoken briefly by Master Gotama, the meaning not analyzed in detail. It would be good if Master Gotama would teach us the Dhamma in such a way that we might understand in detail the meaning of this that has been spoken briefly by Master Gotama, the meaning not analyzed in detail.” “Then, householders, listen and attend closely; I will speak.” “Yes, sir,” the brahmins and householders of Sālā said in reply to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn41:8: “And how, householders, is there threefold wrong conduct and unrighteous conduct by body? Here, householders, someone is a killer of living beings—cruel, with bloody hands, devoted to killing and striking, without mercy toward living beings. And they are one who takes what is not given: whatever is another’s belongings and property, whether in a village or in the wilderness, they take it as theft, taking what is not given. And they engage in sexual misconduct: with those who are protected by mother, protected by father, protected by both mother and father, protected by brother, protected by sister, protected by relatives, protected by clan, protected by Dhamma, who have a husband, who are punishable, even those enclosed with a garland of flowers—they commit conduct with such women. Thus, householders, there is threefold wrong conduct and unrighteous conduct by body.”
translations.mn41:9: “And how, householders, is there fourfold wrong conduct and unrighteous conduct by speech? Here, householders, someone is a liar. Having gone to an assembly, or to a meeting, or among relatives, or among a guild, or in the midst of the royal court, when brought and questioned as a witness: ‘Come, good man, say what you know,’ they say, when they do not know, ‘I know’; or when they know, they say, ‘I do not know’; or when they do not see, they say, ‘I see’; or when they see, they say, ‘I do not see.’ Thus they knowingly speak falsehood for their own sake, or for another’s sake, or for the sake of some small material gain. And they are one who speaks divisively: having heard something here, they tell it elsewhere for the sake of dividing these people; or having heard something elsewhere, they tell it to these people for the sake of dividing those. Thus, they are a breaker of the united, an instigator of those already divided; they delight in factions, enjoy factions, rejoice in factions, and they speak words that create factions. And they are one who speaks harshly: the speech that is rough, hard, hurtful to others, abusive, bordering on anger, not leading to concentration—such speech they speak. And they are one who talks frivolously: speaking at the wrong time, speaking what is untrue, speaking what is unbeneficial, speaking contrary to the Dhamma, speaking contrary to the discipline. They speak speech that is not worth treasuring—untimely, without reason, without measure, not connected with benefit. Thus, householders, there is fourfold wrong conduct and unrighteous conduct by speech.”
translations.mn4:20: Then, brahmin, it occurred to me: ‘Why don’t I, on those nights that are recognized and marked out—the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth of the fortnight—dwell on such nights in those kinds of abodes: shrine-grounds in parks, shrine-grounds in forests, shrine-grounds at trees, frightening, hair-raising places; perhaps I might see fear and dread.’ So, brahmin, at a later time, on those nights that are recognized and marked out—the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth of the fortnight—on such nights I dwelt in those kinds of abodes: shrine-grounds in parks, shrine-grounds in forests, shrine-grounds at trees, frightening, hair-raising places. And there, brahmin, while I was dwelling, a deer would come, or a peacock would drop a twig, or the wind would stir a rustling of leaves; then it occurred to me: ‘Surely this is that fear and dread coming.’ Then, brahmin, it occurred to me: ‘Why indeed do I dwell expecting fear? Why don’t I, as that fear and dread comes to me as it really is, dispel that fear and dread as it really is, right as it is?’ When, brahmin, I was walking, that fear and dread came to me. Then, brahmin, I did not stop, nor sit down, nor lie down, until, walking, I dispelled that fear and dread. When, brahmin, I was standing, that fear and dread came to me. Then, brahmin, I did not walk, nor sit down, nor lie down, until, standing, I dispelled that fear and dread. When, brahmin, I was sitting, that fear and dread came to me. Then, brahmin, I did not lie down, nor stand, nor walk, until, sitting, I dispelled that fear and dread. When, brahmin, I was lying down, that fear and dread came to me. Then, brahmin, I did not sit up, nor stand, nor walk, until, lying down, I dispelled that fear and dread.
translations.mn4:22-26: But, brahmin, my energy was aroused, not slack; my mindfulness was established, not confused; my body was tranquil, not agitated; my mind was concentrated, unified.  Then I, brahmin, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, entered upon and dwelt in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.  With the stilling of thought and examination, I entered upon and dwelt in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, without thought, without examination, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration.  And with the fading away of rapture I dwelt equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and I experienced pleasure with the body; I entered upon and dwelt in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, one dwells in pleasure.’  With the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and grief, I entered upon and dwelt in the fourth jhāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
translations.mn4:27: With the mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, free from defilement, pliant, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of recollection of past lives. I recollected many kinds of past lives, that is: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-contraction, many eons of world-expansion, many eons of world-contraction and world-expansion: ‘There I was so named, of such a clan, of such an appearance, such was my food, such was my experience of pleasure and pain, such was my life-span; passing away from there I reappeared elsewhere; there too I was so named, of such a clan, of such an appearance, such was my food, such was my experience of pleasure and pain, such was my life-span; passing away from there I was reborn here.’ Thus with aspects and particulars I recollected many kinds of past lives.
translations.mn4:28: This, brahmin, was my first knowledge attained in the first watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose, as happens in one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn4:29: With the mind thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, free from defilement, pliant, workable, steady, and attained to imperturbability, I directed my mind to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearing of beings. With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood beings according to their actions: ‘These worthy beings, endowed with misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, misconduct of mind, revilers of the noble ones, of wrong view, undertaking actions based on wrong view—on the breaking up of the body, after death, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, in ruin, in hell.  But these worthy beings, endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, good conduct of mind, not revilers of the noble ones, of right view, undertaking actions based on right view—on the breaking up of the body, after death, have reappeared in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Thus with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I saw beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and I understood beings according to their actions.
translations.mn4:3: Even for me, brahmin, before my awakening, while I was still only an unawakened bodhisatta, this occurred to me: ‘Hard to endure indeed are remote forest and jungle thickets, secluded lodgings; it is hard to take delight in solitude, hard to enjoy being alone; the forests, it seems to me, steal away the mind of a monk who does not obtain concentration.’
translations.mn4:30: This, brahmin, was my second knowledge attained in the middle watch of the night; ignorance was destroyed, knowledge arose; darkness was destroyed, light arose, as happens in one who dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute.
translations.mn4:34: It may occur to you, brahmin: ‘Even now the ascetic Gotama is not free from lust, not free from hate, not free from delusion; that is why he resorts to remote forest and jungle thickets, secluded lodgings.’  But, brahmin, it should not be seen thus.  Brahmin, seeing two benefits, I resort to remote forest and jungle thickets, secluded lodgings—seeing my own pleasant abiding here and now, and having compassion for later generations.”
translations.mn4:4: Then it occurred to me, brahmin: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins with impure bodily deeds resort to remote forest and jungle thickets, secluded lodgings, it is because of the fault of impure bodily deeds that those worthy ascetics and brahmins summon up unwholesome fear and dread.  But I do not resort to remote forest and jungle thickets, secluded lodgings with impure bodily deeds; I am one with pure bodily deeds.  I am one of those noble ones with pure bodily deeds who resort to remote forest and jungle thickets, secluded lodgings.’ Seeing in myself this purity of bodily deeds, brahmin, I gained still more confidence for dwelling in the forest.
translations.mn4:5: Then it occurred to me, brahmin: ‘Whatever ascetics or brahmins with impure verbal deeds … with impure mental deeds … with impure livelihood resort to remote forest and jungle thickets, secluded lodgings, it is because of the fault of impure livelihood that those worthy ascetics and brahmins summon up unwholesome fear and dread.
translations.mn4:6: But I do not resort to remote forest and jungle thickets, secluded lodgings with impure livelihood; I am one with pure livelihood.
translations.mn4:7: I am one of those noble ones with pure livelihood who resort to remote forest and jungle thickets, secluded lodgings.’ Seeing in myself this purity of livelihood, brahmin, I gained still more confidence for dwelling in the forest.
translations.mn52:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Vesālī in the village of Beluva.  Now at that time the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara had arrived at Pāṭaliputta on some business.
translations.mn52:12: Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu, by completely surmounting perceptions of form, with the vanishing of perceptions of resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, enters and dwells in the base of infinite space (thinking), ‘Infinite is space’. He reflects thus: ‘This attainment of the base of infinite space, too, is conditioned and volitionally produced. But whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent, of a nature to cease.’ Knowing this, remaining there … he does not attain the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.mn52:14: Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu, by completely surmounting the base of infinite consciousness, enters and dwells in the base of nothingness (thinking), ‘There is nothing’. He reflects thus: ‘This attainment of the base of nothingness, too, is conditioned and volitionally produced. But whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent, of a nature to cease.’ Knowing this, remaining there, he attains the destruction of the taints. But if he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then, by that very desire for the Dhamma, by that delight in the Dhamma, with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who is reborn spontaneously and there attains final Nibbāna, not returning from that world. This too, householder, is one thing declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, whereby, as a bhikkhu dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, his unliberated mind is liberated, his unexhausted taints go to exhaustion, and he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.”
translations.mn52:15: When this was said, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara said this to Venerable Ānanda: “Just as, Venerable Ānanda, a man seeking a single entrance to a treasure would at once find eleven entrances to a treasure; even so, venerable sir, while seeking one door to the deathless I at once obtained eleven doors to the deathless by development. Just as, venerable sir, a man has a house with eleven doors, and if that house were on fire he could save himself by any one of the doors; even so, venerable sir, by any one of these eleven doors to the deathless I will be able to make myself safe. On account of these things, venerable sir, followers of other sects will go in search of a teacher’s fee for their teacher; how much more should I not make an offering to Venerable Ānanda?”
translations.mn52:2: Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara went to the Kukuṭārāma, to a certain bhikkhu. Having gone, he paid homage to that bhikkhu and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara said this to that bhikkhu: “Where, venerable sir, is Venerable Ānanda now dwelling? For we wish to see Venerable Ānanda.” “Householder, Venerable Ānanda is dwelling in Vesālī, in the village of Beluva.”
translations.mn52:3: Then the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara, having finished that business in Pāṭaliputta, went to Vesālī, to the village of Beluva, to where Venerable Ānanda was. Having gone, he paid homage to Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder Dasama of Aṭṭhakanāgara said this to Venerable Ānanda: “Is there, Venerable Ānanda, one thing declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, whereby, as a bhikkhu dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, his unliberated mind is liberated, his unexhausted taints go to exhaustion, and he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage?” “There is, householder, one thing declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, whereby, as a bhikkhu dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, his unliberated mind is liberated, his unexhausted taints go to exhaustion, and he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.” “But what, Venerable Ānanda, is that one thing declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, whereby, as a bhikkhu dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, his unliberated mind is liberated, his unexhausted taints go to exhaustion, and he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage?”
translations.mn52:4: “Here, householder, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, born of seclusion, with rapture and pleasure. He reflects thus: ‘This first jhāna, too, is conditioned and volitionally produced. But whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent, of a nature to cease.’ Knowing this, remaining there, he attains the destruction of the taints. But if he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then, by that very desire for the Dhamma, by that delight in the Dhamma, with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who is reborn spontaneously and there attains final Nibbāna, not returning from that world. This too, householder, is one thing declared by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, whereby, as a bhikkhu dwells diligent, ardent, and resolute, his unliberated mind is liberated, his unexhausted taints go to exhaustion, and he attains the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.mn52:8: Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, without ill will. He reflects thus: ‘This liberation of mind by loving-kindness, too, is conditioned and volitionally produced. But whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent, of a nature to cease.’ Knowing this, remaining there … he does not attain the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.mn54:18: Suppose, householder, there were a pit of glowing coals, deeper than a man’s height, full of coals without flame and without smoke. Then a man might come along, wanting to live, not wanting to die, wanting happiness, repelled by suffering. Two strong men would seize him by both arms and drag him toward the pit of coals. What do you think, householder: would that man not twist and writhe his body right there? “Yes, venerable sir.” “For what reason?” “For that man knows, venerable sir: ‘If I fall into this pit of coals, then because of that I will meet with death or death-like suffering.’” “In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Sense pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a pit of coals—very painful, very distressing; the danger here is even greater.’ Seeing this as it really is with right wisdom … he develops that same equanimity.
translations.mn54:23: That noble disciple, householder, having arrived at this same unsurpassed purity of mindfulness due to equanimity, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good destinations and bad destinations … he understands beings as faring on according to their actions.
translations.mn54:24: That noble disciple, householder, having arrived at this same unsurpassed purity of mindfulness due to equanimity, by the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it.
translations.mn60:10: Here, householders, those ascetics and brahmins who are of such a doctrine and view: ‘There is what is given … who, having directly known and realized this world and the other world for themselves, proclaim it’—of them it is to be expected that, having abandoned these three unwholesome things—bad conduct by body, bad conduct by speech, bad conduct by mind—they will undertake and practice these three wholesome things—good conduct by body, good conduct by speech, good conduct by mind. For what reason? Because those honorable ascetics and brahmins see the danger, the degradation, the defilement in unwholesome states, and the benefit of renunciation, the side of purification, in wholesome states.
translations.mn60:12: Here, householders, a wise man reflects thus: ‘If there is an other world, then this good man, this person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. But even if there were no other world—let the word of those venerable ascetics and brahmins be true—still this good man, this person, is in this very life praised by the wise: “A virtuous person, a person of right view, one who affirms that there is (an other world).” If indeed there is an other world, then for this good man, this person, there is a gain on both sides: what is praise by the wise in this very life, and that with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus this safe course has been well undertaken and adopted; it stands covering both sides, and it leaves the unwholesome position behind.’
translations.mn60:13: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who are of such a doctrine and view: ‘For one who acts and for one who causes to act, for one who cuts and for one who causes to cut, for one who cooks and for one who causes to cook, for one who grieves and for one who causes to grieve, for one who tires and for one who causes to tire, for one who trembles and for one who causes to tremble, for one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, carries off plunder, commits burglary, lies in ambush on the highway, goes to another’s wife, speaks falsehood—when one acts, evil is not done. Even if, with a razor-edged wheel, one were to make the living beings on this earth into one heap of flesh, one pile of flesh, there would be no evil because of that; there would be no coming of evil. Even if one were to go to the south bank of the Ganges, killing and causing killing, cutting and causing cutting, cooking and causing cooking, there would be no evil because of that; there would be no coming of evil. Even if one were to go to the north bank of the Ganges, giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, there would be no merit because of that; there would be no coming of merit. By giving, by self-control, by restraint, by speaking truth, there is no merit; there is no coming of merit.’
translations.mn60:14: But among those very ascetics and brahmins, some ascetics and brahmins, holding the directly opposite doctrine, spoke thus: ‘For one who acts and for one who causes to act, for one who cuts and for one who causes to cut, for one who cooks and for one who causes to cook, for one who grieves and for one who causes to grieve, for one who tires and for one who causes to tire, for one who trembles and for one who causes to tremble, for one who kills living beings, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, carries off plunder, commits burglary, lies in ambush on the highway, goes to another’s wife, speaks falsehood—when one acts, evil is done. Even if, with a razor-edged wheel, one were to make the living beings on this earth into one heap of flesh, one pile of flesh, there is evil because of that; there is the coming of evil. Even if one were to go to the south bank of the Ganges, killing and causing killing, cutting and causing cutting, cooking and causing cooking, there is evil because of that; there is the coming of evil. Even if one were to go to the north bank of the Ganges, giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, there is merit because of that; there is the coming of merit. By giving, by self-control, by restraint, by speaking truth, there is merit; there is the coming of merit.’ What do you think, householders: are not these ascetics and brahmins directly opposed to one another? “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn60:16: Though there indeed is action, there is the view ‘there is no action’; that is his wrong view. Though there indeed is action, he intends: ‘there is no action’; that is his wrong intention. Though there indeed is action, he speaks the words: ‘there is no action’; that is his wrong speech. Though there indeed is action, saying ‘there is no action,’ he contradicts those arahants who speak of action. Though there indeed is action, he persuades others: ‘there is no action’; that is instruction in what is not the true Dhamma. And by that instruction in what is not the true Dhamma he exalts himself and disparages others. Thus, even earlier, his good conduct has been abandoned and misconduct has come to the fore—namely, this wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, opposition to the noble ones, instruction in what is not the true Dhamma, self-exaltation, disparaging of others. In this way these many bad, unwholesome states come to be for him, conditioned by wrong view.
translations.mn60:17: There, householders, a wise person reflects thus: ‘If indeed there is no efficacy of action, then this good man, this person, on the breakup of the body, will make himself safe and secure; but if indeed there is efficacy of action, then this good man, this person, on the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in the plane of misery, a bad destination, perdition, hell. Still, let there not be efficacy of action; let the word of those venerable ascetics and brahmins be true; yet this good man, this person, is blamed by the wise here and now as “an immoral person, of wrong view, who proclaims the non-efficacy of action.” But if indeed there is efficacy of action, then for this good man, this person, there is a bad throw in both ways: what is blamed by the wise here and now, and what—on the breakup of the body, after death—is rebirth in the plane of misery, a bad destination, perdition, hell. Thus this sure teaching is badly adopted by him, stands having spread itself one-sidedly, and abandons the wholesome ground.
translations.mn60:19: But with efficacy of action truly present, his view is: ‘There is efficacy of action’; that is his right view. But with efficacy of action truly present, he thinks: ‘There is efficacy of action’; that is his right intention. But with efficacy of action truly present, he speaks words: ‘There is efficacy of action’; that is his right speech. But with efficacy of action truly present, he says: ‘There is efficacy of action’; he does not oppose those arahants who proclaim efficacy of action. But with efficacy of action truly present, he convinces another: ‘There is efficacy of action’; that is his teaching of the true Dhamma. And by that teaching of the true Dhamma he neither exalts himself nor disparages another. Thus, even before, his immorality has been abandoned, and morality is present—this right view, right intention, right speech, non-opposition to the noble ones, teaching of the true Dhamma, non-exalting of oneself, non-disparaging of others. Thus for him these many wholesome states arise dependent on right view.
translations.mn60:21: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘There is no cause, no condition for the defilement of beings; without cause, without condition beings are defiled. There is no cause, no condition for the purification of beings; without cause, without condition beings are purified. There is no power, no energy, no manly strength, no manly striving; all beings, all living creatures, all beings, all lives are helpless, powerless, without energy, matured by destiny and circumstance, experiencing pleasure and pain in the six classes of rebirth.’
translations.mn60:22: But among those very ascetics and brahmins, householders, some ascetics and brahmins are direct opponents in doctrine. They say thus: ‘There is a cause, there is a condition for the defilement of beings; with cause and with condition beings are defiled. There is a cause, there is a condition for the purification of beings; with cause and with condition beings are purified. There is power, there is energy, there is manly strength, there is manly striving; not all beings, not all living creatures, not all beings, not all lives are helpless, powerless, without energy, matured by destiny and circumstance, experiencing pleasure and pain in the six classes of rebirth.’ What do you think, householders: are not these ascetics and brahmins direct opponents of one another in doctrine?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn60:29: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘There are absolutely no formless realms.’
translations.mn60:30: But among those very ascetics and brahmins, householders, some ascetics and brahmins are direct opponents in doctrine. They say thus: ‘There absolutely are formless realms.’ What do you think, householders: are not these ascetics and brahmins direct opponents of one another in doctrine?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn60:32: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘There is absolutely no cessation of existence.’
translations.mn60:35: These four persons, householders, are found existing in the world. What four? Here, householders, one person is a self-tormenter, devoted to the practice of self-mortification. Here, householders, one person is an other-tormenter, devoted to the practice of mortifying others. Here, householders, one person is both a self-tormenter, devoted to the practice of self-mortification, and an other-tormenter, devoted to the practice of mortifying others. Here, householders, one person is neither a self-tormenter, not devoted to the practice of self-mortification, nor an other-tormenter, not devoted to the practice of mortifying others; being no self-tormenter and no other-tormenter, he dwells here and now without hunger, quenched, cooled, experiencing happiness, with a self become brahman-like.
translations.mn60:36: And what person, householders, is a self-tormenter, devoted to the practice of self-mortification? Here, householders, one person is a naked ascetic, of free conduct, licking the hands … thus he dwells devoted to the practice of various kinds of tormenting and mortifying the body. This is called, householders, a person who is a self-tormenter, devoted to the practice of self-mortification.
translations.mn60:37: And what person, householders, is an other-tormenter, devoted to the practice of mortifying others? Here, householders, one person is a butcher of sheep, a pig butcher … or whatever other cruel occupations there may be. This is called, householders, a person who is an other-tormenter, devoted to the practice of mortifying others.
translations.mn60:38: And what person, householders, is both a self-tormenter, devoted to the practice of self-mortification, and an other-tormenter, devoted to the practice of mortifying others? Here, householders, one person may be a king, a head-anointed khattiya … they too, threatened with punishment, threatened with fear, with tearful faces, weeping, do their tasks. This is called, householders, a person who is both a self-tormenter, devoted to the practice of self-mortification, and an other-tormenter, devoted to the practice of mortifying others.
translations.mn60:39: And what person, householders, is neither a self-tormenter, not devoted to the practice of self-mortification, nor an other-tormenter, not devoted to the practice of mortifying others; being no self-tormenter and no other-tormenter, he dwells here and now without hunger, quenched, cooled, experiencing happiness, with a self become brahman-like?
translations.mn60:4: “But is there, householders, any teacher agreeable to you in whom you have acquired reasoned confidence?” “There is not, venerable sir, any teacher agreeable to us in whom we have acquired reasoned confidence.” “If you do not obtain a teacher agreeable to you, householders, then this sure teaching should be undertaken and practiced. For the sure teaching, householders, well undertaken and adopted, will be for your welfare and happiness for a long time. And what, householders, is the sure teaching?”
translations.mn60:5: There are, householders, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus, who hold such a view: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings who are spontaneously reborn; there are in the world no ascetics and brahmins who have gone rightly, who practice rightly, who, having themselves directly known and realized this world and the other world, make them known.’
translations.mn60:6: But, householders, among those same ascetics and brahmins, some ascetics and brahmins speak in direct opposition. They say this: ‘There is what is given, there is what is offered, there is what is sacrificed; there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world, there is the other world; there is mother, there is father; there are beings who are spontaneously reborn; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have gone rightly, who practice rightly, who, having themselves directly known and realized this world and the other world, make them known.’ What do you think, householders: ‘are not these ascetics and brahmins in direct opposition to one another?’” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn63:8: And why, Māluṅkyaputta, has this not been declared by me? Because this, Māluṅkyaputta, is not connected with the goal, is not fundamental to the holy life, does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, to nibbāna. Therefore it has not been declared by me.
translations.mn64:13: Further, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘infinite is space’, enters and dwells in the base of infinite space. Whatever there is there that is feeling, that is perception, that is formations, that is consciousness … he is of a nature not to return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is a path, this is a practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:14: Further, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking ‘infinite is consciousness’, enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness. Whatever there is there that is feeling, that is perception, that is formations, that is consciousness … he is of a nature not to return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is a path, this is a practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn64:2: “Do you remember, bhikkhus, the five lower fetters taught by me?” When this was said, Venerable Māluṅkyaputta said this to the Blessed One: “I, venerable sir, remember the five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One.” “But how, Māluṅkyaputta, do you remember the five lower fetters taught by me?” “I, venerable sir, remember identity view as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I, venerable sir, remember doubt as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I, venerable sir, remember attachment to rites and observances as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I, venerable sir, remember sensual desire as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One; I, venerable sir, remember ill will as a lower fetter taught by the Blessed One. Thus, venerable sir, do I remember the five lower fetters taught by the Blessed One.”
translations.mn64:4: When this was said, Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “Now is the time, Blessed One, now is the time, Fortunate One, for the Blessed One to teach the five lower fetters. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.” “Then, Ānanda, listen and attend carefully; I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.mn64:7: And that path, Ānanda, that practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters—relying on that path, that practice, that one may know them, or see them, or abandon the five lower fetters: this is possible.
translations.mn64:9: And what, Ānanda, is the path, what is the practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, secluded from acquisitions, with the abandoning of unwholesome states, with the complete calming of bodily inertia, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, born of seclusion, with rapture and pleasure. Whatever there is there that is form, that is feeling, that is perception, that is formations, that is consciousness, he regards those states as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, as an affliction, as a sickness, as alien, as disintegrating, as empty, as not-self. He turns his mind away from those states. Having turned his mind away from those states, he directs his mind to the deathless element: ‘This is peaceful, this is sublime—namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishment of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, nibbāna.’ Standing there, he attains the destruction of the taints; if he does not attain the destruction of the taints, then through that very desire for the Dhamma, through that delight in the Dhamma, with the ending of the five lower fetters, he becomes one who is spontaneously reborn, one who attains final nibbāna there, of a nature not to return from that world. This too, Ānanda, is a path, this is a practice for the abandoning of the five lower fetters.
translations.mn6:14: If a bhikkhu should wish, bhikkhus: ‘May I experience various kinds of spiritual power—having been one, may I become many; having been many, may I become one; may I appear and disappear; may I go unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain, as though through space; may I dive in and out of the earth as though in water; may I walk on water without breaking it, as though on earth; may I travel cross-legged in the sky like a winged bird; may I touch and stroke with my hand even these moon and sun, so mighty, so powerful; may I wield mastery with the body even as far as the brahmā world’—let him be one who fulfills virtue … develop secluded dwellings.
translations.mn6:15: If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should wish: ‘With the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, may I hear both kinds of sounds—divine and human, those far and near,’ let him be a fulfiller of the precepts …pe… a developer of empty huts.
translations.mn6:16: If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May I understand by mind the minds of other beings, of other persons, having encompassed them with my own mind—may I understand a mind with lust as a mind with lust, and a mind without lust as a mind without lust; may I understand a mind with hate as a mind with hate, and a mind without hate as a mind without hate; may I understand a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, and a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; may I understand a contracted mind as a contracted mind, and a distracted mind as a distracted mind; may I understand an exalted mind as an exalted mind, and an unexalted mind as an unexalted mind; may I understand a surpassed mind as a surpassed mind, and an unsurpassed mind as an unsurpassed mind; may I understand a collected mind as a collected mind, and an uncollected mind as an uncollected mind; may I understand a liberated mind as a liberated mind, and an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind,’ let him be a fulfiller of the precepts …pe… a developer of empty huts.
translations.mn6:2: “Live, bhikkhus, possessed of virtue, possessed of the Pātimokkha; live restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, endowed with good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest faults; having undertaken, train in the training rules.
translations.mn6:3: If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May I be dear and pleasing and respected and revered by my companions in the holy life,’ let him be a fulfiller of the precepts, devoted to inner tranquillity of mind, not neglecting jhāna, endowed with vipassanā, a developer of empty huts.
translations.mn6:6: If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should wish: ‘Those relatives of mine, of the same blood, who have died and passed away, remembering me with a serene mind—may that be of great fruit, of great benefit for them,’ let him be a fulfiller of the precepts, devoted to inner tranquillity of mind, not neglecting jhāna, endowed with vipassanā, a developer of empty huts.
translations.mn6:7: If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May I endure discontent and delight, and may discontent not endure me; having overcome discontent that has arisen, may I dwell having overcome it again and again,’ let him be a fulfiller of the precepts …pe… a developer of empty huts.
translations.mn6:8: If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May I endure fear and dread, and may fear and dread not endure me; having overcome fear and dread that has arisen, may I dwell having overcome it again and again,’ let him be a fulfiller of the precepts …pe… a developer of empty huts.
translations.mn6:9: If, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should wish: ‘May I be one who obtains at will, without trouble, without difficulty, the four jhānas that are higher in mind, pleasant dwellings here and now,’ let him be a fulfiller of the precepts …pe… a developer of empty huts.
translations.mn70:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was walking on tour in Kāsi together with a large saṅgha of bhikkhus. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
translations.mn70:11: “And since, bhikkhus, this has been known by me, seen, understood, realized, and touched with wisdom: ‘Here, for someone who experiences such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states grow,’ therefore I say: ‘Enter upon and dwell in such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.’
translations.mn70:12: I do not, bhikkhus, say to all bhikkhus: ‘What is to be done should be done with diligence’; but I also do not say to all bhikkhus: ‘What is to be done should not be done with diligence.’ Those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, who are arahants, with taints destroyed, who have lived the life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetter of becoming, and are liberated by perfect understanding—to such bhikkhus I say: ‘What is to be done should not be done with diligence.’ For what reason? What was to be done with diligence has been done by them. They are incapable of being negligent.
translations.mn70:13: But those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, who are trainees, not yet attained in mind, dwelling aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage—to such bhikkhus I say: ‘What is to be done should be done with diligence.’ For what reason? Perhaps these venerable ones, using suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, bringing the faculties into balance—might realize, here and now, by their own direct knowledge, and having realized it enter upon and dwell in that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. Seeing this fruit of diligence for these bhikkhus, I say: ‘What is to be done should be done with diligence.’
translations.mn70:14: These seven persons, bhikkhus, exist and are found in the world. Which seven? One liberated in both ways, one liberated by wisdom, a body-witness, one attained-to-view, one faith-liberated, a Dhamma-follower, a faith-follower.
translations.mn70:15: And which person, bhikkhus, is liberated in both ways? Here, bhikkhus, some person, having gone beyond forms, dwells having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that are immaterial; and, having seen with wisdom, his taints are destroyed. This is called, bhikkhus, a person liberated in both ways. To such a bhikkhu I say: ‘What is to be done should not be done with diligence.’ For what reason? What was to be done with diligence has been done by him. He is incapable of being negligent.
translations.mn70:17: And which person, bhikkhus, is a body-witness? Here, bhikkhus, some person, having gone beyond forms, dwells having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that are immaterial; and, having seen with wisdom, some of his taints are destroyed. This is called, bhikkhus, a body-witness. To such a bhikkhu I say: ‘What is to be done should be done with diligence.’ For what reason? Perhaps this venerable one, using suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, bringing the faculties into balance—might realize, here and now, by his own direct knowledge, and having realized it enter upon and dwell in that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. Seeing this fruit of diligence for this bhikkhu, I say: ‘What is to be done should be done with diligence.’
translations.mn70:2: “Monks, I eat only apart from eating at night. And when I eat only apart from eating at night, I perceive good health and freedom from illness, lightness, strength, and comfortable living. Come, you too, monks, eat only apart from eating at night. And when you too, monks, eat only apart from eating at night, you too will perceive good health and freedom from illness, lightness, strength, and comfortable living.” The monks replied to the Blessed One: “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn70:20: And what kind of person, monks, is a Dhamma-follower? Here, monks, a certain person does not dwell having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that transcend forms—the formless states; but having seen with wisdom, some taints of his are exhausted. The teachings proclaimed by the Tathāgata are acceptable to him, by wisdom, after limited reflection. And these qualities are found in him, that is to say: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom. This is called, monks, a Dhamma-follower. Even to this monk, monks, I say: “What should be done should be done with diligence.” For what reason? Perhaps this venerable one, using suitable lodgings, associating with good friends, and bringing the faculties into balance—may realize for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the unsurpassed ending of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life to homelessness, and having realized it, may dwell. Seeing this fruit of diligence for this monk, monks, I say: “What should be done should be done with diligence.”
translations.mn70:22: Monks, I do not say that the fulfilling of knowledge is by the very beginning; but rather, monks, the gradual training, the gradual doing, the gradual practice is the fulfilling of knowledge.
translations.mn70:23: And how, monks, is the gradual training, the gradual doing, the gradual practice the fulfilling of knowledge? Here, monks, one who has arisen faith approaches; approaching, he attends; attending, he lends ear; with attentive ear, he hears the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma, he retains it; having retained the teachings, he examines the meaning; as he examines the meaning, the teachings become acceptable to him after reflection; when there is acceptance after reflection on the teachings, desire arises; with desire arisen, he strives; having striven, he weighs; having weighed, he exerts himself; being one who has exerted himself, he realizes with the body the ultimate truth, and he sees it by wisdom, having penetrated it.
translations.mn70:24: That faith, monks, might not have been; that approaching too, monks, might not have been; that attending too, monks, might not have been; that lending of ear too, monks, might not have been; that hearing of the Dhamma too, monks, might not have been; that retaining of the Dhamma too, monks, might not have been; that examination of the meaning too, monks, might not have been; that acceptance after reflection on the Dhamma too, monks, might not have been; that desire too, monks, might not have been; that striving too, monks, might not have been; that weighing too, monks, might not have been; that exertion too, monks, might not have been. They have gone by a wrong path, monks; they have practiced wrongly, monks. How far these worthless men, monks, have departed from this Dhamma and discipline.
translations.mn70:25: There is, monks, a four-footed statement by which, when it is recited, a wise person would quickly understand the meaning. Shall I recite it for you, monks? You will understand it from me.” “And who are we, venerable sir, and who are the understanders of the Dhamma?”
translations.mn70:26: “And that teacher too, monks, who is devoted to material things, an heir to material things, who lives mixed up with material things—mostly he does not come to have such shouting and cheering as this: ‘So it would be for us, and then we would do it; and so it would not be for us, and then we would not do it’; what then, monks, since the Tathāgata lives entirely detached from material things.
translations.mn70:3: Then the Blessed One, wandering on tour in Kāsi by stages, arrived at the Kāsi town named Kīṭāgiri. There the Blessed One dwelt at Kīṭāgiri in the Kāsi town.
translations.mn70:4: Now at that time the monks named Assaji and Punabbasuka were resident at Kīṭāgiri. Then several monks went to the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka; having gone to them, they said this to the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka: “The Blessed One, friends, eats only apart from eating at night, and so does the Saṅgha of monks. And when eating only apart from eating at night, friends, they perceive good health and freedom from illness, lightness, strength, and comfortable living. Come, you too, friends, eat only apart from eating at night. And when you too, friends, eat only apart from eating at night, you too will perceive good health and freedom from illness, lightness, strength, and comfortable living.” When this was said, the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka said this to those monks: “We, friends, eat in the evening, and in the morning, and in the daytime, at the wrong time. And eating in the evening, and in the morning, and in the daytime, at the wrong time, we perceive good health and freedom from illness, lightness, strength, and comfortable living. Why should we abandon what is beneficial here-and-now and run after what is later? We will eat in the evening, and in the morning, and in the daytime, at the wrong time.”
translations.mn70:7: “Monks, do you not understand that I have taught the Dhamma thus: here, for some, when experiencing such a pleasant feeling, unwholesome qualities increase and wholesome qualities decline; but here, for some, when experiencing such a pleasant feeling, unwholesome qualities decline and wholesome qualities increase; here, for some, when experiencing such a painful feeling, unwholesome qualities increase and wholesome qualities decline; but here, for some, when experiencing such a painful feeling, unwholesome qualities decline and wholesome qualities increase; here, for some, when experiencing such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome qualities increase and wholesome qualities decline; but here, for some, when experiencing such a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, unwholesome qualities decline and wholesome qualities increase”?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.mn75:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was living among the Kurus, at the Kuru town named Kammāsadhamma, in the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, on a grass mat.
translations.mn75:10: “But I, Māgaṇḍiya, formerly, when I was living the household life, endowed with and possessing the five cords of sensual pleasure, indulged in forms cognizable by the eye—liked, desired, agreeable, pleasant, lovely, connected with sensuality, enticing; in sounds cognizable by the ear … in odors cognizable by the nose … in flavors cognizable by the tongue … in tangibles cognizable by the body—liked, desired, agreeable, pleasant, lovely, connected with sensuality, enticing. For me, Māgaṇḍiya, there were three mansions—one for the rainy season, one for the winter, one for the summer. In the rainy-season mansion, Māgaṇḍiya, for the four months of the rains, entertained by music without men, I did not go down to the lower mansion. But later, having known as they really are the arising and passing away of sensual pleasures, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them, I abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, dispelled the fever of sensual pleasures, and I dwell without thirst, with a mind inwardly stilled. I see other beings, not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being eaten up by craving for sensual pleasures, being burned by the fever of sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures. I do not envy them; I do not delight there. Why is that? Because this delight, Māgaṇḍiya, apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states—having attained even divine happiness, it stands—delighting in that delight, I do not envy what is inferior; I do not delight there.”
translations.mn75:12: “Just so, Māgaṇḍiya, formerly, when I was living the household life, endowed with and possessing the five cords of sensual pleasure, I indulged in forms cognizable by the eye—liked, desired, agreeable, pleasant, lovely, connected with sensuality, enticing; in sounds cognizable by the ear … in odors cognizable by the nose … in flavors cognizable by the tongue … in tangibles cognizable by the body—liked, desired, agreeable, pleasant, lovely, connected with sensuality, enticing. But later, having known as they really are the arising and passing away of sensual pleasures, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them, I abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, dispelled the fever of sensual pleasures, and I dwell without thirst, with a mind inwardly stilled. I see other beings, not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being eaten up by craving for sensual pleasures, being burned by the fever of sensual pleasures, indulging in sensual pleasures; I do not envy them; I do not delight there. Why is that? Because this delight, Māgaṇḍiya, apart from sensual pleasures, apart from unwholesome states—having attained even divine happiness, it stands—delighting in that delight, I do not envy what is inferior; I do not delight there.”
translations.mn75:13: “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, a leper with sores, with festering limbs, being eaten by worms, scratching the openings of the wounds with his nails, would warm his body at a pit of embers. His friends and companions, relatives and kin would bring a physician, a surgeon. That physician-surgeon would make medicine for him. Having taken that medicine, he would be freed from the leprosy, and would be healthy, happy, independent, self-mastered, able to go wherever he likes. He would see another leper with sores, with festering limbs, being eaten by worms, scratching the openings of the wounds with his nails, warming his body at a pit of embers. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya: would that man envy that leper for warming at a pit of embers, or for taking medicine?” “No indeed, Master Gotama. Why is that? Because, Master Gotama, when there is disease there is need for medicine; when there is no disease there is no need for medicine.”
translations.mn75:16: “Just so, Māgaṇḍiya, in the past too sensual pleasures were painful in their contact and a great scorching and a great fever; in the future too sensual pleasures will be painful in their contact and a great scorching and a great fever; and now too in the present sensual pleasures are painful in their contact and a great scorching and a great fever. And these beings, Māgaṇḍiya, not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being eaten up by craving for sensual pleasures, being burned by the fever of sensual pleasures, with faculties impaired, have fallen into a perverted perception that in those very sensual pleasures with painful contact there is happiness.”
translations.mn75:17: “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, a leper with sores, with festering limbs, being eaten by worms, scratching the openings of the wounds with his nails, warms his body at a pit of embers. In whatever way, Māgaṇḍiya, that leper with sores, with festering limbs, being eaten by worms, scratching the openings of the wounds with his nails, warms his body at a pit of embers, in that very way those wound-openings become more and more unclean, more foul-smelling, more putrid; and yet there is a certain mere pleasure, a mere gratification—namely, due to the itching of the wound-openings. Just so, Māgaṇḍiya, beings not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being eaten up by craving for sensual pleasures and being burned by the fever of sensual pleasures, indulge in sensual pleasures.
