In whatever way, Māgaṇḍiya, beings not free from lust for sensual pleasures, being eaten up by craving for sensual pleasures and being burned by the fever of sensual pleasures, indulge in sensual pleasures, in that very way the craving for sensual pleasures of those beings increases, and they are burned by the fever of sensual pleasures; and yet there is a certain mere pleasure, a mere gratification—namely, dependent on the five cords of sensual pleasure.”
translations.mn75:18: “What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Have you ever seen or heard of a king or royal minister who, endowed with and enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure, without abandoning craving for sensual pleasures, without dispelling the fever for sensual pleasures, being free of thirst, with a mind inwardly stilled, dwelt or dwells or will dwell?” “No, Master Gotama.” “Good, Māgaṇḍiya. I too, Māgaṇḍiya, have neither seen nor heard of a king or royal minister who, endowed with and enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure, without abandoning craving for sensual pleasures, without dispelling the fever for sensual pleasures, being free of thirst, with a mind inwardly stilled, dwelt or dwells or will dwell. But, Māgaṇḍiya, whatever ascetics or brahmins there are who were or are or will be free of thirst, with minds inwardly stilled, all of them, having known as they really are the arising and passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to sensual pleasures, having abandoned craving for sensual pleasures and dispelled the fever for sensual pleasures, were or are or will be free of thirst, with minds inwardly stilled.”
translations.mn75:2: Then the Blessed One, in the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, entered Kammāsadhamma for alms. Having wandered for alms in Kammāsadhamma, after the meal, on returning from the alms round, he went to a certain grove for the day’s abiding. Having plunged into that grove, he sat down at the root of a certain tree for the day’s abiding.
translations.mn75:22: “Thus I am confident in Master Gotama. Let Master Gotama be able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might know the healthy state, that I might see Nibbāna.” “Suppose, Māgaṇḍiya, there were a man blind from birth: he would not see black and white forms; he would not see blue forms; he would not see yellow forms; he would not see red forms; he would not see crimson forms; he would not see what is even and uneven; he would not see the forms of stars; he would not see the moon and sun. His friends and companions, relatives and kin would provide a physician and surgeon for him. That physician-surgeon would make medicine for him. Having taken that medicine, he would not produce eyes, nor would he cleanse his eyes. What do you think, Māgaṇḍiya? Would not that doctor be a partaker only of weariness and vexation?” “Yes, Master Gotama.” “So too, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma: ‘This is health; this is Nibbāna,’ you would not know health; you would not see Nibbāna. That would be weariness for me; that would be harassment for me.”
translations.mn75:24: So too, Māgaṇḍiya, if I were to teach you the Dhamma: ‘This is health; this is Nibbāna,’ you would know health; you would see Nibbāna. With the arising of vision in you, whatever desire and lust there is regarding the five aggregates subject to clinging would be abandoned; and it might occur to you: ‘For a long time indeed, sirs, have I been cheated, deceived, and betrayed by this mind. For I, clinging to form alone, clung; clinging to feeling alone, clung; clinging to perception alone, clung; clinging to formations alone, clung; clinging to consciousness alone, clung. For me, with clinging as condition there is existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be; thus there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.’”
translations.mn75:25: “Thus I am confident in Master Gotama. Let Master Gotama be able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might rise from this seat no longer blind.” “Then, Māgaṇḍiya, you should associate with good persons. For when you, Māgaṇḍiya, associate with good persons, then you will hear the true Dhamma; when you, Māgaṇḍiya, hear the true Dhamma, then you will practice in accordance with the Dhamma; when you, Māgaṇḍiya, practice in accordance with the Dhamma, then you will know for yourself, you will see for yourself—these diseases, boils, darts; here diseases, boils, darts cease without remainder. For me, with the cessation of clinging there is the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease; thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”
translations.mn75:26: When this was said, Māgaṇḍiya the wanderer said this to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Master Gotama, excellent, Master Gotama. Just as, Master Gotama, one might set upright what had been overturned, or uncover what had been concealed, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the dark so that those with eyes might see forms; so too has the Dhamma been made clear by Master Gotama in many ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May I obtain the going forth in the presence of Master Gotama; may I obtain the higher ordination.”
translations.mn75:27: “Whoever, Māgaṇḍiya, having formerly belonged to another sect, in this Dhamma and Discipline desires the going forth, desires the higher ordination, he lives on probation for four months; after four months have passed, monks with a willing mind give him the going forth, they give him the higher ordination, for the state of a monk. But here I have recognized differences among persons.” “If, venerable sir, those who formerly belonged to other sects, desiring the going forth and desiring the higher ordination in this Dhamma and Discipline, live on probation for four months, and after four months have passed monks with a willing mind give the going forth and give the higher ordination for the state of a monk; I will live on probation for four years, and after four years have passed monks with a willing mind may give me the going forth, may give me the higher ordination for the state of a monk.”
translations.mn75:3: Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, while walking and strolling for exercise, approached the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. Māgaṇḍiya the wanderer saw that a grass mat had been spread out in the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan. Having seen it, he said this to the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta: “For whom, sir Bhāradvāja, has this grass mat been spread out in the fire-hall? It seems suitable for a recluse’s bed.”
translations.mn75:6: The Blessed One heard, with the divine ear element that is purified and surpasses the human, this conversation between the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan and the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya. Then, in the evening, the Blessed One rose from seclusion and approached the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan; having approached, the Blessed One sat down on the prepared grass mat. Then the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had concluded the greetings and the courteous talk, he sat down to one side. As the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta sat to one side, the Blessed One said this to him: “But, Bhāradvāja, was there some conversation with the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya concerning just this very grass mat?” When this was said, the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta, stirred and with hair standing on end, said this to the Blessed One: “It is indeed that which we were wanting to report to Master Gotama. And yet Master Gotama has stated what was not told.”
translations.mn75:7: And this talk between the Blessed One and the brahmin Bhāradvājagotta had been left unfinished. Then the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya, while walking and strolling for exercise, approached the fire-hall of the brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, where the Blessed One was; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had concluded the greetings and the courteous talk, he sat down to one side. As the wanderer Māgaṇḍiya sat to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
translations.mn77:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground.
translations.mn77:10: There are, Udāyi, five other things by which my disciples honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me, and having honored and respected me, they live in dependence on me. What five? Here, Udāyi, my disciples commend me in higher virtue: ‘The recluse Gotama is virtuous, endowed with the supreme aggregate of virtue.’
translations.mn77:15: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have taught my disciples the way, such that, practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the four establishments of mindfulness. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … he dwells contemplating mind in mind … he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. And there, too, many of my disciples dwell having reached the far shore in the consummation of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:16: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have taught my disciples the way, such that, practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the four right efforts. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states; he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states; he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states; he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, applies his mind, and strives for the maintenance of arisen wholesome states, for their non-confusion, for increase, for expansion, for development, for fulfillment. And there, too, many of my disciples dwell having reached the far shore in the consummation of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:17: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have taught my disciples the way, such that, practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the four bases of spiritual power. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops the base of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to desire and with the formations of striving; he develops the base of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to energy and with the formations of striving; he develops the base of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to mind and with the formations of striving; he develops the base of spiritual power endowed with concentration due to investigation and with the formations of striving. And there, too, many of my disciples dwell having reached the far shore in the consummation of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:18: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have taught my disciples the way, such that, practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the five faculties. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops the faculty of faith leading to peace, leading to awakening; he develops the faculty of energy … he develops the faculty of mindfulness … he develops the faculty of concentration … he develops the faculty of wisdom leading to peace, leading to awakening. And there, too, many of my disciples dwell having reached the far shore in the consummation of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:2: At that time several well-known, renowned wanderers were residing in the wanderers’ park at Moranivāpa, that is: Annabhāra, Varadhara, and the wanderer Sakuludāyī, and other well-known, renowned wanderers.
translations.mn77:20: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have taught my disciples the way, such that, practicing accordingly, my disciples develop the seven factors of awakening. Here, Udāyi, a bhikkhu develops the mindfulness awakening factor, supported by seclusion, supported by dispassion, supported by cessation, culminating in relinquishment; he develops the investigation-of-states awakening factor … he develops the energy awakening factor … he develops the rapture awakening factor … he develops the tranquility awakening factor … he develops the concentration awakening factor … he develops the equanimity awakening factor, supported by seclusion, supported by dispassion, supported by cessation, culminating in relinquishment. And there, too, many of my disciples dwell having reached the far shore in the consummation of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:21: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to the disciples the course of practice, following which my disciples develop the noble eightfold path. Here, Udāyi, a monk develops right view, develops right intention, develops right speech, develops right action, develops right livelihood, develops right effort, develops right mindfulness, develops right concentration. And in that my disciples—many—dwell having reached the far shore and culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:22: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to the disciples the course of practice, following which my disciples develop the eight liberations. Possessed of form, one sees forms: this is the first liberation. Perceiving non-form internally, one sees forms externally: this is the second liberation. One is resolved only on the beautiful: this is the third liberation. By completely surmounting perceptions of form, with the vanishing of perceptions of resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, one enters upon and dwells in the base of infinite space, thinking, ‘Infinite is space’: this is the fourth liberation. By completely surmounting the base of infinite space, one enters upon and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness, thinking, ‘Infinite is consciousness’: this is the fifth liberation. By completely surmounting the base of infinite consciousness, one enters upon and dwells in the base of nothingness, thinking, ‘There is nothing’: this is the sixth liberation. By completely surmounting the base of nothingness, one enters upon and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception: this is the seventh liberation. By completely surmounting the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters upon and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling: this is the eighth liberation. And in that my disciples—many—dwell having reached the far shore and culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:24: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to the disciples the course of practice, following which my disciples develop the ten kasiṇa spheres. One perceives the earth kasiṇa above, below, and across, non-dual, immeasurable; one perceives the water kasiṇa …; one perceives the fire kasiṇa …; one perceives the air kasiṇa …; one perceives the blue kasiṇa …; one perceives the yellow kasiṇa …; one perceives the red kasiṇa …; one perceives the white kasiṇa …; one perceives the space kasiṇa …; one perceives the consciousness kasiṇa above, below, and across, non-dual, immeasurable. And in that my disciples—many—dwell having reached the far shore and culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:25: Furthermore, Udāyi, I have declared to the disciples the course of practice, following which my disciples develop the four jhānas. Here, Udāyi, a monk—quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states—enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna, which has thought and examination, born of seclusion, with rapture and pleasure. He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his whole body not pervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Just as, Udāyi, a skilled bathman or a bathman’s apprentice, having poured bath powder into a bronze basin, would knead it again and again with water, sprinkling it again and again, so that the ball of bath powder becomes saturated with moisture, permeated with moisture, within and without, yet would not drip; even so, Udāyi, the monk drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his whole body not pervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.
translations.mn77:26: Furthermore, Udāyi, with the calming of thought and examination, a monk … enters upon and dwells in the second jhāna. He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of concentration, so that there is no part of his whole body not pervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of concentration. Just as, Udāyi, there is a deep lake fed by a spring. It has no inflow of water from the eastern direction, no inflow of water from the western direction, no inflow of water from the northern direction, no inflow of water from the southern direction, and the sky would not, from time to time, send down rain in proper streams; but from that very lake a cool stream of water would well up and, with cool water, drench, steep, fill, and pervade that very lake, so that there would be no part of the whole lake not pervaded by cool water; even so, Udāyi, the monk drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and pleasure born of concentration, so that there is no part of his whole body not pervaded by the rapture and pleasure born of concentration.
translations.mn77:27: Furthermore, Udāyi, with the fading away of rapture … a monk enters upon and dwells in the third jhāna. He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with pleasure without rapture, so that there is no part of his whole body not pervaded by pleasure without rapture. Just as, Udāyi, in a pond of blue lotuses or a pond of red lotuses or a pond of white lotuses, some blue lotuses or red lotuses or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, remain immersed in the water, nourished from within; and from their tips to their roots they are drenched, steeped, filled, and pervaded with cool water, so that there would be no part at all of those blue lotuses or red lotuses or white lotuses not pervaded by cool water; even so, Udāyi, the monk drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with pleasure without rapture, so that there is no part of his whole body not pervaded by pleasure without rapture.
translations.mn77:28: Furthermore, Udāyi, with the abandoning of pleasure and with the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a monk enters upon and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purification of mindfulness by equanimity. He sits having pervaded this very body with a purified mind, cleansed and bright, so that there is no part of his whole body not pervaded by a purified mind, cleansed and bright. Just as, Udāyi, a man might sit having wrapped himself, head and all, in a white cloth, so that there would be no part of his whole body not covered by the white cloth; even so, Udāyi, the monk sits having pervaded this very body with a purified mind, cleansed and bright, so that there is no part of his whole body not pervaded by a purified mind, cleansed and bright. And in that my disciples—many—dwell having reached the far shore and culmination of direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:3: Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms. Then it occurred to the Blessed One: “It is too early yet to wander for alms in Rājagaha. Why don’t I go to the wanderers’ park at Moranivāpa, to where the wanderer Sakuludāyī is, and approach him?”
translations.mn77:32: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have proclaimed to my disciples a practice such that, when my disciples have practiced accordingly, with the divine element of hearing, purified and surpassing the human, they hear both kinds of sounds—divine and human, those far and near. Just as, Udāyī, a strong conch-blower would without difficulty make himself heard in the four directions; even so, Udāyī, I have proclaimed to my disciples a practice such that, when my disciples have practiced accordingly, with the divine element of hearing, purified and surpassing the human, they hear both kinds of sounds—divine and human, those far and near. And there my disciples dwell, many having reached the consummation and perfection in direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:34: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have proclaimed to my disciples a practice such that, when my disciples have practiced accordingly, they recollect various kinds of past lives, that is: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births; many eons of contraction, many eons of expansion, many eons of contraction and expansion: ‘There I was named thus, of such a clan, of such an appearance, such was my food, such was my experience of pleasure and pain, such was the end of my life; passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere; there too I was named thus, of such a clan, of such an appearance, such was my food, such was my experience of pleasure and pain, such was the end of my life; passing away from there, I was reborn here.’ Thus they recollect various kinds of past lives with details and particulars. Just as, Udāyī, a man might go from his own village to another village, and from that village to another village; and from that village he might return again to his own village; and it might occur to him: ‘I went from my own village to another village; there I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, was silent thus; and from that village I went to that village; there too I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, was silent thus; and now from that village I have returned again to my own village’—even so, Udāyī, I have proclaimed to my disciples a practice such that, when my disciples have practiced accordingly, they recollect various kinds of past lives, that is: one birth … thus with details and particulars they recollect various kinds of past lives. And there my disciples dwell, many having reached the consummation and perfection in direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:35: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have proclaimed to my disciples a practice such that, when my disciples have practiced accordingly, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, they see beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and they understand beings as faring on according to their deeds: ‘These worthy beings, endowed with misconduct by body, misconduct by speech, misconduct by mind, revilers of the noble ones, of wrong view, undertaking actions based on wrong view—on the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in the plane of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, hell. But these worthy beings, endowed with good conduct by body, good conduct by speech, good conduct by mind, not revilers of the noble ones, of right view, undertaking actions based on right view—on the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a good destination, the heavenly world.’ Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, they see beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and they understand beings as faring on according to their deeds. Just as, Udāyī, there were two houses with doors, and there a man with eyes, standing in the middle, could see people entering a house and leaving, walking back and forth and moving about; even so, Udāyī, I have proclaimed to my disciples a practice such that, when my disciples have practiced accordingly, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, they see beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and they understand beings as faring on according to their deeds … and there my disciples dwell, many having reached the consummation and perfection in direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:36: Furthermore, Udāyī, I have proclaimed to my disciples a practice such that, when my disciples have practiced accordingly, by the destruction of the taints, they dwell having realized for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it. Just as, Udāyī, a clear, calm, unclouded lake in a mountain cleft: there a man with eyes, standing on the shore, could see shells and snails, and pebbles and stones, and schools of fish, moving about and staying still; and it might occur to him: ‘This lake is clear, calm, unclouded; and there are these shells and snails, these pebbles and stones, and these schools of fish, moving about and staying still’—even so, Udāyī, I have proclaimed to my disciples a practice such that, when my disciples have practiced accordingly, by the destruction of the taints, they dwell having realized for themselves with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it. And there my disciples dwell, many having reached the consummation and perfection in direct knowledge.
translations.mn77:5: Then the Blessed One approached the wanderer Sakuludāyī. Then the wanderer Sakuludāyī said this to the Blessed One: “Come, venerable sir, Blessed One. Welcome, venerable sir, to the Blessed One. It has been a long time, venerable sir, since the Blessed One made an occasion such as this, namely coming here. Sit down, venerable sir, Blessed One; this seat is prepared.” The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. And the wanderer Sakuludāyī, having taken a certain low seat, sat down to one side. When the wanderer Sakuludāyī was seated to one side, the Blessed One said this to him: “What now, Udāyī, are you seated together talking about, and what was your discussion that was interrupted?”
translations.mn77:7: “But how many qualities, Udāyī, do you see in me and in the Dhamma, by which my disciples honor me, respect me, esteem me, venerate me, and, having honored and respected, live in reliance on me?”
translations.mn77:9:
"‘The ascetic Gotama is of little food, and he praises little eating’: if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me for that, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me; but there are, Udāyi, disciples of mine who live on a measure of food, on half a measure of food, on a beluva-fruit’s measure of food, on half a beluva-fruit’s measure of food. But I, Udāyi, sometimes eat a full bowl with this bowl, and I eat even more. ‘The ascetic Gotama is of little food, and he praises little eating’: if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me for that, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me—those disciples of mine, Udāyi, who live on a measure of food … on half a beluva-fruit’s measure of food would not, by this principle, honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me.

‘The ascetic Gotama is content with whatever kind of robe, and he praises contentment with whatever kind of robe’: if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me for that, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me; but there are, Udāyi, disciples of mine who are rag-robe wearers, wear coarse robes; they gather cast-off cloth from charnel grounds or rubbish heaps or shops, and after making an outer robe they wear it. But I, Udāyi, sometimes wear householders’ robes—strong, rough to the touch, like bottle-gourd hair. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with whatever kind of robe, and he praises contentment with whatever kind of robe’: if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me for that, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me—those disciples of mine, Udāyi, who are rag-robe wearers … after making an outer robe they wear it would not, by this principle, honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me.

‘The ascetic Gotama is content with whatever kind of almsfood, and he praises contentment with whatever kind of almsfood’: if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me for that, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me; but there are, Udāyi, disciples of mine who are almsfood eaters, who go from house to house in order, who delight in the observance of gleaning; when they have entered among houses, even if invited to a seat they do not accept. But I, Udāyi, sometimes eat when invited—rice, well-cooked, with black grains picked out, with many curries and many side-dishes. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with whatever kind of almsfood, and he praises contentment with whatever kind of almsfood’: if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me for that, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me—those disciples of mine, Udāyi, who are almsfood eaters … even if invited to a seat they do not accept would not, by this principle, honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me.

‘The ascetic Gotama is content with whatever kind of lodging, and he praises contentment with whatever kind of lodging’: if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me for that, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me; but there are, Udāyi, disciples of mine who are tree-root dwellers, open-air dwellers; for eight months they do not go to a roofed place. But I, Udāyi, sometimes dwell even in gabled houses, plastered inside and out, sheltered from the wind, with close-fitting bolts, with shut windows. ‘The ascetic Gotama is content with whatever kind of lodging, and he praises contentment with whatever kind of lodging’: if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me for that, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me—those disciples of mine, Udāyi, who are tree-root dwellers, open-air dwellers, for eight months do not go to a roofed place would not, by this principle, honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me.

‘The ascetic Gotama is secluded, and he praises seclusion’: if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me for that, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me; but there are, Udāyi, disciples of mine who are forest dwellers, with remote lodgings; having entered forest thickets, remote lodgings, they dwell there; they come down into the midst of the Saṅgha every half-month for the recitation of the Pātimokkha. But I, Udāyi, sometimes dwell crowded with monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, and with kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and disciples of sectarians. ‘The ascetic Gotama is secluded, and he praises seclusion’: if, Udāyi, my disciples were to honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me for that, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me. Those disciples of mine, Udāyi, who are forest dwellers with remote lodgings … come down into the midst of the Saṅgha every half-month for the recitation of the Pātimokkha would not, by this principle, honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me, having honored and respected me they would live relying on me.

So, Udāyi, my disciples do not honor me, respect me, esteem me, and venerate me by these five principles, and having honored and respected me they do not live relying on me."
translations.mn7:11: ‘Insofar as what is mine has been abandoned, vomited up, released, given up, relinquished’: he gains understanding of the meaning, he gains understanding of the Dhamma, he gains gladness connected with the Dhamma; in one who is gladdened, rapture is born; in one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil; one whose body is tranquil feels pleasure; in one who is pleased, the mind becomes concentrated.
translations.mn7:13: He dwells having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere, to all as to oneself, he dwells having pervaded the entire world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, without ill will;
translations.mn7:17: He understands: ‘There is this; there is what is inferior; there is what is superior; there is an escape beyond this perception-attainment.’
translations.mn7:18: As he knows thus, as he sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensuality; his mind is liberated from the taint of becoming; his mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance. When it is liberated, there is the knowledge: ‘Liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’ This is called, bhikkhus: ‘a bhikkhu bathed with the inner bathing’”ti.
translations.mn7:19: Now at that time the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja was seated not far from the Blessed One. Then the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja said this to the Blessed One: “Does Master Gotama go to bathe in the Bāhuka river?” “What, brahmin, is the Bāhuka river? What will the Bāhuka river do?” “For the Bāhuka river, Master Gotama, is regarded by the world as (bringing merit) for many people; the Bāhuka river, Master Gotama, is regarded as meritorious for many people; and in the Bāhuka river many people wash away the evil deeds they have done.”
translations.mn7:2: “Just as, bhikkhus, a cloth is soiled and stained with grime; whatever dye a dyer would apply it to—whether blue dye, or yellow dye, or red dye, or crimson dye—it would come out with a bad color, with an impure color. For what reason? Because the cloth is impure, bhikkhus. In the same way, bhikkhus, when the mind is defiled, a bad destination is to be expected. Just as, bhikkhus, a cloth is pure and bright; whatever dye a dyer would apply it to—whether blue dye, or yellow dye, or red dye, or crimson dye—it would come out with a good color, with a pure color. For what reason? Because the cloth is pure, bhikkhus. In the same way, bhikkhus, when the mind is undefiled, a good destination is to be expected.
translations.mn7:20: Then the Blessed One addressed the brahmin Sundarikabhāradvāja with verses: “The Bāhuka and Adhikakka, and Gaya and Sundarika too; the Sarasvatī and Payāga, and also the river Bāhumatī; though the fool plunges in them constantly, one with dark deeds is not purified. What will Sundarikā do? What Payāga, what the Bāhuka river? A man who is hostile, who has done evil deeds—they do not cleanse him, an evil-doer. For the purified, indeed, it is always auspicious; for the purified, the uposatha is always; for the purified, one of clean deeds, the observance always succeeds. Here itself bathe, brahmin; in regard to all beings, make safety. If you do not speak falsely, if you do not harm living beings; if you do not take what is not given, faithful, not stingy—what will you do by going to Gaya? Even a well will be your Gaya”ti.
translations.mn7:3: And what, bhikkhus, are the defilements of the mind? Covetousness and unrighteous greed are a defilement of the mind; ill will is a defilement of the mind; anger is a defilement of the mind; resentment is a defilement of the mind; denigration is a defilement of the mind; spite is a defilement of the mind; envy is a defilement of the mind; stinginess is a defilement of the mind; deceit is a defilement of the mind; fraud is a defilement of the mind; obstinacy is a defilement of the mind; impetuosity is a defilement of the mind; conceit is a defilement of the mind; arrogance is a defilement of the mind; vanity is a defilement of the mind; negligence is a defilement of the mind.
translations.mn7:6: He is endowed with confirmed confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well proclaimed by the Blessed One, visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be known individually by the wise.’
translations.mn7:7: He is endowed with confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Blessed One’s community of disciples is practicing well; the Blessed One’s community of disciples is practicing straight; the Blessed One’s community of disciples is practicing rightly; the Blessed One’s community of disciples is practicing properly; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This community of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.’
translations.mn82:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One, wandering on tour among the Kurus, arrived at a Kuru market town named Thullakoṭṭhika, together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
translations.mn82:11: Then the friends of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla went to Raṭṭhapāla’s mother and father; having gone, they said this to Raṭṭhapāla’s mother and father: “Mother and father, this Raṭṭhapāla, the clansman, is lying right there on the bare ground: ‘Here itself there will be death for me, or the going forth.’ If you will not permit Raṭṭhapāla the clansman to go forth from the home life into homelessness, death will come to him right there. But if you permit Raṭṭhapāla the clansman to go forth from the home life into homelessness, you will see him even after he has gone forth. If Raṭṭhapāla the clansman would not take delight in the going forth from the home life into homelessness, what other course would there be for him? He would come back right here. Permit Raṭṭhapāla the clansman to go forth from the home life into homelessness.” “We permit Raṭṭhapāla the clansman to go forth from the home life into homelessness, dear. But after going forth he should show himself to his mother and father.” Then the friends of the clansman Raṭṭhapāla went to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla; having gone, they said this to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla: “Get up, friend Raṭṭhapāla; you are permitted by your mother and father to go forth from the home life into homelessness. But after going forth you should show yourself to your mother and father.”
translations.mn82:12: Then Raṭṭhapāla the clansman, having got up and regained strength, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Raṭṭhapāla the clansman said this to the Blessed One: “I am permitted, venerable sir, by my mother and father to go forth from the home life into homelessness. Let the Blessed One ordain me.”
translations.mn82:13: The clansman Raṭṭhapāla received the going forth in the Blessed One’s presence; he received the full admission. Then the Blessed One, after staying at Thullakoṭṭhika as long as he wished, departed on a walking tour toward Sāvatthī, when Venerable Raṭṭhapāla had been fully admitted for half a month. Wandering on tour step by step, he arrived at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park.
translations.mn82:14: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, in no long time—having realized for himself with direct knowledge and having attained in this very life the unsurpassed end of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness—abided. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.” And Venerable Raṭṭhapāla became one of the arahants.
translations.mn82:16: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and, having circled him keeping the right side toward him, put his lodging in order; then, taking bowl and robe, he departed on a walking tour toward Thullakoṭṭhika. Wandering on tour step by step, he arrived at Thullakoṭṭhika. There Venerable Raṭṭhapāla was staying at Thullakoṭṭhika, in King Korabya’s Migacīra. Then in the morning Venerable Raṭṭhapāla dressed, took bowl and robe, and entered Thullakoṭṭhika for alms. Going for alms from house to house in Thullakoṭṭhika, he approached his own father’s dwelling.
translations.mn82:17: Now at that time Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father was having the middle gatehouse plastered. Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father saw Venerable Raṭṭhapāla coming from afar. Seeing him, he said this: “By these shaven little ascetics our only son—dear and pleasing—has been made to go forth.” Then at his own father’s dwelling Venerable Raṭṭhapāla got neither a gift nor a refusal; rather, he got only abuse.
translations.mn82:18: Now at that time Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s family slave woman wanted to throw away some leftover porridge from the day before. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said this to that slave woman: “If it is to be thrown away, sister, pour it here into my bowl.” Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s family slave woman, as she poured that leftover porridge from the day before into Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s bowl, recognized the marks of his hands and feet and his voice. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s family slave woman approached Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s mother; having approached, she said this to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s mother: “Mistress, you should know: ‘Master Raṭṭhapāla has arrived.’” “If, dear, you speak the truth, I will make you a freedwoman.” Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s mother approached Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father; having approached, she said this to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father: “Surely, householder, you should know: ‘They say the clansman Raṭṭhapāla has arrived’?”
translations.mn82:19: Now at that time Venerable Raṭṭhapāla was eating that leftover porridge from the day before, leaning against the root of a certain wall. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father approached Venerable Raṭṭhapāla; having approached, he said this to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: “Is it possible, dear Raṭṭhapāla, that you would eat leftover porridge from the day before? Dear Raṭṭhapāla, surely you should go to your own home.” “How could we have a home, householder, we who have gone forth from the household life into homelessness? We are homeless, householder. We did come to your house, householder; there we got neither a gift nor a refusal; rather, we got only abuse.” “Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, let us go home.” “Enough, householder; today my meal-duty is done.” “Then, dear Raṭṭhapāla, consent to tomorrow’s meal.” Venerable Raṭṭhapāla consented by silence.
translations.mn82:20: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father, knowing Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s consent, approached his own dwelling; having approached, he had a great pile of gold and silver made and covered with screens, and he addressed Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s former wives: “Come, daughters-in-law, adorn yourselves with the adornment by which you were formerly dear and pleasing to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla; adorn yourselves with that adornment.”
translations.mn82:21: Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father, when that night had passed, in his own dwelling had excellent food and provisions prepared, and he announced the time to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: “It is time, dear Raṭṭhapāla; the meal is ready.”
translations.mn82:22: Then in the morning Venerable Raṭṭhapāla dressed, took bowl and robe, and approached his own father’s dwelling; having approached, he sat down on the seat that had been prepared. Then Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father had that pile of gold and silver uncovered and said this to Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: “This is, dear Raṭṭhapāla, your mother’s maternal wealth; this is other paternal wealth; this is other grandfather’s. It is possible, dear Raṭṭhapāla, to enjoy possessions and to make merit. Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, turn back to the lower way and enjoy possessions and make merit.” “If you would do my word, householder, you would load this pile of gold and silver onto a cart, have it taken out, and sink it in midstream in the current of the Ganges river. For what reason? Because, householder, for you there would arise from that cause sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.”
translations.mn82:23: Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s former wives, each taking him by the feet, said this to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: “What kind, dear sir, are the nymphs for whose sake you live the holy life?” “We do not, sisters, live the holy life for the sake of nymphs.” “The dear sir Raṭṭhapāla addresses us with the word ‘sisters’.” Right there they fainted and fell.
translations.mn82:24: Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla said this to his father: “If, householder, food is to be given, give it; do not trouble us.” “Eat, dear Raṭṭhapāla; the meal is ready.” Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla’s father with his own hands satisfied and served the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla with choice solid food and soft food. Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, having eaten, with his bowl and hands washed, still standing, recited these verses:
translations.mn82:26: Then the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, still standing, having spoken these verses, approached King Korabya’s Migacīra; having approached, he sat down at the root of a certain tree for the day’s abiding.
translations.mn82:27: Then King Korabya addressed the park-keeper: “Clean up, my good park-keeper, the Migacīra pleasure-ground; let us go to see the lovely ground.” “Yes, sire,” the park-keeper replied to King Korabya; while cleaning the Migacīra he saw the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla sitting at the root of a certain tree for the day’s abiding. Having seen him, he approached King Korabya; having approached, he said this to King Korabya: “The Migacīra is clean for you, sire. There is here a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, in this very Thullakoṭṭhika the son of the foremost family, whom you were often praising; he is sitting at the root of a certain tree for the day’s abiding.” “Then, my good park-keeper, enough now of the pleasure-ground. Now we will attend upon that Venerable Raṭṭhapāla.”
translations.mn82:28: Then King Korabya, saying, “Let all that prepared solid food and soft food be distributed,” had fine vehicles yoked; mounting a fine vehicle, he set out from Thullakoṭṭhika with fine vehicles, with great royal splendor, to see the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla. Going by vehicle as far as the ground for vehicles, he dismounted from the vehicles and, on foot, with an ever-growing retinue, approached the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla. After exchanging greetings and courteous talk, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, King Korabya said this to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla: “Let the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla sit here on the spread of leather.” “Enough, great king, sit you; I am seated on my own seat.” King Korabya sat down on the seat that had been prepared. Having sat down, King Korabya said this to the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla:
translations.mn82:29: “There are, Raṭṭhapāla, these four kinds of decline, endowed with which some here shave off hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. What four? Decline through old age, decline through illness, decline of wealth, decline of relatives.
translations.mn82:3: Then the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika approached the Blessed One; having approached, some paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and, after exchanging courteous and friendly talk, sat down to one side; some, with hands raised in reverence toward the Blessed One, sat down to one side; some, in the Blessed One’s presence, announced their name and clan and sat down to one side; some sat down to one side in silence. When the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhika were seated to one side, the Blessed One instructed, encouraged, inspired, and gladdened them with a talk on Dhamma.
translations.mn82:34: “These, Raṭṭhapāla, are the four kinds of decline, endowed with which some here shave off hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness. Those are not present in the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla. Having known what, or seen what, or heard what, did the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla go forth from the household life into homelessness?”
translations.mn82:35: “There are, great king, four summaries of Dhamma that were stated by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the perfectly awakened one; having known and seen and heard them, I went forth from the household life into homelessness. What four?
translations.mn82:4: Now at that time a clansman named Raṭṭhapāla, in that very Thullakoṭṭhika the son of the foremost family, was sitting in that assembly. Then it occurred to the clansman Raṭṭhapāla: “As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy, living in a home, to live the holy life that is utterly complete, utterly pure, like a polished conch-shell. What if I were to shave off hair and beard, put on ochre robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?”
translations.mn82:6: Then Raṭṭhapāla the clansman, when the brahmins and householders of Thullakoṭṭhita had not long departed, went to the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Raṭṭhapāla the clansman said this to the Blessed One: “As I, venerable sir, understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, it is not easy, while living the household life, to live the holy life that is utterly complete, utterly pure, like a polished shell. I wish, venerable sir, having shaved off hair and beard and having put on ochre robes, to go forth from the home life into homelessness. May I obtain going forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may I obtain the higher ordination. Let the Blessed One ordain me.” “But have you been permitted, Raṭṭhapāla, by your mother and father to go forth from the home life into homelessness?” “I have not, venerable sir, been permitted by my mother and father to go forth from the home life into homelessness.” “Raṭṭhapāla, Tathāgatas do not ordain a son who has not been permitted by his mother and father.” “Then, venerable sir, I will do so in such a way that my mother and father will permit me to go forth from the home life into homelessness.”
translations.mn95:1: Thus have I heard—At one time the Blessed One, wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, arrived at a Kosalan brahmin village called Opāsāda. There the Blessed One was staying at Opāsāda, to the north of Opāsāda in the deva grove, the sāla grove.
translations.mn95:10: Then Caṅkī the brahmin, together with a large group of brahmins, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When he had concluded the courteous and friendly talk, he sat down to one side.
translations.mn95:11: Now at that time the Blessed One was sitting after having exchanged some courteous and friendly talk with very old brahmins. Now at that time a young man named Kāpaṭika, young, with hair in a topknot, about sixteen years of age by birth, who had gone to the far shore of the three Vedas with their vocabularies and ritual and phonology, with the divisions of syllables, the histories as a fifth, skilled in the word-lists, a grammarian, unexcelled in world-lore and in the marks of a great man, was sitting in that assembly. He kept interjecting talk in the midst of the old brahmins who were consulting with the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One rebuked the young man Kāpaṭika: “Let the venerable Bhāradvāja not interject talk in the midst of the old brahmins who are consulting. Let the venerable Bhāradvāja wait until the talk is concluded.” When this was said, Caṅkī the brahmin said this to the Blessed One: “Let Master Gotama not rebuke the young man Kāpaṭika. The young man Kāpaṭika is well-born, learned, wise, and a fine speaker; and the young man Kāpaṭika is capable of conversing with Master Gotama in this matter.”
translations.mn95:2: Now at that time Caṅkī the brahmin was residing at Opāsāda, teeming with living beings, with grass, wood, and water, with grain, a royal benefice given by King Pasenadi of Kosala, a royal gift, a brahmin endowment.
translations.mn95:20: When, while investigating, he sees him as purified of deluding states; then he places faith in him. With faith arisen he approaches; approaching, he attends on him; attending on him, he lends ear; with attentive ear he hears the Dhamma; having heard the Dhamma he retains it; he examines the meaning of the teachings that he has retained; as he examines the meaning, the teachings are approved by reflection; when there is approval by reflection on the teachings, desire arises; having desire he makes an effort; having made an effort he weighs; having weighed he strives; striving, with resolute mind, he realizes the supreme truth with the body and penetrates it with wisdom and sees it. To this extent, Bhāradvāja, there is awakening to the truth; to this extent one awakens to the truth; and to this extent we describe awakening to the truth; but there is not yet attainment of the truth.”
translations.mn95:33: “But, Master Gotama, which quality is of great help for approaching? We ask Master Gotama about the quality that is of great help for approaching.” “For approaching, Bhāradvāja, faith is of great help. If faith did not arise, one would not approach. And because faith arises, one approaches. Therefore faith is of great help for approaching.”
translations.mn95:5: Now at that time Caṅkī the brahmin had gone to the upper palace for his midday rest. Caṅkī the brahmin saw the brahmins and householders of Opāsāda, having come out from Opāsāda, in groups and bands, going northwards to the deva grove, the sāla grove. Seeing this, he addressed Khatta: “Why now, good Khatta, are the brahmins and householders of Opāsāda, having come out from Opāsāda, in groups and bands, going northwards to the deva grove, the sāla grove?”
translations.mn9:11: And what, friend, is nutriment? what is the origin of nutriment? what is the cessation of nutriment? what is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment? There are these four nutriments, friend, for the maintenance of beings that have come to be, or for the support of those seeking existence. What four? Edible food, coarse or fine, is the first; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; consciousness is the fourth. With the arising of craving there is the arising of nutriment; with the cessation of craving there is the cessation of nutriment; this very Noble Eightfold Path is the way leading to the cessation of nutriment, that is: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration.
translations.mn9:12: When, friend, a noble disciple thus understands nutriment, thus understands the origin of nutriment, thus understands the cessation of nutriment, thus understands the way leading to the cessation of nutriment, then, having abandoned entirely the underlying tendency to lust, having removed the underlying tendency to aversion, having eradicated the underlying tendency to the view and conceit “I am”, having abandoned ignorance and arisen knowledge, he is one who makes an end of suffering in this very life—to this extent too, friend, a noble disciple is of right view, his view is straight, he is endowed with confirmed confidence in the Dhamma, he has arrived at this true Dhamma.”
translations.mn9:15: "But, friends, what is suffering, what is the origin of suffering, what is the cessation of suffering, what is the way leading to the cessation of suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair are suffering, association with the disliked is suffering, separation from the liked is suffering, not to get what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering—this, friends, is called suffering."
translations.mn9:16: "And what, friends, is the origin of suffering? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and passion, delighting here and there, that is: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence—this, friends, is called the origin of suffering."
translations.mn9:17: "And what, friends, is the cessation of suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving—its giving up, relinquishing, release, and non-attachment—this, friends, is called the cessation of suffering."
translations.mn9:18: "And what, friends, is the way leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this very noble eightfold path, that is: right view … right concentration—this, friends, is called the way leading to the cessation of suffering."
translations.mn9:2: "‘Right view, right view’, friends, is what is said. To what extent, friends, is a noble disciple one of right view, with view made straight, possessing confirmed confidence in the Dhamma, arrived at this true Dhamma?" "Even from far away, friends, we would come to the presence of venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. Let venerable Sāriputta himself explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from venerable Sāriputta, the monks will remember it." "Then, friends, listen, attend carefully; I will speak." "Yes, friend," those monks replied to venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.mn9:20: "Very good, friend," those monks, having delighted in and approved of venerable Sāriputta’s words, asked venerable Sāriputta a further question: "But might there be, friend, another way in which a noble disciple is one of right view, with view made straight, possessing confirmed confidence in the Dhamma, arrived at this true Dhamma?"
translations.mn9:3: "When, friends, a noble disciple understands the unwholesome and understands the root of the unwholesome, understands the wholesome and understands the root of the wholesome—then to that extent too, friends, a noble disciple is one of right view, with view made straight, possessing confirmed confidence in the Dhamma, arrived at this true Dhamma."
translations.mn9:4: But what, friends, is the unwholesome, what is the root of the unwholesome, what is the wholesome, what is the root of the wholesome? Killing living beings, friends, is unwholesome; taking what is not given is unwholesome; sexual misconduct in sensual pleasures is unwholesome; false speech is unwholesome; divisive speech is unwholesome; harsh speech is unwholesome; idle chatter is unwholesome; covetousness is unwholesome; ill will is unwholesome; wrong view is unwholesome—this, friends, is called the unwholesome.
translations.mn9:5: And what, friends, is the root of the unwholesome? Greed is the root of the unwholesome, hatred is the root of the unwholesome, delusion is the root of the unwholesome—this, friends, is called the root of the unwholesome.
translations.mn9:7: And what, friends, is the root of the wholesome? Non-greed is the root of the wholesome, non-hatred is the root of the wholesome, non-delusion is the root of the wholesome—this, friends, is called the root of the wholesome.
translations.mn9:70: And what, friends, is an influx, what is the origin of influxes, what is the cessation of influxes, what is the way leading to the cessation of influxes? These, friends, are the three influxes: the influx of sensuality, the influx of existence, the influx of ignorance. With the arising of ignorance is the origin of influxes; with the cessation of ignorance is the cessation of influxes; this very noble eightfold path is the way leading to the cessation of influxes, that is: right view … right concentration.
translations.mn9:8: "When, friends, a noble disciple thus understands the unwholesome, thus understands the root of the unwholesome, thus understands the wholesome, thus understands the root of the wholesome, then, having completely abandoned the underlying tendency to lust, having dispelled the underlying tendency to aversion, having uprooted the underlying tendency to the view and conceit ‘I am’, having abandoned ignorance and arisen knowledge, they are one who makes an end of suffering in this very life—then to that extent too, friends, a noble disciple is one of right view, with view made straight, possessing confirmed confidence in the Dhamma, arrived at this true Dhamma."
translations.sn1.10:2: "For those dwelling in the forest, peaceful, living the spiritual life; eating one meal—by what does their complexion become bright?"
translations.sn1.10:3: "They do not sorrow over the past, they do not yearn for the future; they live sustained by the present—by that their complexion becomes bright."
translations.sn1.17:1: "Hard and difficult to endure is the ascetic life for one untrained; many are the hardships there, where the fool sinks down."
translations.sn1.17:2: "How long should one live the ascetic life, if one does not restrain the mind? At every step one would sink down, following the power of intentions."
translations.sn1.17:3: "Like a tortoise drawing its limbs into its own shell, the monk should gather in mental thoughts; independent, not harassing another, having become fully quenched, one should not reproach anyone."
translations.sn1.18:1: "A man restrained by conscience—someone like that is found in the world; one who realizes blame, like a good horse at a touch of the whip."
translations.sn1.18:2: "Those restrained by conscience, subtle, who always live as mindful ones, reaching the end of suffering, walk evenly in the uneven."
translations.sn1.1:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. Then a certain deity, in the deep of night, of outstanding beauty, illuminating the whole of Jeta’s Grove, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity said this to the Blessed One: "How, sir, did you cross the flood?" "Friend, it was by not standing still and by not struggling that I crossed the flood." "But how, sir, did you cross the flood by not standing still and by not struggling?" "When, friend, I stood still, then I sank; when, friend, I struggled, then I was swept away. Thus, friend, by not standing still and by not struggling I crossed the flood."
translations.sn1.1:2: "After a long time indeed I see a brahmin fully quenched; not standing still, not struggling, having crossed beyond the clingings in the world."
translations.sn1.1:3: That deity said this. The Teacher approved. Then that deity, thinking, "The Teacher approves of me," paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to the right, and then vanished right there.
translations.sn1.20:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha, in the Tapodā park. Then Venerable Samiddhi, rising at the crack of dawn, approached the Tapodā to bathe his limbs. Having bathed his limbs in the Tapodā and come out again, he stood wearing a single robe, drying his limbs. Then a certain deity, in the late night, of surpassing radiance, illuminating the entire Tapodā, approached Venerable Samiddhi; having approached, standing in the air, she addressed Venerable Samiddhi in verse:
translations.sn1.20:2: “Without having eaten you go to beg, monk; for you do not go to beg after eating. Having eaten, monk, go to beg; do not let the time pass you by.”
translations.sn1.20:20: “Beings who perceive what is expressible, established in what is expressible: not fully understanding what is expressible, they come under the yoke of death.
translations.sn1.20:21: But having fully understood what is expressible, he does not conceive an expounder; for for him that is not—there is nothing by which one could speak of him as such. If you know, speak, yakkha.”
translations.sn1.20:22: “I do not, sir, understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One. It would be good, sir, if the Blessed One would speak so that I might understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One.”
translations.sn1.20:23: “Equal, superior, or inferior—whoever conceives so would dispute on that account. Not wavering among the three kinds, for him there is no ‘equal’ or ‘superior’. If you know, speak, yakkha.”
translations.sn1.20:25: “He abandoned conceit and did not fall into arrogance; he cut off craving here in name-and-form. That one, with the knot cut, free of affliction, without longing, seeking him they did not find him—gods and humans here or elsewhere, or in the heavens, in all abodes.
translations.sn1.20:3: “I do not know the time; the hidden time is not seen. Therefore I beg without having eaten—may time not pass me by.”
translations.sn1.20:4: Then that deity, having stood upon the ground, said this to Venerable Samiddhi: “You are young, monk, recently gone forth, with black hair, endowed with blessed youth, in the first stage of life, unindulged in sensual pleasures. Enjoy, monk, human sensual pleasures; do not, abandoning what is visible here and now, run after what is later.”
translations.sn1.20:5: “I do not, friend, abandoning what is visible here and now, run after what is later. Rather, friend, abandoning what is later, I run after what is visible here and now. For later, friend, sensual pleasures are said by the Blessed One to be much suffering, much distress; the danger here is greater. This Dhamma is visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be known individually by the wise.”
translations.sn1.20:6: “And how, monk, are sensual pleasures later, said by the Blessed One to be much suffering, much distress, with greater danger therein? And how is this Dhamma visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be known individually by the wise?”
translations.sn1.20:7: “I, friend, am new, recently gone forth, newly come to this Dhamma and discipline. I am not able to explain in detail. That Blessed One, the arahant, the perfectly awakened one, is staying at Rājagaha in the Tapodā park. Approach the Blessed One and ask him this matter. As the Blessed One answers you, so should you remember it.”
translations.sn1.20:8: “It is not easy, monk, for us to approach that Blessed One, surrounded by other mighty deities. But if you, monk, approach that Blessed One and ask him this matter, we too will come for hearing the Dhamma.” “So be it, friend,” Venerable Samiddhi replied to that deity, and he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Samiddhi said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.21:2: “As if pierced by a spear, as if his head were on fire, for the abandoning of sensual desire, mindful, a monk should wander.”
translations.sn1.21:3: “As if pierced by a spear, as if his head were on fire, for the abandoning of identity-view, mindful, a monk should wander.”
translations.sn1.25:1: “A monk who is an arahant, one who has done what had to be done, with the taints ended, bearing his final body: would he say ‘I speak’, or would he say ‘they speak about me’?”
translations.sn1.25:2: “A monk who is an arahant, one who has done what had to be done, with the taints ended, bearing his final body: he would say ‘I speak’, and he would say ‘they speak about me’; having understood worldly conventions, skilled, he would speak by mere usage.”
translations.sn1.25:3: “A monk who is an arahant, one who has done what had to be done, with the taints ended, bearing his final body: does that monk, having approached conceit, say ‘I speak’, or say ‘they speak about me’?”
translations.sn1.25:4: “For one whose conceit is abandoned there are no knots; all knots of conceit are blown away. That wise one has gone beyond conceiving: he would say ‘I speak’;
translations.sn1.25:5: and he would say ‘they speak about me’; having understood worldly conventions, skilled, he would speak by mere usage.”
translations.sn1.2:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain deity, in the late night, of surpassing radiance, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Blessed One; having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn1.2:5: “By the ending of delight in becoming, by the destruction of perception and consciousness; by the cessation and calming of feelings—thus, friend, I understand the release, the full release, the seclusion of beings.”
translations.sn1.36:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. Then several Satullapakāyikā deities, in the late night, of surpassing radiance, illuminating the entire Jeta’s Grove, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one deity in the Blessed One’s presence recited this verse:
translations.sn1.36:2: “Faith is a man’s companion, if he does not stand in faithlessness; and for him there is honor and fame; and he goes to heaven, leaving the body behind.”
translations.sn1.36:4: “Let one abandon anger, let one abandon conceit; let one go beyond every fetter. For one who does not cling to name-and-form, who has nothing, bonds do not pursue.”
translations.sn1.36:5: “Fools, witless people, devote themselves to heedlessness; but the wise one guards heedfulness as the best wealth.
translations.sn1.36:6: Do not devote yourselves to heedlessness; do not take delight in sensual pleasures and intimacy. For one who is heedful, meditating, attains the highest happiness.”
translations.sn1.38:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha in the Maddakucchi deer-park. At that time the Blessed One’s foot had been injured by a splinter. Violent feelings afflicted the Blessed One—bodily feelings, painful, sharp, severe, bitter, unpleasant, disagreeable; the Blessed One endured them, mindful and fully aware, untroubled. Then the Blessed One, having spread out his outer robe fourfold, lay down in the lion’s posture on his right side, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and fully aware.
translations.sn1.38:10: Overcome by craving, bound by vows and observances, practicing rough austerities for a hundred years; yet their mind is not rightly freed—of inferior aim and form, they do not go to the far shore.
translations.sn1.38:11: There is no self-control here for one who desires conceit; there is no calm for one who is not concentrated. Alone in the forest, living heedlessly, one would not cross beyond the realm of Death.”
translations.sn1.38:12: “Having abandoned conceit, with a well-composed mind, with a purified mind, freed everywhere; alone in the forest, living diligently, one would cross beyond the realm of Death.”
translations.sn1.38:2: Then seven hundred Satullapakāyika deities, in the depth of the night, of radiant appearance, illuminating the whole of Maddakucchi, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, one deity in the presence of the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance: “Truly, good sir, the ascetic Gotama is a nāga; and like a nāga he endures the arisen bodily feelings—painful, sharp, severe, bitter, unpleasant, disagreeable—mindful and fully aware, untroubled.”
translations.sn1.38:3: Then another deity in the presence of the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance: “Truly, good sir, the ascetic Gotama is a lion; and like a lion he endures the arisen bodily feelings—painful, sharp, severe, bitter, unpleasant, disagreeable—mindful and fully aware, untroubled.”
translations.sn1.38:8: Then another deity in the presence of the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance: “See the concentration well developed, and the mind well freed—not leaning forward, not leaning back, not gone to being restrained and held down by formations. Whoever would think such a person-nāga, person-lion, thoroughbred person, bull person, chief burden-bearer person, tamed person should be surpassed—what else but from not seeing?”
translations.sn1.38:9: “The five Vedas, a hundred sacrifices, the ascetic brahmins practicing; yet their mind is not rightly freed—of inferior aim and form, they do not go to the far shore.
translations.sn1.41:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then a certain deity, in the depth of the night, of radiant appearance, illuminating the whole of Jetavana, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, she paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, that deity in the presence of the Blessed One spoke these verses:
translations.sn1.41:4: What is given bears happy fruit; what is not given is not so. Thieves take it, kings take it; fire burns it, it perishes.
translations.sn1.41:5: Then in the end one leaves it, the body together with its possessions. Knowing this, the wise should enjoy and should give; and having given and enjoyed according to one’s means, one goes to a place in heaven, blameless.”
translations.sn1.42:1: “What-giver is a giver of strength, what-giver is a giver of beauty; what-giver is a giver of happiness, what-giver is a giver of sight; and who is a giver of all—tell me that when asked.”
translations.sn1.42:2: “A giver of food is a giver of strength; a giver of cloth is a giver of beauty. A giver of a vehicle is a giver of happiness; a giver of a lamp is a giver of sight.
translations.sn1.42:3: And a giver of all is the one who gives a dwelling; and he is a giver of the deathless, the one who instructs in the Dhamma.”
translations.sn1.51:1: “What indeed is good until old age, what is good when established; what is the jewel of people, what is hard for thieves to take away?”
translations.sn1.51:2: “Virtue is good until old age; faith is good when established. Wisdom is the jewel of people; merit is hard for thieves to take away.”
translations.sn1.55:1: “What produces a person, what runs about for him; what leads one into saṁsāra, what is his great fear?”
translations.sn1.55:2: “Craving produces a person; his mind runs about. A being has entered saṁsāra; suffering is his great fear.”
translations.sn1.56:1: “What produces a person, what runs about for him; what leads one into saṁsāra, why is one not released?”
translations.sn1.56:2: “Craving produces a person; his mind runs about. A being has entered saṁsāra; from suffering one is not released.”
translations.sn1.57:1: “What produces a person, what runs about for him; what leads one into saṁsāra, what is his resort?”
translations.sn1.57:2: “Craving produces a person; his mind runs about. A being has entered saṁsāra; kamma is his resort.”
translations.sn1.59:1: “What is a person’s companion, what rules over him; delighting in what does a mortal get released from all suffering?”
translations.sn1.59:2: “Faith is a person’s companion; wisdom rules over him. Delighting in Nibbāna, a mortal is released from all suffering.”
translations.sn1.62:1: “By what is the world led, by what is it dragged along; under the control of what one thing have all come?”
translations.sn1.62:2: “By mind the world is led; by mind it is dragged along. Under the control of mind, the one thing, all have come.”
translations.sn1.63:2: “By craving the world is led; by craving it is dragged along. Under the control of craving, the one thing, all have come.”
translations.sn1.64:1: “By what is the world fettered, what is its thinking; by the abandoning of what is it said ‘Nibbāna’?”
translations.sn1.64:2: “The world is fettered by delight; thinking is its pondering. By the abandoning of craving it is said ‘Nibbāna’.”
translations.sn1.65:1: “By what is the world bound, what is its thinking; by the abandoning of what does one cut off every bond?”
translations.sn1.65:2: “The world is bound by delight; thinking is its pondering. By the abandoning of craving one cuts off every bond.”
translations.sn1.69:1: “By what is the world bound, by the discipline of what is it freed; by the abandoning of what does one cut off every bond?”
translations.sn1.69:2: “By desire the world is bound; by the discipline of desire it is freed. By the abandoning of desire one cuts off every bond.”
translations.sn1.71:2: “Having cut what does one sleep happily, having cut what does one not sorrow; whose killing, of the one thing, do you approve of, Gotama?”
translations.sn1.71:3: “Having cut anger one sleeps happily; having cut anger one does not sorrow. Of anger, with its poisoned root, and sweet tip, deity—the noble praise the killing; for having cut that, one does not sorrow.”
translations.sn1.73:1: “What here is a man’s best wealth, what well practiced brings happiness; what indeed is the sweetest of tastes, living how is life said to be best?”
translations.sn1.7:2:
"Those whose teachings are not penetrated
are led away in other doctrines;
asleeping, they do not awaken—
for them it is time to awaken."
translations.sn1.8:2:
"Those whose teachings are well forgotten
are led away in other doctrines;
asleeping, they do not awaken—
for them it is time to awaken."
translations.sn11.14:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus." "Venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn11.14:3: Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the Tāvatiṁsa devas: ‘Do not, sirs, disparage this deva-son. This deva-son, sirs, when he was formerly a human being, undertook faith in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata; undertook virtue; undertook learning; undertook generosity; undertook wisdom. Having undertaken faith in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, having undertaken virtue, having undertaken learning, having undertaken generosity, having undertaken wisdom, with the breakup of the body, after death, he has arisen in a good destination, the heavenly world, in companionship with the Tāvatiṁsa devas. He outshines the other devas in both beauty and glory.’ Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, placating the Tāvatiṁsa devas, at that time recited these verses:
translations.sn11.14:6:
‘Therefore faith and virtue,
confidence, and seeing the Dhamma—
the wise person should cultivate them,
mindful of the Buddhas’ dispensation.’
translations.sn11.15:1: At Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to the Blessed One: "What, venerable sir, is the delightfulness of the earth?"
translations.sn11.15:2:
"Park shrines, forest shrines,
and well-made lotus ponds—
of human delightfulness
they are not worth even a sixteenth part."
translations.sn11.22:1: At Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove. There … said this: "Once in the past, bhikkhus, a certain yakkha, ugly and misshapen, was sitting on the seat of Sakka, lord of the devas.
