There, bhikkhus, the Tāvatiṁsa devas complained, grumbled, and criticized: ‘It is wonderful indeed, sirs, it is amazing indeed, sirs: this yakkha, ugly and misshapen, is sitting on the seat of Sakka, lord of the devas!’ But as the Tāvatiṁsa devas complained, grumbled, and criticized, so that yakkha became more and more handsome, more and more beautiful, more and more pleasing.
translations.sn11.22:3: Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, approached that yakkha who feeds on anger. Having approached, he arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and with hands joined in reverence toward that yakkha who feeds on anger, he announced his name three times: ‘I am Sakka, sir, lord of the devas; I am Sakka, sir, lord of the devas.’ As Sakka, lord of the devas, announced his name, so that yakkha became uglier and more misshapen. Having become uglier and more misshapen, right there he vanished. Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, sitting on his own seat and placating the Tāvatiṁsa devas, at that time recited these verses:
translations.sn11.22:4:
‘I am not one with a well-struck mind,
nor am I one who is led by turning back;
I do not get angry for long,
anger does not remain in me.
translations.sn11.22:5:
When angry I do not speak harshly,
nor do I extol myself for my ways;
I restrain myself,
seeing what is for my own good.’
translations.sn11.24:2: "These two, bhikkhus, are fools: one who does not see a fault as a fault, and one who does not accept, in accordance with the Dhamma, a fault from one who confesses a fault—these, bhikkhus, are the two fools. These two, bhikkhus, are wise: one who sees a fault as a fault, and one who accepts, in accordance with the Dhamma, a fault from one who confesses a fault—these, bhikkhus, are the two wise.
translations.sn11.24:3: Once in the past, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, in the Sudhammā assembly hall, placating the Tāvatiṁsa devas, at that time recited this verse:
translations.sn11.3:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus." "Venerable sir," those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn11.3:10: If you do not recollect me, then recollect the Dhamma: "Well-proclaimed by the Blessed One is the Dhamma, visible here and now, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally known by the wise." For you, bhikkhus, recollecting the Dhamma, whatever fear or trepidation or hair-raising may arise will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:11: If you do not recollect the Dhamma, then recollect the Saṅgha: "The Blessed One’s disciple Saṅgha is practising well; the Blessed One’s disciple Saṅgha is practising straight; the Blessed One’s disciple Saṅgha is practising the true way; the Blessed One’s disciple Saṅgha is practising properly—namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight individuals: this is the Blessed One’s disciple Saṅgha, worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world." For you, bhikkhus, recollecting the Saṅgha, whatever fear or trepidation or hair-raising may arise will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:12: For what reason? For the Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is an arahant, a perfectly awakened one, free from lust, free from hatred, free from delusion, fearless, unafraid, unperturbed, not fleeing." Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Fortunate One then further said this, the Teacher:
translations.sn11.3:13:
"In a forest, at the root of a tree,
or in an empty dwelling, bhikkhus,
recollect the fully awakened one;
there will be no fear for you.
translations.sn11.3:14:
If you do not remember the Buddha,
the world’s eldest, the bull among men,
then remember the Dhamma,
leading out, well taught.
translations.sn11.3:15:
If you do not remember the Dhamma,
leading out, well taught,
then remember the Saṅgha,
the unsurpassed field of merit.
translations.sn11.3:16:
Thus, for those remembering the Buddha,
the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, bhikkhus,
fear or trepidation,
or hair-raising will not occur."
translations.sn11.3:2: "In the past, bhikkhus, a battle between the devas and the asuras was joined. Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas:
translations.sn11.3:3: 'If, friends, when the devas have gone to battle, fear or trepidation or horripilation should arise, then at that time you should look up at the top of my banner. For when you look up at the top of my banner, whatever fear or trepidation or horripilation there will be will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:4: But if you do not look up at the top of my banner, then you should look up at the top of the banner of Pajāpati, the deva king. For when you look up at the top of the banner of Pajāpati, the deva king, whatever fear or trepidation or horripilation there will be will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.3:8: For what reason? For Sakka, bhikkhus, lord of the devas, is not without lust, not without hate, not without delusion; he is afraid, timid, frightened, and flees.
translations.sn11.3:9: And I, bhikkhus, say this: 'If, bhikkhus, when you have gone to a forest, or gone to the root of a tree, or gone to an empty dwelling, fear or trepidation or horripilation should arise, then at that time you should recollect me: “Such indeed is the Blessed One: the Arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, accomplished in knowledge and conduct, the Fortunate One, knower of the world, unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, awakened, Blessed One.” For when you recollect me, bhikkhus, whatever fear or trepidation or horripilation there will be will be abandoned.
translations.sn11.5:12: He practices for the welfare of both, for his own and for another's; knowing that the other has been provoked, one who is mindful becomes calm.
translations.sn11.5:14: Now, bhikkhus, when the verses had been spoken by Sakka, lord of the devas, the devas rejoiced, but the asuras were silent. Then, bhikkhus, the assemblies of devas and asuras said this: 'Verses have been spoken by Vepacitti, the asura lord. And those were accompanied by the rod, accompanied by weapons—thus: quarrel, thus: strife, thus: dispute. Verses have been spoken by Sakka, lord of the devas. And those were not accompanied by the rod, not accompanied by weapons—thus: non-quarrel, thus: non-strife, thus: non-dispute. By the well-spoken words of Sakka, lord of the devas, there is victory.' Thus, bhikkhus, by the well-spoken words of Sakka, lord of the devas, there was victory".
translations.sn11.5:2: 'The fools would break out even more, and there would be no one to stop him; therefore with a heavy rod the wise man should restrain a fool.'
translations.sn11.5:3: Now, bhikkhus, when the verse had been spoken by Vepacitti, the asura lord, the asuras rejoiced, but the devas were silent. Then, bhikkhus, Vepacitti, the asura lord, said this to Sakka, lord of the devas: 'Speak, lord of the devas, a verse.' When this was said, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:4: 'This indeed, I think, is the restraint of a fool: knowing that the other has been provoked, one who is mindful becomes calm.'
translations.sn11.5:5: Now, bhikkhus, when the verse had been spoken by Sakka, lord of the devas, the devas rejoiced, but the asuras were silent. Then, bhikkhus, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to Vepacitti, the asura lord: 'Speak, Vepacitti, a verse.' When this was said, bhikkhus, Vepacitti, the asura lord, spoke this verse:
translations.sn11.5:6: 'In this endurance I see a fault, Vāsava: when the fool thinks, “He endures me out of fear,” the stupid one becomes overbearing, like a bull that runs away even more.'
translations.sn11.5:8: 'Let him think it or not, “He endures me out of fear”; there is no benefit greater than patience.
translations.sn12.11:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika's park … "There are, bhikkhus, these four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of beings that have come to be, and for the support of those seeking existence. What four? Edible food, coarse or fine, is the first; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; consciousness is the fourth. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of beings that have come to be, and for the support of those seeking existence.
translations.sn12.12:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. "There are, bhikkhus, these four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of beings that have come to be, and for the support of those seeking existence. What four? Edible food, coarse or fine, is the first; contact is the second; mental volition is the third; consciousness is the fourth. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of nutriment for the maintenance of beings that have come to be, and for the support of those seeking existence".
translations.sn12.15:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Kaccānagotta approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Kaccānagotta said this to the Blessed One: "'Right view, right view,' venerable sir, it is said. To what extent, venerable sir, is there right view"?
translations.sn12.15:2: "This world, Kaccāna, for the most part depends on a duality—on existence and on non-existence. But for one who sees the origin of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, that which is non-existence in the world does not occur. For one who sees the cessation of the world as it really is with correct wisdom, that which is existence in the world does not occur. This world, Kaccāna, for the most part is bound by engagement, clinging, and adherence. But one does not engage in or cling to or take up that engagement and clinging—this standpoint of mind, this adherence and underlying tendency—[thinking:] 'my self.' One does not doubt or waver that 'only suffering arising arises; suffering ceasing ceases'; knowledge of this is for him independent of another. To this extent, Kaccāna, there is right view.
translations.sn12.17:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels' feeding ground. Then the Blessed One, in the morning, having dressed and taken bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. The naked ascetic Kassapa saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Having seen him, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had concluded their courteous and memorable talk, he stood to one side. Standing to one side, the naked ascetic Kassapa said this to the Blessed One: "We would ask the Master Gotama a certain question, if Master Gotama grants us an opportunity for the answering of the question." "It is not the right time yet, Kassapa, for a question; we have entered among the houses."
translations.sn12.17:5: “‘The one who acts is the one who experiences,’ Kassapa: for one who is mindful from the start, saying ‘suffering is self-made’—this falls into eternalism. ‘One acts, another experiences,’ Kassapa: for one who is mindful, having been struck by feeling, saying ‘suffering is made by another’—this falls into annihilationism. Without approaching either of these extremes, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness …pe… thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness …pe… thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering’”ti.
translations.sn12.17:6: When this was said, the naked ascetic Kassapa said this to the Blessed One: “Excellent, bhante, excellent, bhante. Seyyathāpi, bhante, nikkujjitaṁ vā ukkujjeyya …pe… ‘Those with eyes might see forms’; even so, the Dhamma has been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May I obtain the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may I obtain the full admission”ti.
translations.sn12.17:7: “Kassapa, one who was formerly from another sect, who in this Dhamma and discipline desires the going forth, desires the full admission, dwells on probation for four months. After four months have passed, monks with minds satisfied give the going forth and give the full admission for the state of monkhood. But I have known the diversity of persons”ti.
translations.sn12.18:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. Then the wanderer Timbaruka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had concluded the greetings and courteous talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the wanderer Timbaruka said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.18:4: “‘That feeling is the one who feels,’ Timbaruka: for one who is mindful from the start, saying ‘pleasure and pain are self-made’—I do not say so. ‘One feeling, another who feels,’ Timbaruka: for one who is mindful, having been struck by feeling, saying ‘pleasure and pain are made by another’—I do not say so. Without approaching either of these extremes, Timbaruka, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness …pe… thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, cessation of consciousness …pe… thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering’”ti.
translations.sn12.19:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, for the fool who is covered by ignorance, connected with craving, this body has arisen thus. Thus there is both this body and external name-and-form; here there is this dyad. Dependent on the dyad there is contact, the six sense bases, by which, when touched, the fool experiences pleasure and pain by these or by one of them.
translations.sn12.19:2: Bhikkhus, for the wise person who is covered by ignorance, connected with craving, this body has arisen thus. Thus there is both this body and external name-and-form; here there is this dyad. Dependent on the dyad there is contact, the six sense bases, by which, when touched, the wise person experiences pleasure and pain by these or by one of them.
translations.sn12.19:3: In that case, bhikkhus, what is the difference, what is the distinction, what is the difference in character between the wise person and the fool?” “Our teachings, bhante, are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, sheltered by the Blessed One. It would be good, bhante, if the Blessed One himself would make the meaning of this statement clear. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will retain it”ti.
translations.sn12.19:5: “For the fool who is covered by whatever ignorance, and for whom this body has arisen connected with whatever craving, that ignorance of the fool is not abandoned and that craving is not exhausted. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, the fool did not live the spiritual life properly for the complete ending of suffering. Therefore, with the breakup of the body the fool goes to a body; and as one who has gone to a body, he is not freed from birth, aging-and-death, from sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, and despairs. ‘He is not freed from suffering,’ I say.
translations.sn12.23:5: And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for craving? It should be said: ‘Feeling’ …pe… It should be said: ‘Contact’ … It should be said: ‘The six sense bases’ … It should be said: ‘Name-and-form’ … It should be said: ‘Consciousness’ … It should be said: ‘Formations.’ Formations, bhikkhus, I say are with a supporting condition, not without a supporting condition. And what, bhikkhus, is the supporting condition for formations? It should be said: ‘Ignorance.’
translations.sn12.23:6: Thus, bhikkhus, formations have ignorance as their supporting condition, consciousness has formations as its supporting condition, name-and-form has consciousness as its supporting condition, the six sense bases have name-and-form as their supporting condition, contact has the six sense bases as its supporting condition, feeling has contact as its supporting condition, craving has feeling as its supporting condition, clinging has craving as its supporting condition, existence has clinging as its supporting condition, birth has existence as its supporting condition, suffering has birth as its supporting condition, faith has suffering as its supporting condition, gladness has faith as its supporting condition, rapture has gladness as its supporting condition, tranquility has rapture as its supporting condition, happiness has tranquility as its supporting condition, concentration has happiness as its supporting condition, knowledge and vision of things as they really are has concentration as its supporting condition, disenchantment has knowledge and vision of things as they really are as its supporting condition, dispassion has disenchantment as its supporting condition, liberation has dispassion as its supporting condition, knowledge of destruction has liberation as its supporting condition.
translations.sn12.23:7: Just as, bhikkhus, when it rains with heavy drops on the upper mountain, that water, flowing down according to the slope, fills the mountain clefts, gullies, and branches. When the mountain clefts, gullies, and branches are full, they fill the pools. When the pools are full, they fill the great pools. When the great pools are full, they fill the small rivers. When the small rivers are full, they fill the great rivers. When the great rivers are full, they fill the great ocean.
translations.sn12.25:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Bhūmija, in the evening, having risen from seclusion, approached Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. When they had concluded the greetings and courteous talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Bhūmija said this to Venerable Sāriputta:
translations.sn12.25:10: When there is bodily intention, Ānanda, due to bodily intention internal pleasure and pain arise. When there is verbal intention, Ānanda, due to verbal intention internal pleasure and pain arise. When there is mental intention, Ānanda, due to mental intention internal pleasure and pain arise, and with ignorance as condition.
translations.sn12.25:11: Either they themselves, Ānanda, construct that bodily formation, dependent on which that internal pleasure and pain arises in them; or others, Ānanda, construct that bodily formation, dependent on which that internal pleasure and pain arises in them; or knowingly, Ānanda, they construct that bodily formation, dependent on which that internal pleasure and pain arises in them; or unknowingly, Ānanda, they construct that bodily formation, dependent on which that internal pleasure and pain arises in them.
translations.sn12.25:2: "Friend Sāriputta, there are some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of action and who assert pleasure and pain as self-made. And there are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of action and who assert pleasure and pain as made by others. There are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of action and who assert pleasure and pain as both self-made and made by others. And there are, friend Sāriputta, some ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of action and who assert pleasure and pain as neither self-made nor made by others, arisen by chance. Here, friend Sāriputta, what does the Blessed One say, what does he proclaim? How, when answering, would we be speakers of what has been said by the Blessed One, and not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue, and explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, so that no fellow practitioner would come to a blameworthy conclusion of fault in our statement?"
translations.sn12.25:3: "Dependent arisen, friend, is pleasure and pain, said the Blessed One. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. Saying so, one would be a speaker of what has been said by the Blessed One, and would not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is untrue, and would explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, so that no fellow practitioner would come to a blameworthy conclusion of fault in one’s statement.
translations.sn12.25:4: There, friend, those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of action and who assert pleasure and pain as self-made— that too is conditioned by contact. And those … and those … and those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of action and who assert pleasure and pain as neither self-made nor made by others, arisen by chance— that too is conditioned by contact.
translations.sn12.25:5: There, friend, those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of action and who assert pleasure and pain as self-made— that they would experience it apart from contact: no such possibility exists. And those … and those … and those ascetics and brahmins who are proponents of action and who assert pleasure and pain as neither self-made nor made by others, arisen by chance— that they would experience it apart from contact: no such possibility exists."
translations.sn12.25:6: Venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between venerable Sāriputta and venerable Bhūmija. Then venerable Ānanda went to the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One the whole of the conversation that had taken place between venerable Sāriputta and venerable Bhūmija.
translations.sn12.25:7: "Good, good, Ānanda, just as Sāriputta, answering rightly, would answer. Dependent arisen, Ānanda, is pleasure and pain, said by me. Dependent on what? Dependent on contact. Saying so, one would be a speaker of what has been said by me, and would not misrepresent me with what is untrue, and would explain the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma, so that no fellow practitioner would come to a blameworthy conclusion of fault in one’s statement.
translations.sn12.2:11: And what, bhikkhus, is name-and-form? Feeling, perception, intention, contact, attention—this is called name. And the four great elements, and form derived from the four great elements—this is called form. Thus this name and this form. This is called, bhikkhus, name-and-form.
translations.sn12.2:12: And what, bhikkhus, is consciousness? These, bhikkhus, are the six classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This is called, bhikkhus, consciousness.
translations.sn12.2:13: And what, bhikkhus, are formations? These, bhikkhus, are the three formations: bodily formation, verbal formation, mental formation. These are called, bhikkhus, formations.
translations.sn12.2:14: And what, bhikkhus, is ignorance? Not knowing, bhikkhus, regarding suffering; not knowing regarding the origin of suffering; not knowing regarding the cessation of suffering; not knowing regarding the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This is called, bhikkhus, ignorance.
translations.sn12.2:5: And what, bhikkhus, is becoming? These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of becoming: sense-sphere becoming, form becoming, formless becoming. This is called, bhikkhus, becoming.
translations.sn12.2:6: And what, bhikkhus, is clinging? These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of clinging: clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, clinging to a doctrine of self. This is called, bhikkhus, clinging.
translations.sn12.31:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One addressed venerable Sāriputta: "This was said, Sāriputta, in the Pārāyana, in Ajita’s questions:
translations.sn12.31:2: 'And those who have understood the Dhamma, and those trainees, many here— tell me their conduct, O wise one, being asked, sir.'
translations.sn12.31:3: For this, Sāriputta, spoken in brief, how is the meaning to be seen in detail?" When this was said, venerable Sāriputta was silent.
translations.sn12.31:7: "Do you see, Sāriputta, ‘This is real’?” “I see, Blessed One, ‘This is real’ as it really is with right wisdom. Having seen ‘This is real’ as it really is with right wisdom, he practices for the disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of what is real. He sees, as it really is with right wisdom, ‘This has nutriment as its source.’ Having seen, as it really is with right wisdom, ‘This has nutriment as its source,’ he practices for the disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of what has nutriment as its source. He sees, as it really is with right wisdom, ‘With the cessation of that nutriment, what is real is of the nature to cease.’ Having seen, as it really is with right wisdom, ‘With the cessation of that nutriment, what is real is of the nature to cease,’ he practices for the disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation of what is of the nature to cease. Thus, Blessed One, one is a trainee.
translations.sn12.31:8: And how, venerable sir, is one of a nature that is understood? ‘This is what has come to be,’ venerable sir, they see as it really is with right wisdom. Having seen ‘This is what has come to be’ as it really is with right wisdom, through disillusionment with what has come to be, through fading away, through cessation, freed by non-clinging they are liberated. ‘This has arisen from nutriment,’ they see as it really is with right wisdom. Having seen ‘This has arisen from nutriment’ as it really is with right wisdom, through disillusionment with what has arisen from nutriment, through fading away, through cessation, freed by non-clinging they are liberated. ‘With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is of a nature to cease,’ they see as it really is with right wisdom. Having seen ‘With the cessation of that nutriment, what has come to be is of a nature to cease’ as it really is with right wisdom, through disillusionment with what is of a nature to cease, through fading away, through cessation, freed by non-clinging they are liberated. Thus, venerable sir, one is of a nature that is understood. Thus, venerable sir, what was said in the Pārāyana in Ajita’s questions:
translations.sn12.35:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. “With ignorance as condition, monks, formations; with formations as condition, consciousness … thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering.” When this was said, a certain monk said this to the Blessed One: “Which, venerable sir, is aging-and-death, and of whom is this aging-and-death?” “The question is not fitting,” the Blessed One said. “If, monk, one were to say, ‘Which is aging-and-death, and of whom is this aging-and-death?’ or if one were to say, ‘Aging-and-death is one thing, and this aging-and-death belongs to another,’ either way—both have the same meaning, only the phrasing is different. With the view, monk, ‘The soul is the same as the body,’ there is no living of the holy life. With the view, monk, ‘The soul is one thing, the body another,’ there is no living of the holy life. Without approaching either of these two extremes, monk, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With birth as condition, aging-and-death.’”
translations.sn12.35:2: “Which, venerable sir, is birth, and of whom is this birth?” “The question is not fitting,” the Blessed One said. “If, monk, one were to say, ‘Which is birth, and of whom is this birth?’ or if one were to say, ‘Birth is one thing, and this birth belongs to another,’ either way—both have the same meaning, only the phrasing is different. With the view, monk, ‘The soul is the same as the body,’ there is no living of the holy life. With the view, monk, ‘The soul is one thing, the body another,’ there is no living of the holy life. Without approaching either of these two extremes, monk, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With existence as condition, birth.’”
translations.sn12.35:3: “Which, venerable sir, is existence, and of whom is this existence?” “The question is not fitting,” the Blessed One said. “If, monk, one were to say, ‘Which is existence, and of whom is this existence?’ or if one were to say, ‘Existence is one thing, and this existence belongs to another,’ either way—both have the same meaning, only the phrasing is different. With the view, monk, ‘The soul is the same as the body,’ there is no living of the holy life; with the view, monk, ‘The soul is one thing, the body another,’ there is no living of the holy life. Without approaching either of these two extremes, monk, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With clinging as condition, existence’ … ‘With craving as condition, clinging’ … ‘With feeling as condition, craving’ … ‘With contact as condition, feeling’ … ‘With the six sense bases as condition, contact’ … ‘With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases’ … ‘With consciousness as condition, name-and-form’ … ‘With formations as condition, consciousness.’”
translations.sn12.35:4: “Which, venerable sir, are formations, and of whom are these formations?” “The question is not fitting,” the Blessed One said. “If, monk, one were to say, ‘Which are formations, and of whom are these formations?’ or if one were to say, ‘Formations are one thing, and these formations belong to another,’ either way—both have the same meaning, only the phrasing is different. With the view, monk, ‘The soul is the same as the body,’ there is no living of the holy life; with the view, monk, ‘The soul is one thing, the body another,’ there is no living of the holy life. Without approaching either of these two extremes, monk, the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma by the middle: ‘With ignorance as condition, formations.’”
translations.sn12.35:5: But, monk, with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, whatever of his are those crooked ways, practiced, wriggled about, of whatever kind: ‘Which is aging-and-death, and of whom is this aging-and-death?’ or ‘Aging-and-death is one thing, and this aging-and-death belongs to another’ or ‘The soul is the same as the body’ or ‘The soul is one thing, the body another’—all of these are abandoned for him, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made non-existent, not liable to arise in the future.
translations.sn12.35:7: But, monk, with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, whatever of his are those crooked ways, practiced, wriggled about, of whatever kind: Which is existence … which is clinging … which is craving … which is feeling … which is contact … which are the six sense bases … which is name-and-form … which is consciousness …
translations.sn12.38:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. “And whatever, monks, one intends, and whatever one plans, and whatever one has a tendency toward, this is a support for the persistence of consciousness. When there is a support, there is an establishment of consciousness. When that consciousness is established and has grown, there is the production of renewed existence in the future. When there is the production of renewed existence in the future, in the future there come to be birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.38:2: But if, monks, one does not intend and does not plan, yet one has a tendency toward, this is a support for the persistence of consciousness. When there is a support, there is an establishment of consciousness. When that consciousness is established and has grown, there is the production of renewed existence in the future. When there is the production of renewed existence in the future, in the future there come to be birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.44:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. “Monks, I will teach the arising and the passing away of the world. Listen to that, attend closely, I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.44:2: “And what, bhikkhus, is the origin of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, becoming; with becoming as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. This, bhikkhus, is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.44:3: Dependent on the ear and sounds …pe… dependent on the nose and odors … dependent on the tongue and tastes … dependent on the body and tangibles … dependent on the mind and mind-objects, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling …pe… with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. This, bhikkhus, is the origin of the world.
translations.sn12.44:4: And what, bhikkhus, is the cessation of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. With contact as condition, feeling; with feeling as condition, craving. With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, there is the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of becoming …pe… thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This, bhikkhus, is the cessation of the world.
translations.sn12.46:1: He was staying at Sāvatthī. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When they had concluded a cordial and memorable conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn12.46:2: “Now then, Master Gotama, does the same one act and the same one experience?” “‘The same one acts and the same one experiences’: this, brahmin, is one extreme.”
translations.sn12.46:3: “Then, Master Gotama, does one act and another experience?” “‘One acts and another experiences’: this, brahmin, is the second extreme. Without approaching either of these extremes, brahmin, the Tathāgata teaches Dhamma by the middle: ‘With ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness …pe… thus there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations …pe… thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering’”ti.
translations.sn12.51:10: When he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not delighted in’. When he feels a painful feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not delighted in’. When he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not delighted in’. When he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it unattached. When he feels a painful feeling, he feels it unattached. When he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it unattached.
translations.sn12.51:11: Feeling a feeling that ends with the body, he understands: ‘I am feeling a feeling that ends with the body’; feeling a feeling that ends with life, he understands: ‘I am feeling a feeling that ends with life’. He understands: ‘With the breaking up of the body, after the ending of life, here itself all that is felt, not delighted in, will cool; the bodily remains will be left’.
translations.sn12.51:12: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were to take a hot pot from a potter’s kiln and set it down on level ground. There the heat would subside right there; the shards would remain. So too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu feeling a feeling that ends with the body understands: ‘I am feeling a feeling that ends with the body’; feeling a feeling that ends with life understands: ‘I am feeling a feeling that ends with life’. He understands: ‘With the breaking up of the body, after the ending of life, here itself all that is felt, not delighted in, will cool; the bodily remains will be left’.
translations.sn12.51:13: “What do you think, bhikkhus: would an arahant bhikkhu, one whose taints are ended, generate a meritorious volitional formation, or generate a demeritorious volitional formation, or generate an imperturbable volitional formation?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn12.51:14: “But when formations are utterly absent, with the cessation of formations, would consciousness be discerned?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn12.51:2: “To what extent, bhikkhus, should a bhikkhu, while investigating, investigate for the complete right ending of suffering?” “Our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, venerable sir, guided by the Blessed One, with the Blessed One as refuge. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would make clear the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will retain it.” “Then, bhikkhus, listen and attend carefully; I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.51:3: “Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, while investigating, investigates thus: ‘This manifold and various suffering that arises in the world—aging-and-death—of what is this suffering the source, the origin, what is it born from, what is it produced from? When what exists does aging-and-death come to be? When what does not exist does aging-and-death not come to be?’ While investigating, he understands thus: ‘This manifold and various suffering that arises in the world—aging-and-death—this suffering has birth as its source, birth as its origin, is born from birth, produced from birth. When birth exists, aging-and-death comes to be; when birth does not exist, aging-and-death does not come to be.’
translations.sn12.51:4: He understands aging-and-death, he understands the origin of aging-and-death, he understands the cessation of aging-and-death, and he understands the practice that leads in accordance with the Dhamma to the cessation of aging-and-death; and practicing accordingly, he is one who practices in accordance with the Dhamma. This is called, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has practiced for the complete right ending of suffering, for the cessation of aging-and-death.
translations.sn12.51:5: Then further, while investigating, he investigates: ‘And this birth—of what is it the source, the origin, what is it born from, what is it produced from? When what exists does birth come to be? When what does not exist does birth not come to be?’ While investigating, he understands thus: ‘Birth has becoming as its source, becoming as its origin, is born from becoming, produced from becoming; when becoming exists, birth comes to be; when becoming does not exist, birth does not come to be.’
translations.sn12.51:6: He understands birth, and he understands the origin of birth, and he understands the cessation of birth, and he understands the way of practice leading to what is appropriate for the cessation of birth, and he practices accordingly, one who practices in conformity with the Dhamma; this is called, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has practiced entirely rightly for the ending of suffering, for the cessation of birth.
translations.sn12.51:7: Then again, examining he examines: ‘But of what is this existence the cause … of what is this clinging the cause … of what is this craving the cause … feeling … contact … of what is this sixfold sense base the cause … what about this name-and-form … what about this consciousness … of what are these volitional formations the cause, what is their origin, what are they born from, what do they arise from; when what exists do volitional formations come to be, when what does not exist do volitional formations not come to be?’ Examining, he understands thus: ‘Volitional formations have ignorance as their cause, ignorance as their origin, are born of ignorance, arise from ignorance; when ignorance exists, volitional formations come to be; when ignorance does not exist, volitional formations do not come to be.’
translations.sn12.51:8: He understands volitional formations, and he understands the origin of volitional formations, and he understands the cessation of volitional formations, and he understands the way of practice leading to what is appropriate for the cessation of volitional formations, and he practices accordingly, one who practices in conformity with the Dhamma; this is called, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has practiced entirely rightly for the ending of suffering, for the cessation of volitional formations.
translations.sn12.51:9: A person, bhikkhus, who has gone to ignorance—if he forms a meritorious volitional formation, consciousness becomes tending toward the meritorious. If he forms a demeritorious volitional formation, consciousness becomes tending toward the demeritorious. If he forms an imperturbable volitional formation, consciousness becomes tending toward the imperturbable. But when, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s ignorance has been abandoned and knowledge has arisen, then through the fading away of ignorance, through the arising of knowledge, he neither forms a meritorious volitional formation, nor forms a demeritorious volitional formation, nor forms an imperturbable volitional formation. Not forming, not intending, he does not cling to anything in the world; not clinging, he is not agitated; not agitated, he personally attains final Nibbāna. He understands: ‘Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’
translations.sn12.52:2: Just as, bhikkhus, a great bonfire would burn from ten cartloads of wood, or twenty cartloads of wood, or thirty cartloads of wood, or forty cartloads of wood. There a man from time to time would throw in dry grass, would throw in dry cow-dung, and would throw in dry sticks. For thus, bhikkhus, that great bonfire, with that as its fuel, with that as its support, would burn for a long time, for a long period. Even so, bhikkhus, for one dwelling contemplating gratification in things that can be clung to, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging … thus there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.52:3: For one dwelling contemplating danger in things that can be clung to, bhikkhus, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair cease. Thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. “For one dwelling contemplating gratification in things that can be clung to, bhikkhus, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence … thus there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:2: Just as, bhikkhus, a great tree: whatever roots it has that go downward and whatever go across, all of them carry nourishment upward. For thus, bhikkhus, that great tree, with that as its fuel, with that as its support, would stand for a long time, for a long period. Even so, bhikkhus, for one dwelling contemplating gratification in things that can be clung to, craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging … thus there is the origin of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.55:3: For one dwelling contemplating danger in things that can be clung to, bhikkhus, craving ceases. With the cessation of craving, the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of existence … thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn12.61:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jetavana, in Anāthapiṇḍika’s park … “An uninstructed worldling, bhikkhus, might become disenchanted with this body made of the four great elements, might become dispassionate toward it, might be released from it. For what reason? There is seen, bhikkhus, with this body made of the four great elements, both accumulation and diminution, taking up and laying down. Therefore, there an uninstructed worldling might become disenchanted, might become dispassionate, might be released.
translations.sn12.61:2: But as to what is called mind, or mentality, or consciousness, there an uninstructed worldling is not able to become disenchanted, not able to become dispassionate, not able to be released. For what reason? For a long time, bhikkhus, this has been adhered to, made ‘mine’, and grasped by the uninstructed worldling: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self.’ Therefore, there an uninstructed worldling is not able to become disenchanted, not able to become dispassionate, not able to be released.
translations.sn12.61:3: It would be better, bhikkhus, for an uninstructed worldling to take this body made of the four great elements as self, rather than the mind. For what reason? Because this body made of the four great elements is seen to stand for one year, to stand for two years, to stand for three years, to stand for four years, to stand for five years, to stand for ten years, to stand for twenty years, to stand for thirty years, to stand for forty years, to stand for fifty years, to stand for a hundred years, and to stand even longer.
translations.sn12.61:5: There, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple carefully attends with wise attention to dependent origination itself: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises; when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases— that is, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness … thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of volitional formations; with the cessation of volitional formations, the cessation of consciousness … thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering’.”
translations.sn12.62:3: There, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple carefully attends with wise attention to dependent origination itself: ‘When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises; when this does not exist, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.’ Depending on pleasant feeling contact, bhikkhus, pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that same pleasant-feeling contact, the feeling that is born of it—pleasant feeling arisen depending on pleasant-feeling contact—ceases, it subsides. Depending on painful feeling contact, bhikkhus, painful feeling arises. With the cessation of that same painful-feeling contact, the feeling that is born of it—painful feeling arisen depending on painful-feeling contact—ceases, it subsides. Depending on neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling contact, bhikkhus, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that same neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling contact, the feeling that is born of it—neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arisen depending on neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling contact—ceases, it subsides.
translations.sn12.62:4: Just as, bhikkhus, from the rubbing and striking together of two sticks heat is born, fire is produced. With the separation and different arrangement of those same two sticks, the heat that is born of that ceases, it subsides; so too, bhikkhus, depending on pleasant-feeling contact pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that same pleasant-feeling contact, the feeling that is born of it—pleasant feeling arisen depending on pleasant-feeling contact—ceases, it subsides … painful-feeling contact depending on … depending on neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling contact neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that same neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling contact, the feeling that is born of it—neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arisen depending on neither-painful-nor-pleasant-feeling contact—ceases, it subsides.
translations.sn12.63:3: What do you think, bhikkhus: would they take food for the sake of play, or would they take food for the sake of intoxication, or would they take food for the sake of adornment, or would they take food for the sake of beautification?” “No indeed, bhante.” “Would they not, bhikkhus, take food only for the sake of crossing the desert?” “Yes, bhante.” “So too, bhikkhus, I say that solid food should be regarded. When solid food, bhikkhus, is fully understood, sensual lust for the five strands of sense pleasures is fully understood. When sensual lust for the five strands of sense pleasures is fully understood, there is no fetter by which, fettered, a noble disciple would come again to this world.
translations.sn12.63:4: And how, bhikkhus, should contact as nutriment be regarded? Suppose, bhikkhus, a flayed cow were to stand leaning against a wall. Whatever creatures are dependent on the wall would eat it. If it were to stand leaning against a tree, whatever creatures are dependent on the tree would eat it. If it were to stand leaning against water, whatever creatures are dependent on the water would eat it. If it were to stand leaning against the air, whatever creatures are dependent on the air would eat it. For whatever it is, bhikkhus, that the flayed cow stands leaning against, whatever creatures are dependent on that would eat it. So too, bhikkhus, I say: ‘contact as nutriment should be regarded.’ When contact as nutriment, bhikkhus, is fully understood, the three feelings are fully understood. When the three feelings are fully understood, I say that for the noble disciple there is nothing further to be done.
translations.sn12.63:5: And how, bhikkhus, should mental volition as nutriment be regarded? Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a pit of glowing coals, deeper than a man’s height, full of coals, without ash, without smoke. Then a man would come along, wishing to live, not wishing to die, wishing for happiness, repelled by suffering. Two strong men would seize him by his arms and drag him toward that pit of glowing coals. Then, bhikkhus, for that man his intention would be far away, his wish far away, his resolve far away. For what reason? For thus, bhikkhus, it occurs to that man: ‘If I fall into this pit of glowing coals, then on that account I will meet with death or deadly suffering.’ So too, bhikkhus, I say: ‘mental volition as nutriment should be regarded.’ When mental volition as nutriment, bhikkhus, is fully understood, the three cravings are fully understood. When the three cravings are fully understood, I say that for the noble disciple there is nothing further to be done.
translations.sn12.64:2: If, bhikkhus, in solid food there is lust, there is delight, there is craving, consciousness is established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and grows, there is descent of name-and-form. Where there is descent of name-and-form, there is growth of volitional formations. Where there is growth of volitional formations, there is in the future the production of renewed existence. Where there is in the future the production of renewed existence, there is in the future birth, aging, and death. Where there is in the future birth, aging, and death, that, bhikkhus, I say, is with sorrow, with lamentation, with suffering, with distress.
translations.sn12.64:4: Suppose, bhikkhus, a dyer or a painter, with dye or lac or turmeric or indigo or madder, would create on a well-polished board or wall or cloth a woman’s form or a man’s form, complete in all its parts and features; even so, bhikkhus, if in edible food there is lust, there is delight, there is craving, consciousness is established there and grows. Where consciousness is established and has grown, there is the descent of name-and-form. Where there is the descent of name-and-form, there is increase of formations. Where there is increase of formations, there is future production of renewed existence. Where there is future production of renewed existence, there is future birth, aging, and death. Where there is future birth, aging, and death, that, bhikkhus, I say, is with sorrow, with lamentation, with despair.
translations.sn12.64:6: But if, bhikkhus, in edible food there is no lust, no delight, no craving, consciousness is not established there and does not grow. Where consciousness is not established and does not grow, there is no descent of name-and-form. Where there is no descent of name-and-form, there is no increase of formations. Where there is no increase of formations, there is no future production of renewed existence. Where there is no future production of renewed existence, there is no future birth, aging, and death. Where there is no future birth, aging, and death, that, bhikkhus, I say, is without sorrow, without lamentation, without despair.
translations.sn12.64:8: Suppose, bhikkhus, in a peaked house or a hall with a peaked roof there is a window to the north or south or east; when the sun rises, having entered through the window, where would the sunbeam be established?” “On the western wall, venerable sir.” “But if, bhikkhus, there were no western wall, where would it be established?” “On the ground, venerable sir.” “But if, bhikkhus, there were no ground, where would it be established?” “In water, venerable sir.” “But if, bhikkhus, there were no water, where would it be established?” “Unestablished, venerable sir.” “Even so, bhikkhus, if in edible food there is no lust, no delight, no craving …”
translations.sn12.65:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. “Formerly, bhikkhus, before my awakening, when I was still an unawakened bodhisatta, this thought occurred to me: ‘Hard indeed has this world fallen into: it is born and it ages and it dies and it passes away and it is reborn. Yet it does not know an escape from this suffering, from aging and death. When indeed will an escape from this suffering, from aging and death, be discerned?’ Then, bhikkhus, this thought occurred to me: ‘When what exists does aging-and-death come to be? Aging-and-death is dependent on what as condition?’ Then, bhikkhus, through wise attention there was for me a breakthrough by wisdom: ‘When birth exists, aging-and-death comes to be; aging-and-death is conditioned by birth.’
translations.sn12.65:3: Then, bhikkhus, this thought occurred to me—this consciousness turns back from name-and-form; it does not go beyond. To this extent one may be born or age or die or pass away or be reborn, that is, with name-and-form as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact … thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering. ‘Arising, arising’: thus, bhikkhus, regarding things unheard of before, the eye arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
translations.sn12.65:5: Then, bhikkhus, this thought occurred to me: ‘When what does not exist is consciousness not? With the cessation of what is there the cessation of consciousness?’ Then, bhikkhus, through wise attention there was for me a breakthrough by wisdom: ‘When name-and-form does not exist, consciousness is not; with the cessation of name-and-form there is the cessation of consciousness.’
translations.sn12.65:6: Then, bhikkhus, this thought occurred to me—this path has been discovered by me for awakening, that is: with the cessation of name-and-form there is the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness there is the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form there is the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases there is the cessation of contact … thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. ‘Cessation, cessation’: thus, bhikkhus, regarding things unheard of before, the eye arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.
translations.sn12.65:7: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man wandering through a forest wilderness would see an ancient road, an ancient path, followed by people in the past. He would follow it. Following it, he would see an ancient city, an ancient capital, inhabited by people in the past, furnished with parks, furnished with groves, furnished with lotus ponds, with raised ramparts, delightful. Then, bhikkhus, that man would inform a king or a royal minister: ‘Come, sir, you should know—I, wandering through a forest wilderness, saw an ancient road, an ancient path, followed by people in the past; I followed it. Following it, I saw an ancient city, an ancient capital, inhabited by people in the past, furnished with parks, furnished with groves, furnished with lotus ponds, with raised ramparts, delightful. Build that city, sir.’ Then, bhikkhus, the king or the royal minister would build that city. After some time, that city would become prosperous and thriving, rich in food, crowded with people, having attained growth and expansion. Even so, bhikkhus, I saw an ancient road, an ancient path, followed by the perfectly awakened ones of the past.
translations.sn12.66:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus at a Kuru town named Kammāsadhamma. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Do you contemplate, bhikkhus, contemplation of the interval?” When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: “I, venerable sir, contemplate contemplation of the interval.” “But how, bhikkhu, do you contemplate contemplation of the interval?” Then that bhikkhu answered. As that bhikkhu answered, he did not satisfy the Blessed One’s mind.
translations.sn12.66:2: When this was said, Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “Now is the time, Blessed One; now is the time, Fortunate One, for the Blessed One to speak a summary in brief. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.” “Then, Ānanda, listen and attend closely, I will speak,” he said. “Yes, sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn12.66:5: And further reflecting, he reflects on a summary in brief: ‘Now where does this craving arise as it arises, and where does it settle as it settles?’ Reflecting thus, he understands: whatever in the world is dear and pleasing—there this craving arises as it arises, there it settles as it settles. And what in the world is dear and pleasing? The eye in the world is dear, pleasing—there this craving arises as it arises, there it settles as it settles. The ear in the world is dear, pleasing … the nose in the world is dear, pleasing … the tongue in the world is dear, pleasing … the body in the world is dear, pleasing … the mind in the world is dear, pleasing—there this craving arises as it arises, there it settles as it settles.
translations.sn12.66:6: For whatever ascetics or brahmins in the past saw what in the world is dear and pleasing as permanent, saw it as happiness, saw it as self, saw it as health, saw it as secure— they increased craving. Those who increased craving increased acquisition. Those who increased acquisition increased suffering. Those who increased suffering were not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, and despairs; I say they were not freed from suffering.
translations.sn12.66:7: And whatever ascetics or brahmins in the future will see what in the world is dear and pleasing as permanent, will see it as happiness, will see it as self, will see it as health, will see it as secure— they will increase craving. Those who will increase craving will increase acquisition. Those who will increase acquisition will increase suffering. Those who will increase suffering will not be freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, and despairs; I say they will not be freed from suffering.
translations.sn12.66:8: And whatever ascetics or brahmins at present see what in the world is dear and pleasing as permanent, see it as happiness, see it as self, see it as health, see it as secure— they increase craving. Those who increase craving increase acquisition. Those who increase acquisition increase suffering. Those who increase suffering are not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, and despairs; I say they are not freed from suffering.
translations.sn12.67:1: At one time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika, in the evening, having emerged from seclusion, approached Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. When the greetings and polite talk were finished, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said this to Venerable Sāriputta: “Now what, friend Sāriputta: is aging-and-death self-made, is aging-and-death made by another, is aging-and-death both self-made and made by another, or is aging-and-death arisen by chance, without self-making and without other-making?” “No, friend Koṭṭhika, aging-and-death is not self-made, aging-and-death is not made by another, aging-and-death is not both self-made and made by another, nor is aging-and-death arisen by chance, without self-making and without other-making. But rather, with birth as condition there is aging-and-death.”
translations.sn12.67:2: “Now what, friend Sāriputta: is birth self-made, is birth made by another, is birth both self-made and made by another, or is birth arisen by chance, without self-making and without other-making?” “No, friend Koṭṭhika, birth is not self-made, birth is not made by another, birth is not both self-made and made by another, nor is birth arisen by chance, without self-making and without other-making. But rather, with existence as condition there is birth.”
translations.sn12.67:4: “Now what, friend Sāriputta: is consciousness self-made, is consciousness made by another, is consciousness both self-made and made by another, or is consciousness arisen by chance, without self-making and without other-making?” “No, friend Koṭṭhika, consciousness is not self-made, consciousness is not made by another, consciousness is not both self-made and made by another, nor is consciousness arisen by chance, without self-making and without other-making. But rather, with name-and-form as condition there is consciousness.”
translations.sn12.67:5: “Just now we understand Venerable Sāriputta’s statement thus: ‘No, friend Koṭṭhika, name-and-form is not self-made, name-and-form is not made by another, name-and-form is not both self-made and made by another, nor is name-and-form arisen by chance, without self-making and without other-making. But rather, with consciousness as condition there is name-and-form.’
translations.sn12.67:7: “But in what way, friend Sāriputta, is the meaning of what has been said to be seen?” — “In that case, friend, I will give you a simile. By a simile, too, some wise men understand the meaning of what is said. Suppose, friend, that two bundles of reeds were to stand leaning against each other. In the same way, friend, with name-and-form as condition, consciousness; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases; with the six sense bases as condition, contact … thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering. And if, friend, one of those bundles of reeds were to be pulled away, the other would fall; and if the other were to be pulled away, the first would fall. In the same way, friend, with the cessation of name-and-form there is the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness there is the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form there is the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases there is the cessation of contact … thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.”
translations.sn12.67:8: “Wonderful, friend Sāriputta; amazing, friend Sāriputta. How well this has been spoken by the venerable Sāriputta. And we approve of what the venerable Sāriputta has said with these thirty-six grounds:”
translations.sn12.68:13: “Then is the venerable Nārada an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed?” — “ ‘The cessation of existence is Nibbāna’: this has been truly seen by me with correct wisdom, friend, but I am not an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. Suppose, friend, there were a well on a desert road, but there was neither a rope nor a water-drawer there. Then a man would come along, scorched by the heat, overcome by the heat, weary, thirsty, parched with thirst; he would look down at that well. Knowledge would occur to him: ‘Water’, but he would not dwell having touched it with his body. In the same way, friend, ‘the cessation of existence is Nibbāna’ has been truly seen by me with correct wisdom, but I am not an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed.”
translations.sn12.68:6: “Then is the venerable Musīla an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed?” When this was said, the venerable Musīla was silent.
translations.sn12.69:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. There … “The great ocean, bhikkhus, as it approaches, causes great rivers to approach; great rivers, as they approach, cause small rivers to approach; small rivers, as they approach, cause great pools to approach; great pools, as they approach, cause small pools to approach. Even so, bhikkhus, ignorance, as it approaches, causes formations to approach; formations, as they approach, cause consciousness to approach; consciousness, as it approaches, causes name-and-form to approach; name-and-form, as it approaches, causes the six sense bases to approach; the six sense bases, as they approach, cause contact to approach; contact, as it approaches, causes feeling to approach; feeling, as it approaches, causes craving to approach; craving, as it approaches, causes clinging to approach; clinging, as it approaches, causes existence to approach; existence, as it approaches, causes birth to approach; birth, as it approaches, causes aging-and-death to approach.”
translations.sn12.70:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel sanctuary. Now at that time the Blessed One was honored, respected, revered, venerated, and paid homage, and was a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. The Saṅgha of bhikkhus, too, was honored, respected, revered, venerated, and paid homage, and was a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick. But the wanderers of other sects were not honored, not respected, not revered, not venerated, not paid homage, and were not recipients of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and supplies for the sick.
translations.sn12.70:10: “But do you venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, dwell having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that, having passed beyond forms, are formless?” — “No indeed, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:11: “Then now, venerable ones—this declaration and the nonattainment of these states—what is this for us, friend?” — “We are liberated by wisdom, friend Susīma.”
translations.sn12.70:12: “I do not understand in detail the meaning of what has been spoken in brief by these venerable ones. It would be good if the venerable ones would speak in such a way that I might understand in detail the meaning of what has been spoken in brief by these venerable ones.” — “Whether you understand, friend Susīma, or whether you do not understand, still we are liberated by wisdom.”
translations.sn12.70:13: Then the venerable Susīma, rising from his seat, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the venerable Susīma reported to the Blessed One the whole of whatever conversation and talk he had had with those bhikkhus. “First, Susīma, knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma; afterward, knowledge in Nibbāna.”
translations.sn12.70:14: “I do not understand in detail the meaning of what has been spoken in brief by the Blessed One, venerable sir. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would speak in such a way that I might understand in detail the meaning of what has been spoken in brief by the Blessed One.” — “Whether you understand, Susīma, or whether you do not understand, still: knowledge of the stability of the Dhamma first, afterward knowledge in Nibbāna.
translations.sn12.70:16: “Therefore, Susīma, whatever form there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—every form: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self’; thus it should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom. Whatever feeling there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—every feeling: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self’; thus it should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom. Whatever perception … Whatever formations there are—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—every formation: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self’; thus it should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom. Whatever consciousness there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—every consciousness: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self’; thus it should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom.”
translations.sn12.70:17: Seeing thus, Susima, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted even with form, becomes disenchanted even with feeling, becomes disenchanted even with perception, becomes disenchanted even with formations, becomes disenchanted even with consciousness. Becoming disenchanted, they become dispassionate; through dispassion they are liberated; when liberated, there is the knowledge: ‘Liberated.’ They understand: ‘Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’
translations.sn12.70:18: “‘With birth as condition, aging-and-death’—do you see thus, Susima?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘With existence as condition, birth’—do you see thus, Susima?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘With clinging as condition, existence’—do you see thus, Susima?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “‘With craving as condition, clinging’—do you see thus, Susima?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “With feeling as condition, craving … with contact as condition, feeling … with the six sense bases as condition, contact … with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases … with consciousness as condition, name-and-form … with formations as condition, consciousness … with ignorance as condition, formations—do you see thus, Susima?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.sn12.70:2: At that time the wanderer Susima was living at Rājagaha together with a large assembly of wanderers. Then the wanderers’ assembly said this to the wanderer Susima: “Come, friend Susima, live the holy life under the ascetic Gotama. Having learned the Dhamma, you will recite it to us. Having learned that Dhamma, we will speak it to householders. In this way we too will be honored, respected, esteemed, revered, venerated, and gain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicines and requisites for the sick.” “Yes, friends,” the wanderer Susima replied to his own assembly, and he approached Venerable Ānanda. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda. When they had concluded the greetings and polite conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the wanderer Susima said this to Venerable Ānanda: “I desire, friend Ānanda, to live the holy life in this Dhamma and discipline.”
translations.sn12.70:21: “But, Susima, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you, with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, those far and near?” “No indeed, venerable sir.”
translations.sn12.70:25: “But, Susima, knowing thus and seeing thus, do you dwell having touched with the body those peaceful liberations that are immaterial, having passed beyond forms?” “No indeed, venerable sir.”
translations.sn12.70:27: Then Venerable Susima fell with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and said this to the Blessed One: “An offense overcame me, venerable sir, so foolish, so deluded, so unskillful, in that in this well-proclaimed Dhamma and discipline I went forth as one seeking gain in Dhamma. Let the Blessed One accept my offense as an offense, for my restraint in the future.”
translations.sn12.70:3: Then Venerable Ānanda took the wanderer Susima and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, this wanderer Susima says: ‘I desire, friend Ānanda, to live the holy life in this Dhamma and discipline.’” “Then, Ānanda, ordain Susima.” The wanderer Susima received the going forth in the Blessed One’s presence; he received full ordination.
translations.sn12.70:5: “But do you venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, experience various kinds of psychic power: having been one you become many, having been many you become one; you appear, you vanish; you go unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as though through space; you dive in and out of the earth as though in water; you walk on water without sinking as though on earth; seated cross-legged you travel through the sky like a winged bird; you touch and stroke with the hand these moon and sun so mighty, so powerful; with the body you exercise mastery as far as the Brahmā world?” “No indeed, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:6: “But do you venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, with the divine ear element, purified and surpassing the human, hear both kinds of sounds, divine and human, those far and near?” “No indeed, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:7: “But do you venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, understand the minds of other beings, other persons with your own mind, having encompassed their mind with your mind: you understand a mind with lust as a mind with lust; you understand a mind without lust as a mind without lust; you understand a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred; you understand a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred; you understand a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion; you understand a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion; you understand a contracted mind as a contracted mind; you understand a distracted mind as a distracted mind; you understand an expanded mind as an expanded mind; you understand an unexpanded mind as an unexpanded mind; you understand a mind with something superior as a mind with something superior; you understand an unsurpassed mind as an unsurpassed mind; you understand a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind; you understand an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind; you understand a liberated mind as a liberated mind; you understand an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind?” “No indeed, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:8: “But do you venerable ones, knowing thus and seeing thus, recollect various kinds of past lives, that is: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births; many eons of contraction, many eons of expansion, many eons of contraction and expansion: ‘There I was so named, of such a clan, such in appearance, such was my food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, with such a life span; passing away from there, I arose elsewhere; and there too I was so named, of such a clan, such in appearance, such was my food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, with such a life span; passing away from there, I was reborn here’—thus you recollect various kinds of past lives with their aspects and details?” “No indeed, friend.”
translations.sn12.70:9: “But, venerable sirs, do you—knowing thus and seeing thus—with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good destinations and bad destinations, and understand beings as faring according to their deeds: ‘Indeed these beings, sirs, endowed with bodily misconduct, endowed with verbal misconduct, endowed with mental misconduct, revilers of the noble ones, wrong-viewed, undertaking action based on wrong view—upon the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in the plane of deprivation, the bad destination, the lower realm, hell; but these beings, sirs, endowed with bodily good conduct, endowed with verbal good conduct, endowed with mental good conduct, not revilers of the noble ones, right-viewed, undertaking action based on right view—upon the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in the good destination, the heavenly world’?—thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, do you see beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in good destinations and bad destinations, and understand beings as faring according to their deeds?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn16.11:1: At one time Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground. Now at that time Venerable Ānanda was traveling on tour in the Southern Hills together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
translations.sn16.11:10: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: “Strong moral shame and moral dread will be present in me toward elders, newcomers, and those in the middle.” For in this way, Kassapa, you should train.
translations.sn16.11:11: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: “Whatever teaching I shall hear connected with the wholesome, I shall listen to it making it as bone, attending to it, bringing all of my mind to bear, with ear alert.” For in this way, Kassapa, you should train.
translations.sn16.11:12: Therefore, Kassapa, you should train thus: “And my mindfulness of the body, accompanied by joy, will not be abandoned.” For in this way, Kassapa, you should train.”
translations.sn16.11:13: Then, friend, the Blessed One, having advised me with this exhortation, rose from his seat and departed. For seven days, friend, I ate only alms from one district; on the eighth, knowledge arose.
translations.sn16.11:14: Then, friend, the Blessed One left the road and approached a certain tree root.
