Then, friend, having spread out a patchwork outer robe folded in four, I said this to the Blessed One: ‘Here, venerable sir, let the Blessed One sit—this would be for my welfare and happiness for a long time.’ The Blessed One sat down, friend, on the prepared seat. Having sat down, friend, the Blessed One said this to me: ‘Soft is this patchwork outer robe of yours, Kassapa.’ ‘Let the Blessed One accept my patchwork outer robe out of compassion.’ ‘But will you wear my hempen rag-robes, Kassapa, cast-off garments?’ ‘I will wear, venerable sir, the Blessed One’s hempen rag-robes, cast-off garments.’ So then, friend, I gave the patchwork outer robe to the Blessed One, and I took up the Blessed One’s hempen rag-robes, cast-off garments.
translations.sn16.11:17: I, friend, by the destruction of the taints, dwell having realized for myself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. And, friend, one might think that a seven-jewel nāga, or an eight-and-a-half-jewel one, should be covered with a palm leaf—so might one think my six direct knowledges should be covered.”
translations.sn16.11:2: Now at that time about thirty bhikkhus, companions of Venerable Ānanda, having renounced the training, reverted to a lower state, mostly being youths. Then Venerable Ānanda, having traveled on tour in the Southern Hills as he liked, went to Rājagaha, to the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground, to where Venerable Mahākassapa was. Having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Mahākassapa and sat down to one side. As Venerable Ānanda was sitting to one side, Venerable Mahākassapa said this to him: “How many reasons, friend Ānanda, have been given by the Blessed One for instituting the three-meal limit in families?”
translations.sn16.11:3: “There are, Venerable Kassapa, three reasons for which the Blessed One instituted the three-meal limit in families: for the restraint of bad people, for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus, so that those with evil desires would not, relying on a faction, split the Saṅgha, and out of compassion for families. These, Venerable Kassapa, are the three reasons for which the Blessed One instituted the three-meal limit in families.”
translations.sn16.11:4: “Then why now, friend Ānanda, do you travel on tour together with these new bhikkhus—with sense doors unguarded, immoderate in eating, and not devoted to wakefulness? I think you travel bringing slaughter to the crops; I think you travel bringing ruin to families. Your following, friend Ānanda, is collapsing; your new recruits, friend, are falling away. This young man does not know moderation.”
translations.sn16.11:6: The bhikkhunī Thullanandā heard: “It is said that the master Mahākassapa has rebuked the master Ānanda, the sage of Videha, with ‘young man’ talk.”
translations.sn16.11:7: Then the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, displeased, uttered displeased speech: “How can the master Mahākassapa—formerly of another sect—think it right to disparage the master Ānanda, the sage of Videha, with ‘young man’ talk?” Venerable Mahākassapa heard the bhikkhunī Thullanandā speaking these words.
translations.sn16.11:8: Then the Venerable Mahākassapa said this to the Venerable Ānanda: “Truly, friend Ānanda, a hasty, unconsidered speech has been spoken by the bhikkhunī Thullanandā. From the time, friend, that I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness, I do not recall having pointed to any other teacher, apart from that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Formerly, friend, when I was still living the household life, this occurred to me: ‘The home life is confining, a dusty path; going forth is open air. It is not easy, while living in a home, to live the holy life that is utterly complete, utterly purified, like a polished conch-shell. What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness?’ Then, friend, at a later time, having made a patchwork outer robe, and directing my mind to those in the world who are arahants, I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the ochre robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.
translations.sn16.13:2: Just as, Kassapa, there is no disappearance of gold so long as counterfeit gold does not arise in the world; but when, Kassapa, counterfeit gold arises in the world, then there is the disappearance of gold—so too, Kassapa, there is no disappearance of the true Dhamma so long as a counterfeit of the true Dhamma does not arise in the world; but when, Kassapa, a counterfeit of the true Dhamma arises in the world, then there is the disappearance of the true Dhamma.
translations.sn16.13:4: There are, Kassapa, five things that lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma. What five? Here, Kassapa, bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male lay followers, and female lay followers dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Teacher; they dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Dhamma; they dwell without reverence and without deference toward the Saṅgha; they dwell without reverence and without deference toward the training; they dwell without reverence and without deference toward concentration—these, Kassapa, are the five things that lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma.
translations.sn16.2:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Venerable Mahākassapa and the Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling at Bārāṇasī, at Isipatana in the Deer Park. Then the Venerable Sāriputta, in the evening, having emerged from seclusion, approached the Venerable Mahākassapa; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Mahākassapa. When they had finished exchanging courteous and friendly words, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa: “It is said, friend Kassapa: ‘One who is not ardent and has no moral dread is incapable of awakening, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage; but one who is ardent and has moral dread is capable of awakening, capable of Nibbāna, capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage.’”
translations.sn16.2:3: And how, friend, is one without moral dread? Here, friend, a bhikkhu does not have moral dread that ‘unarisen bad unwholesome states, arising in me, would lead to harm’; he does not have moral dread that ‘arisen bad unwholesome states, not being abandoned, would lead to harm’; he does not have moral dread that ‘unarisen wholesome states, not arising in me, would lead to harm’; he does not have moral dread that ‘arisen wholesome states, ceasing, would lead to harm.’ Thus, friend, one is without moral dread. Thus, friend, one who is not ardent and without moral dread is incapable of awakening, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage.
translations.sn16.2:4: And how, friend, is one ardent? Here, friend, a bhikkhu makes an effort that ‘unarisen bad unwholesome states, arising in me, would lead to harm’; he makes an effort that ‘arisen bad unwholesome states, not being abandoned, would lead to harm’; unarisen wholesome states … he makes an effort. Thus, friend, one is ardent.
translations.sn16.5:1: Thus have I heard … at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As the Venerable Mahākassapa was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him: “You are now old, Kassapa, and these rough hemp rag-robes of yours are heavy garments. Therefore, Kassapa, wear householders’ robes, eat invitations, and dwell near me.”
translations.sn21.10:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground. Now at that time a certain bhikkhu named Thera was a solitary dweller and a praiser of solitary dwelling. Alone he entered the village for alms, alone he returned, alone he sat in private, and alone he undertook walking meditation. Then several bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One: “Here, bhante, a certain bhikkhu named Thera is a solitary dweller and a praiser of solitary dwelling.”
translations.sn21.10:3: “There is such a thing, Thera, as solitary dwelling; I do not say there is not. But, Thera, listen to how solitary dwelling is fulfilled in detail; attend closely; I will speak.” “Yes, bhante,” … “And how, Thera, is solitary dwelling fulfilled in detail? Here, Thera, what is past is abandoned, what is future is relinquished, and in regard to present acquisitions of personality, desire and lust are well removed. Thus, Thera, solitary dwelling is fulfilled in detail.”
translations.sn21.1:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. There the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus!” “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
translations.sn21.1:2: Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this: “Here, friend, when I was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in my mind: ‘“Noble silence, noble silence” is said. Now what is noble silence?’ Then it occurred to me: ‘Here a bhikkhu, with the stilling of thought and examination, enters and dwells in the second jhāna—internal clarity, unification of mind, without thought, without examination, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This is called noble silence.’ So I, friend, with the stilling of thought and examination, entered and dwelt in the second jhāna—internal clarity, unification of mind, without thought, without examination, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. But while I was dwelling in that dwelling, perceptions and attentions accompanied by thought occurred to me.”
translations.sn21.2:1: At Sāvatthī. There venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus.” “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn21.2:2: “Here, friend, when I was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in my mind: ‘Is there anything in the world such that, with its change and alteration, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and distress would arise in me?’ Then it occurred to me: ‘There is nothing in the world such that, with its change and alteration, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and distress would arise in me.’”
translations.sn21.3:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. Now at that time venerable Sāriputta and venerable Mahāmoggallāna were dwelling at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrel-feeding place, in the same lodging. Then venerable Sāriputta, in the evening, having emerged from seclusion, approached venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with venerable Mahāmoggallāna. After they had concluded the greetings and polite talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, venerable Sāriputta said this to venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
translations.sn21.3:2: “Your faculties are serene, friend Moggallāna; your complexion is pure, bright, and clear. Surely venerable Mahāmoggallāna today has dwelt in a peaceful dwelling.” “I have dwelt today in a rather coarse dwelling, friend. But I had a talk on Dhamma.” “And with whom did venerable Mahāmoggallāna have a talk on Dhamma?” “I had a talk on Dhamma with the Blessed One, friend.” “But the Blessed One is far away, friend, now dwelling at Sāvatthī, in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. Then did venerable Mahāmoggallāna approach the Blessed One by psychic power, or did the Blessed One approach venerable Mahāmoggallāna by psychic power?” “I did not approach the Blessed One by psychic power, friend; nor did the Blessed One approach me by psychic power. But to the extent that the Blessed One has, to that extent is purified the divine eye and the divine element of hearing; and to the extent that I have, to that extent is purified the divine eye and the divine element of hearing.” “Then in what way did venerable Mahāmoggallāna have a talk on Dhamma with the Blessed One?”
translations.sn21.3:3: “Here, friend, I said this to the Blessed One: ‘“One with aroused energy, one with aroused energy,” lord, is said. To what extent, lord, is one with aroused energy?’ When this was said, friend, the Blessed One said this to me: ‘Here, Moggallāna, a bhikkhu dwells with aroused energy—let only skin, sinews, and bones remain, and let the flesh and blood in the body dry up; without attaining that which can be attained by human strength, human energy, and human striving, there will be no stopping of energy. In this way, Moggallāna, one is with aroused energy.’ Thus, friend, I had a talk on Dhamma with the Blessed One.”
translations.sn21.3:6: ‘Sāriputta indeed is foremost in wisdom, in virtue and in serenity too; and even a bhikkhu who has gone to the far shore would be at most just so.’
translations.sn21.6:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then venerable Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya approached the Blessed One. The Blessed One saw venerable Lakuṇḍakabhaddiya coming from afar. Seeing him, he addressed the bhikkhus: “Do you see, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu coming—ugly, unsightly, stunted, of a form despised by bhikkhus?” “Yes, lord.” “That bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is of great psychic power, of great might, and there is no attainment that is easy to obtain that has not been attained before by that bhikkhu. He dwells having entered upon and abiding in that unsurpassed consummation of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, having realized it for himself with direct knowledge here and now.” The Blessed One said this … the Teacher:
translations.sn21.6:2: “Swans, herons, and peacocks, elephants and buffalo and deer— all are afraid of the lion; there is no equality in body.”
translations.sn21.8:1: He was dwelling at Sāvatthī. Then venerable Nanda, the Blessed One’s maternal aunt’s son, having put on robes that were well-pressed and well-smoothed, having applied collyrium to his eyes, and taking a bright bowl, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said this to venerable Nanda as he sat to one side: “It is not fitting for you, Nanda, for a clansman who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, that you should wear well-pressed and well-smoothed robes, apply collyrium to your eyes, and carry a bright bowl. But this is fitting for you, Nanda, for a clansman who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith: that you should be a forest-dweller, an almsfood-eater, a rag-robe wearer, and dwell without longing for sensual pleasures.” The Blessed One said this … the Teacher:
translations.sn21.8:2: “When shall I see Nanda, a forest-dweller, a rag-robe wearer, living on scraps, without longing for sensual pleasures?”
translations.sn21.9:1: He dwells at Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Tissa, the Blessed One’s cousin, approached the Blessed One; having approached, having paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side, sad and dejected, shedding tears. Then the Blessed One said this to Venerable Tissa: “Why now, Tissa, do you sit to one side sad and dejected, shedding tears?” “For, venerable sir, the monks on all sides have mocked me with words and with water.” “For you, Tissa, are one who admonishes but is not patient with admonition; that is not fitting for you, Tissa, a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness, that you be one who admonishes but is not patient with admonition. This is fitting for you, Tissa, a clansman who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness: ‘that you should be one who admonishes and is patient with admonition.’”
translations.sn22.100:2: Have you seen, bhikkhus, a picture called ‘a painting’?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “That too, bhikkhus, a picture called ‘a painting’ is painted by mind. Yet even more, bhikkhus, than that painted mind, mind itself is more variegated. Therefore, bhikkhus, again and again one should review one’s own mind: ‘For a long time this mind has been defiled by greed, by hate, by delusion.’ By defilement of mind, bhikkhus, beings are defiled; by purification of mind beings are purified.
translations.sn22.100:3: I do not see, bhikkhus, any other single class as having mind so variegated as this, bhikkhus, namely animals. Those too, bhikkhus, animals are fashioned by mind; yet even more, bhikkhus, than those animals, mind itself is more variegated. Therefore, bhikkhus, again and again one should review one’s own mind: ‘For a long time this mind has been defiled by greed, by hate, by delusion.’ By defilement of mind, bhikkhus, beings are defiled; by purification of mind beings are purified.
translations.sn22.101:1: At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of the taints is for one who knows and sees, not for one who does not know and does not see. And what, bhikkhus, does one know and see such that the destruction of the taints comes to be? ‘Such is form, such is the arising of form, such is the vanishing of form; such is feeling … such is perception … such are formations … such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the vanishing of consciousness’—thus, bhikkhus, for one who knows thus, who sees thus, the destruction of the taints comes to be.
translations.sn22.101:2: For a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, dwelling not devoted to the practice of cultivation, even if such a wish were to arise: ‘Oh, may my mind be freed from the taints by non-clinging,’ still his mind is not freed from the taints by non-clinging. For what reason? ‘Because it has not been developed’ is what should be said. Not developed with respect to what? Because of not developing the four establishments of mindfulness, because of not developing the four right strivings, because of not developing the four bases of spiritual power, because of not developing the five faculties, because of not developing the five powers, because of not developing the seven factors of awakening, because of not developing the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn22.101:3: Just as, bhikkhus, a hen has eight or ten or twelve eggs. If those eggs are not properly sat upon by the hen, not properly warmed, not properly nurtured, then even if such a wish were to arise in that hen: ‘Oh, may my chicks break the eggshell with the tip of their claws or with their beak and hatch safely,’ still those chicks are unable to break the eggshell with the tip of their claws or with their beak and hatch safely. For what reason? For those eggs of that hen, bhikkhus, eight or ten or twelve, are not properly sat upon by the hen, not properly warmed, not properly nurtured. So too, bhikkhus, for a bhikkhu dwelling not devoted to the practice of cultivation, even if such a wish were to arise: ‘Oh, may my mind be freed from the taints by non-clinging,’ still his mind is not freed from the taints by non-clinging. For what reason? ‘Because it has not been developed’ is what should be said. Not developed with respect to what? Because of not developing the four establishments of mindfulness … the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn22.1:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira, in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, the Deer Park. Then Nakulapitā the householder approached the Blessed One; having approached, having paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. While sitting to one side, Nakulapitā the householder said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn22.1:10: He regards feeling as self, or self as possessing feeling; or feeling in self, or self in feeling. He is obsessed with ‘I am feeling; feeling is mine.’ For one who is obsessed with ‘I am feeling; feeling is mine,’ that feeling changes and becomes otherwise. With the change and becoming otherwise of feeling, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise for him.
translations.sn22.1:11: He regards perception as self, or self as possessing perception; or perception in self, or self in perception. He is obsessed with ‘I am perception; perception is mine.’ For one who is obsessed with ‘I am perception; perception is mine,’ that perception changes and becomes otherwise. With the change and becoming otherwise of perception, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise for him.
translations.sn22.1:12: He regards formations as self, or self as possessing formations; or formations in self, or self among formations. He is obsessed with ‘I am formations; formations are mine.’ For one who is obsessed with ‘I am formations; formations are mine,’ those formations change and become otherwise. With the change and becoming otherwise of formations, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair arise for him.
translations.sn22.1:13: He regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness; or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness. He is obsessed with: ‘I am consciousness, consciousness is mine.’ For one who is obsessed with: ‘I am consciousness, consciousness is mine,’ that consciousness changes and becomes otherwise. As his consciousness changes and becomes otherwise, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Thus, householder, he is one with a sick body and a sick mind.
translations.sn22.1:14: And how, householder, is one sick in body but not sick in mind? Here, householder, a well-taught noble disciple, a seer of the noble ones, skilled in the noble Dhamma, well trained in the noble Dhamma, a seer of good persons, skilled in the Dhamma of good persons, well trained in the Dhamma of good persons, does not regard form as self, or self as possessing form; or form in self, or self in form. He is not obsessed with: ‘I am form, form is mine.’ For one who is not obsessed with: ‘I am form, form is mine,’ that form changes and becomes otherwise. As his form changes and becomes otherwise, there do not arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.sn22.1:2: “Venerable sir, I am old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the end of life; my body is sick, frequently afflicted. But I, venerable sir, am one who sees impermanence, in regard to the Blessed One and the monks who are dear to me. Advise me, venerable sir, the Blessed One; instruct me, venerable sir, the Blessed One, for my welfare and happiness for a long time.”
translations.sn22.1:3: “So it is, householder, so it is, householder. For this body, householder, is sick, a mass of sores, enveloped. For who, householder, while caring for this body, would claim even for a moment to be healthy—unless out of foolishness? Therefore, householder, you should train thus: ‘Though my body is sick, my mind will be not sick.’ For thus, householder, you should train.”
translations.sn22.1:4: Then Nakulapita the householder, having delighted in and approved of what the Blessed One had said, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and having walked around him on the right, went to Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Sāriputta and sat down to one side. As Nakulapita the householder was sitting to one side, Venerable Sāriputta said this to him: “Your faculties are bright, householder; your complexion is pure and clear. Did you obtain today, in the Blessed One’s presence, a Dhamma talk to listen to?”
translations.sn22.1:7: “But, householder, did it not occur to you to question the Blessed One further: ‘To what extent, venerable sir, is one sick in body and sick in mind, and to what extent is one sick in body but not sick in mind?’” “Even from far away, venerable sir, we would come to Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good if the meaning of this statement were to occur to Venerable Sāriputta himself.”
translations.sn22.1:8: “Then, householder, listen and attend closely; I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” Nakulapita the householder replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn22.1:9: “And how, householder, is one sick in body and sick in mind? Here, householder, an untaught ordinary person, not a seer of the noble ones, unskilled in the noble Dhamma, untrained in the noble Dhamma, not a seer of good persons, unskilled in the Dhamma of good persons, untrained in the Dhamma of good persons, regards form as self, or self as possessing form; or form in self, or self in form. He is obsessed with: ‘I am form, form is mine.’ For one who is obsessed with: ‘I am form, form is mine,’ that form changes and becomes otherwise. As his form changes and becomes otherwise, there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair.
translations.sn22.22:2: And what, monks, is the bearer of the burden? The person is to be said to be so. This venerable one of such a name, of such a clan: this is called, monks, the bearer of the burden.
translations.sn22.22:3: And what, monks, is taking up the burden? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there, that is: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for nonexistence. This is called, monks, taking up the burden.
translations.sn22.22:4: And what, monks, is laying down the burden? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving—relinquishment, letting go, release, non-attachment. This is called, monks, laying down the burden.”
translations.sn22.22:6: “The five aggregates are indeed the burden, and the person is the bearer of the burden; taking up the burden is suffering in the world; laying down the burden is happiness.
translations.sn22.2:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Devadaha, a town of the Sakyans. Then several monks who were going to the back country approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said this to the Blessed One: “We wish, venerable sir, to go to the back country, to take up residence in the back-country region.”
translations.sn22.2:10: If, friend, for one who has attained and dwells in unwholesome states there would be in this very life a pleasant abiding, without affliction, without distress, without fever, and with the breakup of the body, after death, a good destination could be expected, the Blessed One would not commend the abandoning of unwholesome states. But since, friend, for one who has attained and dwells in unwholesome states there is in this very life a painful abiding, with affliction, with distress, with fever, and with the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination can be expected, therefore the Blessed One commends the abandoning of unwholesome states.
translations.sn22.2:2: “But, monks, has Sāriputta been consulted by you?” “No, venerable sir, Venerable Sāriputta has not been consulted by us.” “Consult Sāriputta, monks. Sāriputta, monks, is wise, a helper of the monks, a fellow practitioner.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
translations.sn22.2:3: Now at that time Venerable Sāriputta was sitting not far from the Blessed One, in a certain clump of goat-herd’s bushes. Then those monks, having approved and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and, keeping him on their right, went to where Venerable Sāriputta was; having approached, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Sāriputta. After exchanging courteous and friendly talk, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said to Venerable Sāriputta: “We wish, friend Sāriputta, to go to the outlying districts, to take up residence in the outlying districts. The Teacher has been consulted by us.”
translations.sn22.2:5: “Even from far away, friend, we would come to the presence of Venerable Sāriputta to understand the meaning of this statement. It would be good indeed if the meaning of this statement were to occur to Venerable Sāriputta himself.” “Then, friends, listen, attend carefully, I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to Venerable Sāriputta. Venerable Sāriputta said this:
translations.sn22.36:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One … and, sitting to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: “It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, resolute.” “Whatever, monk, one has a latent tendency to, that is conceived; whatever is conceived, by that one is reckoned. Whatever one has no latent tendency to, that is not conceived; whatever is not conceived, by that one is not reckoned.” “Understood, Blessed One, understood, Fortunate One.”
translations.sn22.3:1: Thus have I heard—at one time Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling among the Avantīs at Kuraraghara, on the precipice mountain. Then Hāliddikāni the householder approached Venerable Mahākaccāna; having approached, he paid homage to Venerable Mahākaccāna and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Hāliddikāni the householder said to Venerable Mahākaccāna: “This was said, venerable sir, by the Blessed One in the Aṭṭhakavagga, in the Māgaṇḍiya’s Questions:
translations.sn22.3:10: And how, householder, is one not void of sensual pleasures? Here, householder, someone has not rid themselves of lust for sensual pleasures, has not rid themselves of desire, has not rid themselves of affection, has not rid themselves of thirst, has not rid themselves of fever, has not rid themselves of craving. Thus, householder, one is not void of sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:11: And how, householder, is one void of sensual pleasures? Here, householder, someone has rid themselves of lust for sensual pleasures, has rid themselves of desire, has rid themselves of affection, has rid themselves of thirst, has rid themselves of fever, has rid themselves of craving. Thus, householder, one is void of sensual pleasures.
translations.sn22.3:12: And how, householder, is one who holds up (expectations)? Here, householder, someone thinks: ‘May I be such in the future; may I be such a feeler in the future; may I be such a perceiver in the future; may I be such a volitional-formations one in the future; may I be such a consciousness one in the future.’ Thus, householder, one is one who holds up (expectations).
translations.sn22.3:14: And how, householder, is one a maker of talk, having quarreled with people? Here, householder, someone is a maker of talk of this kind: ‘You do not understand this Dhamma and discipline; I understand this Dhamma and discipline. How could you understand this Dhamma and discipline? You are practicing wrongly; I am practicing rightly. What should be said first you said afterward; what should be said afterward you said first. What is consistent is with me; what is inconsistent is with you. What you have long practiced is overturned. Your thesis is refuted; go, free yourself from your doctrine. You are defeated; disentangle yourself, if you can.’ Thus, householder, one is a maker of talk, having quarreled with people.
translations.sn22.3:17: “Having abandoned the home, wandering without a fixed abode, not making intimacies with people in the village; void of sensual pleasures, not holding up (expectations), how could one make talk, having quarreled with people?”
translations.sn22.3:6: And how, householder, is one a wanderer with a fixed abode? Bound, entangled, and tied by a dwelling-place in the sign of forms, householder—this is called ‘a wanderer with a fixed abode.’ Bound, entangled, and tied by a dwelling-place in the sign of sounds … bound, entangled, and tied by a dwelling-place in the sign of odors … in the sign of tastes … in the sign of tangibles … bound, entangled, and tied by a dwelling-place in the sign of mental phenomena, householder—this is called ‘a wanderer with a fixed abode.’ Thus, householder, one is a wanderer with a fixed abode.
translations.sn22.3:8: And how, householder, is one one who has formed intimacy in the village? Here, householder, someone dwells closely connected with householders, rejoicing together, grieving together, happy when they are happy, suffering when they are suffering; when duties and tasks have arisen, they themselves engage in those endeavors. Thus, householder, one has formed intimacy in the village.
translations.sn22.3:9: And how, householder, is one not one who has formed intimacy in the village? Here, householder, a monk dwells not closely connected with householders, not rejoicing together, not grieving together, not happy when they are happy, not suffering when they are suffering; when duties and tasks have arisen, they do not themselves engage in those endeavors. Thus, householder, one has not formed intimacy in the village.
translations.sn22.47:1: At Sāvatthī. “Whatever recluses or brahmins, monks, who regard the self in many ways, all of them regard the five aggregates subject to clinging, or one among them. What five? Here, monks, an uninstructed ordinary person, not seeing the noble ones, unskilled in the noble Dhamma, untrained in the noble Dhamma; not seeing good persons, unskilled in the Dhamma of good persons, untrained in the Dhamma of good persons, regards form as self, or self as possessing form; or form in self, or self in form. He regards feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness; or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness.
translations.sn22.47:2: Thus this very kind of regarding remains for him as ‘I am.’ And when, monks, ‘I am’ has not disappeared, there is a descent of the five faculties—of the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty. There is, monks, mind; there are mental phenomena; there is the element of ignorance. For an uninstructed ordinary person touched by feeling born of contact with ignorance, ‘I am’ also occurs; ‘I am this’ also occurs; ‘I shall be’ also occurs; ‘I shall not be’ also occurs; ‘I shall be with form’ also occurs; ‘I shall be formless’ also occurs; ‘I shall be percipient’ also occurs; ‘I shall be non-percipient’ also occurs; ‘I shall be neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient’ also occurs.
translations.sn22.48:1: At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I will teach the five aggregates and the five aggregates subject to clinging. Listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, are the five aggregates? Whatever form there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is called the form aggregate. Whatever feeling … whatever perception … whatever formations there are—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle … this is called the formations aggregate. Whatever consciousness there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is called the consciousness aggregate. These, bhikkhus, are called the five aggregates.”
translations.sn22.53:1: At Sāvatthī. “One with appropriation, bhikkhus, is unfreed; one without appropriation is freed. If, bhikkhus, consciousness, standing, were to stand with appropriation of form, having form as its object, established upon form, with delight as its moisture, it would come to growth, increase, and expansion. If with appropriation of feeling … If with appropriation of perception … If, bhikkhus, with appropriation of formations, consciousness, standing, were to stand, having formations as its object, established upon formations, with delight as its moisture, it would come to growth, increase, and expansion.”
translations.sn22.53:2: Bhikkhus, if one were to say thus: ‘Apart from form, apart from feeling, apart from perception, apart from formations, I will describe the coming, the going, the passing away, the rebirth, the growth, the increase, or the expansion of consciousness’—that is not possible.
translations.sn22.54:2: If, bhikkhus, consciousness, standing, were to stand with appropriation of form, having form as its object, established upon form, with delight as its moisture, it would come to growth, increase, and expansion. Or if, bhikkhus, consciousness, standing, were to stand with appropriation of feeling … Or if, bhikkhus, consciousness, standing, were to stand with appropriation of perception … Or if, bhikkhus, with appropriation of formations, consciousness, standing, were to stand, having formations as its object, established upon formations, with delight as its moisture, it would come to growth, increase, and expansion.
translations.sn22.55:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Blessed One uttered this inspired utterance: “‘May I not be, and may it not be mine; it would not be, and it will not be mine’—a bhikkhu firmly resolved thus would cut off the lower fetters.” When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, would a bhikkhu firmly resolved thus—‘May I not be, and may it not be mine; it would not be, and it will not be mine’—cut off the lower fetters?”
translations.sn22.55:10: “But how, venerable sir, knowing how and seeing how is there the immediate destruction of the taints?” “Here, bhikkhu, an unlearned ordinary person comes to dread in a place that should not be dreaded. This dread, bhikkhu, is for the unlearned ordinary person: ‘May I not be, and may it not be mine; it would not be, and it will not be mine.’”
translations.sn22.55:4: He does not understand as it really is: form is suffering, ‘form is suffering’; feeling is suffering … perception is suffering … formations are suffering … consciousness is suffering, ‘consciousness is suffering.’
translations.sn22.55:5: He does not understand as it really is: form is not-self, ‘form is not-self’; feeling is not-self, ‘feeling is not-self’; perception is not-self, ‘perception is not-self’; formations are not-self, ‘formations are not-self’; consciousness is not-self, ‘consciousness is not-self.’
translations.sn22.55:6: He does not understand as it really is: form is conditioned, ‘form is conditioned’; feeling is conditioned … perception is conditioned … formations are conditioned … consciousness is conditioned, ‘consciousness is conditioned.’ He does not understand as it really is: form will cease. Feeling will cease … perception will cease … formations will cease … consciousness will cease, as it really is.
translations.sn22.55:8: He understands as it really is: form is impermanent, ‘form is impermanent.’ Feeling is impermanent … perception is impermanent … formations are impermanent … consciousness is impermanent, ‘consciousness is impermanent,’ as it really is. Form is suffering … consciousness is suffering … form is not-self … consciousness is not-self … form is conditioned … consciousness is conditioned, ‘consciousness is conditioned,’ as it really is. He understands as it really is: form will cease. Feeling … perception … formations … he understands as it really is: consciousness will cease.
translations.sn22.55:9: Through the ceasing of form, the ceasing of feeling, the ceasing of perception, the ceasing of formations, the ceasing of consciousness—thus, bhikkhu, ‘May I not be, and may it not be mine; it would not be, and it will not be mine’—a bhikkhu firmly resolved thus would cut off the lower fetters.” “Thus firmly resolved, venerable sir, ‘a bhikkhu would cut off the lower fetters.’”
translations.sn22.56:13: And what, bhikkhus, is consciousness? There are these six classes of consciousness, bhikkhus—eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness. This, bhikkhus, is called consciousness. With the arising of name-and-form there is the arising of consciousness; with the cessation of name-and-form there is the cessation of consciousness. This very Noble Eightfold Path is the practice leading to the cessation of consciousness, that is to say—right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.56:14: For whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, having directly known consciousness in this way, having directly known the origin of consciousness in this way, having directly known the cessation of consciousness in this way, having directly known the way of practice leading to the cessation of consciousness in this way, have practiced for disenchantment with consciousness, for dispassion, for cessation—they are practicing well. Those who are practicing well enter deeply into this Dhamma and Discipline.
translations.sn22.56:2: And how is it fourfold? I directly knew form, I directly knew the origin of form, I directly knew the cessation of form, I directly knew the way of practice leading to the cessation of form; I directly knew feeling … I directly knew perception … I directly knew formations … I directly knew consciousness, I directly knew the origin of consciousness, I directly knew the cessation of consciousness, I directly knew the way of practice leading to the cessation of consciousness.
translations.sn22.56:5: And whatever ascetics or brahmins there are, bhikkhus, having directly known form in this way … having directly known the way of practice leading to the cessation of form in this way, by disenchantment with form, by dispassion, by cessation, freed through non-clinging—they are well freed. Those who are well freed are complete. For those who are complete there is no description of a round to be made.
translations.sn22.57:1: Thus have I heard at Sāvatthī. “A bhikkhu, bhikkhus, skilled in seven bases and investigating in three ways, in this Dhamma and Discipline is called one who is complete, one who has lived the holy life, a supreme person. And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu skilled in seven bases? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands form, understands the origin of form, understands the cessation of form, understands the way of practice leading to the cessation of form; understands the gratification in form, understands the danger in form, understands the escape from form; understands feeling … understands perception … understands formations … understands consciousness, understands the origin of consciousness, understands the cessation of consciousness, understands the way of practice leading to the cessation of consciousness; understands the gratification in consciousness, understands the danger in consciousness, understands the escape from consciousness.”
translations.sn22.57:11: And what, bhikkhus, are formations? There are these six classes of volition, bhikkhus—volition regarding forms … volition regarding mental phenomena. These, bhikkhus, are called formations. With the origin of contact is the origin of formations; with the cessation of contact is the cessation of formations. This very noble eightfold path is the way of practice leading to the cessation of formations, that is—right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:15: The pleasure and joy that arises dependent on consciousness—this is the gratification in consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, of a nature to change—this is the danger in consciousness. The removal of desire and lust for consciousness, the abandoning of desire and lust—this is the escape from consciousness.
translations.sn22.57:17: And whatever ascetics or brahmins there are, bhikkhus, having directly known consciousness in this way, having directly known the origin of consciousness in this way, having directly known the cessation of consciousness in this way, having directly known the way of practice leading to the cessation of consciousness in this way; having directly known the gratification in consciousness in this way, having directly known the danger in consciousness in this way, having directly known the escape from consciousness in this way, by disenchantment with consciousness, by dispassion, by cessation, freed through non-clinging—they are well freed. Those who are well freed are complete. For those who are complete there is no description of a round to be made. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is skilled in seven bases.
translations.sn22.57:2: And what, bhikkhus, is form? The four great elements, and form derived from the four great elements. This, bhikkhus, is called form. With the origin of nutriment is the origin of form; with the cessation of nutriment is the cessation of form. This very noble eightfold path is the way of practice leading to the cessation of form, that is—right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:5: And whatever ascetics or brahmins there are, bhikkhus, having directly known form in this way, having directly known the origin of form in this way, having directly known the cessation of form in this way, having directly known the way of practice leading to the cessation of form in this way; having directly known the gratification in form in this way, having directly known the danger in form in this way, having directly known the escape from form in this way, by disenchantment with form, by dispassion, by cessation, freed through non-clinging—they are well freed. Those who are well freed are complete. For those who are complete there is no description of a round to be made.
translations.sn22.57:6: And what, bhikkhus, is feeling? There are these six classes of feeling, bhikkhus—feeling born of eye-contact … feeling born of mind-contact. This, bhikkhus, is called feeling. With the origin of contact is the origin of feeling; with the cessation of contact is the cessation of feeling. This very noble eightfold path is the way of practice leading to the cessation of feeling, that is—right view … right concentration.
translations.sn22.57:7: The pleasure and joy that arises dependent on feeling—this is the gratification in feeling. That feeling is impermanent, suffering, of a nature to change—this is the danger in feeling. The removal of desire and lust for feeling, the abandoning of desire and lust—this is the escape from feeling.
translations.sn22.58:1: Thus have I heard at Sāvatthī. “The Tathāgata, bhikkhus, the Arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, is freed through non-clinging by disenchantment with form, by dispassion, by cessation, and is therefore called the perfectly enlightened one. A bhikkhu too, bhikkhus, freed by wisdom, is freed through non-clinging by disenchantment with form, by dispassion, by cessation, and is therefore called ‘freed by wisdom.’”
translations.sn22.58:3: The Tathāgata, bhikkhus, the Arahant, the perfectly enlightened one, is freed through non-clinging by disenchantment with perception … with formations … with consciousness, by dispassion, by cessation, and is therefore called the perfectly enlightened one. A bhikkhu too, bhikkhus, freed by wisdom, is freed through non-clinging by disenchantment with consciousness, by dispassion, by cessation, and is therefore called ‘freed by wisdom.’
translations.sn22.59:10: Whatever consciousness there is, past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near— all consciousness is to be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’
translations.sn22.59:7: “Therefore, bhikkhus, whatever form there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’
translations.sn22.5:11: Consciousness does not delight, does not welcome, does not remain holding on. For one who does not delight in consciousness, does not welcome it, does not remain holding on, the delight in consciousness ceases. With the cessation of delight, cessation of clinging … thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:2: And what, bhikkhus, is the arising of form, what is the arising of feeling, what is the arising of perception, what is the arising of formations, what is the arising of consciousness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu delights, welcomes, and remains holding on.
translations.sn22.5:3: And what does he delight in, welcome, and remain holding on to? He delights in form, welcomes it, and remains holding on to it. For one who delights in form, welcomes it, and remains holding on to it, delight arises. Whatever delight there is in form, that is clinging. Dependent on that clinging, there is becoming; dependent on becoming, birth; dependent on birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair come to be. Thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:4: He delights in feeling … he delights in perception … he delights in formations … he delights in consciousness, welcomes it, and remains holding on. For one who delights in consciousness, welcomes it, and remains holding on to it, delight arises. Whatever delight there is in consciousness, that is clinging. Dependent on that clinging, there is becoming; dependent on becoming, birth; dependent on birth … thus there is the arising of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.5:8: And what does he not delight in, not welcome, not remain holding on to? He does not delight in form, does not welcome it, does not remain holding on to it. For one who does not delight in form, does not welcome it, does not remain holding on to it, whatever delight there is in form ceases. With the cessation of delight, cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, cessation of becoming … thus there is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering.
translations.sn22.60:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof. Then Mahāli the Licchavi approached the Blessed One … and, sitting to one side, Mahāli the Licchavi said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn22.60:2: “Pūraṇa Kassapa, venerable sir, says thus: ‘There is no cause, there is no condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled without cause, without condition. There is no cause, there is no condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified without cause, without condition.’ What does the Blessed One say here?”
translations.sn22.60:3: “There is, Mahāli, a cause, there is a condition for the defilement of beings; beings are defiled with cause, with condition. There is, Mahāli, a cause, there is a condition for the purification of beings; beings are purified with cause, with condition.”
translations.sn22.60:4: “But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition for the defilement of beings? How are beings defiled with cause, with condition?”
translations.sn22.60:5: “If, Mahāli, form were exclusively suffering, immersed in suffering, entered upon suffering, not entered upon by pleasure, beings would not lust after form. But because, Mahāli, form is pleasant, immersed in pleasure, entered upon pleasure, not entered upon by suffering, therefore beings lust after form; through lust they are bound; through being bound they are defiled. This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the defilement of beings; thus beings are defiled with cause, with condition.
translations.sn22.60:8: If, Mahāli, consciousness were exclusively suffering, immersed in suffering, entered upon suffering, not entered upon by pleasure, beings would not lust after consciousness. But because, Mahāli, consciousness is pleasant, immersed in pleasure, entered upon pleasure, not entered upon by suffering, therefore beings lust after consciousness; through lust they are bound; through being bound they are defiled. This too, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the defilement of beings. Thus too beings are defiled with cause, with condition.”
translations.sn22.60:9: “But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition for the purification of beings? How are beings purified with cause, with condition?” “If, Mahāli, form were exclusively pleasant, immersed in pleasure, entered upon pleasure, not entered upon by suffering, beings would not become disenchanted with form. But because, Mahāli, form is suffering, immersed in suffering, entered upon suffering, not entered upon by pleasure, therefore beings become disenchanted with form; becoming disenchanted they become dispassionate; through dispassion they are purified. This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the purification of beings. Thus beings are purified with cause, with condition.
translations.sn22.76:2: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form as well, with feeling as well … with perception as well … with formations as well … with consciousness as well. Becoming disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion he is liberated. When liberated, there is knowledge: ‘Liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’ As far as there are abodes of beings, as far as the summit of existence, these are the foremost, these are the best in the world, namely the arahants.”
translations.sn22.76:4: “Happy indeed are the arahants,  craving is not found in them;  the conceit ‘I am’ is cut off,  the net of delusion is torn apart.
translations.sn22.76:6: Having fully understood the five aggregates,  they are of seven true-Dhamma ranges;  praiseworthy good persons,  sons of the Buddha, born of him.
translations.sn22.76:7: Endowed with the seven treasures,  trained in the three trainings;  the great heroes wander about,  fears and terrors abandoned.
translations.sn22.76:8: Endowed with ten factors,  great nāgas, collected;  these indeed are the best in the world,  craving is not found in them.
translations.sn22.76:9: The untrained-knowledge has arisen,  this is the last accumulation;  whatever is the essence of the holy life,  in that they are not dependent on another.”
translations.sn22.79:1: At Sāvatthī. “Whatever ascetics or brahmins, bhikkhus, recollect manifold kinds of past lives as they recollect, all of them recollect the five aggregates subject to clinging, or one of them. Which five? ‘I was of such a form in the past’—thus, bhikkhus, as they recollect, they recollect only form. ‘I was of such a feeling in the past’—thus, bhikkhus, as they recollect, they recollect only feeling. ‘I was of such a perception in the past’ … ‘I was of such volitional formations in the past’ … ‘I was of such consciousness in the past’—thus, bhikkhus, as they recollect, they recollect only consciousness.
translations.sn22.79:10: ‘Now I am being eaten up by consciousness. In the past too I was eaten up by consciousness in just this way, just as now I am being eaten up by present consciousness. And if I were to delight in future consciousness, in the future too I would be eaten up by consciousness in just this way, just as now I am being eaten up by present consciousness.’ Reflecting thus, he is without concern for past consciousness; he does not delight in future consciousness; and he is practicing for disenchantment with, dispassion toward, and cessation of present consciousness.
translations.sn22.79:7: Therein, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Now I am being eaten up by form. In the past too I was eaten up by form in just this way, just as now I am being eaten up by present form. And if I were to delight in future form, in the future too I would be eaten up by form in just this way, just as now I am being eaten up by present form.’ Reflecting thus, he is without concern for past form; he does not delight in future form; and he is practicing for disenchantment with, dispassion toward, and cessation of present form.
translations.sn22.80:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu, in the Nigrodha Park. Then the Blessed One, in connection with some matter, dismissed the community of bhikkhus and, in the forenoon, having dressed and taken bowl and robe, entered Kapilavatthu for alms. Having walked for alms in Kapilavatthu, after the meal, on returning from the almsround, he went to the Great Wood for the day’s abiding. Having entered the Great Wood, he sat for the day’s abiding at the root of the Beluvala sapling.
translations.sn22.80:4: The Blessed One consented by silence. Then Brahmā Sahampati, knowing the Blessed One’s consent, paid homage to the Blessed One, and after circumambulating him on the right, disappeared right there.
translations.sn22.80:5: Then the Blessed One, in the evening, having risen from seclusion, went to the Nigrodha Park; having gone there, he sat down on a seat that had been spread. Sitting, the Blessed One formed such an exertion of spiritual power that those bhikkhus, on the second day, came to me looking abashed. Those bhikkhus, on the second day, came to the Blessed One looking abashed; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. When those bhikkhus were seated to one side, the Blessed One said this:
translations.sn22.80:6: “This, bhikkhus, is an extreme of livelihoods, namely, going for alms. This, bhikkhus, is a curse in the world: ‘You wander for alms with bowl in hand.’ And yet, bhikkhus, sons of good families take it up for a reason, depending on a reason; not forced by a king, not forced by thieves, not pressured by debt, not pressured by fear, not because it is a way of making a living; but rather: ‘We are afflicted by birth, aging, and death, by sorrows, lamentations, pains, displeasures, and despairs—afflicted by suffering, overwhelmed by suffering—perhaps an ending of this whole mass of suffering might be discerned.’
translations.sn22.80:7: Thus gone forth, bhikkhus, is this son of a good family. Yet he is covetous for sensual pleasures, with intense lust, with a mind of ill will, with corrupted intentions of mind, forgetful, not clearly comprehending, unconcentrated, with a wandering mind, with faculties unguarded. Just as, bhikkhus, a firebrand lit at both ends and smeared with dung in the middle does not serve as timber either in a village or in a forest, so too I say this person is similar: he has fallen away from the enjoyments of a householder, and he does not fulfill the purpose of asceticism.
translations.sn22.80:9: There are these two views, bhikkhus: the view of existence and the view of nonexistence. Therein, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Is there anything in the world such that, by clinging to it, I would be blameless?’ He understands thus: ‘There is nothing in the world such that, by clinging to it, I would be blameless. For by clinging to form alone I would cling; by clinging to feeling alone … by clinging to perception alone … by clinging to volitional formations alone; by clinging to consciousness alone I would cling. For me, with clinging as condition, there would be existence; with existence as condition, birth; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair would come to be. Thus there would be the arising of this whole mass of suffering.’
translations.sn22.81:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī, in Ghosita’s Park. Then the Blessed One, in the forenoon, having dressed and taken bowl and robe, entered Kosambī for alms. Having walked for alms in Kosambī, after the meal, on returning from the almsround, having himself put the dwelling in order and taken bowl and robe, without informing, without taking leave of the attendants, without notifying the community of bhikkhus, alone and without a second he set out on wandering.
translations.sn22.81:10: He does not regard form as self, he does not regard feeling as self, he does not regard perception … he does not regard volitional formations … he does not regard consciousness as self; but he has this view: ‘That self is that world; after death I shall be that—permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change.’ But that, bhikkhus, which is the eternalist view, that is a volitional formation. And that volitional formation—dependent on what … pe … thus too, bhikkhus, for one who knows thus and sees thus, without delay there is the destruction of the taints.
translations.sn22.81:3: Then the Blessed One, wandering on tour by stages, came to Pāḷileyyaka. There the Blessed One stayed at Pāḷileyyaka, at the root of the Bhaddasāla tree. Then several bhikkhus approached Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda. After exchanging greetings and pleasantries, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said this to Venerable Ānanda: “It has been a long time, friend Ānanda, since we heard a talk on Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One. We wish, friend Ānanda, to hear a talk on Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One.”
translations.sn22.82:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī, in the Eastern Monastery, in Migāramātā’s mansion, together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Now at that time, on that uposatha day, the fifteenth, the night of the full moon, the Blessed One was sitting in the open air surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
translations.sn22.82:10: “What, venerable sir, is the gratification in form, what is the danger, what is the escape; what is the gratification in feeling … what is the gratification in perception … what is the gratification in volitional formations … what is the gratification in consciousness, what is the danger, what is the escape?” “Bhikkhu, the pleasure and joy that arises dependent on form—this is the gratification in form. That form is impermanent, suffering, of a nature to change—this is the danger in form. The removal of desire and lust for form, the abandoning of desire and lust—this is the escape from form. That feeling dependent on … that perception dependent on … those volitional formations dependent on … the pleasure and joy that arises dependent on consciousness—this is the gratification in consciousness. That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, of a nature to change—this is the danger in consciousness. The removal of desire and lust for consciousness, the abandoning of desire and lust—this is the escape from consciousness.” Then that bhikkhu, pleased with and approving the Blessed One’s words, asked the Blessed One a further question:
translations.sn22.82:11: “How, venerable sir, for one who knows and sees, are there no underlying tendencies to ‘I-making’, ‘mine-making’, and conceit in regard to this conscious body and in regard to all signs externally?” “Bhikkhu, whatever form there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—he sees it as it really is with correct wisdom. Whatever feeling … whatever perception … whatever volitional formations … whatever consciousness there is—past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all consciousness: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’—he sees it as it really is with correct wisdom. Thus, bhikkhu, for one who knows thus and sees thus, there are no underlying tendencies to ‘I-making’, ‘mine-making’, and conceit in regard to this conscious body and in regard to all signs externally.”
translations.sn22.82:12: Now at that time this thought arose in the mind of a certain bhikkhu: “So it seems, sirs, form is not-self, feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is not-self; how will actions done by what is not-self touch a self?” Then the Blessed One, having known that bhikkhu’s thought with his mind, addressed the bhikkhus:
translations.sn22.82:13: “There is, bhikkhus, this possibility: that here some foolish man, unlearned, overwhelmed by ignorance, with a mind dominated by craving, might think to outrun the Teacher’s dispensation: ‘So it seems, sirs, form is not-self, feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is not-self. How will actions done by what is not-self touch a self?’ You have been guided by me by way of cross-questioning, bhikkhus, here and there in those various things.”
translations.sn22.82:4: “But, venerable sir, these five clinging-aggregates are rooted in what?” “Bhikkhu, these five clinging-aggregates are rooted in desire.” …pe… “Is that same clinging the five clinging-aggregates, venerable sir, or is clinging something apart from the five clinging-aggregates?” “Bhikkhu, clinging is not just those five clinging-aggregates, nor is clinging apart from the five clinging-aggregates; rather, whatever desire and lust there is there, that is the clinging there.” “Good, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu …pe… asked a further question:
translations.sn22.82:5: “But, venerable sir, could there be difference in desire and lust with respect to the five clinging-aggregates?” “There could be, bhikkhus,” the Blessed One said: “Here, bhikkhu, in the case of some person it is thus: ‘May I be of such form in the future, may I be of such feeling in the future, may I be of such perception in the future, may I be of such volitional formations in the future, may I be of such consciousness in the future.’ Thus, bhikkhu, there could be difference in desire and lust with respect to the five clinging-aggregates.” “Good, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu …pe… asked a further question:
translations.sn22.82:7: “What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the form aggregate; what is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the feeling aggregate; what is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the perception aggregate; what is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the volitional formations aggregate; what is the cause, what is the condition for the designation of the consciousness aggregate?” “Bhikkhu, the four great elements are the cause, the four great elements are the condition, for the designation of the form aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition, for the designation of the feeling aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition, for the designation of the perception aggregate. Contact is the cause, contact is the condition, for the designation of the volitional formations aggregate. Name-and-form is the cause, name-and-form is the condition, for the designation of the consciousness aggregate.” “Good, venerable sir,” that bhikkhu …pe… asked:
translations.sn22.82:8: “And how, bhante, is there identity view?” — “Here, bhikkhu, an uninstructed ordinary person, one who does not see the noble ones, unskilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, undisciplined in the Dhamma of the noble ones; one who does not see the good persons, unskilled in the Dhamma of the good persons, undisciplined in the Dhamma of the good persons, regards form as self, or self as possessing form; or form in self, or self in form; feeling … perception … formations … regards consciousness as self, or self as possessing consciousness; or consciousness in self, or self in consciousness. Thus, bhikkhu, there is identity view.” — “Good, bhante,” that bhikkhu … asked:
translations.sn22.82:9: “And how, bhante, is there no identity view?” — “Here, bhikkhu, an instructed noble disciple, one who sees the noble ones, skilled in the Dhamma of the noble ones, well trained in the Dhamma of the noble ones; one who sees the good persons, skilled in the Dhamma of the good persons, well trained in the Dhamma of the good persons, does not regard form as self, does not regard self as possessing form; does not regard form in self, does not regard self in form; does not regard feeling … does not regard perception … does not regard formations … does not regard consciousness as self, does not regard self as possessing consciousness; does not regard consciousness in self, does not regard self in consciousness. Thus, bhikkhu, there is no identity view.” — “Good, bhante,” that bhikkhu … asked:
translations.sn22.83:1: At Sāvatthī. There the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus.” — “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this:
translations.sn22.83:3: Just as, friend Ānanda, a woman or a man, young, youthful, fond of adornment, looking at the reflection of their own face in a mirror that is pure and bright, or in a clear bowl of water, would see it with clinging, not without clinging; even so, friend Ānanda, with clinging to form there is ‘I am’, not without clinging. With clinging to feeling … perception … formations … with clinging to consciousness there is ‘I am’, not without clinging.
translations.sn22.84:10: This simile has been made by me, Tissa, to convey the meaning. And this here is the meaning: ‘A person unskilled in the path’—this, Tissa, is a designation for an ordinary person. ‘A person skilled in the path’—this, Tissa, is a designation for the Tathāgata, the arahant, the perfectly awakened one. ‘A fork in the road’—this, Tissa, is a designation for doubt. ‘The left path’—this, Tissa, is a designation for the wrong eightfold path, that is: wrong view … wrong concentration. ‘The right path’—this, Tissa, is a designation for the noble eightfold path, that is: right view … right concentration. ‘A dense jungle thicket’—this, Tissa, is a designation for ignorance. ‘A great swampy hollow’—this, Tissa, is a designation for sensual pleasures. ‘A pit, a precipice’—this, Tissa, is a designation for anger and vexation. ‘A level stretch of ground, delightful’—this, Tissa, is a designation for Nibbāna. Delight, Tissa, delight, Tissa. With my exhortation, with my assistance, with my instruction.”
translations.sn22.84:5: “Good, good, Tissa. That is so, Tissa. For one whose lust has not departed from formations, whose lust for consciousness has not departed—whose desire has not departed, whose affection has not departed, whose thirst has not departed, whose fever has not departed, whose craving has not departed—because of the change and alteration of that consciousness there arise sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and distress.” — “So it is, bhante.”
translations.sn22.84:6: “Good, good, Tissa. That is so, Tissa. For one whose lust has not departed from consciousness. What do you think, Tissa: for one whose lust for form has departed, whose desire has departed, whose affection has departed, whose thirst has departed, whose fever has departed, whose craving has departed—because of the change and alteration of that form, do sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and distress arise?” — “No indeed, bhante.”
translations.sn22.85:1: At one time the Venerable Sāriputta was staying at Sāvatthī in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. Now at that time a bad view had arisen in a bhikkhu named Yamaka, of this sort: “I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: that a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, with the breaking up of the body, is annihilated and perishes; after death he does not exist.”
translations.sn22.85:10: “What do you think, friend Yamaka: do you regard form … feeling … perception … formations … consciousness as the Tathāgata?” — “No indeed, friend.”
translations.sn22.85:11: “What do you think, friend Yamaka: do you regard the Tathāgata as this one who is without form … without feeling … without perception … without formations … without consciousness?” — “No indeed, friend.” “And when, friend Yamaka, the Tathāgata is not found in this very life as real and true, is it fitting for you to make that statement: ‘I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: that a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, with the breaking up of the body, is annihilated and perishes; after death he does not exist’?”
translations.sn22.85:12: “That bad view occurred to me before, friend Sāriputta, when I was unwise; but having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Venerable Sāriputta, that bad view has been abandoned and the Dhamma has been understood by me.”
translations.sn22.85:16: He does not understand as it really is impermanent form as ‘impermanent form’. He does not understand as it really is impermanent feeling as ‘impermanent feeling’. He does not understand as it really is impermanent perception as ‘impermanent perception’. He does not understand as it really is impermanent formations as ‘impermanent formations’. He does not understand as it really is impermanent consciousness as ‘impermanent consciousness’.
translations.sn22.85:19: He does not understand as it really is conditioned form as ‘conditioned form’. Conditioned feeling … conditioned perception … conditioned formations … he does not understand as it really is conditioned consciousness as ‘conditioned consciousness’.
translations.sn22.85:20: They do not truly understand form as it really is: ‘Form is a killer.’ They do not truly understand feeling as it really is: ‘Feeling is a killer’ … perception as it really is: ‘Perception is a killer’ … they do not truly understand volitional formations as they really are: ‘Volitional formations are killers.’ They do not truly understand consciousness as it really is: ‘Consciousness is a killer.’
translations.sn22.85:21: They approach form, take it up, and cling to it: ‘This is my self.’ Feeling … perception … volitional formations … they approach consciousness, take it up, and cling to it: ‘This is my self.’ For them these five clinging-aggregates, approached and taken up, lead for a long time to harm and suffering.
translations.sn22.85:23: They truly understand impermanent form as it really is: ‘Form is impermanent.’ Impermanent feeling … impermanent perception … impermanent volitional formations … they truly understand impermanent consciousness as it really is: ‘Consciousness is impermanent.’
translations.sn22.85:25: They truly understand not-self form as it really is: ‘Form is not-self.’ Not-self feeling … not-self perception … not-self volitional formations … they truly understand not-self consciousness as it really is: ‘Consciousness is not-self.’
translations.sn22.85:5: When those monks were unable to dissuade the venerable Yamaka from that bad view, then those monks, having risen from their seats, approached the venerable Sāriputta; having approached, they said this to the venerable Sāriputta: “Venerable Sāriputta, a bad view like this has arisen in the monk Yamaka: ‘I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: that a monk whose taints are ended, with the breakup of the body, is annihilated and perishes, and does not exist after death.’ Let the venerable Sāriputta approach the monk Yamaka out of compassion.” The venerable Sāriputta consented by silence. Then the venerable Sāriputta, in the evening, having emerged from seclusion, approached the venerable Yamaka; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the venerable Yamaka … Having sat down to one side, the venerable Sāriputta said this to the venerable Yamaka:
translations.sn22.85:6: “Is it true, friend Yamaka, that a bad view like this has arisen in you: ‘I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: that a monk whose taints are ended, with the breakup of the body, is annihilated and perishes, and does not exist after death’?” “Indeed, friend, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One thus: that a monk whose taints are ended, with the breakup of the body, is annihilated and perishes, and does not exist after death.”
translations.sn22.85:9: “What do you think, friend Yamaka: do you regard form as the Tathāgata?” “No, friend.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata as apart from form?” “No, friend.” “Do you regard feeling … as apart from feeling … perception … as apart from perception … volitional formations … as apart from volitional formations … do you regard consciousness as the Tathāgata?” “No, friend.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata as apart from consciousness?” “No, friend.”
translations.sn22.86:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof. Now at that time the venerable Anurādha was staying not far from the Blessed One, in a forest hut. Then several wanderers of other sects approached the venerable Anurādha; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the venerable Anurādha. After exchanging greetings and courtesies, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those wanderers of other sects said this to the venerable Anurādha: “Friend Anurādha, that Tathāgata—the supreme person, the highest person, who has attained the highest attainment—does the Tathāgata, when describing him, describe him in these four positions: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’?”
translations.sn22.86:10: “What do you think, Anurādha: do you regard form … feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as the Tathāgata?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn22.86:11: “What do you think, Anurādha: do you regard this Tathāgata as formless … without feeling … without perception … without volitional formations … without consciousness?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn22.86:12: “And since for you, Anurādha, the Tathāgata is not found here and now, in this very life, as real and actual, is it fitting for you to make that declaration: ‘That Tathāgata—the supreme person, the highest person, who has attained the highest attainment—the Tathāgata, when describing him, describes him apart from these four positions—“The Tathāgata exists after death,” or … “does not exist,” or “both exists and does not exist,” or “neither exists nor does not exist after death”’?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn22.86:2: When this was said, the venerable Anurādha said this to those wanderers of other sects: “Friend, that Tathāgata—the supreme person, the highest person, who has attained the highest attainment—the Tathāgata, when describing him, describes him apart from these four positions: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,’ or ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.’” When this was said, those wanderers of other sects said this to the venerable Anurādha: “This monk must be new, recently gone forth, or else an elder who is foolish and incompetent.” Then those wanderers of other sects, having disparaged the venerable Anurādha with charges of being new and of being foolish, rose from their seats and departed.
translations.sn22.86:3: Then, when those wanderers of other sects had recently departed, it occurred to the venerable Anurādha: “If those wanderers of other sects were to ask me a further question—how, answering, could I be one who repeats what the Blessed One has said, and yet not misrepresent the Blessed One with what is not so; could I answer in accordance with the Dhamma, and so that no fellow practitioner, following the Dhamma, would arrive at a blameworthy ground for criticism?”
translations.sn22.86:8: “What do you think, Anurādha: do you regard form as ‘the Tathāgata’?” — “No, venerable sir.” “Do you regard feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness as ‘the Tathāgata’?” — “No, venerable sir.”
