translations.sn22.86:9: “What do you think, Anurādha: do you regard the Tathāgata as in form?” — “No, venerable sir.” “Do you regard the Tathāgata as apart from form?” — “No, venerable sir.” “In feeling … apart from feeling … in perception … apart from perception … in volitional formations … apart from volitional formations … in consciousness … apart from consciousness do you regard (any of these) as ‘the Tathāgata’?” — “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn22.89:10: “Just as, friend, there is the fragrance of a blue lotus, or a pink lotus, or a white lotus. Now if someone were to say: ‘the fragrance is of the petal’, or ‘the fragrance is of the color’, or ‘the fragrance is of the stamens’—would he, speaking thus, be speaking correctly?” — “No, friend.” “Then how, friend, would one speaking correctly explain it?” — “Speaking correctly, friend, he would explain: ‘the fragrance is of the flower.’” “So too, friend, I do not say of form, ‘I am’; nor do I say, apart from form, ‘I am’. I do not say of feeling … of perception … of volitional formations … of consciousness, ‘I am’; nor do I say, apart from consciousness, ‘I am’. Yet, friend, in the five clinging-aggregates ‘I am’ has been attained by me, but I do not regard (it as) ‘I am this.’”
translations.sn22.89:11: “Although, friend, the five lower fetters are abandoned in a noble disciple, still there remains for him: ‘the “I am” conceit, “I am” desire, “I am” underlying tendency connected with the five clinging-aggregates has not been uprooted. After some time he dwells contemplating rise and fall in the five clinging-aggregates: ‘such is form, such is the arising of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling … such is perception … such are volitional formations … such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’ As he dwells contemplating rise and fall in these five clinging-aggregates, whatever “I am” conceit, “I am” desire, “I am” underlying tendency connected with the five clinging-aggregates that has not been uprooted—even that comes to be uprooted.”
translations.sn22.89:12: “Just as, friend, a cloth is soiled, stained with dirt. Its owners would hand it over to a washerman. The washerman, having kneaded it with salt or lye or cow dung, rinses it in clean water. Although that cloth becomes clean and bright, still there remains in it an unremoved smell of salt, or a smell of lye, or a smell of cow dung. The washerman gives it back to its owners. They put it in a scented casket. Whatever unremoved smell of salt, or smell of lye, or smell of cow dung remained in it—even that comes to be removed. So too, friend, although the five lower fetters are abandoned in a noble disciple, still there remains an unremoved “I am” conceit, “I am” desire, “I am” underlying tendency connected with the five clinging-aggregates. After some time he dwells contemplating rise and fall in the five clinging-aggregates: ‘such is form, such is the arising of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling … such is perception … such are volitional formations … such is consciousness, such is the arising of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’ As he dwells contemplating rise and fall in these five clinging-aggregates, whatever “I am” conceit, “I am” desire, “I am” underlying tendency connected with the five clinging-aggregates that has not been uprooted—even that comes to be removed.”
translations.sn22.89:13: When this was said, the elder bhikkhus said this to Venerable Khemaka: “We did not question Venerable Khemaka with the wish to trouble him. Rather, Venerable Khemaka was able to explain, teach, point out, establish, disclose, analyze, and make plain in detail the Blessed One’s teaching. And this Blessed One’s teaching has been explained, taught, pointed out, established, disclosed, analyzed, and made plain in detail by Venerable Khemaka.”
translations.sn22.90:1: At one time several elder bhikkhus were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then Venerable Channa, in the evening, having risen from seclusion, taking a key, went from dwelling to dwelling and addressed the elder bhikkhus: “Let the venerable elders admonish me; let the venerable elders instruct me; let the venerable elders give me a Dhamma talk, so that I might see the Dhamma.”
translations.sn22.90:2: When this was said, the elder bhikkhus said this to Venerable Channa: “Form, friend Channa, is impermanent; feeling is impermanent; perception is impermanent; volitional formations are impermanent; consciousness is impermanent. Form is not-self; feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is not-self. All formations are impermanent; all phenomena are not-self.”
translations.sn22.90:3: Then it occurred to Venerable Channa: “This too is so for me: ‘form is impermanent, feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is impermanent; form is not-self, feeling … perception … volitional formations … consciousness is not-self. All formations are impermanent; all phenomena are not-self.’ And yet my mind does not leap up, does not become confident, does not become settled, does not become resolved in the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the ending of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna. Anxiety and clinging arise; the mind turns back: ‘Then who now is my self?’ But it is not so for one who sees the Dhamma in this way. Who indeed might teach me the Dhamma so that I might see the Dhamma?”
translations.sn22.90:4: Then it occurred to Venerable Channa: “Venerable Ānanda is dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery, praised and esteemed by the Teacher and by wise companions in the holy life; and Venerable Ānanda is able to teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might see the Dhamma; and I have that much confidence in Venerable Ānanda. Why don’t I go to Venerable Ānanda?” Then Venerable Channa, having put his dwelling in order and taking up bowl and robe, went to Kosambī, to Ghosita’s monastery, to Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda …pe… and sitting to one side Venerable Channa said this to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn22.90:8: “Even by this much we are pleased with Venerable Channa—if only Venerable Channa has made it clear and cut off the stake. Lend ear, friend Channa; you are capable of understanding the Dhamma.” Then, by just that much, great rapture and gladness arose in Venerable Channa: “Surely I am capable of understanding the Dhamma.”
translations.sn22.94:1: At Sāvatthī. “Monks, I do not dispute with the world; rather, the world disputes with me. A speaker of Dhamma, monks, does not dispute with anyone in the world. Whatever, monks, is agreed in the world by the wise to be nonexistent, I too say of that, ‘It does not exist.’ Whatever, monks, is agreed in the world by the wise to exist, I too say of that, ‘It exists.’”
translations.sn22.94:3: And what, monks, is agreed in the world by the wise to exist, that I say, ‘It exists’? Form, monks, is impermanent, suffering, of a nature to change; it is agreed in the world by the wise to exist; I too say of it, ‘It exists.’ Feeling is impermanent …pe… consciousness is impermanent, suffering, of a nature to change; it is agreed in the world by the wise to exist; I too say of it, ‘It exists.’ This, monks, is agreed in the world by the wise to exist; I too say of that, ‘It exists.’
translations.sn22.94:4: There is, monks, in the world what pertains to the world; the Tathāgata fully awakens to it, fully comprehends it; having fully awakened to it, having fully comprehended it, he explains it, teaches it, points it out, establishes it, discloses it, analyzes it, and makes it plain.
translations.sn22.94:7: One who, monks, when the Tathāgata is explaining in this way, teaching, pointing out, establishing, disclosing, analyzing, and making plain, does not know and does not see—to that one I say, monks, ‘a foolish ordinary person, blind, without eyes, unknowing, unseeing’; what can I do with him?
translations.sn22.95:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Ayujjhā on the bank of the Ganges river. There the Blessed One addressed the monks:
translations.sn22.95:10: As one reflects and examines wisely, it becomes empty and hollow for one who sees it wisely.
translations.sn22.95:11: And concerning this body, taught by one of great wisdom: see form as discarded, the abandoning of the three things.
translations.sn22.95:12: When life and heat and consciousness leave this body, then it lies cast aside, a senseless thing, food for others.
translations.sn22.95:13: Such is this continuity: this is illusion, the talk of fools; it is declared a killer; no essence is found here.
translations.sn22.95:2: “Suppose, monks, this Ganges river were to carry along a great lump of foam. A man with good eyesight would see it, would reflect on it, would examine it wisely. As he sees it, reflects on it, and examines it wisely, it would appear to him as just empty, as just hollow, as just without substance. For what substance could there be, monks, in a lump of foam? In the same way, monks, whatever form there is—past, future, or present …pe… whether far or near—a monk sees it, reflects on it, examines it wisely. As he sees it, reflects on it, and examines it wisely, it appears to him as just empty, as just hollow, as just without substance. For what substance could there be, monks, in form?”
translations.sn22.95:3: “Suppose, monks, in the autumn season, when it is raining with large drops, a water bubble arises and ceases in the water. A man with good eyesight would see it, would reflect on it, would examine it wisely. As he sees it, reflects on it, and examines it wisely, it would appear to him as just empty, as just hollow, as just without substance. For what substance could there be, monks, in a water bubble? In the same way, monks, whatever feeling there is—past, future, or present …pe… whether far or near—a monk sees it, reflects on it, examines it wisely. As he sees it, reflects on it, and examines it wisely, it appears to him as just empty, as just hollow, as just without substance. For what substance could there be, monks, in feeling?”
translations.sn22.95:4: “Suppose, monks, in the last month of the hot season, at midday, a mirage shimmers. A man with good eyesight would see it, would reflect on it, would examine it wisely. As he sees it, reflects on it, and examines it wisely, it would appear to him as just empty, as just hollow …pe… for what substance could there be, monks, in a mirage? In the same way, monks, whatever perception there is …pe….”
translations.sn22.95:5: “Suppose, monks, a man wanting heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, would take a sharp axe and enter a forest. There he would see a great banana trunk, straight, fresh, not yet with the crown cut off. He would cut it at the root; having cut it at the root, he would cut off the top; having cut off the top, he would strip off the leaf-sheaths. As he stripped off the leaf-sheaths, he would not find even sapwood, much less heartwood. A man with good eyesight would see it, would reflect on it, would examine it wisely. As he sees it, reflects on it, and examines it wisely, it would appear to him as just empty, as just hollow, as just without substance. For what substance could there be, monks, in a banana trunk? In the same way, monks, whatever volitional formations there are—past, future, or present …pe… whether far or near—a monk sees them, reflects on them, examines them wisely. As he sees them, reflects on them, and examines them wisely, they appear to him as just empty, as just hollow, as just without substance. For what substance could there be, monks, in volitional formations?”
translations.sn22.95:6: Suppose, bhikkhus, a magician or a magician’s apprentice were to display a magic illusion at a crossroads. A man with good eyesight would see it, observe it, and examine it carefully. As he sees it, observes it, and examines it carefully, it would appear to him as empty, it would appear to him as hollow, it would appear to him as without substance. For what substance could there be in a magic illusion, bhikkhus? Even so, bhikkhus, whatever consciousness there is—past, future, or present … whatever is far or near—a bhikkhu sees it, observes it, and examines it carefully. As he sees it, observes it, and examines it carefully, it appears to him as empty, it appears to him as hollow, it appears to him as without substance. For what substance could there be in consciousness, bhikkhus?
translations.sn22.95:7: Seeing thus, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form, with feeling … with perception … with volitional formations … with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion he is liberated. When liberated, there is the knowledge: “Liberated” … he understands: “There is no more of this state of being.””
translations.sn22.95:9: “Form is like a lump of foam; feeling is like a bubble; perception is like a mirage; volitional formations are like a plantain trunk; and consciousness is like an illusion, taught by the Kinsman of the Sun.
translations.sn22.96:1: At Sāvatthī. Then that bhikkhu, sitting to one side, said this to the Blessed One: “Is there, venerable sir, any form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain the same for eternity? Is there, venerable sir, any feeling that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain the same for eternity? Is there, venerable sir, any perception that is … Is there, venerable sir, any volitional formations that are permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain the same for eternity? Is there, venerable sir, any consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain the same for eternity?” “There is not, bhikkhu, any form that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain the same for eternity. There is not, bhikkhu, any feeling … any perception … any volitional formations … any consciousness that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain the same for eternity.”
translations.sn22.96:2: Then the Blessed One, taking up a small lump of cow dung in his hand, said this to that bhikkhu: “Even this much, bhikkhu, of acquisition of identity does not exist that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain the same for eternity. If even this much, bhikkhu, of acquisition of identity existed that was permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, this living of the holy life would not be evident for the complete ending of suffering. But since, bhikkhu, even this much of acquisition of identity does not exist that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, therefore this living of the holy life is evident for the complete ending of suffering.
translations.sn22.96:3: In the past, bhikkhu, I was a king, a khattiya anointed on the head. For me, bhikkhu, as a king, a khattiya anointed on the head, there were eighty-four thousand cities, with Kusāvatī as the royal capital at their head. For me, bhikkhu, as a king, a khattiya anointed on the head, there were eighty-four thousand mansions, with the Dhamma Mansion at their head. For me, bhikkhu, as a king, a khattiya anointed on the head, there were eighty-four thousand gabled houses, with the Great Array gabled house at their head. For me, bhikkhu, as a king, a khattiya anointed on the head, there were eighty-four thousand couches—made of ivory, of teak, of gold, covered with long-fleeced rugs, with white woolen covers, with embroidered covers, with antelope-skin coverlets of the finest kadali-deer, with canopies above, with crimson pillows at both ends. For me, bhikkhu, as a king, a khattiya anointed on the head, there were eighty-four thousand elephants with golden ornaments, with golden banners, covered with golden netting, with the royal elephant Uposatha at their head. For me, bhikkhu, as a king, a khattiya anointed on the head, there were eighty-four thousand horses with golden ornaments, with golden banners, covered with golden netting, with the royal horse Valāhaka at their head. For me, bhikkhu, as a king, a khattiya anointed on the head, there were eighty-four thousand chariots with golden ornaments, with golden banners, covered with golden netting, with the chariot Vejayanta at their head. For me, bhikkhu, as a king, a khattiya anointed on the head, there were eighty-four thousand gems, with the jewel treasure at their head. For me, bhikkhu … there were eighty-four thousand women, with Queen Subhaddā at their head. For me, bhikkhu … there were eighty-four thousand khattiyas, attendants, with the counselor treasure at their head. For me, bhikkhu … there were eighty-four thousand milch cows, clothed in fine cloth, with bronze milk-pails. For me, bhikkhu … there were eighty-four thousand million garments of cloth—fine linen, fine silk, fine wool, fine cotton. For me, bhikkhu … there were eighty-four thousand bowls of rice; in the evening and in the morning, food was brought.
translations.sn22.97:2: Then the Blessed One, having placed a little dust on the tip of his fingernail, said this to that bhikkhu: “Even this much, bhikkhu, of form does not exist that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, that will remain the same for eternity. If even this much, bhikkhu, of form existed that was permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, this living of the holy life would not be evident for the complete ending of suffering. But since, bhikkhu, even this much of form does not exist that is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, therefore this living of the holy life is evident for the complete ending of suffering.”
translations.sn35.101:4: Suppose, bhikkhus, that whatever grass, sticks, branches, and leaves there are in this Jeta Grove, people were to carry them off, or burn them, or use them as they wished—would it occur to you: ‘People are carrying us off, or burning us, or using us as they wish’?”
translations.sn35.116:2: Then it occurred to those monks: “Venerable Ānanda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by wise spiritual companions. And Venerable Ānanda is able to explain in detail the meaning of this brief summary that has been recited by the Blessed One, and to analyze in detail the meaning that has not been analyzed in detail. Why don’t we go to Venerable Ānanda; having gone, we will ask Venerable Ānanda about this matter?”
translations.sn35.116:3: Then those monks went to Venerable Ānanda; having gone, they exchanged greetings with Venerable Ānanda. When they had exchanged greetings and concluded polite and cordial talk, they sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said this to Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn35.116:5: “Just as, friends, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, looking for heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, would pass by the root, would pass by the trunk of a great standing tree that has heartwood, and would think that the heartwood should be sought among the branches and leaves; so too, with the Teacher present face to face, you think, having passed by that Blessed One, that you should ask us about this matter. For, friends, the Blessed One knows and sees—he has become vision, has become knowledge, has become the Dhamma, has become Brahmā; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the deathless, the master of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata. And that was the right time for you to ask the Blessed One himself about this matter. As the Blessed One would explain it to you, so should you remember it.”
translations.sn35.116:6: “Indeed, friend Ānanda, the Blessed One knows and sees—he has become vision, has become knowledge, has become the Dhamma, has become Brahmā; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the deathless, the master of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata. And that was the right time for us to ask the Blessed One himself about this matter. As the Blessed One would explain it to us, so we would remember it. But Venerable Ānanda is praised by the Teacher and esteemed by wise spiritual companions. And Venerable Ānanda is able to explain in detail the meaning of this brief summary that has been recited by the Blessed One, and to analyze in detail the meaning that has not been analyzed in detail. Let Venerable Ānanda analyze it without making it burdensome.”
translations.sn35.116:7: “Then, friends, listen and attend carefully; I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to Venerable Ānanda. Venerable Ānanda said this:
translations.sn35.116:9: “Yes, friend,” those monks, having agreed with Venerable Ānanda, rose from their seats and went to the Blessed One; having gone, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, those monks said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn35.117:1: “Before my awakening, monks, while I was still an unawakened bodhisatta, it occurred to me: ‘When those five strands of sensual pleasure that have previously touched the mind are past, ceased, and changed, my mind, going there again and again, would go to what is present, or a little to what is future.’ Then, monks, it occurred to me: ‘When those five strands of sensual pleasure that have previously touched the mind are past, ceased, and changed, there should be heedfulness in regard to the self, mindfulness, and guarding of the mind.’ Therefore, monks, when those five strands of sensual pleasure that have previously touched the mind are past, ceased, and changed, your mind, going there again and again, would go to what is present, or a little to what is future. Therefore, monks, when those five strands of sensual pleasure that have previously touched the mind are past, ceased, and changed, there should be heedfulness in regard to yourselves, mindfulness, and guarding of the mind. Therefore, monks, that base should be understood where the eye ceases and perception of forms ceases; that base should be understood … where the tongue ceases and perception of tastes ceases; that base should be understood … where the mind ceases and perception of mental phenomena ceases—that base should be understood.” Having said this, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered the dwelling.
translations.sn35.118:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, went to the Blessed One; having gone, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, Sakka, lord of the devas, said this to the Blessed One: “What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition by which some beings here do not attain final extinguishment in this very life? And what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition by which some beings here attain final extinguishment in this very life?”
translations.sn35.118:2: “There are, lord of the devas, forms cognizable by the eye—desired, pleasing, agreeable, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in them, welcomes them, and remains holding to them, then for him—delighting in them, welcoming them, and remaining holding to them—there is consciousness dependent on that, there is clinging to that. With clinging, lord of the devas, a monk does not attain final extinguishment …”
translations.sn35.118:3: “There are, lord of the devas, tastes cognizable by the tongue … There are, lord of the devas, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind—desired, pleasing, agreeable, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in them, welcomes them, and remains holding to them, then for him—delighting in them, welcoming them, and remaining holding to them—there is consciousness dependent on that, there is clinging to that. With clinging, lord of the devas, a monk does not attain final extinguishment. This, lord of the devas, is the cause; this is the condition by which some beings here do not attain final extinguishment in this very life.”
translations.sn35.118:4: “And there are, lord of the devas, forms cognizable by the eye—desired, pleasing, agreeable, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain holding to them, then for him—not delighting in them, not welcoming them, and not remaining holding to them—there is no consciousness dependent on that, there is no clinging to that. Without clinging, lord of the devas, a monk attains final extinguishment …”
translations.sn35.127:1: At one time Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja was living at Kosambī in Ghosita’s monastery. Then King Udena went to Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja; having approached, he exchanged greetings with Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja. When they had concluded their cordial and memorable conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, King Udena said this to Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja: “What, master Bhāradvāja, is the reason, what is the condition, by which these young monks—youthful, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first stage of life, not indulging in sensual pleasures—live the complete and perfectly pure holy life for life, and they go the whole way?” “This, great king, was said by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the perfectly awakened Buddha: ‘Come, bhikkhus: in women old enough to be your mother, establish the perception of a mother; in women old enough to be your sister, establish the perception of a sister; in women old enough to be your daughter, establish the perception of a daughter.’ This, great king, is the reason, this is the condition, by which these young monks—youthful, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first stage of life, not indulging in sensual pleasures—live the complete and perfectly pure holy life for life, and they go the whole way.”
translations.sn35.127:2: “The mind is fickle, master Bhāradvāja. Sometimes lustful states arise even toward women old enough to be one’s mother; lustful states arise even toward women old enough to be one’s sister; lustful states arise even toward women old enough to be one’s daughter. Is there, master Bhāradvāja, another reason and another condition by which these young monks—youthful, with black hair … they go the whole way?”
translations.sn35.127:3: “This, great king, was said by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the perfectly awakened Buddha: ‘Come, bhikkhus: review this very body from the soles of the feet up, and from the top of the hair down, bounded by skin, full of many kinds of impurities—there are in this body: hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, mucus, synovial fluid, urine.’ This too, great king, is the reason, this is the condition, by which these young monks—youthful, with black hair … they go the whole way.” “For those monks, master Bhāradvāja, who have developed body, developed virtue, developed mind, developed wisdom, that is easy. But for those monks, master Bhāradvāja, who have not developed body, not developed virtue, not developed mind, not developed wisdom, that is hard. Sometimes, master Bhāradvāja, when one attends to it as unattractive, it appears as attractive all the same. Is there, master Bhāradvāja, another reason and another condition by which these young monks—youthful, with black hair … they go the whole way?”
translations.sn35.127:4: “This, great king, was said by that Blessed One who knows and sees, the Arahant, the perfectly awakened Buddha: ‘Come, bhikkhus: live with doors guarded in the sense faculties. Having seen a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs or its details. For if, by dwelling with the eye faculty unrestrained, evil unwholesome states of longing and displeasure might invade one, then practice restraint for its restraint. Guard the eye faculty; enter upon restraint with regard to the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear … having smelled an odor with the nose … having tasted a flavor with the tongue … having touched a tangible with the body … having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, do not grasp at its signs or its details. For if, by dwelling with the mind faculty unrestrained, evil unwholesome states of longing and displeasure might invade one, then practice restraint for its restraint. Guard the mind faculty; enter upon restraint with regard to the mind faculty.’ This too, great king, is the reason, this is the condition, by which these young monks—youthful, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first stage of life, not indulging in sensual pleasures—live the complete and perfectly pure holy life for life, and they go the whole way.”
translations.sn35.136:2: Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, touches, and mental phenomena in their entirety; desirable, lovely, pleasing—so far as this is said to be.
translations.sn35.136:3: For the world with its devas, these are agreed to be happiness; where these cease, that is agreed by them to be suffering.
translations.sn35.136:4: Happiness seen by the noble ones: the cessation of identity; this is contrary to what is seen by the whole world.
translations.sn35.136:5: What others call happiness, the noble ones call suffering; what others call suffering, the noble ones know as happiness.
translations.sn35.136:6: See the Dhamma hard to know; here the unwise are confused. For those covered over there is darkness; for those who do not see there is gloom.
translations.sn35.136:7: But for the mindful it is opened up, like a light for those who see; those unskilled in the Dhamma do not understand, though close by, the path.
translations.sn35.136:8: For those obsessed with craving for existence, following craving for existence, who have entered Māra’s domain, this Dhamma is not well understood.
translations.sn35.63:1: At Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Migajāla went to the Blessed One … Sitting to one side, Venerable Migajāla said this to the Blessed One: “ ‘One who lives alone, one who lives alone,’ venerable sir, is said. To what extent, venerable sir, is one a ‘one who lives alone,’ and to what extent is one a ‘one who lives with a second’?”
translations.sn35.69:1: At one time Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Upasena were living at Rājagaha on the slope of Sappasoṇḍika in the Cool Forest. Now at that time a snake had fallen on Venerable Upasena’s body. Then Venerable Upasena addressed the monks: “Come, friends, lift this body of mine onto a bed and carry it outside, before this body breaks up right here—just like a handful of chaff.”
translations.sn35.74:1: At Sāvatthī. Then a certain monk went to the Blessed One … Sitting to one side, that monk said this to the Blessed One: “In such-and-such a monastery, venerable sir, there is a certain monk, new, unknown, sick, suffering, seriously ill. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would go to that monk, out of compassion.”
translations.sn35.74:12: “Good, good, bhikkhu. It is good indeed, bhikkhu, that you understand the Dhamma taught by me for the purpose of fading away of lust. For the Dhamma is taught by me, bhikkhu, for the purpose of fading away of lust. What do you think, bhikkhu: is the eye permanent or impermanent?”
translations.sn35.74:18: “But what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—is it fit to be regarded thus: ‘This is mine, I am this, this is my self’?”
translations.sn35.74:2: Then the Blessed One, having heard a report and having heard a report of illness, and having known, “An unknown monk,” went to where that monk was. That monk saw the Blessed One coming from afar. Having seen him, he arranged himself on the bed. Then the Blessed One said to that monk: “Enough, monk; do not arrange yourself on the bed. There are seats laid out; I will sit there.” The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One said to that monk: “I hope you are bearing up, monk, I hope you are getting by; I hope your painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing; that their subsiding is evident, not their increasing?”
translations.sn35.74:3: “For me, sir, it is not bearable, not sustainable. My painful feelings are severe; they increase and do not subside. Their increasing is evident, not their subsiding.”
translations.sn35.75:7: “Sir, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One for the purpose of final extinguishment without clinging.”
translations.sn35.75:8: “Good, good, monk. It is good that you, monk, understand the Dhamma taught by me for the purpose of final extinguishment without clinging. For the Dhamma has been taught by me, monk, for the purpose of final extinguishment without clinging.
translations.sn35.88:1: Then Venerable Puṇṇa went to the Blessed One; having gone up …pe… and sitting to one side, Venerable Puṇṇa said to the Blessed One: “It would be good, sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that I, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, might dwell alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and resolute.”
translations.sn35.88:12: “If, sir, the people of Sunāparanta give me a blow with a stick, then it will occur to me thus: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are indeed good, these people of Sunāparanta are indeed very good, in that they do not give me a blow with a weapon.’ Thus it will be in this matter, Blessed One; thus it will be in this matter, Fortunate One.”
translations.sn35.88:14: “If, sir, the people of Sunāparanta give me a blow with a weapon, then it will occur to me thus: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are indeed good, these people of Sunāparanta are indeed very good, in that they do not take my life with a sharp weapon.’ Thus it will be in this matter, Blessed One; thus it will be in this matter, Fortunate One.”
translations.sn35.88:16: “If, sir, the people of Sunāparanta take my life with a sharp weapon, then it will occur to me thus: ‘There are disciples of that Blessed One who, wearied, ashamed, and disgusted with body and life, seek a knife-bearer; this knife-bearer has come to me without my seeking it.’ Thus it will be in this matter, Blessed One; thus it will be in this matter, Fortunate One.”
translations.sn35.88:17: “Good, good, Puṇṇa. Endowed with this taming and calming, Puṇṇa, you will be able to dwell in the country of Sunāparanta. Now, Puṇṇa, do as you think it is time.”
translations.sn35.88:18: Then Venerable Puṇṇa, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and, having made a respectful circumambulation, set in order his lodging, and taking up bowl and robe, set out on a wandering tour to the country of Sunāparanta. Walking on tour in due course, he arrived at the country of Sunāparanta. There Venerable Puṇṇa dwelt in the country of Sunāparanta. Then within that very rainy season Venerable Puṇṇa brought about the realization of about five hundred male lay followers. Within that very rainy season he brought about the realization of about five hundred female lay followers. Within that very rainy season he realized the three knowledges. Within that very rainy season he attained final extinguishment.
translations.sn35.88:19: Then several monks went to the Blessed One …pe… and sitting to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: “Sir, that Puṇṇa, the clansman, who was instructed by the Blessed One with a brief exhortation, has died. What is his destination, what is his future course?”
translations.sn35.88:4: “Puṇṇa, having been instructed by me with this brief exhortation, in which country will you dwell?” “Sir, there is a country called Sunāparanta; I will dwell there.”
translations.sn35.88:5: “The people of Sunāparanta are fierce, Puṇṇa; the people of Sunāparanta are rough, Puṇṇa. If the people of Sunāparanta insult and abuse you, then, Puṇṇa, what will occur to you?”
translations.sn35.88:6: “If, sir, the people of Sunāparanta insult and abuse me, then it will occur to me thus: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are indeed good, these people of Sunāparanta are indeed very good, in that they do not give me a blow with the hand.’ Thus it will be in this matter, Blessed One; thus it will be in this matter, Fortunate One.”
translations.sn35.88:8: “If, sir, the people of Sunāparanta give me a blow with the hand, then it will occur to me thus: ‘These people of Sunāparanta are indeed good, these people of Sunāparanta are indeed very good, in that they do not give me a blow with a clod.’ Thus it will be in this matter, Blessed One; thus it will be in this matter, Fortunate One.”
translations.sn35.95:1: Then Venerable Mālukyaputta went to the Blessed One …pe… and sitting to one side, Venerable Mālukyaputta said to the Blessed One: “It would be good, sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that I, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, might dwell alone, withdrawn, heedful, ardent, and resolute.”
translations.sn35.95:10: “And in this, Mālukyaputta, regarding things to be seen, heard, sensed, and cognized: in the seen there will be only the seen; in the heard there will be only the heard; in the sensed there will be only the sensed; in the cognized there will be only the cognized. When for you, Mālukyaputta, regarding things to be seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, in the seen there will be only the seen; in the heard there will be only the heard; in the sensed there will be only the sensed; in the cognized there will be only the cognized—then you, Mālukyaputta, will not be by that. When you, Mālukyaputta, are not by that, then you, Mālukyaputta, are not there. When you, Mālukyaputta, are not there, then you, Mālukyaputta, are neither here, nor beyond, nor in between the two. This is the end of suffering.”
translations.sn35.95:12:
‘Having seen a form, mindfulness is lost,
Attending in the mind to a pleasing sign;
With a lustful mind one feels,
And on that one remains fastened.
translations.sn35.95:14:
Having heard a sound, mindfulness is lost,
Attending in the mind to a pleasing sign;
With a lustful mind one feels,
And on that one remains fastened.
translations.sn35.95:16:
Having smelled an odor, mindfulness is lost,
Attending in the mind to a pleasing sign;
With a lustful mind one feels,
And on that one remains fastened.
translations.sn35.95:18: Having tasted a flavor, mindfulness is lost for one who attends to the pleasing sign; with a mind inflamed he feels, and he stands clinging to that.
translations.sn35.95:2: “Now here, Māluṅkyaputta, what shall we say to the young monks? For you, monk, being old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, having come to old age, ask for instruction in brief.”
translations.sn35.95:20: Having contacted a touch, mindfulness is lost for one who attends to the pleasing sign; with a mind inflamed he feels, and he stands clinging to that.
translations.sn35.95:22: Having cognized a mind-object, mindfulness is lost for one who attends to the pleasing sign; with a mind inflamed he feels, and he stands clinging to that.
translations.sn35.95:24: He does not lust after forms; having seen a form, mindful; with a dispassionate mind he feels, and he does not stand clinging to that.
translations.sn35.95:25: As he sees a form, and also experiences the feeling: it is exhausted, not accumulated; thus he lives mindful. Thus, as he diminishes suffering, “nibbāna nearby” is spoken of.
translations.sn35.95:26: He does not lust after sounds; having heard a sound, mindful; with a dispassionate mind he feels, and he does not stand clinging to that.
translations.sn35.95:27: As he hears a sound, and also experiences the feeling: it is exhausted, not accumulated; thus he lives mindful. Thus, as he diminishes suffering, “nibbāna nearby” is spoken of.
translations.sn35.95:28: He does not lust after odors; having smelled an odor, mindful; with a dispassionate mind he feels, and he does not stand clinging to that.
translations.sn35.95:3: “Even though I, venerable sir, am old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, having come to old age, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief; let the Fortunate One teach me the Dhamma in brief—perhaps I might understand the meaning of what the Blessed One has said; perhaps I might become an heir to what the Blessed One has said.”
translations.sn35.95:30: He does not lust after flavors; having tasted a flavor, mindful; with a dispassionate mind he feels, and he does not stand clinging to that.
translations.sn35.95:35: As he knows a mind-object, and also experiences the feeling: it is exhausted, not accumulated; thus he lives mindful. Thus, as he diminishes suffering, “nibbāna nearby” is spoken of.”
translations.sn35.95:36: “I understand the meaning of this that was spoken by the Blessed One in brief in such detailed way, venerable sir.” “Good, good, Māluṅkyaputta. Good indeed, Māluṅkyaputta: you understand in detail the meaning of what was spoken by me in brief:
translations.sn35.95:4: “What do you think, Māluṅkyaputta: those forms cognizable by the eye that you have not seen, never seen before—you do not see them, and it does not occur to you, ‘I might see them’: is there for you there any desire or lust or affection?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn35.95:9: “Those mind-objects cognizable by the mind that you have not cognized, never cognized before—you do not cognize them, and it does not occur to you, ‘I might cognize them’: is there for you there any desire or lust or affection?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn36.19:12: And what, Ānanda, is there another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a monk, completely surmounting the base of infinite space, enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness, (thinking) ‘Consciousness is infinite’. This, Ānanda, is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness. Those, Ānanda, who would say thus: ‘They experience this as the ultimate peaceful happiness and gladness’—this I do not allow for them. For what reason? There is, Ānanda, another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.
translations.sn36.19:15: And what, Ānanda, is there another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a monk, completely surmounting the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. This, Ānanda, is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.
translations.sn36.19:7: And what, Ānanda, is there another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a monk, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, born of seclusion, with rapture and happiness. This, Ānanda, is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness. Those, Ānanda, who would say thus: ‘They experience this as the ultimate peaceful happiness and gladness’—this I do not allow for them. For what reason? There is, Ānanda, another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.
translations.sn36.19:8: And what, Ānanda, is there another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a monk, with the stilling of thought and examination, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal clarity and unification of mind, is without thought and without examination, born of concentration, with rapture and happiness. This, Ānanda, is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness. Those, Ānanda, who would say thus: ‘They experience this as the ultimate peaceful happiness and gladness’—this I do not allow for them. For what reason? There is, Ānanda, another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.
translations.sn36.19:9: And what, Ānanda, is there another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness? Here, Ānanda, a monk, with the fading away of rapture too, dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and feels happiness with the body, that of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, one dwells happily’; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna. This, Ānanda, is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness. Those, Ānanda, who would say thus: ‘They experience this as the ultimate peaceful happiness and gladness’—this I do not allow for them. For what reason? There is, Ānanda, another happiness more excellent and more sublime than this happiness.
translations.sn36.21:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the squirrels’ feeding ground. Then Moḷiyasīvaka the wanderer approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. When the courteous and cordial talk was finished, he sat down at one side. Seated at one side, Moḷiyasīvaka the wanderer said this to the Blessed One: “There are, Master Gotama, some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus, who hold such a view: ‘Whatever this person experiences—pleasant or painful or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—all that is due to what was done before.’ What does Master Gotama say here?”
translations.sn36.21:2: “Even so, Sīvaka, some feelings arise here that are originated from bile. This too, Sīvaka, should be known by oneself, that some feelings arise here that are originated from bile. And this too, Sīvaka, is acknowledged by the world as truth, that some feelings arise here that are originated from bile. Therein, Sīvaka, those ascetics and brahmins who are of such a doctrine and such a view: ‘Whatever this person experiences—pleasure or pain or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that is due to what was done before’—they go beyond what is known by themselves, and they go beyond what is acknowledged by the world as truth. Therefore I say that those ascetics and brahmins are wrong.”
translations.sn36.21:4: When this was said, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said this to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama, magnificent, Master Gotama … Up to life’s end, let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from today.”
translations.sn36.23:1: Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: “Which, venerable sir, is feeling? Which is the arising of feeling? Which is the practice leading to the arising of feeling? Which is the cessation of feeling? Which is the practice leading to the cessation of feeling? What is the gratification in feeling? What is the danger? What is the escape?”
translations.sn36.31:2: And what, bhikkhus, is unworldly rapture? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal placidity and unification of mind, without applied thought and without sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This is called, bhikkhus, unworldly rapture.
translations.sn36.31:3: And what, bhikkhus, is unworldly rapture that is more unworldly? Whatever rapture arises for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed as he reviews his mind liberated from lust, as he reviews his mind liberated from hate, as he reviews his mind liberated from delusion—this is called, bhikkhus, unworldly rapture that is more unworldly.
translations.sn36.31:5: And what, bhikkhus, is unworldly pleasure? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal placidity and unification of mind, without applied thought and without sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. And with the fading away of rapture, he dwells equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, and he experiences pleasure with the body; he enters and dwells in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, one dwells in pleasure.’ This is called, bhikkhus, unworldly pleasure.
translations.sn36.31:6: And what, bhikkhus, is unworldly pleasure that is more unworldly? Whatever pleasure and gladness arise for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed as he reviews his mind liberated from lust, as he reviews his mind liberated from hate, as he reviews his mind liberated from delusion—this is called, bhikkhus, unworldly pleasure that is more unworldly.
translations.sn36.31:8: And what, bhikkhus, is unworldly equanimity? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu—with the abandoning of pleasure and with the abandoning of pain, and with the earlier ending of gladness and sadness—enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-pain-nor-pleasure and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This is called, bhikkhus, unworldly equanimity.
translations.sn36.31:9: And what, bhikkhus, is unworldly equanimity that is more unworldly? Whatever equanimity arises for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed as he reviews his mind liberated from lust, as he reviews his mind liberated from hate, as he reviews his mind liberated from delusion—this is called, bhikkhus, unworldly equanimity that is more unworldly.
translations.sn36.4:2: Whoever does not endure these, the painful feelings that have arisen—bodily, life-taking—touched by which he trembles.
translations.sn36.4:3: He cries out and weeps, weak and without strength; he did not rise up from the underworld, nor did he reach firm ground.
translations.sn36.6:2: But, bhikkhus, an instructed noble disciple, when touched by a painful feeling, does not sorrow, does not lament, does not weep, does not beat his breast and cry, and does not fall into confusion. He feels one feeling—bodily, not mental.
translations.sn36.6:4: The wise one does not feel feeling; even though he is learned, both pleasure and pain. And this is a great distinction of the skillful man from the ordinary person.
translations.sn36.6:5: For one who has understood the Dhamma, learned, seeing this world and the other: agreeable things do not disturb the mind; from the disagreeable he does not come to aversion.
translations.sn36.7:3: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu mindful? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … he dwells contemplating mind in mind … he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is mindful.
translations.sn36.7:4: And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu clearly comprehending? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking away; he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing the saṅghāṭi, bowl, and robes; he acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension when urinating and defecating; he acts with clear comprehension when walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and keeping silent. Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu acts with clear comprehension. Mindful, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should await the time. This is our instruction to you.
translations.sn36.7:5: If, bhikkhus, while that bhikkhu is thus mindful and fully aware, diligent, ardent, and resolute as he dwells, a pleasant feeling arises, he understands thus: ‘This pleasant feeling has arisen in me. And that is dependent, not independent. Dependent on what? Dependent on this very body. But this body is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen. A pleasant feeling that has arisen dependent on the body—which is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen—how could it be permanent?’ He dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and in the pleasant feeling, he dwells contemplating vanishing, he dwells contemplating fading away, he dwells contemplating cessation, he dwells contemplating relinquishment. As he dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and in the pleasant feeling, contemplating vanishing, contemplating fading away, contemplating cessation, contemplating relinquishment, whatever underlying tendency to lust there is toward the body and toward the pleasant feeling, that is abandoned.
translations.sn36.7:8: If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not delighted in’. If he feels a painful feeling … If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not delighted in’. If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached; if he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached; if he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached. Feeling a feeling limited by the body, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling limited by the body’; feeling a feeling limited by life, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling limited by life’. He understands: ‘With the breakup of the body, after the termination of life, here itself all that is felt, not delighted in, will become cool’.
translations.sn4.13:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, in the Maddakucchi deer-park. Now at that time the Blessed One’s foot had been injured by a splinter, and severe feelings came upon the Blessed One—bodily painful, sharp, intense, harsh, bitter, unpleasant, disagreeable. The Blessed One endured them, mindful and fully aware, untroubled. Then the Blessed One, having spread out the outer robe folded in four, lay down in the lion’s posture on the right side, placing one foot on the other, mindful and fully aware. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.13:2: “Do you lie down from lethargy, or are you drunk on poetry? Do you not have aims in plenty? Alone in a secluded lodging, with drowsy face—what is this: are you sleeping?”
translations.sn4.13:3: “I do not lie down from lethargy, nor am I drunk on poetry. Having realized the goal, I am without sorrow. Alone in a secluded lodging, I lie down, compassionate toward all beings.
translations.sn4.13:4: Even those in whose breast a dart has entered, again and again shaking the heart—those too would obtain sleep though pierced; therefore I, with the dart removed, do not sleep.
translations.sn4.13:5: Awake, I do not doubt nor do I fear; night and day do not afflict me. I see no loss anywhere in the world; therefore I sleep, compassionate toward all beings.”
translations.sn4.18:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Magadhans, at Pañcasālā, a brahmin village. Now at that time in the brahmin village of Pañcasālā there were guests for the young girls. Then the Blessed One, in the morning, having dressed and taken bowl and robe, entered the brahmin village of Pañcasālā for alms. Now at that time the brahmins and householders of Pañcasālā were obsessed by Māra the Evil One: “Let the ascetic Gotama not get alms.”
translations.sn4.18:2: Then the Blessed One entered the brahmin village of Pañcasālā for alms with his bowl as well-washed as it was, and returned with his bowl as well-washed as it was. Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One: “Well then, ascetic, did you get alms?” “So you did, Evil One, such that I did not get alms.” “Then, sir, let the Blessed One enter the brahmin village of Pañcasālā for alms a second time. Then I will act so that the Blessed One will get alms.”
translations.sn4.19:4: “What they speak of as ‘mine’ and ‘this is mine’, and those who speak of ‘mine’—if your mind is there, you will not escape me, ascetic.”
translations.sn4.19:5: “What they speak of is not mine; those who speak of ‘mine’ are not me. Thus know, Evil One: you will not even see my path.”
translations.sn4.1:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā, on the bank of the river Nerañjarā, at the root of the Ajapāla banyan tree, newly awakened. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind: “I am indeed freed from that difficult practice. Good that I am freed from that difficult practice which was not connected with the goal. Good indeed that I am freed; I have attained awakening.”
translations.sn4.1:2: Then Māra the Evil One, having known with his mind the thought in the Blessed One’s mind, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.1:3: “Having abandoned the practices of austerity by which young men become pure, you think ‘impure’ is ‘pure’; you have missed the path to purity.”
translations.sn4.1:6: “Developing virtue, concentration, and wisdom, the path to awakening, I have attained the supreme purity; you are defeated, End-maker.”
translations.sn4.1:7: Then Māra the Evil One—“The Blessed One knows me, the Fortunate One knows me”—sorrowful and dejected, vanished right there.
translations.sn4.20:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans, in the Himalayan region, in a forest hut. Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind: “Is it possible to govern a kingdom without killing, without causing killing, without conquering, without causing conquering, without sorrowing, without causing sorrowing, by Dhamma?”
translations.sn4.20:3: “Even if there were a whole mountain of gold, of solid gold: not even twice that would suffice for one. Thus the wise one should live evenly.
translations.sn4.20:4: One who has seen suffering and from where it originates—how could that being incline toward sensual pleasures? Having known acquisition as attachment in the world, that being should train for the removal of that very thing.”
translations.sn4.21:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was living among the Sakyans at Silāvatī. Now at that time several bhikkhus were living not far from the Blessed One, diligent, ardent, resolute. Then Māra the Evil One, having created the appearance of a brahmin—wearing a cloak of antelope hide, with a great matted-hair topknot, old, bent like a roof-beam, breathing with a wheeze, taking an udumbara staff—went to those bhikkhus. Having gone to them, he said this to those bhikkhus: “Sirs, you have gone forth while young, very youthful, with black hair, endowed with the blessing of youth, in the first stage of life, without having played with sensual pleasures. Let the sirs enjoy human sensual pleasures. Do not, abandoning what is visible here and now, run after what is for later.” “We do not, brahmin, abandoning what is visible here and now, run after what is for later. Rather, brahmin, abandoning what is for later, we run after what is visible here and now. For sensual pleasures, brahmin, have been called by the Blessed One as very painful, very distressing; the danger therein is even greater. This Dhamma is visible here and now, immediate, inviting inspection, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise.” When this was said, Māra the Evil One, shaking his head, sticking out his tongue, raising three wrinkles on his forehead, leaning on his staff, departed.
translations.sn4.24:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was living at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the Ajapāla banyan tree. Now at that time Māra the Evil One had been following the Blessed One for seven years, looking for an opening, not finding an opening. Then Māra the Evil One went to the Blessed One; having gone to him, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.24:10: “Having gained no relish there, let the crow-king depart; like a crow striking a rock, we will depart, disappointed with Gotama.”
translations.sn4.24:2: “Have you fallen into sorrow, meditating in the forest, or have you lost wealth and long for it? Or have you done some wrong in a village—why do you not make a witness among the people? No witness is found for you by anyone.”
translations.sn4.24:3: “Having dug up the root of sorrow entirely, I meditate without wrongdoing, not grieving. Having cut off all craving and lust for existence, without taints I meditate, bound to heedless ones.”
translations.sn4.24:6: “If you have understood the path, the safe one leading to the deathless, go away—go, you alone; why do you instruct another?”
translations.sn4.24:7: “Those people who go beyond ask about the undying state. When I am asked, I declare to them what is true, that which is without acquisition.”
translations.sn4.24:8: “Just as, venerable sir, there might be a pond not far from a village or town. There a crab might be. Then, venerable sir, several boys or girls, having come out from that village or town, would go to that pond; having gone, they would lift that crab out of the water and place it on dry land. Whatever limb, venerable sir, that crab would extend, that very limb those boys or girls would cut off with a stick or a stone, would break, would smash, would crush. Thus, venerable sir, with all its limbs cut off, broken, smashed, crushed, that crab would be unable to enter that pond. In the same way, venerable sir, whatever devious, crooked, writhing things have been practiced, all of them have been cut off, broken, smashed, crushed by the Blessed One. Now I am unable, venerable sir, to approach the Blessed One again, looking for an opening.” Then Māra the Evil One, in the presence of the Blessed One, spoke these verses of disillusionment:
translations.sn4.24:9: “Just as a crow went about a stone the color of fat: ‘Perhaps we might find something soft here; perhaps there would be some relish.’
translations.sn4.25:10: “‘An arahant, the Fortunate One in the world, not led by lust; having gone beyond Māra’s domain, therefore I grieve exceedingly.’”
translations.sn4.25:12: Then Taṇhā and Aratī and Ragā, Māra’s daughters, went to the Blessed One; having gone to him, they stood to one side. Standing to one side, Taṇhā, Māra’s daughter, addressed the Blessed One in verse:
translations.sn4.25:14: “Having attained the goal, the heart’s peace, having conquered the army, attractive in forms—alone, meditating, I realized happiness; therefore I do not make a witness among the people; no witness is found for me by anyone.”
translations.sn4.25:16: “A bhikkhu who dwells in what way is much here, having crossed the five floods, does he cross here the sixth? How does one who meditates much, to whom perceptions of sensual pleasures are external, not obtain that?”
translations.sn4.25:17: “With body calmed, mind well-freed, unconstructing, mindful, without a home; having directly known the Dhamma, meditating without thought, he does not get angry, does not recall, and is not sluggish.
translations.sn4.25:2: “Why are you downcast, dear? What man do you grieve for? We will bind him with the snare of lust like a bull elephant in the forest; having bound him, we will lead him—he will come under your control.”
translations.sn4.25:20: “He will cut off craving, one who wanders among assemblies and communities; surely many of faith will practice. This man, without a home, will lead the multitude—he will cut through to the far shore of King Death.”
translations.sn4.25:23: “Fools, with lotus stalks, you attack a mountain; with your nails you dig a mountain; with your teeth you chew iron.
translations.sn4.25:24: Having struck your head against a rock, you seek depth in the underworld; like leaning your chest against a post, you will depart disappointed with Gotama.”
translations.sn4.25:4: Then Taṇhā and Aratī and Ragā, Māra’s daughters, went to the Blessed One; having gone to him, they said this to the Blessed One: “We will attend on your feet, ascetic.” Then the Blessed One did not give attention, since he was freed in the unsurpassed destruction of acquisitions.
translations.sn4.25:5: Then Taṇhā and Aratī and Ragā, Māra’s daughters, having withdrawn to one side, considered thus: “Men’s intentions are of many kinds. Suppose we create a hundred and a hundred forms of young women.” Then Taṇhā and Aratī and Ragā, Māra’s daughters, having created a hundred and a hundred forms of young women, went to the Blessed One; having gone to him, they said this to the Blessed One: “We will attend on your feet, ascetic.” But the Blessed One did not give attention to that either, since he was freed in the unsurpassed destruction of acquisitions.
translations.sn4.8:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. Then Māra the Evil One went to the Blessed One; having gone to him, he spoke this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
translations.sn4.8:2: “One with sons delights in sons; one with cattle delights likewise in cattle. Delighting for a man is in acquisitions; for one without acquisitions does not delight.”
translations.sn4.8:3: “A man with sons grieves because of his sons; one with cattle likewise grieves because of his cattle. A person’s grief is because of acquisitions; for one without acquisitions does not grieve.”
translations.sn44.1:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. Now at that time Khemā the nun, wandering on tour among the Kosalans, had come to stay at Toraṇavatthu, between Sāvatthī and Sāketa. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, traveling from Sāketa to Sāvatthī, came to stay for one night at Toraṇavatthu, between Sāketa and Sāvatthī. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed a certain man: “Come, good man, at Toraṇavatthu find such an ascetic or brahmin as I might visit today.”
translations.sn44.1:2: “Yes, sire,” that man replied to King Pasenadi of Kosala. Having wandered all around Toraṇavatthu, he did not see such an ascetic or brahmin as King Pasenadi of Kosala might visit. But he saw Khemā the nun who had come to stay at Toraṇavatthu. Having seen her, he approached King Pasenadi of Kosala; and having approached, he said this to King Pasenadi of Kosala:
translations.sn44.1:3: “There is no such ascetic or brahmin at Toraṇavatthu as your majesty might visit. But there is, sire, a nun named Khemā, a disciple of that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. And this good report of that lady has spread: ‘She is wise, competent, intelligent, learned, a speaker on the Dhamma, with good ready wit.’ Let your majesty visit her.”
translations.sn44.1:6: “Then, great king, I will question you on this very matter. Answer me as you see fit. What do you think, great king: do you have any calculator or accountant or reckoner who would be able to count the sand in the Ganges—so much sand, or so many hundreds of sand, or so many thousands of sand, or so many hundreds of thousands of sand?” “No, lady.” “But do you have any calculator or accountant or reckoner who would be able to count the water in the great ocean—so many water-measures, or so many hundreds of water-measures, or so many thousands of water-measures, or so many hundreds of thousands of water-measures?” “No, lady.” “For what reason?” “Because, lady, the ocean is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom.” “So too, great king: by whatever form one would describe the Tathāgata, that form has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made into nonexistence, not liable to arise in the future. The Tathāgata is freed from reckoning in terms of form, great king—deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom, like the great ocean. ‘The Tathāgata exists after death’ does not apply; ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death’ does not apply; ‘the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ does not apply; ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’ does not apply.
translations.sn44.1:9: By whatever consciousness one would describe the Tathāgata, that consciousness has been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, made into nonexistence, not liable to arise in the future. The Tathāgata is freed from reckoning in terms of consciousness, great king—deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom, like the great ocean. ‘The Tathāgata exists after death’ does not apply; ‘the Tathāgata does not exist after death’ does not apply; ‘the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’ does not apply; ‘the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’ does not apply.” Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having delighted in and approved of what Khemā the nun said, rose from his seat, paid homage to Khemā the nun, and, having circumambulated her on the right, departed.
translations.sn45.1:2: “Ignorance, bhikkhus, is the forerunner in entering upon unwholesome states, and along with it come lack of conscience and lack of fear of wrongdoing. For one who is caught up in ignorance, bhikkhus, and is unlearned, wrong view arises; for one with wrong view, wrong intention arises; for one with wrong intention, wrong speech arises; for one with wrong speech, wrong action arises; for one with wrong action, wrong livelihood arises; for one with wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises; for one with wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises; for one with wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises.
translations.sn45.2:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was staying among the Sakyans at a Sakyan town called Nagaraka. Then Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “Half of this holy life, venerable sir, is this—good friendship, good companionship, good camaraderie.”
translations.sn45.2:2: “Not so, Ānanda, not so, Ānanda. This entire holy life, Ānanda, is this—good friendship, good companionship, good camaraderie. For a bhikkhu who has a good friend, Ānanda, who has good companions, good comrades, it is to be expected that he will develop the noble eightfold path, that he will cultivate the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn45.2:3: And how, Ānanda, does a bhikkhu who has good friends, good companions, good comrades develop the noble eightfold path, cultivate the noble eightfold path? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu develops right view that is dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, maturing in relinquishment; he develops right intention dependent on seclusion … he develops right speech … he develops right action … he develops right livelihood … he develops right effort … he develops right mindfulness … he develops right concentration that is dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. Thus, Ānanda, a bhikkhu who has good friends, good companions, good comrades develops the noble eightfold path, cultivates the noble eightfold path.
translations.sn45.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then Venerable Ānanda, in the forenoon, having dressed and taken bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Venerable Ānanda saw the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi driving out of Sāvatthī in an all-white mare-drawn chariot. White horses were yoked, with white adornments; the chariot was white, the retinue was white, the reins were white, the goad-stick was white, the parasol was white, the turban was white, the clothes were white, the sandals were white, and he was fanned with a white fan. Seeing him, people said this: “Indeed, sirs, what a divine vehicle! Indeed, sirs, it is like a divine vehicle!”
translations.sn45.4:10: Non-ill will, non-harming, seclusion as whose weapon; endurance as the armor and coat of mail— it proceeds toward security from yoking.
translations.sn45.4:2: Then Venerable Ānanda, having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, on returning from the alms-round, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn45.4:4: “It is possible, Ānanda,” the Blessed One said. “For this, Ānanda, is a designation for this very noble eightfold path: ‘the divine vehicle’ and also ‘the Dhamma-vehicle’ and also ‘the unsurpassed victory in battle.’”
translations.sn45.4:8: “For one whose faith and wisdom are yoked, always bearing the burden; conscience is the pole, mind the yoke; mindfulness is the guarding charioteer.
translations.sn45.4:9: The chariot’s equipment is virtue; absorption is the axle, energy the wheels; equanimity is the yoke, concentration the shaft; desirelessness is the enclosure.
translations.sn45.8:1: At Sāvatthī. “Monks, I will teach you the noble eightfold path; I will analyze it. Listen to that, pay close attention, I will speak.” “Yes, bhante,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn45.8:3: And what, monks, is right view? The knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin of suffering, the knowledge of the cessation of suffering, the knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—this is called right view, monks.
translations.sn45.8:4: And what, monks, is right intention? The intention of renunciation, the intention of non-ill will, the intention of non-harming—this is called right intention, monks.
translations.sn45.8:5: And what, monks, is right speech? Abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter—this is called right speech, monks.
translations.sn45.8:6: And what, monks, is right action? Abstaining from killing living beings, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from unchastity—this is called right action, monks.
translations.sn45.8:7: And what, monks, is right livelihood? Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, makes a living by right livelihood—this is called right livelihood, monks.
translations.sn45.8:8: And what, monks, is right effort? Here, monks, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, upholds and exerts the mind for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states; for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states … for the arising of unarisen wholesome states … for the continuance, non-confusion, increase, expansion, development, and fulfillment of arisen wholesome states he generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, upholds and exerts the mind—this is called right effort, monks.
translations.sn45.8:9: And what, monks, is right mindfulness? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; he dwells contemplating mind in mind—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world—this is called right mindfulness, monks.
translations.sn46.11:1: “Just as, monks, whatever living beings pursue the four postures—at times walking, at times standing, at times sitting, at times lying down—all of them, relying on the earth, established on the earth, pursue these four postures; so too, monks, a monk, relying on virtue, established in virtue, develops the seven factors of awakening, makes much of the seven factors of awakening.
translations.sn46.14:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding-ground. Now at that time Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling in the Pippali Cave, sick, suffering, gravely ill. Then the Blessed One, in the evening, having emerged from seclusion, approached Venerable Mahākassapa; having approached, he sat down on a seat spread out. Seated, the Blessed One said this to Venerable Mahākassapa:
translations.sn46.14:2: “Is it bearable for you, Kassapa, is it manageable? Are the painful feelings subsiding, not increasing? Is their subsiding evident, not their increasing?” “It is not bearable for me, bhante, not manageable. My painful feelings are increasing, not subsiding; their increasing is evident, not their subsiding.”
translations.sn46.29:2: Here, monks, a monk develops the mindfulness factor of awakening, supported by seclusion … he develops the equanimity factor of awakening, supported by seclusion, supported by dispassion, supported by cessation, culminating in relinquishment. Thus developed, monks, the seven factors of awakening, thus made much of, lead to the abandoning of fettering states.
translations.sn46.30:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sumbhas, in a Sumbhan village named Setaka. Then Venerable Udāyī approached the Blessed One … seated to one side, Venerable Udāyī said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.30:2: "It is amazing, sir, it is astonishing, sir. To such an extent, sir, have affection and reverence and shame and dread of wrongdoing for the Blessed One been made much of by me. For formerly, sir, when I was a householder, I was not one who had made much of the Dhamma, not one who had made much of the Saṅgha. But then, seeing affection and reverence and shame and dread of wrongdoing for the Blessed One, I went forth from the household life into homelessness. The Blessed One taught me the Dhamma: ‘such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling … such is perception … such are formations … such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’
translations.sn46.30:3: Then, sir, having gone to an empty hut, turning over and over these five clinging-aggregates, I directly knew as it really is: ‘this is suffering’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘this is the origin of suffering’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘this is the cessation of suffering’; I directly knew as it really is: ‘this is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.’ And the Dhamma has been penetrated by me, sir, and the path has been obtained by me; which, developed and made much of by me, will lead one dwelling thus and thus to suchness, so that I shall know: ‘birth is ended, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’
translations.sn46.38:1: At whatever time, bhikkhus, a noble disciple listens to the Dhamma making it a matter of vital concern, attending with the mind, bringing the whole mind to bear, and lending ear, at that time these five hindrances are not present in him. At that time the seven awakening factors go to fulfillment by development.
