translations.sn46.3:1: "Those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, who are accomplished in virtue, accomplished in concentration, accomplished in knowledge, accomplished in liberation, accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation—to those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, I declare seeing to be of great benefit; to those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, I declare listening to be of great benefit; to those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, I declare approaching to be of great benefit; to those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, I declare attending on them to be of great benefit; to those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, I declare recollection to be of great benefit; to those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, I declare going forth in accordance to be of great benefit. For what reason? Having heard the Dhamma from such bhikkhus, one dwells withdrawn with a twofold withdrawal—withdrawal of body and withdrawal of mind. Dwelling thus withdrawn, one recollects that Dhamma and thinks it over.
translations.sn46.3:2: At whatever time, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwelling thus withdrawn recollects that Dhamma and thinks it over, at that time the mindfulness awakening factor has been aroused in the bhikkhu; at that time the bhikkhu develops the mindfulness awakening factor; at that time the mindfulness awakening factor goes to fulfillment by development in the bhikkhu. Dwelling thus mindful, he investigates that Dhamma with wisdom, examines it, and enters upon investigation.
translations.sn46.51:20: And what, bhikkhus, is the non-nutriment for the arising of the unarisen energy awakening factor, and for the development and fulfillment of the arisen energy awakening factor? There are, bhikkhus, the element of initiative, the element of exertion, the element of striving. Therein, making much of non-attention—this is the non-nutriment for the arising of the unarisen energy awakening factor, and for the development and fulfillment of the arisen energy awakening factor.
translations.sn46.51:21: And what, bhikkhus, is the non-nutriment for the arising of the unarisen rapture awakening factor, and for the development and fulfillment of the arisen rapture awakening factor? There are, bhikkhus, things that are a basis for the rapture awakening factor. Therein, making much of non-attention—this is the non-nutriment for the arising of the unarisen rapture awakening factor, and for the development and fulfillment of the arisen rapture awakening factor.
translations.sn46.51:22: And what, bhikkhus, is the non-nutriment for the arising of the unarisen tranquility awakening factor, and for the development and fulfillment of the arisen tranquility awakening factor? There are, bhikkhus, tranquility of body and tranquility of mind. Therein, making much of non-attention—this is the non-nutriment for the arising of the unarisen tranquility awakening factor, and for the development and fulfillment of the arisen tranquility awakening factor.
translations.sn46.51:23: And what, bhikkhus, is the non-nutriment for the arising of the unarisen concentration awakening factor, and for the development and fulfillment of the arisen concentration awakening factor? There are, bhikkhus, the sign of calm and the sign of non-distraction. Therein, making much of non-attention—this is the non-nutriment for the arising of the unarisen concentration awakening factor, and for the development and fulfillment of the arisen concentration awakening factor.
translations.sn46.52:1: Then several bhikkhus, in the morning, having dressed and taken bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Then those bhikkhus thought: "It is too early yet to wander for alms in Sāvatthī. Suppose we were to go to the park of the wanderers of other sects."
translations.sn46.52:10: And what, bhikkhus, is the method, relying on which the seven awakening factors become fourteen? Whatever, bhikkhus, is mindfulness regarding internal phenomena, that too is the mindfulness awakening factor; whatever is mindfulness regarding external phenomena, that too is the mindfulness awakening factor. ‘Mindfulness awakening factor’—thus this comes under the heading. Yet by this method it is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:11: Whatever, bhikkhus, one investigates with wisdom, examines, and enters upon investigation regarding internal phenomena, that too is the investigation-of-phenomena awakening factor; whatever one investigates with wisdom, examines, and enters upon investigation regarding external phenomena, that too is the investigation-of-phenomena awakening factor. ‘Investigation-of-phenomena awakening factor’—thus this comes under the heading. Yet by this method it is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:12: Whatever, bhikkhus, is bodily energy, that too is the energy awakening factor; whatever is mental energy, that too is the energy awakening factor. ‘Energy awakening factor’—thus this comes under the heading. Yet by this method it is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:13: Whatever, bhikkhus, is rapture with thinking and examining, that too is the rapture awakening factor; whatever is rapture without thinking and examining, that too is the rapture awakening factor. ‘Rapture awakening factor’—thus this comes under the heading. Yet by this method it is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:14: Whatever, bhikkhus, is tranquility of body, that too is the tranquility awakening factor; whatever is tranquility of mind, that too is the tranquility awakening factor. ‘Tranquility awakening factor’—thus this comes under the heading. Yet by this method it is twofold.
translations.sn46.52:15: Whatever concentration there is with applied thought and sustained thought, that too is the awakening factor of concentration; whatever concentration there is without applied thought and without sustained thought, that too is the awakening factor of concentration. ‘The awakening factor of concentration’: that is how this statement goes. And that, by way of exposition, becomes twofold.
translations.sn46.52:2: Then those bhikkhus went to the park of the wanderers of other sects; having gone, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects. After exchanging courteous and memorable talk, they sat down to one side. When the bhikkhus were seated to one side, the wanderers of other sects said this to them:
translations.sn46.52:3: “Friends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to his disciples like this: ‘Come, bhikkhus, abandon the five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—and develop the seven awakening factors as they really are.’ We too, friends, teach the Dhamma to our disciples like this: ‘Come, friends, abandon the five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—and develop the seven awakening factors as they really are.’ In this, friends, what difference is there, what distinction, what divergence between the ascetic Gotama and us, that is to say—between teaching and teaching, between instruction and instruction?”
translations.sn46.52:4: Then the bhikkhus neither approved nor rejected what those wanderers of other sects had said. Without approving and without rejecting, they rose from their seats and left, thinking: “We will understand the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.” Then those bhikkhus, having wandered for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, on returning from the almsround, approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. When they were seated to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
translations.sn46.52:8: “Bhikkhus, wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be addressed like this: ‘But, friends, is there a way such that, relying on that way, the five hindrances become ten, and the seven awakening factors become fourteen?’ When asked thus, bhikkhus, the wanderers of other sects will not be able to answer, and they will fall into further vexation. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, it is outside their domain. I do not see, bhikkhus, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this population with its ascetics and brahmins, with devas and humans, anyone who could satisfy the mind by answering these questions, except the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from here.
translations.sn46.52:9: “And what, bhikkhus, is the way such that, relying on that way, the five hindrances become ten? Whatever internal sensual desire there is, that too is a hindrance; whatever external sensual desire there is, that too is a hindrance. ‘The hindrance of sensual desire’: that is how this statement goes. And that, by way of exposition, becomes twofold. Whatever internal ill will there is, that too is a hindrance; whatever external ill will there is, that too is a hindrance. ‘The hindrance of ill will’: that is how this statement goes. And that, by way of exposition, becomes twofold. Whatever sloth there is, that too is a hindrance; whatever torpor there is, that too is a hindrance. ‘The hindrance of sloth and torpor’: that is how this statement goes. And that, by way of exposition, becomes twofold. Whatever restlessness there is, that too is a hindrance; whatever remorse there is, that too is a hindrance. ‘The hindrance of restlessness and remorse’: that is how this statement goes. And that, by way of exposition, becomes twofold. Whatever doubt regarding phenomena there is internally, that too is a hindrance; whatever doubt regarding phenomena there is externally, that too is a hindrance. ‘The hindrance of doubt’: that is how this statement goes. And that, by way of exposition, becomes twofold. This, bhikkhus, is the way such that, relying on that way, the five hindrances become ten.”
translations.sn46.53:10: At the time, bhikkhus, when the mind is restless, it is not the time for developing the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena; it is not the time for developing the awakening factor of energy; it is not the time for developing the awakening factor of rapture. For what reason? A restless mind, bhikkhus, is calmed down with difficulty by these things.
translations.sn46.53:11: Suppose, bhikkhus, a person wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire. He would throw on dry grass, throw on dry cow-dung, throw on dry sticks, and give it a gust of wind, and would not sprinkle it with dust. Could that person extinguish a great mass of fire?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn46.53:13: And at the time, bhikkhus, when the mind is restless, it is the time for developing the awakening factor of tranquillity; it is the time for developing the awakening factor of concentration; it is the time for developing the awakening factor of equanimity. For what reason? A restless mind, bhikkhus, is well calmed down by these things.
translations.sn46.53:14: Suppose, bhikkhus, a person wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire. He would throw on wet grass, throw on wet cow-dung, throw on wet sticks, and give it a gust of water, and sprinkle it with dust. Could that person extinguish a great mass of fire?” “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.sn46.53:2: “Bhikkhus, wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be addressed like this: ‘Friends, at the time when the mind is sluggish, for which awakening factors is it not the time for development, and for which awakening factors is it the time for development? And friends, at the time when the mind is restless, for which awakening factors is it not the time for development, and for which awakening factors is it the time for development?’ When asked thus, bhikkhus, the wanderers of other sects will not be able to answer, and they will fall into further vexation. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, it is outside their domain.
translations.sn46.53:3: I do not see, bhikkhus, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this population with its ascetics and brahmins, with devas and humans, anyone who could satisfy the mind by answering these questions, except the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from here.
translations.sn46.53:4: At a time, bhikkhus, when the mind is sluggish, it is not the time for developing the awakening factor of tranquility, not the time for developing the awakening factor of concentration, not the time for developing the awakening factor of equanimity. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the sluggish mind is hard to rouse by these qualities.
translations.sn46.53:5: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man wanted to kindle a small fire. He would throw on it wet grass, throw on it wet cow-dung, throw on it wet sticks, and pour water and wind on it, and sprinkle it with dust. Would that man be able to kindle a small fire? “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn46.53:7: And at a time, bhikkhus, when the mind is sluggish, it is the time for developing the awakening factor of investigation of states, the time for developing the awakening factor of energy, the time for developing the awakening factor of rapture. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the sluggish mind is easy to rouse by these qualities.
translations.sn46.53:8: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man wanted to kindle a small fire. He would throw on it dry grass, throw on it dry cow-dung, throw on it dry sticks, and blow with his mouth, and would not sprinkle it with dust. Would that man be able to kindle a small fire? “Yes, venerable sir.”
translations.sn46.54:1: At one time the Blessed One was living among the Koliyans at a Koliyan town named Haliddavasana. Then several bhikkhus, having dressed in the forenoon and taken bowl and robe, entered Haliddavasana for alms. Then it occurred to those bhikkhus: “It is too early to wander for alms in Haliddavasana. Why don’t we go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?”
translations.sn46.54:11: “Bhikkhus, wanderers of other sects who speak thus should be addressed as follows: ‘But how, friends, is the liberation of mind by loving-kindness developed, what is it headed for, what is its culmination, what is its fruit, what is its ending? And how, friends, is the liberation of mind by compassion developed, what is it headed for, what is its culmination, what is its fruit, what is its ending? And how, friends, is the liberation of mind by empathetic joy developed, what is it headed for, what is its culmination, what is its fruit, what is its ending? And how, friends, is the liberation of mind by equanimity developed, what is it headed for, what is its culmination, what is its fruit, what is its ending?’ When asked thus, bhikkhus, the wanderers of other sects would not be able to answer, and further would fall into vexation. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, it is outside their domain. I do not see, bhikkhus, in this world with its devas, with its Māras, with its Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, anyone who could satisfy the mind by answering these questions, except the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from here.
translations.sn46.54:12: And how, bhikkhus, is the liberation of mind by loving-kindness developed, what is it headed for, what is its culmination, what is its fruit, what is its ending? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the awakening factor of mindfulness accompanied by loving-kindness … he develops the awakening factor of equanimity accompanied by loving-kindness, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in what is not repulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the repulsive. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the not-repulsive in what is repulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the not-repulsive. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in both what is not repulsive and what is repulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the repulsive. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the not-repulsive in both what is repulsive and what is not repulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the not-repulsive. If he wishes, ‘Avoiding both what is not repulsive and what is repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending,’ he dwells there equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending, or else he enters upon and dwells in the beautiful liberation. I say, bhikkhus, that the liberation of mind by loving-kindness has the beautiful as its culmination, for a bhikkhu who possesses wisdom and has not penetrated a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:13: And how, bhikkhus, is the liberation of mind by compassion developed, what is it headed for, what is its culmination, what is its fruit, what is its ending? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the awakening factor of mindfulness accompanied by compassion … he develops the awakening factor of equanimity accompanied by compassion, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in what is not repulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the repulsive … if he wishes, ‘Avoiding both what is not repulsive and what is repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending,’ he dwells there equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending. Or else, by completely surmounting perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, he enters upon and dwells in the base of infinite space: ‘Infinite is space.’ I say, bhikkhus, that the liberation of mind by compassion has the base of infinite space as its culmination, for a bhikkhu who possesses wisdom and has not penetrated a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:14: And how, bhikkhus, is the liberation of mind by empathetic joy developed, what is it headed for, what is its culmination, what is its fruit, what is its ending? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the awakening factor of mindfulness accompanied by empathetic joy … he develops the awakening factor of equanimity accompanied by empathetic joy, dependent on seclusion, dependent on dispassion, dependent on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. If he wishes, ‘May I dwell perceiving the repulsive in what is not repulsive,’ he dwells there perceiving the repulsive … if he wishes, ‘Avoiding both what is not repulsive and what is repulsive, may I dwell equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending,’ he dwells there equanimous, mindful and clearly comprehending. Or else, having completely surmounted the base of infinite space, he enters upon and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness: ‘Infinite is consciousness.’ I say, bhikkhus, that the liberation of mind by empathetic joy has the base of infinite consciousness as its culmination, for a bhikkhu who possesses wisdom and has not penetrated a higher liberation.
translations.sn46.54:3: “The ascetic Gotama, friend, teaches the Dhamma to his disciples like this: ‘Come, bhikkhus, having abandoned the five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—dwell having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to oneself, having pervaded the entire world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, without ill will—dwell. Having pervaded one direction with a mind accompanied by compassion … with a mind accompanied by sympathetic joy … with a mind accompanied by equanimity; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to oneself, having pervaded the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, without ill will—dwell.’”
translations.sn46.8:1: At one time the Venerable Upavāna and the Venerable Sāriputta were dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. Then the Venerable Sāriputta, in the evening, having emerged from seclusion, approached the Venerable Upavāna; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Upavāna. When they had concluded their exchange of greetings and courteous talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Upavāna:
translations.sn46.8:2: “Could a bhikkhu know, friend Upavāna: ‘Through internal wise attention, my seven awakening factors are thus well aroused and lead to comfortable abiding’?” “A bhikkhu could know, friend Sāriputta: ‘Through internal wise attention, my seven awakening factors are thus well aroused and lead to comfortable abiding.’”
translations.sn47.10:1: Then the Venerable Ānanda, in the morning, having dressed and taken his bowl and robe, approached a certain nuns’ residence; having approached, he sat down on a seat that had been prepared. Then several bhikkhunīs approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those bhikkhunīs said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
translations.sn47.10:2: “Here, Venerable Ānanda, several bhikkhunīs, dwelling with minds well established in the four establishments of mindfulness, perceive lofty distinction from earlier to later.” “So it is, sisters, so it is, sisters. For whatever bhikkhu or bhikkhunī, sisters, dwells with a mind well established in the four establishments of mindfulness, this can be expected of them: ‘They will perceive lofty distinction from earlier to later.’”
translations.sn47.10:7: Again further, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells observing phenomena in phenomena … observing feeling … observing mind … ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. As he dwells observing phenomena in phenomena, either an object of Dhamma arises and there is bodily burning, or the mind becomes sluggish, or the mind is distracted outwardly. Therefore, Ānanda, that bhikkhu should direct the mind toward some inspiring sign. As he directs the mind toward some inspiring sign, gladness is born. For one who is gladdened, rapture is born. For one with rapture, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, one feels pleasure. For one who is pleased, the mind becomes concentrated. He reflects thus: ‘For the sake of what I directed my mind, that purpose of mine has been accomplished. Come now, I will withdraw it.’ And he withdraws, and does not think and does not ponder. He understands: ‘I am without thought, without pondering; inwardly mindful, I am comfortable.’ Thus, Ānanda, there is development by directing.
translations.sn47.10:9: Thus, Ānanda, development by directing has been taught by me, and development without directing has been taught. What should be done by a teacher who seeks his disciples’ welfare, out of compassion, has been done for you by me. These, Ānanda, are the roots of trees; these are empty huts. Meditate, Ānanda; do not be negligent; do not later become remorseful. This is my instruction to you.”
translations.sn47.13:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. At that time the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling among the Magadhans at the village of Nālakagāma, afflicted, suffering, gravely ill. And Cunda the novice was the attendant of the Venerable Sāriputta.
translations.sn47.13:2: Then the Venerable Sāriputta, due to that very illness, attained final Nibbāna. Then Cunda the novice, taking the Venerable Sāriputta’s bowl and robe, approached Sāvatthī, Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park, to the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Cunda the novice said this to the Venerable Ānanda: “The Venerable Sāriputta, sir, has attained final Nibbāna. This is his bowl and robe.”
translations.sn47.13:3: “This, friend Cunda, is a message to be brought for seeing the Blessed One. Come, friend Cunda, let us approach the Blessed One; having approached, we will report this matter to the Blessed One.” “Yes, sir,” Cunda the novice replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
translations.sn47.13:4: Then the Venerable Ānanda and Cunda the novice approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “This, sir, Cunda the novice says thus: ‘The Venerable Sāriputta, sir, has attained final Nibbāna; this is his bowl and robe.’ And moreover, sir, my body is as though made of sweet rice; the directions do not appear to me; the teachings are not clear to me, having heard: ‘The Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna.’”
translations.sn47.19:1: At one time the Blessed One was living among the Sumbhas, at a Sumbha town called Sedaka. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Once in the past, bhikkhus, a bamboo acrobat, having set up a bamboo pole, addressed his apprentice, the ‘Grease-pot’: ‘Come you, my dear Grease-pot, climb the bamboo pole and stand on my shoulders.’ ‘Yes, teacher,’ bhikkhus, the apprentice Grease-pot replied to the bamboo acrobat; and having climbed the bamboo pole, he stood on the teacher’s shoulders. Then, bhikkhus, the bamboo acrobat said this to the apprentice Grease-pot: ‘You, my dear Grease-pot, protect me, and I will protect you. In this way, guarded by one another, protected by one another, we will display our skills, obtain profit, and safely climb down from the bamboo poles.’ When this was said, bhikkhus, the apprentice Grease-pot said this to the bamboo acrobat: ‘But, teacher, that will not be so. You, teacher, protect yourself; I will protect myself. In this way, guarding ourselves, protecting ourselves, we will display our skills, obtain profit, and safely climb down from the bamboo poles.’”
translations.sn47.19:2: “That is the proper way there,” the Blessed One said, “as the apprentice Grease-pot said to the teacher. ‘I will protect myself,’ bhikkhus: the establishments of mindfulness should be practiced. ‘I will protect another’: the establishments of mindfulness should be practiced. Protecting oneself, bhikkhus, one protects another; protecting another, one protects oneself.”
translations.sn47.20:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was living among the Sumbhas, at a Sumbha town called Sedaka. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus.” “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this:
translations.sn47.20:2: “Suppose, bhikkhus, a great crowd would gather thinking, ‘A beauty of the countryside, a beauty of the countryside!’ And suppose, bhikkhus, that beauty of the countryside would be supremely skilled in dancing, supremely skilled in singing. Thinking, ‘The beauty of the countryside is dancing and singing!’ an even greater crowd would gather. Then a man would come along, wishing to live, not wishing to die, wishing for happiness, averse to suffering. They would say this to him: ‘Here, good man, is a bowl filled to the brim with oil; it must be carried between the great crowd and the beauty of the countryside. And a man with a drawn sword will follow right behind you. Wherever you spill even a little of it, right there he will cut off your head.’ What do you think, bhikkhus: would that man, without paying attention to that bowl of oil, allow negligence outwardly?” “No, venerable sir.”
translations.sn47.25:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was living at Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having concluded the courteous and memorable conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One: “What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the condition, whereby, when the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the true Dhamma does not last long? And what, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the condition, whereby, when the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the true Dhamma lasts long?”
translations.sn47.25:2: “Because, brahmin, the four establishments of mindfulness are not developed, not made much of, when the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the true Dhamma does not last long. And because, brahmin, the four establishments of mindfulness are developed, made much of, when the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the true Dhamma lasts long.
translations.sn47.29:2: Then the Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the morning and taken bowl and robe, approached the residence of the householder Sirivaḍḍha; having approached, he sat down on a seat that had been prepared. Having sat down, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the householder Sirivaḍḍha: “I hope it is bearable for you, householder, I hope you are managing; I hope the painful feelings are subsiding and not increasing; that their subsiding, not their increasing, is evident?” “It is not bearable for me, venerable sir, I am not managing. Strong painful feelings are increasing for me and not subsiding; their increasing, not their subsiding, is evident.”
translations.sn47.29:3: “Therefore, householder, you should train like this: ‘I will dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world; with feelings … with mind … I will dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world.’ For in this way, householder, you should train.”
translations.sn47.33:1: “For anyone, bhikkhus, for whom the four establishments of mindfulness are neglected, for them the noble path that rightly goes to the ending of suffering is neglected. For anyone, bhikkhus, for whom the four establishments of mindfulness are undertaken, for them the noble path that rightly goes to the ending of suffering is undertaken.
translations.sn47.37:1: “These, bhikkhus, are the four establishments of mindfulness. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. As he dwells contemplating the body in the body, whatever desire there is in regard to the body is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.37:2: He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. As he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, whatever desire there is in regard to feelings is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.37:3: He dwells contemplating mind in mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. As he dwells contemplating mind in mind, whatever desire there is in regard to mind is abandoned. With the abandoning of desire, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:1: “These, bhikkhus, are the four establishments of mindfulness. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. As he dwells contemplating the body in the body, the body is fully understood. Because the body is fully understood, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:2: He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. As he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, feelings are fully understood. Because feelings are fully understood, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.38:3: He dwells contemplating mind as mind—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. For one dwelling contemplating mind as mind, the mind comes to be fully understood. Because the mind is fully understood, the deathless is realized.
translations.sn47.40:1: “I will teach you, bhikkhus, the establishments of mindfulness, and the development of the establishments of mindfulness, and the way of practice leading to the development of the establishments of mindfulness. Listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, are the establishments of mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as body—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world; he dwells contemplating feelings as feelings … he dwells contemplating mind as mind … he dwells contemplating phenomena as phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. This is called, bhikkhus, the establishments of mindfulness.”
translations.sn47.40:2: “And what, bhikkhus, is the development of the establishments of mindfulness? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells in the body contemplating the nature of arising; he dwells in the body contemplating the nature of vanishing; he dwells in the body contemplating the nature of arising-and-vanishing—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. He dwells in feelings contemplating the nature of arising … he dwells in mind contemplating the nature of arising … he dwells in phenomena contemplating the nature of arising; he dwells in phenomena contemplating the nature of vanishing; he dwells in phenomena contemplating the nature of arising-and-vanishing—ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure for the world. This is called, bhikkhus, the development of the establishments of mindfulness.”
translations.sn47.4:1: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans at Sālā, a brahmin village. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus … and said this:
translations.sn47.4:2: “Those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, who are new, recently gone forth, newly come to this Dhamma and Vinaya—those bhikkhus, bhikkhus, should be encouraged, engaged, and established in the development of the four establishments of mindfulness. Which four? Come, friends, dwell contemplating the body as body—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a clear mind, collected, with one-pointed mind—for knowledge of the body as it really is; dwell contemplating feelings as feelings—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a clear mind, collected, with one-pointed mind—for knowledge of feelings as they really are; dwell contemplating mind as mind—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a clear mind, collected, with one-pointed mind—for knowledge of the mind as it really is; dwell contemplating phenomena as phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a clear mind, collected, with one-pointed mind—for knowledge of phenomena as they really are.”
translations.sn47.4:3: “Those bhikkhus too, bhikkhus, who are trainees, who have not attained the mind’s goal, dwelling aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage—they too dwell contemplating the body as body—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a clear mind, collected, with one-pointed mind—for full understanding of the body; they dwell contemplating feelings as feelings—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a clear mind, collected, with one-pointed mind—for full understanding of feelings; they dwell contemplating mind as mind—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a clear mind, collected, with one-pointed mind—for full understanding of mind; they dwell contemplating phenomena as phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a clear mind, collected, with one-pointed mind—for full understanding of phenomena.”
translations.sn47.4:4: “Those bhikkhus too, bhikkhus, who are arahants, with taints destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, exhausted the fetters of becoming, liberated by right knowledge—they too dwell contemplating the body as body—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a clear mind, collected, with one-pointed mind—disjoined from the body; they dwell contemplating feelings as feelings—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a clear mind, collected, with one-pointed mind—disjoined from feelings; they dwell contemplating mind as mind—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a clear mind, collected, with one-pointed mind—disjoined from the mind; they dwell contemplating phenomena as phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a clear mind, collected, with one-pointed mind—disjoined from phenomena.”
translations.sn47.6:1: “Once upon a time, bhikkhus, a hawk suddenly swooped down upon a lapwing and seized it. Then, bhikkhus, while the lapwing was being carried off by the hawk, it lamented thus: ‘We are unlucky indeed, we are of little merit, in that we wandered in ground not our own, in another’s domain. If only we had wandered in our own ground, in our ancestral domain, this hawk would not have been enough for me, that is, for battle!’ ‘But what, lapwing, is your own ground, your ancestral domain?’ ‘That is, ploughed ground and clod-heaps.’ Then, bhikkhus, the hawk, not relying on its own strength, not boasting of its own strength, released the lapwing: ‘Go then, lapwing; even there, having gone, you will not escape me.’
translations.sn47.6:2: Then, bhikkhus, the lapwing went to the ploughed ground and clod-heaps, and, having climbed up onto a large clod, stood calling to the hawk: ‘Come now to me, hawk! Come now to me, hawk!’ Then, bhikkhus, that hawk, not relying on its own strength, not boasting of its own strength, drawing together both wings, suddenly swooped upon the lapwing. But when, bhikkhus, the lapwing knew, ‘This hawk has come very close to me,’ it slipped into the gap of that very clod. Then, bhikkhus, the hawk struck its breast right there. For thus it is, bhikkhus, with one who wanders in ground not his own, in another’s domain.”
translations.sn47.6:3: “Therefore, bhikkhus, do not wander in ground not your own, in another’s domain. For those, bhikkhus, who wander in ground not their own, in another’s domain, Māra finds an opening; Māra finds a footing. And what, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu’s ground not his own, another’s domain? That is, the five cords of sensual pleasure. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are wished for, desired, pleasing, dear, connected with sensuality, enticing; sounds cognizable by the ear … smells cognizable by the nose … tastes cognizable by the tongue … tangibles cognizable by the body that are wished for, desired, pleasing, dear, connected with sensuality, enticing—this, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu’s ground not his own, another’s domain.”
translations.sn47.7:1: “There are, bhikkhus, rough and rugged regions of the Himalayan king of mountains where there is neither the range of monkeys nor of humans. There are, bhikkhus, rough and rugged regions of the Himalayan king of mountains where there is the range of monkeys, but not of humans. There are, bhikkhus, level stretches of ground of the Himalayan king of mountains, delightful, where there is the range both of monkeys and of humans. There, bhikkhus, hunters set out sticky glue on the monkeys’ tracks, to bind the monkeys.”
translations.sn47.8:2: That foolish, incompetent, unskilled cook does not take up the sign from his own master: ‘Today this curry of mine pleases my master, or he reaches for that, or he takes much of that, or he speaks in praise of that. Today this sour curry of mine pleases my master, or he reaches for the sour, or he takes much of the sour, or he speaks in praise of the sour. Today the bitter curry of mine … today the pungent curry of mine … today the sweet curry of mine … today the alkaline curry of mine … today the non-alkaline curry of mine … today the salty curry of mine … today the unsalty curry of mine pleases my master, or he reaches for the unsalty, or he takes much of the unsalty, or he speaks in praise of the unsalty.’
translations.sn47.8:4: So, bhikkhus, that foolish, incompetent, unskilled monk is not a gainer of pleasant dwellings here and now, not a gainer of mindfulness and clear comprehension. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, that foolish, incompetent, unskilled monk does not take up the sign of his own mind.
translations.sn47.8:5: Just as, bhikkhus, a wise, competent, skilled cook would attend on a king or a royal minister with curries of various kinds—sour ones, bitter ones, pungent ones, sweet ones, alkaline ones, non-alkaline ones, salty ones, unsalty ones.
translations.sn5.10:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the bhikkhunī Vajirā, in the morning, having dressed and taken her bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, returned from the alms-round, she approached the Blind Men’s Grove for the day’s abiding. Having entered the Blind Men’s Grove, she sat down for the day’s abiding at the root of a certain tree. Then Māra the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, dread, and horripilation in the bhikkhunī Vajirā, wanting to shake her from concentration, approached the bhikkhunī Vajirā; having approached, he addressed the bhikkhunī Vajirā in a verse:
translations.sn5.10:2: “By whom is this being made? Where is the maker of the being? Where has the being arisen, and where does the being cease?”
translations.sn5.10:3: Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Vajirā: “Who now is this, a human or a non-human, who speaks a verse?” Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Vajirā: “This is Māra the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, dread, and horripilation in me, wanting to shake me from concentration, who speaks a verse.” Then the bhikkhunī Vajirā, having known, “This is Māra the Evil One,” replied to Māra the Evil One with verses:
translations.sn5.10:4: “Why do you assume ‘a being,’ Māra—is that your view? This is merely a heap of formations; no being is found here.
translations.sn5.10:5: Just as, when there is an assemblage of parts, there is the sound ‘a chariot’; so, when the aggregates exist, there is the convention ‘a being.’
translations.sn5.10:6: Only suffering is born, suffering stands and passes away; nothing apart from suffering is born, nothing other than suffering ceases.”
translations.sn5.1:1: Thus have I heard—at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jetavana, Anāthapiṇḍika’s park. Then the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā, in the morning, having dressed and taken her bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms. Having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, after the meal, returned from the alms-round, seeking seclusion, she approached the Blind Men’s Grove. Then Māra the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, dread, and horripilation in the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā, wanting to shake her from seclusion, approached the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā; having approached, he addressed the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā in a verse:
translations.sn5.1:2: “There is no escape in the world—what will you do with seclusion? Enjoy sensual pleasures; do not be one who later regrets.”
translations.sn5.1:3: Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā: “Who now is this, a human or a non-human, who speaks a verse?” Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā: “This is Māra the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, dread, and horripilation in me, wanting to shake me from seclusion, who speaks a verse.” Then the bhikkhunī Āḷavikā, having known, “This is Māra the Evil One,” replied to Māra the Evil One with verses:
translations.sn5.1:4: “There is an escape in the world, well touched by me through wisdom; Evil One, friend of the heedless, you do not know that state.
translations.sn5.1:5: Sense pleasures are like swords and stakes; the aggregates are like a butcher’s block. What you call delight in sensuality—that has become discontent for me.”
translations.sn5.1:6: Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The bhikkhunī Āḷavikā knows me,” sorrowful and unhappy, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.2:2: “That which is to be attained by seers, a state hard to come to—by two-finger wisdom it is not possible for a woman to reach it.”
translations.sn5.2:4: “What could womanhood do, when the mind is well collected, when knowledge is underway, when one sees the Dhamma rightly?
translations.sn5.2:5: Whoever might think like this: ‘I am a woman’ or ‘I am a man,’ or ‘I am something else’—Māra is fit to speak to them.”
translations.sn5.3:2: “Why now do you sit alone, with a weeping face, like one whose child has died? Alone, having gone into the middle of the forest—are you searching for a man?”
translations.sn5.3:3: Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī: “Who now is this, a human or a non-human, who speaks a verse?” Then it occurred to the bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī: “This is Māra the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, dread, and horripilation in me, wanting to shake me from concentration, who speaks a verse.”
translations.sn5.3:5: “Long ago my child died; men are just like that. I do not grieve, I do not weep, I am not afraid of you, friend.
translations.sn5.3:6: Everywhere delight has been struck down; the mass of darkness has been shattered. Having conquered the army of Death, I dwell without taints.”
translations.sn5.3:7: Then Māra the Evil One, thinking, “The bhikkhunī Kisāgotamī knows me,” sorrowful and unhappy, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.4:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the bhikkhunī Vijayā, in the morning, having dressed … she sat down for the day’s abiding at the root of a certain tree. Then Māra the Evil One, wanting to arouse fear, dread, and horripilation in the bhikkhunī Vijayā, wanting to shake her from concentration, approached the bhikkhunī Vijayā; having approached, he addressed the bhikkhunī Vijayā in a verse:
translations.sn5.4:2: “You are young and beautiful, and I too am young, a fine youth; with a fivefold musical instrument, come, let us amuse ourselves.”
translations.sn5.4:4: “Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, and delightful touches—I give them to you alone, Māra; I have no need for that.
translations.sn5.4:5: With this rotting body, breaking up and perishable: I am disgusted, I am ashamed; sensual craving is uprooted.
translations.sn5.4:6: And beings who have gone to form, and those established in the formless; and the attainment that is peaceful—everywhere the darkness has been struck down.”
translations.sn5.5:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Uppalavaṇṇā, in the morning, having dressed … she stood at the root of a certain sala tree in full bloom. Then Māra the Wicked, wanting to arouse fear, trepidation, and terror in the nun Uppalavaṇṇā, wanting to drive her out of concentration, approached the nun Uppalavaṇṇā; having approached, he addressed the nun Uppalavaṇṇā in a verse:
translations.sn5.5:2: “Approaching the top of a well-blooming tree, nun, you stand alone at the root of the sala; there is no second of your beauty—foolish one, are you not afraid of a rogue?”
translations.sn5.5:4: “Even if a hundred thousand rogues, of that sort, were to come here, I do not tremble a hair, I am not frightened; Māra, I do not fear you, not even alone.
translations.sn5.5:6: I am one who has mastery over the mind; the bases of spiritual power are well developed; I am freed from all bonds; friend, I do not fear you.”
translations.sn5.5:7: Then Māra the Wicked, thinking, “The nun Uppalavaṇṇā knows me,” sorrowful and dejected, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.6:2: “Why do you not approve of birth? One who is born enjoys sensual pleasures. Who has persuaded you of this: ‘Do not approve of birth, nun’?”
translations.sn5.6:3: “For one who is born there is death; one who is born encounters sufferings; bondage, slaughter, affliction—therefore I do not approve of birth.
translations.sn5.6:4: The Buddha taught the Dhamma, the crossing beyond birth; for the abandoning of all suffering, he established me in the truth.
translations.sn5.6:5: And beings who have gone to form, and those established in the formless— not understanding cessation, they come again to renewed existence.”
translations.sn5.7:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Upacālā, in the morning, having dressed … she sat down for the day’s abiding at the root of a certain tree. Then Māra the Wicked approached the nun Upacālā; having approached, he said this to the nun Upacālā: “Where then, nun, do you want to be reborn?” “I do not, friend, want to be reborn anywhere.”
translations.sn5.7:2: “The Thirty-three and the Yāma gods, and the Tusita gods too; the gods delighting in creation, the gods who wield power over others—direct your mind there; you will experience delight.”
translations.sn5.7:3: “The Thirty-three and the Yāma gods, and the Tusita gods too; the gods delighting in creation, the gods who wield power over others—bound by the bond of sensuality, they fall again under Māra’s control.
translations.sn5.7:4: All the world is ablaze; all the world is smoking; all the world is burning; all the world is trembling.
translations.sn5.7:5: Unshaken, unburning, resorted to by no ordinary person—where there is no access for Māra, there my mind delights.”
translations.sn5.7:6: Then Māra the Wicked, thinking, “The nun Upacālā knows me,” sorrowful and dejected, vanished right there.
translations.sn5.8:1: At Sāvatthī. Then the nun Sīsupacālā, in the morning, having dressed … she sat down for the day’s abiding at the root of a certain tree. Then Māra the Wicked approached the nun Sīsupacālā; having approached, he said this to the nun Sīsupacālā: “Whose sect, nun, do you approve of?” “I do not, friend, approve of anyone’s sect.”
translations.sn5.8:2: “For the sake of whom did you shave your head? You appear like an ascetic; and you do not approve of a sect—why do you wander about, confused?”
translations.sn5.8:3: “The sects outside of this, they delight in views; I do not approve their Dhamma; they are not skilled in the Dhamma.
translations.sn5.8:5: Freed in every way, without clinging, the one with vision sees all; having reached the ending of all deeds, freed in the destruction of acquisitions—he is my Blessed One, my teacher; his instruction I approve of.”
translations.sn5.9:2: “By whom has this figure been made? Where is the maker of the figure? Where has the figure arisen? Where does the figure cease?”
translations.sn5.9:4: “This figure is not self-made; this suffering is not made by another; having arisen dependent on a cause, with the breaking up of the cause it ceases.
translations.sn5.9:6: So too these aggregates and elements, and these six sense bases: having arisen dependent on a cause, with the breaking up of the cause they cease.”
translations.sn56.11:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Bārāṇasī, in the deer park at Isipatana. There the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
translations.sn56.11:10: But when, monks, in these four noble truths, my knowledge and vision—thus, in three turnings and twelve aspects—was fully purified as it really is, then, monks, I acknowledged: ‘I have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment’ in this world with its devas, with Māra, with Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans. And knowledge and vision arose in me: ‘Unshakable is my liberation; this is my last birth; now there is no renewed existence.’” Thus spoke the Blessed One. Pleased, the group of five monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
translations.sn56.11:11: And while this exposition was being spoken, in the venerable Koṇḍañña there arose the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye: “Whatever is of the nature to arise, all that is of the nature to cease.”
translations.sn56.11:13: Thus, in that moment, at that instant, at that very time, a sound rose up as far as the brahmā world. And this ten-thousandfold world-system shook, quaked, and trembled, and an immeasurable great radiance appeared in the world, surpassing the radiance of the devas.
translations.sn56.11:2: “These two extremes, monks, should not be pursued by one who has gone forth. What two? That pursuit of sensual pleasure in sensual pleasures, which is low, vulgar, of ordinary people, ignoble, and not connected with the goal; and that pursuit of self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and not connected with the goal. Without approaching both these extremes, monks, the middle way has been awakened to by the Tathāgata, producing vision, producing knowledge, leading to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, to Nibbāna.
translations.sn56.11:3: And what, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata, producing vision, producing knowledge, leading to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, to Nibbāna? It is simply this noble eightfold path, that is: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. This, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata, producing vision, producing knowledge, leading to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, to Nibbāna.”
translations.sn56.11:4:
“Now this, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of suffering: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering; association with the unloved is suffering, separation from the loved is suffering; not getting what one wants is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates subject to clinging are suffering.

“Now this, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering: this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there, that is: craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence.

“Now this, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering: the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving—its relinquishment, letting go, release, and non-attachment.

“Now this, bhikkhus, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering: this very noble eightfold path, that is: right view … right concentration.”
translations.sn56.11:5:
“‘This is the noble truth of suffering’: for me, bhikkhus, in things unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.

“‘Now this noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood’: for me, bhikkhus, before … arose.

“‘Now this noble truth of suffering has been fully understood’: for me, bhikkhus, in things unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.”
translations.sn56.11:6:
“‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering’: for me, bhikkhus, in things unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.

“‘Now this noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned’: for me, bhikkhus, before … arose.

“‘Now this noble truth of the origin of suffering has been abandoned’: for me, bhikkhus, in things unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.”
translations.sn56.11:7:
“‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering’: for me, bhikkhus, in things unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.

“‘Now this noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized’: for me, bhikkhus, before … arose.

“‘Now this noble truth of the cessation of suffering has been realized’: for me, bhikkhus, in things unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.”
translations.sn56.11:8:
“‘This is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering’: for me, bhikkhus, in things unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.

“‘Now this noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering is to be developed’: for me, bhikkhus, before … arose.

“‘Now this noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering has been developed’: for me, bhikkhus, in things unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, light arose.”
translations.sn56.11:9: “So long as, bhikkhus, my knowledge and vision of these four noble truths, in this threefold turn and twelvefold mode, as they really are, was not thoroughly purified, I did not claim, bhikkhus, in the world with its devas, with Māra, with Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, to have awakened to the unsurpassed perfect awakening.”
translations.sn56.20:1:
“There are these four, bhikkhus, that are true, not untrue, not otherwise. Which four?

“‘This is suffering’: bhikkhus, this is true, not untrue, not otherwise.

“‘This is the origin of suffering’: this is true, not untrue, not otherwise.

“‘This is the cessation of suffering’: this is true, not untrue, not otherwise.

“‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’: this is true, not untrue, not otherwise.

“These, bhikkhus, are the four that are true, not untrue, not otherwise.”
translations.sn56.26:1: “For anyone, bhikkhus, for whom you would have compassion, and who would think you should be listened to—whether friends or companions, relatives or kinsfolk—such people, bhikkhus, should be encouraged, guided, and established for the realization as it really is of the four noble truths.”
translations.sn56.26:2: “Of which four? Of the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. For anyone, bhikkhus, for whom you would have compassion, and who would think you should be listened to—whether friends or companions, relatives or kinsfolk—such people, bhikkhus, should be encouraged, guided, and established for the realization as it really is of these four noble truths.”
translations.sn56.27:1: “There are these four, bhikkhus, noble truths. Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—these, bhikkhus, are the four noble truths that are true, not untrue, not otherwise; therefore they are called ‘noble truths’.”
translations.sn56.28:1: “There are these four, bhikkhus, noble truths. Which four? The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering. In the world with its devas, with Māra, with Brahmā, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, with its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is noble; therefore they are called ‘noble truths’.”
translations.sn56.30:1: At one time several elder bhikkhus were dwelling among the Cetans at Sahañcanika. Now at that time, after their meal, having returned from the alms round, several elder bhikkhus, seated together, assembled in the pavilion, had this discussion arise: “Whoever, friends, sees suffering, sees also the origin of suffering, sees also the cessation of suffering, and sees also the way leading to the cessation of suffering.”
translations.sn56.31:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Kosambī in the Sīsapā grove. Then the Blessed One, taking a few sīsapā leaves in his hand, addressed the bhikkhus: “What do you think, bhikkhus, which is more: the few sīsapā leaves I have taken in my hand, or those up above in the Sīsapā grove?” “The few sīsapā leaves taken in the Blessed One’s hand are very few, venerable sir; those up above in the Sīsapā grove are far more.” “So too, bhikkhus, what is far more is that which I have directly known but have not declared to you. And why, bhikkhus, have I not declared it? Because, bhikkhus, it is not connected with the goal, not fundamental to the holy life; it does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, to Nibbāna; therefore I have not declared it.
translations.sn56.31:2: And what, bhikkhus, have I declared? ‘This is suffering,’ bhikkhus, I have declared; ‘this is the origin of suffering,’ I have declared; ‘this is the cessation of suffering,’ I have declared; ‘this is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ I have declared.
translations.sn56.31:3: And why, bhikkhus, have I declared this? Because, bhikkhus, this is connected with the goal, this is fundamental to the holy life; this leads to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to awakening, to Nibbāna; therefore I have declared it.
translations.sn56.35:1: “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were a hundred years old, living for a hundred years. Someone would say to him: ‘Come, good man: in the morning they will strike you with three hundred spears; at midday they will strike you with three hundred spears; in the evening they will strike you with three hundred spears. And so, good man, being struck day after day with three hundred spears at a time, though a hundred years old and living for a hundred years, at the end of a hundred years you would comprehend the four noble truths that had not been comprehended.’
translations.sn56.35:2: By an earnest clansman, bhikkhus, it is fitting to make the effort. For what reason? This saṁsāra, bhikkhus, is without discoverable beginning; no first point is found of blows by spear, by sword, by stick, by knife. Even if it were so, bhikkhus, I do not say that the comprehension of the four noble truths is with suffering, with distress; rather, bhikkhus, I say that the comprehension of the four noble truths is with happiness itself, with gladness itself. Of which four? Of the noble truth of suffering … of the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering.
translations.sn56.36:1: “Suppose, bhikkhus, a man, having cut and gathered together all the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jambudīpa into one heap, would make stakes. Having made stakes, he would impale the large creatures in the great ocean on the large stakes, the medium creatures in the great ocean on the medium stakes, and the tiny creatures in the great ocean on the tiny stakes. And still, bhikkhus, there would be coarse creatures in the great ocean not used up.
translations.sn56.36:2: Then in this Jambudīpa the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves would come to exhaustion, to depletion. But far more, bhikkhus, are the tiny creatures in the great ocean that are not easy to impale on stakes. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, the body is so subtle. So vast, bhikkhus, is the plane of misery. And having been freed from so vast a plane of misery, the person accomplished in view understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’
translations.sn56.42:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak. Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Come, bhikkhus, let us go to Patibhānakūṭa for the day’s abiding.” “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, together with several bhikkhus, approached Patibhānakūṭa. Then a certain bhikkhu saw at Patibhānakūṭa a great precipice. Seeing it, he said to the Blessed One: “Great indeed, venerable sir, is this precipice; frightening indeed, venerable sir, is this precipice. Is there, venerable sir, any other precipice greater and more frightening than this precipice?” “There is, bhikkhu, another precipice greater and more frightening than this precipice.”
translations.sn56.42:2: “But which, venerable sir, is that other precipice greater and more frightening than this precipice?” “Those, bhikkhus, whatever ascetics or brahmins who do not understand as it really is ‘This is suffering,’ do not understand as it really is ‘This is the origin of suffering,’ do not understand as it really is ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ do not understand as it really is ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’—they delight in formations that lead to birth, they delight in formations that lead to aging, they delight in formations that lead to death, they delight in formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Delighting in formations that lead to birth … to aging … to death … to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair, they fashion formations that lead to birth, they fashion formations that lead to aging, they fashion formations that lead to death, they fashion formations that lead to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. Having fashioned formations that lead to birth … to aging … to death … to sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair, they fall into the precipice of birth, they fall into the precipice of aging, they fall into the precipice of death, they fall into the precipice of sorrow, lamentation, pain, displeasure, and despair. They are not freed from birth, aging, and death, from sorrows, lamentations, pains, displeasures, and despairs. ‘They are not freed from suffering,’ I say.”
translations.sn56.45:1: At one time the Blessed One was staying at Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the hall with the peaked roof. Then Venerable Ānanda, having dressed in the forenoon and taken his bowl and robe, entered Vesālī for alms. Venerable Ānanda saw several Licchavi youths practicing in the assembly hall, from far off sending an arrow through a fine palm-leaf hole, one after another, without missing. Seeing this, it occurred to him: “These Licchavi youths are trained indeed, well trained indeed; for from far off they will send an arrow through a fine palm-leaf hole, one after another, without missing.”
translations.sn56.45:3: “What do you think, Ānanda: which is more difficult, more hard to accomplish—one who from far off would send an arrow through a fine palm-leaf hole, one after another, without missing; or one who would split the tip of a hair that has been split into seven?” “This, Bhante, is more difficult and more hard to accomplish: that one would split the tip of a hair that has been split into seven.” “But, Ānanda, they pierce what is more hard to pierce—those who as it really is pierce: ‘This is suffering’ … ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering,’ as it really is.”
translations.sn56.46:1: “There are, bhikkhus, the intermundane chasms, unbounded, dark, the gloom of darkness, where the light of these moon and sun, so mighty, so powerful, does not reach.”
translations.sn56.46:2: When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One: “Great indeed, Bhante, is that darkness, very great indeed, Bhante, is that darkness. Is there, Bhante, from this darkness another darkness greater and more terrifying?” “There is, bhikkhu, from this darkness another darkness greater and more terrifying.”
translations.sn56.48:1: “Suppose, bhikkhus, this great earth were a single mass of water. There a man would throw in a yoke with one hole. The east wind would carry it westward; the west wind would carry it eastward; the north wind would carry it southward; the south wind would carry it northward. And there would be a blind turtle. After a hundred years and a hundred years had passed, it would surface once, once. What do you think, bhikkhus: would that blind turtle, surfacing once after a hundred years and a hundred years had passed, put its neck into that one-holed yoke?” “It would be a sheer coincidence, Bhante, that that blind turtle, surfacing once after a hundred years and a hundred years had passed, would put its neck into that one-holed yoke.”
translations.sn56.48:2: “So too is it a sheer coincidence, bhikkhus, that one obtains human status. So too is it a sheer coincidence, bhikkhus, that a Tathāgata arises in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. So too is it a sheer coincidence, bhikkhus, that the Dhamma and discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata shines in the world. And this, bhikkhus, human status has been obtained; a Tathāgata has arisen in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One; and the Dhamma and discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata shines in the world.
